# Mock answer — Paper 1, three wines from one variety

## a) Grape variety (15 marks)

Riesling. All three are unoaked, bone-dry to just off-dry, and share a piercing, tartaric-edged acid line carrying pronounced lime, mandarin and white blossom over a stony, non-fruit core — the transparency and high extract without any oak crutch is Riesling's signature. Alcohol sits in a narrow warm 13–13.5% band across the flight, so it does not discriminate; the acid quality does. Grüner Veltliner was considered but there is no white pepper, lentil or radish and the aromatic lift is too floral; Chenin Blanc is ruled out by the absence of wax, lanolin, quince and phenolic grip. Wine 3's kerosene/wax note as it develops seals the call.

## b) Origin and quality (3 x 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — New Zealand, Central Otago. Exuberant lime blossom and mandarin with generous mid-palate weight, yet a searing, still-malic acid line: high ripeness held by firm acidity reads as high-altitude continental, not maritime Marlborough (which would show more herbal, less floral fruit). Very good quality, single-block estate tier, at the top of NZ dry Riesling.

**Wine 2** — Germany, Rheinhessen, Grosses Gewächs. Drier, stonier, less fruit-forward, with penetrating chalky drive and marked extract. The tension here is the killer point: this ripeness at ~13% would be flabby off a lesser site, so a producer confident enough to ferment fully dry — well inside the GG sugar ceiling rather than up against it — is declaring limestone-driven site power, not vintage heat. Outstanding, benchmark GG.

**Wine 3** — France, Alsace, Haut-Rhin lieu-dit. Broader, softer-edged, honeyed and evolving, with lower acidity and a trace of sugar. Good to very good, above generic Alsace AOC but without Grand Cru depth.

## c) Style and winemaking (3 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — pristine, primary, protectively made: whole-bunch pressed, cool stainless-steel ferment on cultured yeast, no malolactic (malic acid retained), ferment arrested to leave a few grams of sugar, early bottling under screwcap. No lees or oak texture at all.

**Wine 2** — textural and savoury rather than fruity: ripe hand-picked fruit, slow ambient ferment in large neutral casks, giving oxygen without oak flavour, then long gross-lees ageing. Fermented dry; the mealy breadth is lees, not sugar.

**Wine 3** — riper picking with a little passerillage, ambient ferment in old wood/tank running slowly to a natural stop with residual sugar, extended lees and less reductive handling — hence early tertiary honey and breadth.

## d) Drink window and commercial position (3 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — 2–3 years old; drinking now, improving 3–4 years, holding 8–10. £30/NZ$50; allocated to independent specialists and fine-dining lists in the UK, US and Australia; competes with top Eden and Clare Valley dry Riesling.

**Wine 2** — 3–4 years old; needs 5–8 years to unfurl, holding 15–20+. €50–60 ex-cellar, mailing-list and Michelin-listed, strong in Germany, Scandinavia, Japan; rivals Chablis Grand Cru. Challenge: the price ceiling buyers still impose on German dry Riesling.

**Wine 3** — 4–5 years old, at its plateau, holding 5–6. €18–22; specialist off-trade and regional French/Benelux bistros; a wine for Alsace loyalists rather than a trophy buy.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 1 Question 1

## a) Identify the grape variety (9 marks)

Riesling. The unifying signal is very high, racy acidity married to low-to-moderate alcohol, with an aromatic core of lime, lemon zest and white stone fruit over a flinty, stony minerality. Wines 1 and 3 carry that acidity at around 13–13.5% perceived warmth; Wine 2 is lighter-bodied with lower perceived alcohol. No oak-derived vanilla or toast, and no malolactic softening, on any of the three.

Chardonnay was weighed, since it also spans cool to warm sites, but there is no buttery, apple or bread-dough character, and the petrol-adjacent minerality on Wines 1 and 3 argues against it. Chenin Blanc was considered on acidity and stone fruit, but the lanolin texture and quince density are absent; these profiles are linear rather than waxy.

## b) Origin, style, and quality (3 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1 — Pfalz, Germany.** Riper peach and mirabelle with fuller body than a Mosel would give, high but not extreme acidity, finishing dry. A Trocken Spätlese-weight wine from a good site. Very good quality, GG-adjacent, though it lacks the saline drive of Wine 3.

**Wine 2 — Marlborough, New Zealand.** Lime cordial and grapefruit pith, piercing acidity, lighter body. The pure, unreductive fruit separates it from a German or Austrian equivalent. Good quality, premium regional varietal level; commercial in orientation.

**Wine 3 — Wachau, Austria.** The most concentrated: white peach, apricot, crushed-stone minerality and phenolic grip indicating full Smaragd ripeness. Warmth plus steely acidity and salinity suggest a steep gneiss site. Outstanding; the length points to a single vineyard rather than a regional blend.

## c) Key winemaking decisions (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Fermented to full dryness — a deliberate Trocken decision, no arrested sugar. Cool stainless-steel fermentation is indicated by citrus purity without phenolic edge; malic brightness shows no malolactic conversion. Textural mid-palate weight without bread-dough notes suggests several months on fine lees in tank, not barrel.

**Wine 2.** Unlike Wine 1, the emphasis is on retention rather than build: early picking for acidity, stainless steel, and minimal post-fermentation ageing before bottling to protect aromatics. A slight spritz is consistent with early screwcap bottling retaining CO₂.

**Wine 3.** Late harvesting at Smaragd ripeness gives the phenolic grip. The honeyed mid-palate without residual sugar indicates a long, cool ferment of some weeks taken to dryness. The reductive, stony finish points to protective, low-oxygen handling. Weight here is grape-derived, not oak-derived.

## d) Maturity and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Bright lemon and primary stone fruit suggest 2–3 years old. Drinking well now, with concentration to improve 3–4 years further, gaining petrol, honey and dried herb; sound for 8–10 years from vintage. Around €20–30, aimed at independent merchants and specialist on-trade in Germany, Scandinavia and the UK, competing with other dry Pfalz wines below GG price.

**Wine 2.** Vivid primary lime and light structure indicate a very young wine and a drink-now style: it will hold 3–4 years but will not improve, since freshness is the whole appeal. Around NZ$25–35, a by-the-glass and off-trade wine competing with Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc for the aromatic white consumer; strong domestically and in Australia, the UK and North America.

**Wine 3.** Around four years old and still youthful — the tight mineral finish shows it is only beginning to open. It should improve markedly over 5–7 years, developing honey, dried apricot and beeswax, holding at peak beyond fifteen years from vintage. At roughly €45–65 it is a fine-wine list and specialist-retail proposition for collectors in Austria, Germany, the UK and North America. Under the skin, its real commercial argument is that at village-Burgundy money it offers Grand Cru-scale ageing potential — the ripeness is Smaragd, but the acid backbone keeps it from tipping into weight.

## a) Identify the grape variety (4 marks)

Riesling. Both wines share citrus, apple and a stony, slate-like mineral quality pointing toward a high-acid, low-phenolic white variety. The very high, racy acidity is the single most diagnostic structural marker — it eliminates Chardonnay, which rarely achieves this electric acid tension, and Sauvignon Blanc, whose pyrazine or tropical character is absent from both. Chenin Blanc was considered but its characteristic waxy, lanolin quality is absent, and neither wine shows phenolic grip. The two wines are stylistically divergent — one bone dry, the other carrying residual sugar at lower perceived alcohol — yet the varietal spine is consistent: high natural acidity, pure citrus-apple fruit, minimal oak, and slate minerality.

## b) Origin, style and winemaking (2 × 15 marks)

**Wine 1** — Clare Valley, Australia. Smoky citrus, sliced apple, incipient petrol and jasmine florals. The palate is bone dry and very crisp — medium-plus weight held in check by significant diurnal range, consistent with Clare Valley's elevated, continental conditions. Firm structure and dryness distinguish this from Wine 2: cool nights arrest ripening and preserve malic-dominant acidity, producing a lime-cordial grip rather than the lactic-rounded acidity of a German counterpart. Picked at close to full phenolic ripeness, gently pressed and cold-fermented in stainless steel to preserve primary aromatics. Malolactic fermentation deliberately avoided — confirmed by the racy, malic acid character — and bottled early under screwcap. No oak influence detectable.

**Wine 2** — Mosel, Germany, Spätlese level. Lemon-green hue, white tree fruit, wet earth and pronounced slate minerality. Residual sugar is perceptible but precisely balanced by high, steely acidity; very low perceived alcohol and light body confirm fermentation arrested early to retain RS. The sweetness level rules out Kabinett and sits clearly at Spätlese. Hand-harvested from steep slate terraces — mineral intensity and fruit purity rule out mechanisation — then whole-bunch pressed and fermented in stainless steel or large traditional fuder, with no oak detectable.

## c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, estate-level Clare Valley Riesling retailing around AUD $25–35. Primary aromatics indicate 1–2 years of age. Structural acid and concentration suggest improvement over 4–6 years, developing petrol and toast complexity, then holding for 3–4 more. A natural competitor to dry Alsace Riesling at a friendlier price, with export strength in the UK, USA and Japan through specialist off- and on-trade channels.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding quality, retailing around €30–50. Primary white-fruit character suggests 3–4 years of age, barely approaching its drinking window. Significant improvement expected over the next decade as honeyed stone fruit and petrol complexity emerge, with a holding period of 20-plus years. A specialist-merchant and fine-dining wine with a devoted following in the USA, UK and Japan.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety (15 marks)

Riesling. The single most diagnostic feature across all three wines is electric, racy acidity combined with moderate-to-low perceived alcohol and an aromatic profile spanning lime, green apple, and white blossom, with no pyrazines, oak, or phenolic weight. Wine 2 anchors the identification: off-dry, very light-bodied, with piercing acidity and sweet lime-peach character. No other variety produces this acid-weight-sweetness configuration.

The two plausible alternatives were Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc. Sauvignon Blanc was considered for Wine 3's lime and herbaceous lift, but lacks the mineral precision, weightless body, and emerging petrol note diagnostic of Riesling. Chenin Blanc shares high acidity and an off-dry spectrum but is richer-textured and more phenolic; Wine 2's delicate low-alcohol structure rules it out. The consistency of lime, slate-driven minerality, and pencil-fine acid thread across all three wines confirms Riesling.

## b) Origin, climate, and winemaking (3 × 13 marks)

**Wine 1 — Alsace, France (Grand Cru or prestige cuvée level)**

The generous body, fully dry palate, and notable alcohol warmth point to Alsace: Riesling harvested at full physiological ripeness, giving stone-fruit depth alongside classic lime and dried citrus. The continental climate — warm, dry growing seasons sheltered by the Vosges — allows full phenolic maturity without sacrificing acid structure. Broader, rounder texture than any German counterpart indicates extended lees contact in large old foudres; fermentation proceeded to dryness. The richness alongside precise acid integration suggests a single-site selection with particularly deep soils.

**Wine 2 — Mosel, Germany (Spätlese, Einzellage)**

Almost weightless body and barely perceptible warming alcohol indicate the cool, slate-dominated slopes of the Mosel. Marginal, steep, south-facing vineyards produce naturally low alcohol; the off-dry style with sweet lime, lemon custard, and apricot reflects fermentation arrested at around 40–50 g/L residual sugar. Winemaking appears minimal — cool fermentation in stainless steel or large casks, chilled to halt fermentation and lock in primary aromatics. The absence of any lees-derived texture signals early bottling. Honeyed fruit and tropical ripeness suggest a named Einzellage rather than a generic Bereich wine.

**Wine 3 — Eden Valley, South Australia**

Intense lime streaking on a dry palate is immediately recognisable as Australian Riesling, but the slightly softer acid, delicate white floral lift, and dried herb nuance separate Eden Valley from Clare Valley's more searingly linear style. Perceived alcohol sits noticeably above Wine 2, consistent with a warmer harvest window despite the altitude. Winemaking is reductive and minimalist: cool tank fermentation, no oak, early bottling to preserve primary citrus and floral precision. A faint mineral, bath-salts note confirms Eden Valley rather than a warmer plains origin.

## c) Quality and maturity (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding quality, equivalent to Grand Cru or prestige single-vineyard Alsace level; approximately €40–60 retail. The wine appears 3–4 years old, showing primary to early secondary development. Approachable now, it has the concentration and acid architecture to improve for a further 8–10 years, gaining petrol, dried apricot, and waxy complexity before holding for an additional 5 years.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality, Einzellage Spätlese level, approximately €25–35 retail. Currently 4–5 years old with vibrant primary fruit intact; the sweetness-acidity balance is at a beautiful early peak. It will continue to develop honeyed and kerosene tertiary notes over 5–8 years before peaking, then hold for a further 5 years.

**Wine 3** — Very good quality, estate Riesling from a recognised cool-climate sub-region, approximately AUD 25–35 retail. It reads as young — likely 1–2 years old — with primary citrus and floral character entirely dominant. It will gain petrol and toast complexity over 5–7 years and hold comfortably for a further 3–5 years thereafter.

Riesling. The decisive structural feature across the flight is searing acidity carried on low-to-moderate body with no oak influence whatsoever. Sauvignon Blanc was weighed but rejected: no pyrazine, and instead lime, green apple and, in two wines, developing petrol and floral lift. Perceived alcohol ranges from feather-light in Wine 2 to warm and moderately full in Wine 1, yet the acid architecture is constant — Riesling's signature stylistic range. Wine 2's off-dry lime-custard sweetness balanced at that low weight confirms the call.

## b) Region of Origin (3 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1 — Kamptal, Austria.** Stony grip with ripe peach and apricot, firm body and generous warmth indicate a dry continental Riesling. Alsace was the alternative, but Alsatian dry Riesling shows broader, softer phenolics; the saline-stony finish and driving extract here point to Kamptal, with old-vine concentration on loess and amphibolite.

**Wine 2 — Mosel, Germany.** Very light body, perceptible sweetness against electric acidity, lime custard and peach at barely-there perceived alcohol: a Mosel Spätlese. Nahe and Saar were considered; the soft slate minerality and honeyed richness rather than the Saar's steelier austerity place it in the Mittelmosel.

**Wine 3 — Eden Valley, Australia.** Pale straw with green hints, bone-dry, intense lime juice with white pepper. Clare Valley is the obvious alternative, but the softer acid line, blossom rather than sherbet aromatics, and emerging petrol indicate Eden Valley's higher-altitude, cooler sites.

## c) Style and Winemaking (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** No oak character, yet a faint textural roundness suggests large neutral casks rather than pure stainless steel. Concentration and phenolic ripeness imply low-yield old vines picked late; fully dry and built for age.

**Wine 2.** Unlike Wine 1, fermentation was arrested before dryness — by chilling or by high must weight stalling yeast in cold cellars — leaving sweetness as a deliberate counterweight to acidity, not a fault. Pristine fruit purity and reductive freshness indicate stainless steel throughout.

**Wine 3.** Where Wine 2 is protected by sugar, this wine is protected by closure: clean citrus with no oxidative bruising at five-plus years points to screw cap and wholly reductive handling. The petrol and honeyed citrus development is bottle age under inert conditions, consistent with a held-back reserve release.

## d) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1 — Outstanding; Erste Lage / DAC Reserve level**, around €35–50. Intensity, length and structural precision sit clearly above Kamptal DAC entry level. Sold through Austria's premium on-trade and specialist retail, exported to Germany, Switzerland, the UK and US independents. It competes with Alsace Grand Cru and Rheingau Erstes Gewächs, offering sharper terroir definition at the price.

**Wine 2 — Very good; Spätlese from a classified Einzellage**, around €20–35. Mid-tier in the Prädikat hierarchy: more concentrated than Kabinett, short of Auslese. Exports to the UK, US and Scandinavia. Sweetness remains a perception barrier, but at this perceived alcohol and acid structure it owns the low-alcohol, food-friendly niche almost unchallenged.

**Wine 3 — Very good; single-vineyard museum-release Riesling**, around AUD 45–65. The hold-back strategy separates it from commodity Australian Riesling and earns premium specialist listings in Australia, the UK and Scandinavia, competing with mature Clare Valley and German Spätlese as a drink-now proposition. It is peaking now, will hold four to six years, gaining petrol and lime marmalade before slow decline.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety (4 marks)

Riesling. Both wines share lime, lemon curd and honeysuckle aromatics, underpinned by electric, high-pitched acidity and zero oak influence. Crucially they diverge sharply in sweetness, illustrating the variety's unmatched stylistic range. Gewurztraminer was considered but ruled out by the far more piercing acidity and absence of rose-water texture; Pinot Gris lacks Riesling's defining citrus-lime core and acidity intensity.

## b) Identify the origin of each wine (2 × 13 marks)

**Wine 1 — Nahe, Germany, Großes Gewächs.** Pale lemon with green highlights, exceptional purity of lime, wet slate and an incipient petrol mineral quality confirm Germany. The wine is dry, and its fuller body and slightly higher perceived alcohol point away from the steep, leaner Mosel terraces — the first and obvious candidate — toward a warmer, south-facing slate site. The Nahe fits: it delivers Mosel-like mineral precision alongside white peach and apricot depth with more generosity. Extraordinary length and complexity place this at the apex of the German quality hierarchy: a Großes Gewächs from a premier Einzellage.

**Wine 2 — Clare Valley, South Australia.** Deep gold with high viscosity signals substantial residual sugar. The nose is ripe and clean: lime flesh, honeyed citrus, kumquat and a tropical underpinning. The palate is sweet yet the high acidity drives a long, cleansing finish. Critically, there are no botrytis markers — no mushroom or oxidative marmalade character — distinguishing this from a German Beerenauslese where noble rot drives complexity. The concentration here comes from the cordon cut technique rather than botrytis, producing the bright, fruit-forward sweetness that is Clare Valley's signature late-harvest style.

## c) Style and winemaking (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** A dry, full-bodied Riesling of high concentration. Complete absence of oxidative or reductive fault points to cool fermentation in stainless steel, preserving primary aromatics. No malolactic influence preserves the racy tartaric acidity. A slightly creamy mid-palate suggests extended lees contact beneath the mineral frame. The wine is tightly wound now but the acid architecture supports a decade or more of further development.

**Wine 2.** Sweetness was achieved through cordon cut — severing canes to halt water movement and concentrate sugars in situ — rather than botrytis or desiccation, explaining the clean, fruit-forward character absent any fungal complexity. Fermentation was arrested early, preserving elevated residual sugar while retaining the variety's high natural acidity. Stainless steel ageing maintains citrus freshness. The result is unmistakably different from Old World sweet Riesling: brighter and fruitier, positioned as an approachable dessert wine.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 1 Question 1

## a) Identify the grape variety (15 marks)

Riesling. The decisive evidence is very high, racy acidity across a wide weight range — from a barely-warm, feather-light wine near 8% to a fuller, riper example around 13.5% — a variety able to span extreme climatic conditions while keeping its acid architecture intact. All three share lime, citrus and stony minerality, with no pyrazine, no phenolic wax and no aromatic broadness. Chenin Blanc was the closest alternative, sharing high acidity and climate versatility, but the electric, lean acid quality and lime register rule out Chenin's waxy lanolin. Sauvignon Blanc was weighed and dismissed: the mineral depth and structural weight here replace pungent green herb. The flight's ability to run from dry to richly sweet confirms Riesling.

## b) Origin, style, and vintage conditions (3 × 13 marks)

**Wine 1 — Alsace, France.** Fuller body, warmer alcohol presence and generous stone fruit exclude both Mosel and a cool New World site: this is Riesling grown with real heat accumulation. Dry, with high acidity carried on considerable extract and a spiced, waxy richness — Alsace, from deeper soils at Grand Cru level. The warm, dry 2022 vintage explains the ripe concentration and palate warmth; the retained acidity points to early picking.

**Wine 2 — Mosel, Germany.** The barely perceptible alcohol combined with searing acidity is the flight's clearest fingerprint and is achievable almost nowhere else. Gold colour, high viscosity, spiced honey, dried mushroom and a long sweet finish indicate substantial residual sugar at Auslese level; red slate and volcanic soils of the middle Mosel account for the pepper-spice edge. The warm but not hot 2019 vintage delivered ripe fruit with intact acidity, and the tension between honeyed weight and electric acid reads as a textbook fine 2019 Auslese.

**Wine 3 — Central Otago, New Zealand.** Where Wine 1 is broad and Wine 2 sweet, this is angular and bone-dry: lime cordial, crushed stone, white blossom, very high but clean acidity, medium-plus body. Dryness plus weight rules out the Mosel; the absence of Alsatian breadth and spice rules out Alsace. A cool, high-altitude continental New World site fits — Central Otago, where UV intensity and diurnal swing give ripeness and acidity together. The cool, fresh 2023 vintage explains the tension and restraint.

## c) Winemaking: oak, lees ageing, and key decisions (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** No vanilla, toast or coconut: neutral large-format foudre or stainless steel, the Alsatian route to aromatic purity. Slight creamy breadth suggests lees contact without stirring. The key decision was fermenting fully dry in a hot vintage, demanding precise harvest timing to keep freshness.

**Wine 2.** Fermentation was arrested early, most likely by chilling and filtration, to hold Auslese-level sugar. No oak; traditional stainless steel or old cask preserves the crystalline fruit. Viscosity and finish length indicate extended time on fine lees.

**Wine 3.** Linear, precise, with no buttery or toasty note: reductive stainless-steel handling, MLF blocked to protect the acidity. Lees work appears minimal — primary fruit and structural purity are prioritised over texture, the opposite decision to Wine 1.

Cape Point Vineyards, Reserve Sauvignon Blanc 2022. Cape Point, South Africa. (13.5%)

modelAnswer:
## a) Grape variety (6 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc. All three wines share lemon-green colour, high racy acidity, a dry palate and moderate alcohol (~13%). Aromatics confirm the call: green apple and flint in Wine 1, intense passionfruit and gooseberry in Wine 2, and complex citrus, herb and stone-fruit in Wine 3. Riesling was considered but lacks petrol and beeswax and shows no residual sugar here. Chenin Blanc was weighed against the high-acid dry structure, but waxy lanolin, quince and oxidative phenolic texture are absent across the flight.

---

## Wine 1

**b) Origin**

Sancerre, Loire Valley, France. Crushed flint, wet chalk and muted white grapefruit over green apple signal a cool Old World origin. Kimmeridgian chalk minerality — saline and taut — is synonymous with Sancerre's terres blanches soils. Pouilly-Fumé shares the mineral signature but the gun-metal smokiness that appellation often displays is absent, tightening the call to Sancerre. Marlborough (Wine 2) shows far greater tropical intensity.

**c) Style and winemaking**

Precise and site-expressive. Pure citrus and no buttery or toasty character indicate cool-temperature fermentation in stainless steel with no malolactic conversion — a deliberate choice to preserve mineral tension. Subtle textural lift points to brief lees contact. No oak: terroir and variety are the explicit priority.

**d) Quality and maturity**

Very good, with Village-level Sancerre precision approaching Premier Cru ambition. Primary citrus aromatics and youthful colour suggest 1–2 years of age. Drink now or hold 3–4 years as the taut structure resolves into honeyed complexity, then plateau for a further 2–3 years.

**e) Commercial position**

Specialist merchant and premium on-trade in France, the UK and the US at around £18–22, competing directly with Pouilly-Fumé and white Burgundy at the same tier.

---

## Wine 2

**b) Origin**

Marlborough, New Zealand, Wairau Valley. Pungent passionfruit, guava and gooseberry alongside ripe lemon peel signal a warm, sunny New World harvest. Acidity is high but broader and less steely than Wine 1. Loire was eliminated by the overt tropical intensity and absence of chalk-driven minerality; South Africa (Wine 3) carries more structural weight and winemaking complexity.

**c) Style and winemaking**

Vivid and fruit-expressive, built for immediate appeal. Whole-bunch pressing, cool fermentation in stainless steel and early bottling are indicated by the clean, pungent aromatics and absence of phenolic grip. Malolactic fermentation was deliberately bypassed to lock in racy acidity and tropical freshness. A fully reductive, tank-to-bottle approach: no lees texture, no oak.

**d) Quality and maturity**

Good, consistent with a well-made commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc. The entirely primary fruit profile suggests 6–12 months post-harvest. At peak now; drink within 1–2 years before intensity fades.

**e) Commercial position**

Premium supermarket and casual on-trade in New Zealand, the UK and Australia at around £12–15, competing with benchmark Marlborough labels at a slightly more accessible price.

---

## Wine 3

**b) Origin**

Cape Point, South Africa. Green and yellow apple, lemongrass, grapefruit and spice complexity (cardamom, white pepper) combine with a richer, more textured palate and perceptible warmth (~13.5%). This rules out Marlborough — less textural richness, no spice — and Loire, which shows lower alcohol and a more restrained profile. Cape Point's Atlantic-facing slopes deliver this paradox: tropical weight with a saline, flinty backbone. Subtle vanilla and brioche confirm barrel fermentation, pointing to a serious Reserve-level coastal wine.

**c) Style and winemaking**

Ambitious and textured — a deliberate departure from the variety's reductive norm. Barrel fermentation in French oak (small proportion new) gives vanilla and subtle spice; extended lees ageing of over a year accounts for the layered, creamy mid-palate. Malolactic fermentation was likely avoided in part to retain the fresh acid line. Crucially, oak and lees amplify the site's natural salinity rather than masking it — the tension distinguishes this entirely from Marlborough's fruit-forward approach.

**d) Quality and maturity**

Very good, equivalent to a Reserve-level South African coastal white, 2–3 years old with excellent integration. Ready to drink now; structural depth supports improvement over 3–4 years, then holding for a further 3–5 years before primary fruit fades.

**e) Commercial position**

Independent specialist and premium on-trade in South Africa, the UK and Germany at around £20–25, a credible rival to Pessac-Léognan white Bordeaux at the same style tier.

# Mock Answer — Practice Paper 1 (Semillon pair)

## a) Identify the grape variety (4 marks)

Semillon. Both show lemon/lemongrass aromatics over a lean citrus core with a waxy, lanolin texture. No pyrazine, so not Sauvignon Blanc; no stone-fruit weight, so not Viognier; the phenolic waxiness excludes Chardonnay and Chenin. The spread of perceived alcohol — fragile in Wine 1, warm in Wine 2 — reflects Semillon's chameleon response to climate.

## b) Country and region of origin (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1 — Hunter Valley, New South Wales.** Pale lemon-green, very restrained aromatics, razor acidity, and a body/alcohol impression below 11.5% — implausibly light for most New World whites, but the Hunter's signature from early picking. South African Semillon was weighed but would show riper fruit or oak; here there is none, and the lanolin/lemon-juice purity confirms the Hunter.

**Wine 2 — Franschhoek, Western Cape.** Deeper gold, fuller body, warm ~13.5% palate impression, integrated French oak (hazelnut, marzipan) and a saline, pithy finish. Margaret River was considered, but the ginger and star-anise spice with that saline mineral close fits Franschhoek.

## c) Style and winemaking decisions (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** is reductive and unoaked: no vanilla, no buttery MLF character, so stainless steel with minimal oxygen. Early harvest is the foundational decision, capturing acid and green citrus before phenolic ripeness. Deliberately austere young.

**Wine 2** is interventionist: barrique ferment/maturation with a modest new-oak proportion given the integration, full MLF for the creamy breadth, and harvest at full phenolic ripeness. Contrasting philosophies — Wine 1 treats acidity as the asset, Wine 2 texture.

## d) Maturity, potential and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1**, around 6–7 years old, is in a tight, almost dumb phase — not at its best now. Expect toasted-lemon, beeswax and honey over 8–12 years, holding 20 from vintage. A specialist proposition at roughly AUD 50–70 for fine-wine merchants and premium restaurant lists in Australia, the UK and USA, competing with Chablis 1er Cru; the challenge is educating consumers through its austere youth.

**Wine 2**, 2–3 years old, drinks well now, gaining complexity 4–6 years then holding a decade before oak dominates. At roughly £20–25 it suits premium by-the-glass and mid-upper lists in South Africa, the UK, Germany and the USA, against Pessac-Léognan blanc. Rising interest in Cape whites is the opportunity; varietally labelled Semillon remains a harder retail sell than Chardonnay.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety (4 marks)

Riesling. The structural fingerprint is decisive across all four wines: pronounced to very high racy, linear acidity, low to moderate alcohol (the lightest showing watery delicacy consistent with around 8%, the heaviest a fuller warmth suggesting ~13–14%), and a complete absence of oak or MLF influence. Aromatics progress from lime cordial, lemon pith, and white blossom through yellow peach and tangerine to petrol and mineral complexity — the hallmark Riesling arc across climates and age. Chardonnay was eliminated: even the fuller wines show none of the apple-cream or lees-driven texture of oaked or MLF examples, and the tartaric acidity exceeds any Chardonnay baseline. Sauvignon Blanc was briefly considered for Wine 3's floral-citrus register but ruled out by the dry-extract weight and pronounced mineral drive.

## b) Region of origin (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 — Wachau, Austria.** Delicate body and low-moderate alcohol, yet real dry-extract precision: a chiselled, stony mineral line that is firmer and harder than Mosel, and completely dry rather than off-dry. The cool-climate citrus and white stone fruit, combined with slatey phenolic texture, points to Central European river-valley origin. The bone-dry palate and lighter body are consistent with Federspiel level in the Wachau. German Mosel was considered but eliminated by the bone-dry finish and firmer phenolic texture.

**Wine 2 — Rheinhessen, Germany (Grosses Gewächs).** The most powerful wine in the flight: tangerine, blood orange, spicy saline mineral, and apparent ~13–14% warmth in the glass signal a warm vintage in a warmer German region at top-tier ripeness. Rheinhessen's heavier soils yield this broad, spicy fruit profile at GG level; Rheingau was considered but its more restrained, mineral style is inconsistent with the wine's generosity and aromatic span.

**Wine 3 — Eden Valley, South Australia.** Fluorescent pale colour, lifted aromatics of finger lime, jasmine, and blackcurrant leaf, then mouth-watering acidity with chalky mineral texture — classic high-altitude South Australian Riesling. Clare Valley was considered but typically shows a harder, more reductive lime-juice character; the floral, saline-mineral elegance here points to Eden Valley.

**Wine 4 — Mosel, Germany (Spätlese).** Barely perceptible alcohol warmth, off-dry balance of green apple, white peach, and fresh lime held in tension by searing acidity — the definitive Mosel signature. Spätlese level fits the weight: more substance than Kabinett, without Auslese's honey. Saar and Nahe were considered but the ripe tropical inflection alongside classic green apple-peach character narrows the call to the Mittelmosel.

## c) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Dry, reductive, minimal-intervention style: stainless steel or large neutral vessel, temperature-controlled fermentation, early protective handling. Malic acidity is preserved intact — no MLF. Early bottling retains freshness; lighter alcohol reflects cooler vintage or harvest management at Federspiel ripeness.

**Wine 2.** Extended lees contact in neutral vessel builds spicy, saline texture without obscuring the mineral cut. Harvested at full GG ripeness, explaining the ~13–14% perceived alcohol. Stainless steel fermentation — the wine's transparency and racy acidity are incompatible with new oak — likely with extended cold maceration before pressing to extract phenolic structure and aromatic complexity.

**Wine 3.** Entirely stainless steel throughout; no oak or MLF detectable. Night harvesting or cold-chain protection likely accounts for the fluorescent lifted aromatics; whole-bunch pressing preserves purity. The chalky mineral texture reflects soil character rather than winemaking intervention. Early bottling locks in freshness.

**Wine 4.** Fermentation arrested — chilling and sterile filtration — to preserve the off-dry Spätlese balance. Low-temperature stainless steel fermentation retains apple blossom and fresh peach aromatics. No oak. The achieved tension between residual sugar and racy acidity is the winemaking intent.

## d) Quality and maturity (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1.** Very good quality; precise Wachau Federspiel at around €15–20. Drinking well now. The delicate body limits improvement; will hold cleanly for 3–5 years, developing some petrol character, then fade.

**Wine 2.** Outstanding quality — top-tier Grosses Gewächs at €50–80+. Still tightly wound and youthful; concentration and acidity will drive improvement for 8–10 years, adding complex petrol, dried citrus, and spice. Will hold a further 10–15 years at peak.

**Wine 3.** Very good quality; upper-tier Eden Valley at around AUD $30–40. Currently in its primary window at its freshest. Petrol and toast will develop over 3–5 years; will hold a further 3–4 years before fruit attenuates.

**Wine 4.** Very good quality; classic Mittelmosel Spätlese at around €25–35. Approachable now, but concentration and acidity give 5–8 years of improvement, adding honey, dried apricot, and petrol, then holding a further 10 years.

# Mock Answer — Practice Paper 1 (Riesling Pair)

## a) Grape Variety (6 marks)

Riesling. Both show lime zest, white peach and a steely, flinty mineral edge over very high, racy acidity, and both are bone dry. Chenin Blanc was the closest alternative — it shares the acid and mineral drive — but neither wine offers waxy lanolin, quince or phenolic grip. Chardonnay is ruled out by the absence of a broad, creamy mid-palate; Sauvignon Blanc by the absence of pyrazines. The electric citrus purity and fine-boned structure confirm Riesling.

## b) Region of Origin (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1 — Wachau, Austria.** Generous body with noticeable warmth (~13.5% by feel) alongside very high acidity indicates a warm continental site with dramatic diurnal range. Grapefruit and apricot concentration over a stony, schistous backbone, plus real palate weight, points to the Wachau rather than the cooler Kamptal or Kremstal, at Smaragd ripeness.

**Wine 2 — Niagara Peninsula, Canada.** Lighter body, lime cordial and green apple, lower apparent warmth: cool-climate New World. Acidity is high but less searing, suggesting continental climate with lake moderation. Clare Valley was weighed and rejected — Australian Riesling shows more piercing lime intensity and a drier, more angular finish than this rounder texture.

## c) Style and Winemaking (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Full-bodied, dry, age-worthy. Pure fruit with no phenolic edge suggests whole-bunch pressing and clean settling; no buttery or lactic notes indicates stainless-steel fermentation with malolactic blocked to protect the acid line. A creamy mid-palate and faint leesy character point to extended fine-lees contact building density. No oak — the richness is site concentration.

**Wine 2.** Cool stainless-steel fermentation for primary aromatic purity, MLF suppressed (acidity malic-edged, not soft), no oak. Where Wine 1 gains weight from lees ageing, this reads early-bottled with little textural development — a commercial choice for freshness.

## d) Quality, Maturity, and Commercial Position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding; Smaragd, the top Wachau tier, around €40–60. Around two years old and not yet at peak: it should improve five to seven years, gaining petrol, dried apricot and honey, then plateau a further five. Specialist merchants and high-end on-trade, competing with Alsace Grand Cru and German GG; strongest export appeal in Germany, the UK and Japan.

**Wine 2.** Very good, entry-to-mid tier, around CAD $20–30, for premium supermarket, specialist retail and by-the-glass on-trade. Drinking well at about two years; limited structural reserve means it will hold three to four years without improving before the fruit flattens. Competes with Mosel Kabinett and Clare Valley for consumers wanting unoaked aromatic dry whites in Canadian and US east-coast markets.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 1 Practice Question (Three Chardonnays)

---

#### Section A · For the flight as a whole

## a) Grape Variety (6 marks)

Chardonnay. All three share a lemon-gold colour without oxidative browning, an apple-to-stone-fruit core free of pyrazine or petrol, moderate warmth suggesting 13–13.5%, and — decisively — lees and oak handling that sits comfortably on the fruit rather than fighting it.

Riesling was the most credible alternative: similar citrus and mineral clarity, but the palate warmth and fuller body contradict Riesling's low-alcohol, high-acid frame, and no petrol or slate development appears. Pinot Gris was weighed for Wine 2's richer mid-palate and eliminated by the complete absence of phenolic grip or waxy texture. Only Chardonnay accounts for stone fruit, lees creaminess, toasty hazelnut and saline finish coexisting across three very different climates.

---

#### Section B · For each wine individually

## b) + c) Wine 1 — Mâconnais, Southern Burgundy

**Origin, style and winemaking:** White peach, citrus blossom and crushed limestone with restrained body and high but polished acidity point to cool-to-moderate France. Subtle vanilla without weight of extract places it in the Mâconnais rather than the richer, more oak-driven Côte de Beaune, and the modest concentration argues against Pouilly-Fuissé. Partial barrel fermentation in older oak alongside tank; malolactic partial or suppressed, preserving the saline edge.

**Quality and commercial position:** Good quality at village Mâconnais level, £18–25 in UK independent specialists, with export appeal in North America and Germany for affordable Burgundian Chardonnay. Competes with Viré-Clessé and the named Mâcon communes. Drink now, holding freshness three to four years; it will not gain.

---

## b) + c) Wine 2 — Auckland region, New Zealand

**Origin, style and winemaking:** Nectarine, toasted hazelnut and brioche over a saline back-palate with struck-flint reduction: cool-climate New World Chardonnay, barrel-fermented with extended lees contact and full malolactic in barrel, roughly 40–50% new French oak, wild yeast and deliberately reductive handling. Unlike Wine 1, the oak is a texture-builder rather than a seasoning. Acid precision and the salinity rule out Australia and California; the linear, very long finish and flint signature indicate Auckland's clay and volcanic sites.

**Quality and commercial position:** Outstanding, the equal of a good Côte de Beaune Premier Cru, at £45–60 UK / NZ$90–120. Placement is the top premium on-trade in London, New York and Tokyo, alongside village Meursault, and specialist retail selling New World Burgundian style. Constraints are tiny volume and low regional recognition. Drinking now, improving two to three years, then a tertiary plateau to the early 2030s.

---

## b) + c) Wine 3 — Napa Valley hillside, California

**Origin, style and winemaking:** The most revealing wine here because it refuses to behave like its appellation. Green apple, preserved lemon and crushed limestone, no tropical fruit and no new-oak vanilla; neutral or old French oak, minimal malolactic, high tartaric acidity reading as cool-site precision. The beeswax and chamomile lift and low extraction suggest a hillside volcanic or calcareous site with fog-moderated ripeness far below the valley floor. Where Wine 2 pursues Burgundy through texture, this one pursues it through subtraction — proof that site selection and winemaker intent can override appellation expectation.

**Quality and commercial position:** Very good to outstanding, $60–80 in the US. Its buyer is the Napa collector who came to Chardonnay via Burgundy — Californian fine-dining lists and premium independents in the US and UK. Commercially it is caught between consumers expecting opulent Napa, who will find it austere, and Burgundy loyalists sceptical of the address; the growing cool-site, low-intervention segment in the US and Asia is the opening. At peak now, holding to 2030 as citrus fades to dried fruit and hazelnut.

# Mock answer — 2025 Paper 1 Question 2

---

## Section A · For the flight as a whole

### a) Grape variety (7 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc. All four share racy, linear acidity with a thiolic register — gooseberry, passion fruit, lime zest — over pyrazine herbaceousness (cut grass, tomato leaf, capsicum), strongest in Wines 3 and 4. Riesling is ruled out: no petrol/kerosene development at this aromatic intensity, and no residual sugar variation across the set. Viognier was weighed for Wine 1's stonefruit weight but fails on the absence of apricot and exotic florals and on the taut acidity. Chardonnay is eliminated by the lack of broad, creamy palate weight and apple-core fruit; every wine keeps a piercing green-citrus tension Chardonnay does not deliver.

### e) Commercial positioning (9 marks)

Wine 1 sits at £30–40 through independent specialists and premium on-trade in France, the UK and Japan, competing against top Pouilly-Fumé. Wine 2 is the volume anchor: premium supermarkets, on-trade chains and travel retail across the US, UK and Asia at £15–20, and the reference point by which consumers judge the category. Wine 3, at £20–28, targets sommeliers and adventurous drinkers in the US west coast and Scandinavia who want cool-climate New World precision without the Marlborough price of entry. Wine 4 is the most niche — German-speaking specialist merchants and starred restaurant lists at £25–35 — constrained by low awareness of Styrian Sauvignon but benefiting from sommelier advocacy for alternative European expressions.

---

## Section B · For each wine individually

### Wine 1 — France, Sancerre

**b) Origin (7 marks)**

Lemon-gold, medium-plus viscosity and a waxy, rich palate rule out entry-level Loire Sauvignon and Muscadet (aromatically far too intense). Gun-flint spice with waxy lemon indicates silex soils; Pouilly-Fumé shares the flint but rarely this palate weight and old-vine concentration. A top hillside cru of Sancerre is the conclusion.

**c) Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Serious and textural rather than aromatically simple. The waxy mid-palate roundness points to fermentation in neutral old oak or large format — texture, not flavour, so used barrels rather than new. No buttery character: MLF blocked or minimal. The persistent mineral finish suggests 6–9 months on lees.

**d) Quality, maturity, drinking window (6 marks)**

Outstanding; single-vineyard cru level, around £35. Primary-dominated aromatics at 2–3 years old. Drinking now, with the concentration to improve 3–5 years, gaining dried citrus peel, honeyed wax and flint, then holding a further 4–6.

---

### Wine 2 — Marlborough, New Zealand

**b) Origin (7 marks)**

Pale lemon-green, near-brilliant clarity and explosive passion fruit, ripe gooseberry and kaffir lime over a saline edge and mouthwatering grapefruit finish are the Marlborough fingerprint. California would show fig, melon and lower acid with rounder body. Chile (Wine 3) was the closest call, but Wine 2 is riper and more tropical and lacks the jalapeño and chalky grip of the Pacific-cooled coast.

**c) Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Reductive winemaking to maximise thiols: whole-bunch pressing, cool ferment, predominantly stainless steel — hence the brilliant clarity and absence of phenolic bitterness. Faint beeswax and wet stone imply a small fraction in old oak or concrete for texture. Sharp malic acidity confirms no MLF.

**d) Quality, maturity, drinking window (6 marks)**

Very good; the commercial-premium benchmark for the region at around £17. One to two years old. At its peak now; will hold 2–3 years but the thiol intensity that is its whole proposition will fade. No improvement window.

---

### Wine 3 — San Antonio Valley, Chile

**b) Origin (7 marks)**

Grapefruit pith, lime, nettle and pronounced jalapeño over chalky-saline minerality point to a cool coastal South American site with direct Pacific influence. The capsicum-plus-salinity combination separates it from Marlborough (more tropical) and Austria (elderflower and flint). Humboldt-cooled San Antonio/Leyda fits the acid retention at modest body; Casablanca was considered but typically shows more stone fruit and less green heat.

**c) Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Wholly unoaked and uncompromising: cool stainless-steel fermentation, careful sulphur management to protect thiols, no lees or oak markers. Unlike Wine 1, no textural amplification is attempted — the emphasis is varietal purity and mineral linearity.

**d) Quality, maturity, drinking window (6 marks)**

Very good; top of its regional tier at £22–26. One to two years old, no development. Drink now to two years; structurally it could last 2–3 more, gaining waxy, dried-herb notes, but it is not built for ageing.

---

### Wine 4 — Südsteiermark, Austria

**b) Origin (7 marks)**

Elderflower, nettle and white grapefruit over crushed-stone flint, with a faint pumpkin-seed-oil inflection, plus medium-plus body and finesse, indicate central Europe rather than the New World. Alsace shares the floral register but lacks this chalky mineralité and structural weight. Südsteiermark on Opok marl-limestone is the conclusion; the saline length suggests a single-vineyard classified site.

**c) Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Dry, mineral-driven, with unusual body for an unoaked wine — the Styrian route to site expression through neutral vessels. Stainless steel, no MLF, so malic acidity carries the taut structure; the long finish and palate weight imply 6–8 months' lees contact.

**d) Quality, maturity, drinking window (6 marks)**

Outstanding; top-tier single-vineyard Austrian Sauvignon at £28–35. Three to four years old, integration just beginning. Improves over 3–5 years, gaining mineral depth and dried floral complexity, then holds 3–5 more — the most age-worthy wine in the flight, and evidence that Sauvignon's longevity comes from soil-driven structure, not oak.

**Wine 1** — Bone-dry, extended sur lie ageing of 18 months or more in large neutral vessels; the brioche note and slight creamy mid-palate texture result from lees contact without added aromatic complexity. No oak influence is detectable. Piercing, malic-edged acidity — rather than a broader lactic quality — indicates MLF was suppressed to preserve saline freshness.

**Wine 2** — Partial fermentation and ageing in small French oak barriques is suggested by subtle vanilla and toasted hazelnut alongside the primary aromatics, though the modest new-oak proportion leaves fruit unmasked; integration points to approximately 12 months barrel maturation. The 2021 vintage's cooler conditions have produced tighter acidity and mineral precision relative to riper years.

**Wine 3** — High physiological ripeness at harvest from a single classified site. No detectable botrytis; this is a Vendange Normale of exceptional concentration. Acidity retains grip consistent with suppressed MLF. Ageing in old large barrels, possibly combined with stainless steel, preserves aromatic intensity without adding oak character.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality; equivalent to Clos-level Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie, retailing around €18–25. Best placed with independent wine merchants and premium by-the-glass lists in Scandinavia, Japan, and the UK specialist sector. It competes with Picpoul de Pinet and entry-level Chablis at a lower price, with genuine terroir identity as its advantage. The challenge is limited consumer recognition of Muscadet beyond commodity pricing. Drink now to 2030.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding quality; one of only a handful of single-appellation AOCs in France. Retails at €120–200, distributed through fine wine merchants and Michelin-starred restaurant lists in France, the UK, the US, and Japan. Tiny production restricts volume, but genuine rarity and growing prestige of Northern Rhône whites support the price. Will improve for 8–10 years, developing dried apricot and waxy tertiary complexity, with a plateau at 15 years.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding quality; Alsace Grand Cru equivalent, retailing at €60–90. Natural market is fine-dining on-trade and specialist off-trade across Europe and North America. Richness and weight make it a compelling match for rich poultry, game, and aged cheese, aiding premium gastronomy positioning. The principal commercial challenge is varietal unfamiliarity relative to Burgundy Chardonnay or German Riesling. Will improve over 5–8 years, gaining tertiary smoke and honey, then hold for a further decade.

The under-the-skin point: near-fat texture arrives at only moderate alcohol, so richness is extract from low-yielding old vines and long lees contact, not sugar ripeness — a producer pushing Aligoté well past its reputation as Burgundy's second grape.

Châteauneuf Blanc was the other option, but the wine has more mineral tension and less blowsy fennel. The pepper-and-granite signature with this weight points to the northern Rhône hill of Hermitage.

**Wine 3 — Chardonnay, Puligny-Montrachet 1er Cru.** Lemon-gold, high viscosity, pronounced and strikingly pure: citrus zest, white peach, white flowers, a hazelnut undertone and an iron-mineral core. b) For each wine, identify the grape variety and the sub-region of origin as closely as possible. (2 x 6 marks)

c) For each wine, comment on the style and on the key winemaking decisions that have shaped it. (2 x 7 marks)

d) For each wine, assess the quality, the state of maturity and the potential to develop further, and comment on the commercial position of the wine. (2 x 8 marks)

wines.fullText: Cantina Tramin, Nussbaumer Gewurztraminer, 2021. Alto Adige, Italy. (14.5%)
Abbazia di Novacella, Kerner, 2024. Valle Isarco, Alto Adige, Italy. (13.5%)

modelAnswer:
## a) Region of origin (8 marks)

Alto Adige (Südtirol). High, crisp acidity in both wines combined with pronounced aromatic intensity points to a cool, high-altitude mountain environment with wide diurnal variation. Alsace was the main alternative: Alsace Gewurztraminer shows lower acidity and broader texture, and the saline mineral thread of Wine 2 is untypical of French aromatic whites. Linear acid structures allied to intense aromatics narrow the origin to the Italian Alps.

## b) Variety and sub-region (2 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Gewurztraminer, Termeno/Tramin (Oltradige-Bassa Atesina). Lychee and white rose identify the variety; lemon-oil precision distinguishes it from warmer Alsace expressions. Full body and palate warmth, perceived around 14%, confirm generous ripeness tempered by altitude. Tramin, in the lower, warmer Adige, is its historic home.

**Wine 2** — Kerner, Valle Isarco (Eisacktal). Elderflower, white pepper and saline minerality rule out Gewurztraminer's overt spice and Riesling's petrol note; Kerner, a Riesling × Trollinger cross, explains the profile. The near-bone-dry palate and saline finish indicate cool, high-altitude Valle Isarco rather than the warmer Bolzano basin.

## c) Style and winemaking (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Rich, dry aromatic white. Absence of toast or vanilla confirms stainless steel throughout, preserving primary aromatics; a creamy mid-palate suggests lees contact adding body without masking freshness. Peach and melon ripeness indicates late harvest from warmer lower-valley sites, held in balance by the variety's brisk acidity.

**Wine 2** — Linear and saline by contrast. Stainless steel again, protecting Kerner's high-toned aromatics. A few grams of residual sugar, buried under high acidity, reads as dry but adds textural weight. Herbal freshness and blood orange point to early picking of high-altitude fruit to lock in acidity.

## d) Quality, maturity, commercial position (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good to excellent; a Südtirol DOC single-vineyard Gewurztraminer at €25–35, justified by aromatic depth, length and acid-ripeness balance. At three to four years it drinks well now, holding two to three more before the florals fade; drink within six years. Sells strongly in German-speaking markets and northern Italy, with specialist importers in the UK and USA. It competes with top Alsace Gewurztraminer, offering better freshness at a lower price — persuasive for independent merchants and premium on-trade.

**Wine 2** — Very good; a Valle Isarco Kerner at €18–25. The saline precision alongside citrus and stone fruit lifts it above simpler Alto Adige whites. At one to two years it shows well now and should gain complexity over two to three years, holding four to five from vintage. The commercial challenge is recognition: Kerner is unknown outside specialist circles, which is also its opportunity. Target Germany, Scandinavia and UK independents, with by-the-glass placement in wine-focused restaurants the most effective route to new consumers.

wines.fullText: Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé 2023. Mâconnais, Burgundy, France. (13.0%)
Lucien Crochet Sancerre Blanc Le Chêne Marchand 2022. Loire Valley, France. (13.5%)

modelAnswer:
## a) Country, region and grape variety (2 × 10 marks)

Both wines are from France.

**Wine 1** — Mâconnais, Burgundy; Chardonnay. White peach, pear and chalk with a restrained toasty lift point to Chardonnay. Riesling was considered — the saline, crushed-limestone finish could fit dry Alsace — but the warm, medium-plus body and absence of petrol rule it out. Chenin Blanc was weighed for its floral/stone-fruit pairing, but the waxy phenolic bite is absent. Within Burgundy, moderate concentration with a crisp limestone finish places this in the Mâconnais: a Côte de Beaune 1er Cru would show deeper concentration and tertiary development; generic Bourgogne Blanc less mineral definition.

**Wine 2** — Sancerre, Loire; Sauvignon Blanc. Flinty-chalk minerality, lemon-meringue citrus and a saline, iodine-laced palate with racy acidity confirm Sauvignon Blanc. Loire Chenin was considered — shared high acidity and provenance — but would bring lanolin, quince and a rounder texture. The flinty-chalk signature of Kimmeridgian and caillottes soils rules out Verdejo or Grüner. Its mineral weight distinguishes it from Pouilly-Fumé and Menetou-Salon.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, mid-weight, mineral-driven. Clean stone fruit without phenolic edge points to gentle whole-bunch pressing. Subtle vanilla and toasted hazelnut indicate fermentation and short ageing in French oak, perhaps 20–25% new, the rest neutral. Completed malolactic explains the round mid-palate; several months on lees give the creamy, saline finish.

**Wine 2** — Dry, racy, structure over fruit richness. Gooseberry-citrus purity points to whole-bunch pressing and cool stainless-steel fermentation, with four to six months on fine lees for the faint pastry note. No oak. Malolactic appears blocked: the tartaric precision would be erased by lactic softening — as deliberate a decision here as allowing it was in Wine 1.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good, at Mâcon-Villages level, €18–25. It surpasses generic Mâcon Blanc in mineral definition but lacks Pouilly-Fuissé's concentration. Independent specialists and mid-range on-trade in France, the UK and Benelux: real Burgundy provenance for drinkers priced out of the Côte de Beaune. Competes with Saint-Véran and Viré-Clessé. Drink now to 2027–28; moderate structure limits cellaring.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding, at premier lieu-dit Sancerre level, €35–50. Mineral depth and enveloping texture set it above village Sancerre. Fine-wine specialists, Michelin accounts and premium independents in France, Germany, the UK, Japan and the US, competing with top-tier Pouilly-Fumé. Structured acidity and chalky spine suggest improvement over four to five years, holding to 2030–32.

Domaine des Roches Neuves, Saumur Blanc, 2022. Loire Valley, France. (13%)
Mas de Daumas Gassac, Blanc, 2022. IGP Hérault, Languedoc, France. (13.5%)

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — a) Region of Origin (8 marks)

Alsace, France. Rose petal, jasmine, and stone-fruit intensity set against a bone-dry palate points immediately to Alsace. The restrained sweetness rules out Vouvray, where Chenin Blanc would show quince and wax rather than floral spice. Waxy lanolin alongside grapefruit zest and flinty minerality narrows the call to Riesling: Gewurztraminer would show oilier texture with lower acidity, while Pinot Gris would tend toward muted aromatics and heavier mouthfeel. Medium-plus perceived alcohol is consistent with Grand Cru or high-quality single-vineyard Riesling.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Dry, with no perceptible residual sugar — a deliberate choice against the appellation's historical off-dry tendencies. Pure citrus and stone-fruit character with no vanilla or toast indicates stainless steel fermentation. Flinty, slightly waxy texture points to extended lees contact, building mid-palate weight without sacrificing freshness. No MLF: the acidity remains zesty and tartaric rather than broad or creamy.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (9 marks)

Outstanding quality, equivalent to Grand Cru or single-vineyard Alsace Riesling, retailing around €30–50. Aromatic complexity, length, and structural precision exceed simple AOC Alsace level. The dry, mineral-driven style positions this for independent merchants and premium on-trade in Germany, the UK, and Japan, competing with German GGs at a similar or lower price. Structured to develop over five to eight more years, building petrol and apricot-preserve complexity.

## Wine 2 — a) Region of Origin (8 marks)

Saumur Blanc, Loire Valley, France. Quince, lemon curd, and waxy lanolin alongside linear acidity identifies Chenin Blanc. Muscadet was eliminated — Melon de Bourgogne would be lighter and more neutral. Vouvray was considered but the taut, austere mineral drive rather than honeyed roundness points to Saumur's tuffeau soils over Vouvray's softer profile. Medium-plus body with slight textural grip confirms dry Saumur rather than Anjou Blanc.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Reductive and mineral-driven. No oak-derived characters point to stainless steel or older large-format vessels. Subtle phenolic grip suggests partial skin contact or extended maceration on solids, a signature of biodynamically farmed Chenin. No MLF: the acidity remains cutting and tartaric, preserving the appellation's hallmark tension.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (9 marks)

Very good quality, equivalent to premier-domaine Saumur Blanc, retailing at approximately €20–30. The key commercial challenge is appellation recognition: Saumur Blanc struggles for shelf presence against Savennières or Vouvray. The ideal channel is specialist merchants and sommelier-driven on-trade in the UK, Benelux, and the US natural-wine market, where biodynamic credentials amplify appeal. Drink now or over the next six to ten years as it develops honeyed, waxy tertiary complexity.

## Wine 3 — a) Region of Origin (8 marks)

Languedoc, southern France — specifically an IGP-level origin such as the Hérault. Garrigue, fennel, white pepper, and exotic stone-fruit aromatics alongside a saline, herb-edged finish are distinctively southern French. The floral lift initially suggested a Viognier-led Rhône, but the anise-and-garrigue echo with saline mineral finish and textural grip without oak points to a multi-variety Languedoc Blanc rather than a single-variety Condrieu.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A structured, aromatic blend — possibly Viognier, Petit Manseng, and Marsanne — vinified to emphasise freshness despite the warm origin. No vanilla or toast indicates neutral vessel ageing or stainless steel, preserving herb and mineral detail. Subtle textural grip without tannin suggests brief skin contact on some components. The saline finish points to earlier harvest on certain lots, a deliberate acid-management decision for this climate.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (9 marks)

Outstanding for its IGP tier, retailing around €25–40, significantly overdelivering on legal classification. The Hérault IGP designation undersells actual quality, creating both an opportunity — strong value perception — and a challenge, as shelf positioning falls below AOC wines of lesser merit. Export markets in the UK, USA, and Scandinavia are the primary audience through specialist importers and premium on-trade. Drink now to eight years, developing spiced dried fruit and deeper garrigue complexity.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 1 Question 1

## a) Region of Origin (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Alsace, France. Honeycomb, stone fruit and a distinctly petrolly mineral lift over medium-plus body and moderate warmth (~13%), with zippy, precise acidity: a Riesling from a continental site with some altitude moderation. The honeyed density and phenolic breadth rule out Mosel, which would be lighter and lower in alcohol; Clare Valley was weighed but lacks this mineral depth and would show a harder, more limey acid line. The generous body and length fit a Grand Cru or top single-parcel Alsace site.

**Wine 2** — Côte de Beaune, Burgundy. Restrained white peach, hazelnut and savoury lees; medium-plus body with high but broad acidity and silky, integrated texture. Chablis was considered and rejected: it would give a leaner, more linear acid profile with a flinty rather than creamy mid-palate. California Chardonnay is excluded by the racy acidity and complete absence of tropical fruit. The depth and precision point to Meursault at 1er Cru level.

**Wine 3** — Pessac-Léognan, Bordeaux. Grapefruit and preserved lemon alongside nectarine and fig, with elderflower and a chalky, saline finish — the Sauvignon Blanc–Sémillon signature of the Graves family. Loire Sauvignon was weighed but the oak integration, mid-palate texture and Sémillon-derived stone fruit rule it out. The salinity, length and structural completeness lift it above generic Graves.

**Wine 4** — Touraine, Loire Valley. Gooseberry, nettle, cut grass and green apple with a flinty edge; light body, low alcohol (~12%), unoaked, saline finish. Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé were considered but this lacks their textural weight and gunflint smoke. Marlborough is excluded by the absence of tropical fruit and the chalky mineral finish. Touraine fits the modest scale and unadorned style.

---

## b) Grape Variety or Varieties (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Riesling. Petrol-inflected minerality with honeyed stone fruit and razor acidity at medium-plus body.

**Wine 2** — Chardonnay. Hazelnut and peach over broad, textured acidity, shaped by malolactic fermentation and barrel.

**Wine 3** — Sauvignon Blanc with Sémillon. Grapefruit and citrus zest are Sauvignon-driven; the fig and creamy mid-palate weight indicate a meaningful Sémillon component.

**Wine 4** — Sauvignon Blanc. Pyrazine-led aromatics, unambiguous.

---

## c) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, concentrated Alsace Riesling. Honeyed ripeness suggests late picking of hand-sorted fruit; fermentation in large old foudre or inert vessel at controlled temperature, since no toast or vanilla is detectable. Several months on fine lees adds the textural breadth without masking the mineral line.

**Wine 2** — The only wine in the flight with full malolactic fermentation, which supplies the creamy roundness. Fermented in French barrique, perhaps 20–30% new, with 12–18 months on lees for mid-palate weight. Retained freshness on the finish points to careful temperature and SO₂ management.

**Wine 3** — Barrel-fermented Bordeaux Blanc, roughly 30–40% new oak, giving toasted hazelnut and light cedar. Unlike Wine 2, malolactic appears only partial: the mid-palate is creamy but grapefruit acidity survives intact. Bâtonnage on lees builds texture, and the Sémillon base supplies body and length the Sauvignon alone would not.

**Wine 4** — Reductive, unoaked and picked early. Cool stainless-steel fermentation preserves the pyrazine aromatics; early bottling retains CO₂ and the saline crispness. No lees work, no oak — the deliberate opposite of Wine 3's approach to the same variety.

---

## d) Quality and Ageing Potential (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; Grand Cru Alsace level, €35–55. Youthful at 2–3 years, primary fruit dominant. Will improve 5–8 years as kerosene, dried apricot and spice emerge, then hold a decade.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding; 1er Cru Meursault, £60–90. Currently closed at 3–4 years and needs a further 3–5; peaking at 8–10 years from vintage with beeswax, truffle and toasted almond, then holding.

**Wine 3** — Very good to outstanding; Cru Classé de Graves, €25–40. Already approachable at 2–3 years but with a 5–8 year improvement window towards preserved citrus, lanolin and struck flint. The under-the-skin point: Sémillon is what buys this wine its ageing curve — the Sauvignon-only Wine 4 has no equivalent reserve, which is why two wines of the same principal variety sit two decades apart in longevity.

**Wine 4** — Good; serious Touraine, €10–15. Varietal pleasure rather than complexity; light extract offers nothing to bottle age. Drink within 2–3 years of vintage.

# Mock Answer — Practice Paper 1 (France, Three Regions)

## a) Region and grape variety (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Viognier, Condrieu, Northern Rhône. Pronounced white peach, apricot and acacia blossom with a lychee lift is varietally decisive for Viognier. The palate is full and round, oily in texture but cut by mandarin-toned freshness, alcohol reading warm at around 13.5%. Alsace Pinot Gris was weighed: it can match the aromatic exuberance but not this oily peach concentration and floral force. Languedoc Viognier rarely sustains this tension alongside the weight, and the mineral definition argues against a New World origin. Within the Northern Rhône, the pine kernel note and textural drive fit Condrieu rather than Côte-Rôtie Blanc; the precision suggests a single-vineyard bottling.

**Wine 2** — Chardonnay, Meursault, Côte de Beaune. Medium-plus intensity of apple and stone fruit beneath hazelnut and pastry oak, with high tartaric acidity carrying real textural weight. Chablis is ruled out — it would be more austere and gunflinty, with far less generosity; Mâconnais rarely reaches this concentration. Pouilly-Fuissé was considered but lacks the lees-built creaminess and emerging tertiary complexity. Meursault.

**Wine 3** — Chenin Blanc, Vouvray, Loire. Woolly lanolin on the nose with savoury herbs and crushed-shell minerality: old-vine Chenin in a dry style. Savennières is the plausible alternative and shares the saline dryness, but the honeyed roundness here belongs to Vouvray's tuffeau rather than Savennières' schist-driven austerity. South African Chenin would give the texture without this savoury-mineral depth.

## b) Style and winemaking (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Full-bodied and dry with pronounced aromatics and no oak character: fermentation and ageing in neutral vessels, stainless steel or old large wood, to protect Viognier's volatile aromatics. Aromatic purity suggests whole-bunch pressing. Unblended with Marsanne or Roussanne, as Condrieu requires.

**Wine 2** — The broad, creamy mid-palate and integrated nutty notes indicate full malolactic fermentation in barrel with roughly 12 months on lees, in about 25–30% new French oak. Cold settling before fermentation would account for the clean fruit.

**Wine 3** — Dry but with a textural impression of 2–4 g/L residual sugar carried by high acidity. Unlike Wine 2, oak plays no part: ambient fermentation in neutral vessels and 8–12 months on lees build savoury complexity without masking site.

## c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding; single-vineyard Condrieu level, around €60–80. At roughly two years it balances primary and secondary character and drinks well now, but will hold 4–6 years as the florals turn honeyed and waxy. Fine wine specialists and premium on-trade with Rhône depth; USA, UK and Japan take most exports.

**Wine 2** — Very good to outstanding, Meursault Premier Cru level at €50–70. At about three years it is only opening; 5–7 years of improvement remain as the oak recedes and dried-mushroom tertiary notes arrive. Fine wine merchants and starred restaurants globally.

**Wine 3** — Very good, leading Vouvray Sec at €25–35 — a third the price of the Meursault for comparable ageing capacity, which is the commercial argument. At two years it is barely open; 10–15 years will take it from savoury-mineral to beeswax and quince. Specialist merchants selling Loire as the value alternative to white Burgundy.

**Wine 3** — Côtes du Rhône Blanc. Grenache Blanc with Clairette. Gold, slightly hazy, with ripe apricot, beeswax, chamomile, fennel and garrigue, and generous warm body. Condrieu Viognier was the alternative given the stone fruit, but Condrieu is silky and apricot-cream; this has phenolic grip and herbal savouriness, and broader, more textural weight than varietal Viognier delivers.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, medium-bodied, restrained. No buttery breadth: partial rather than full malolactic, preserving freshness. Subtle toast and vanilla, well integrated and never dominant, point to used barriques or large-format wood rather than new oak. Gentle roundness and medium-plus length indicate lees ageing; the absence of struck-match reduction suggests racking before bottling.

**Wine 2** — Unlike Wine 1, no wood at all: purity of citrus and gunflint with zero vanilla or toast confirms stainless steel or large neutral vessel. Malolactic blocked — the angular acid line and crisp grapefruit finish rule out lactic softening. The muscular texture comes from extended lees contact, adding weight without touching the acid frame.

**Wine 3** — The most interventionist in intent yet the least technological: haze and phenolic grip indicate skin contact during fermentation; beeswax and dried-fruit notes indicate low sulfur and an oxidative élevage, consistent with a low-intervention or biodynamic grower. ## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; village Mâconnais level, around £25–30 retail. Outperforms generic Mâcon-Villages on mineral precision but lacks the tension of Pouilly-Fuissé. Independent specialists and premium on-trade, selling to drinkers priced out of Côte de Beaune villages; UK, US and Japan.

Fine-dining on-trade and specialist merchants in the UK, US, Scandinavia and Japan; competes directly with top Pouilly-Fumé and carries a following among Sauvignon Blanc buyers who track named parcels rather than brands.

**Wine 3** — Good to very good for the appellation, £20–28. Herb, honeycomb and phenolic texture exceed the generic tier, but the haze and oxidative handling narrow distribution sharply: natural wine bars and advocacy-led independents in France, the UK and urban US. The style polarises — the same phenolic grip that gives it interest will read as a fault to consumers expecting clean fruit — so it cannot be sold on appellation alone. Its route to market is the recommendation, which caps volume but protects margin. Conservative on-trade lists will resist it.

Dry, medium-bodied, mineral-driven. The flinty reduction reflects stainless steel fermentation under inert gas — intrinsic to Fiano, not a fault. Lees contact is modest, retaining freshness without the broad softening of extended sur lie. Oak is absent by design: it would collapse the tension between floral delicacy and mineral austerity that defines the wine.

## Wine 2 — c) Maturity, Development and Commercial Position (7 marks)

About two years old. Drinking well now, with six to eight years ahead as flint and chamomile turn waxy and nutty, then holding four to five more. Very good quality, Fiano di Avellino DOCG, around €18–25. Italian restaurants and fine dining; growing US, UK and Scandinavian demand from drinkers seeking a structured Chablis alternative at similar money.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Deep gold, apricot compote, almond paste and integrated spice: mature Verdicchio. The riper concentration and golden hue rule out Garganega, lighter in weight and colour; the body and almond-paste richness exceed Fiano's leaner register. The textural depth places it in Marche, and Riserva-level concentration points to Castelli di Jesi Classico Riserva rather than Matelica, which shows higher acidity and less generosity.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Dry, full-bodied, ambitious. Gold colour and almond-paste spice indicate oak ageing in medium-sized barrels or tonneaux, part new, adding texture while leaving the varietal bitter almond intact. Softened acidity confirms full malolactic fermentation. Twelve to eighteen months on lees is suggested by the polysaccharide texture and by minerality wrapped in fruit rather than exposed.

## Wine 3 — c) Maturity, Development and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Four to five years old, at or near peak, with three to four years of further improvement as nutty oxidative complexity deepens, then five years holding. Outstanding quality, Riserva DOCG, around €30–45. Premium on-trade and fine wine merchants; strongest in Germany and the US, competing with aged village to Premier Cru Burgundy at a lower price.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Pale yellow with green tints, orange blossom, gunpowder, petrol, saline minerality, anise and almond, long and sapid: Carricante. Petrol plus volcanic salinity is diagnostic and appears in none of the other three varieties. Greco di Tufo shares the almond-citrus note but is broader and more phenolic, without this taut saline freshness. Gunpowder minerality and orange blossom confirm high-elevation Etna, Sicily; the Superiore designation indicates the northern slopes.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Dry, light-to-medium-bodied, aromatically intense. No vanilla or toast confirms stainless steel and no new oak. Four to six months on lees adds texture without dulling the electric freshness. The petrol, blossom and anise complexity comes from the variety's terpene and thiol profile amplified by volcanic soil, not from intervention: the philosophy is to preserve, not construct.

## Wine 4 — c) Maturity, Development and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Three to four years old, drinking very well, with five to seven years of improvement as petrol, wax and mineral tertiaries emerge — as in mature Clare Valley Riesling — then four years holding. Outstanding quality, Etna Bianco Superiore DOC, around €30–50. Fine wine merchants and premium Italian-focused on-trade; rapid growth in the US, UK and Japan, competing with Chablis Premier Cru and German Riesling GG.
