## a) Region of origin (6 marks)

Both wines show moderate rather than racy acidity, generous body and warm ripe fruit, with no pyrazine or green edge — ruling out Margaret River and cooler South Australian zones such as Clare. Wine 1's waxy lanolin and Wine 2's saline, flint-edged stonefruit both fit a warm, humid maritime origin giving textural weight without the phenolic coarseness of hot inland regions. Decisively, one region routinely delivers both low-alcohol aged Semillon and increasingly confident Chardonnay.

**Both wines: Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia.**

## b) Grape variety

**Wine 1 — Semillon.** Deep gold, toasted brioche, beeswax, lemon curd and petrol. Chardonnay was weighed and rejected: it does not develop waxy lanolin with petrol, and the low perceived alcohol (light-bodied, no warmth, ~11%) is far below Wine 2's. Riesling was considered for the petrol, but the wax and honey, without piercing lime acidity, exclude it.

**Wine 2 — Chardonnay.** White peach, struck flint, toasted almond, creamy lees. Viognier was considered for the stonefruit richness but the firm acid line, absence of oily viscosity and cedary oak point to Chardonnay.

## c) Style and winemaking

**Wine 1.** Dry, oxidatively developed. No vanilla or barrel toast: tank or old-vat fermentation, no malolactic. Beeswax and oatmeal texture suggest brief lees contact; the petrol and marmalade are bottle-derived, not winemaking.

**Wine 2.** By contrast, reductive and worked. Struck flint plus creamy texture indicate partial barrel fermentation in older French oak — cedar without new-oak vanilla — with six to nine months on lees. Firm acidity alongside restrained butter suggests partial malolactic only; clean fruit with no phenolic grip implies whole-bunch pressing.

## d) Quality, maturity and commercial position

**Wine 1.** Outstanding: a regional icon style, AUD 70–100. Fully tertiary at seven to eight years, at peak now, holding three to five more as marmalade and nut character build. Sold through independent fine wine merchants, premium on-trade and UK/Asian export where aged Semillon has collector interest; the barrier is consumer unfamiliarity — it needs sommelier explanation to sell.

**Wine 2.** Very good, single-vineyard tier, AUD 45–65. Lemon-gold with primary stonefruit at three to four years; will improve two to three years as lees complexity knits, then hold four to five. Premium restaurant and specialist retail, competing directly with village Burgundy at a lower price — its commercial argument to UK and US fine-dining buyers.

The higher-order point: one climate, two opposite quality routes — Semillon earning complexity from bottle age with minimal intervention, Chardonnay from cellar work at release.

# Mock answer — Paper 1 Question 1

## a) Origin and principal varieties (4 x 9 marks)

**Wine 1 — Pessac-Léognan, Bordeaux, France. Sauvignon Blanc with a substantial Sémillon component.** The nose splits cleanly in two: white grapefruit, lemon zest, box hedge and nettle on one side, lemon curd, fresh fig and a waxy lanolin weight on the other. That second half is not Sauvignon and points to Sémillon. Alcohol reads moderate rather than generous, with medium(+) tartaric acidity and a saline, flinty close — cool-tempered maritime, not warm. Margaret River was weighed, but that origin usually gives more overt passion fruit and a fatter mid-palate; the restraint, the smoky flint and the fine toasted-barrel seasoning narrow to the Graves gravels, and the depth of the finish to a classed-growth property in Pessac-Léognan rather than generic Bordeaux Blanc.

**Wine 2 — Douro (Douro Superior), Portugal. Rabigato, Gouveio and Viosinho, with Arinto.** Lemon-gold with citrus peel, quince, firm pear, dried herbs and a hot-stone, schistous edge. Alcohol is perceptibly warm and the body broad, yet the acid line stays taut and slightly bitter-pithy on the finish — the signature of high-altitude plantings in a hot region. Rioja Blanco was considered and rejected: no oxidative nuttiness, no old-oak sweetness. Vinho Verde is far too light and spritzy for this weight. The combination of warmth, citrus-pith grip and granite/schist salinity is Douro white.

**Wine 3 — Swartland, South Africa. Chenin Blanc-led, with Roussanne and Clairette/Verdelho.** Pale gold, white peach, dried apricot, beeswax and a distinct fynbos-and-chamomile herbal signature. The waxy, lanolin thread and gentle phenolic grip say Chenin; the broad, oily mid-palate says a Rhône white partner. Alcohol is moderate, acidity medium(+) and chalky, with subtle oxidative complexity and no new oak. A Rhône blend proper was eliminated — too fresh, too little fennel and glycerol heat. Loire Chenin was eliminated on the riper stone fruit and the dried-herb scrub character.

**Wine 4 — Vienna, Austria. Wiener Gemischter Satz: Grüner Veltliner-led field blend with Weissburgunder, Riesling and Traminer.** White pepper and fennel over yellow apple, apricot, citrus pith, fresh almond and struck flint, closing saline with light phenolic grip. Alsace Edelzwicker was considered but shows broader, lower acidity and usually some Muscat/Gewurztraminer perfume; here the peppery lift plus a taut, unoaked line is unmistakably Viennese.

## b) Blend construction and key winemaking decisions (4 x 6 marks)

**Wine 1**: Sauvignon picked early for pyrazine and acid, Sémillon later for flesh; the pure citrus with no phenolic bitterness suggests whole-bunch pressing, then fermentation in barrel — perhaps a third new — with lees stirring for the creamy underlay. Malolactic clearly blocked: the acid is still linear.

**Wine 2**: co-fermentation or early blending of neutral-but-structural Douro varieties, harvested at altitude to hold acid; cool stainless fermentation with brief lees contact, minimal wood, prioritising freshness over texture.

**Wine 3**: separate parcel fermentations, spontaneous, with some skin contact for the grip; ageing in old, large-format neutral wood, unfined and lightly protected, blended late — the subtle oxidative note is deliberate rather than accidental.

**Wine 4**: a genuine field blend, interplanted and co-harvested. The insight here is that a mixed planting cannot ripen evenly, so some varieties come in slightly under-ripe and others over — that internal spread is precisely what delivers a long textural mid-palate at only moderate alcohol. Whole-cluster pressing, large old oak or steel, no malolactic.

## c) Quality and maturity (4 x 5 marks)

**Wine 1**: outstanding, Cru Classé de Graves level; 3–4 years old, drinking well now, will improve 5–6 years and hold 10–12, gaining toast and honeyed depth.
**Wine 2**: good quality, Douro DOC estate white; 2 years old, at its peak, drink over 2–3 years — freshness will fade first.
**Wine 3**: very good to outstanding, top independent Swartland tier; youthful at 3 years, improving 4–5 years, holding a decade as the wax turns honeyed.
**Wine 4**: very good, top-site Ried/Alte Reben level; drink now to 5 years, holding 7–8.

## d) Style and commercial position (4 x 5 marks)

**Wine 1** is a serious, barrel-built, ageworthy white for fine-dining lists and specialist merchants at around £50–60, competing with Village white Burgundy. **Wine 2** is a fresh, food-friendly modern white at £15–18, sold through independents and Portuguese on-trade to consumers exploring beyond Vinho Verde. **Wine 3** is a low-intervention terroir statement, allocated through specialist retail and sommelier lists at £30–35, competing with Savennières and Northern Rhône whites; its challenge is Chenin's soft price ceiling. **Wine 4** is an authenticity-led, geographically unique wine, ~£30, ideal for by-the-glass programmes in wine-focused restaurants — its strength and weakness both being that Gemischter Satz needs explaining.

## b) Style and winemaking (2 x 10 marks)

**Wine 1.** The clean citrus core with no phenolic bitterness suggests whole-bunch pressing; the gold hue and toast indicate barrel fermentation in French oak, perhaps 30% new, medium toast. ## Wine 1 — Marsanne, Pyrenees, Australia

### a) Variety and origin (8 marks)

Deep gold, full-bodied, with a waxy, lanolin nose over honeysuckle and stone fruit, and a broad, unctuous palate: Marsanne. Oaked Chardonnay was ruled out by the absence of a citrus spine and the presence of that waxy phenolic grip. Warm, generous alcohol reading around 13.5–14% and more flesh and phenolic bite than a Hermitage Blanc indicate a warm New World continental site — the Pyrenees of Victoria, altitude tempering heat, fits the mix of ripeness and residual freshness. Fruit-driven rather than reductive, so a premium regional interpretation rather than a cellar-aged Goulburn style.

### b) Winemaking (9 marks)

Ripe picking with brief skin contact giving phenolic grip on the finish; no toast or vanillin, so fermentation and ageing in tank or neutral oak, protecting varietal character. The broad, low-acid mid-palate indicates full malolactic. Concentration suggests low yields and a late harvest date.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good; a premium estate-tier Australian white, around AUD 35–45. Specialist retail and premium on-trade, with export appeal to UK independents and US by-the-glass lists wanting an alternative to oaked Chardonnay. Competes with Heathcote and Goulburn Marsanne but is more immediately approachable. At peak; will hold 3–5 years without gaining aged Semillon-style complexity.

---

## Wine 2 — Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, Abruzzo, Italy

### a) Variety and origin (8 marks)

Gold with a faint haze; a pronounced nose of apple, raw almond, iodine, ginger, musky pear and salty mineral. That complexity excludes high-yielding bulk whites. Vermentino was considered for the salinity but lacks the almond and musk and carries less palate weight; Fiano would show hazelnut rather than this iodine drive. Apple, apricot and Adriatic salinity, with medium-high alcohol, point to Trebbiano d'Abruzzo from a low-intervention producer — a variety whose name suggests industrial thinness but which here reads as seriously terroir-expressive.

### b) Winemaking (9 marks)

The haze indicates no filtration. Aromatic breadth and textural depth come from extended lees contact in large old botti — no new-oak imprint whatsoever. The musk and complexity suggest native-yeast fermentation; the glass weight, a late harvest for full phenolic ripeness.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Outstanding — a benchmark of the variety, at DOC Riserva level, €40–60 in Italy, £50–70 UK. Collector's wine for fine-dining lists and specialist Italian importers, with strong potential in Japan and the US natural-wine trade. The commercial obstacle is the name itself, which will deter buyers who have never tasted the variety at this level. Drink now, developing over 5–8 years.

---

## Wine 3 — Pinot Gris, Alsace, France

### a) Variety and origin (8 marks)

Deep gold, full-bodied, slightly oily, with rose petal, smoke, white pepper and apricot, and a faintly sweet impression on a technically dry finish: Pinot Gris. Gewurztraminer shares the breadth but would deliver overt lychee and Turkish delight; the smoky restraint here settles it. Warm alcohol near 14% and the ripeness of the fruit indicate Alsace, and the concentration and mineral drive suggest a named cru site rather than generic Alsace.

### b) Winemaking (9 marks)

Whole-bunch pressing with limited but real phenolic extraction; full malolactic behind the buttery mid-palate; ageing in large neutral casks, adding weight without aromatic interference. The ripeness and residual impression point to a late harvest with some botrytis influence in a warm vintage.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good to outstanding, at cru level, €25–45. On-trade in France, Germany and Scandinavia, plus UK and US Alsace specialists. Its generosity makes it a food wine for richer dishes, which is where its margin lies. Drink now to 2030, then honeyed spice complexity for a further five years.

---

## Wine 4 — Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough, New Zealand

### a) Variety and origin (8 marks)

Pale lemon-green with passionfruit, gooseberry, elderflower and yuzu: Sauvignon Blanc. Loire origin was rejected — Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé show capsicum, flint and smoke rather than this tropical charge. Marlborough, then; but the dry, chalky, faintly fennel-edged palate and baked-apple depth exceed the commodity norm, indicating a premium producer with a wild-fermented component.

### b) Winemaking (9 marks)

Predominantly stainless steel to protect thiols. A wild-fermented portion in old oak supplies the nectarine and baked-apple layer without oak on the nose. Extended lees contact gives the creamy mid-palate; the finish is bone-dry with mineral grip and no bottling intervention evident.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good — the appellation's top tier, NZD 40–55 (roughly £20–28 UK), above commodity Marlborough but below the micro-terroir elite. UK premium retail and independents, plus the US, Germany and Scandinavia. It undercuts premium Sancerre for consumers seeking textured aromatic whites, and suits premium by-the-glass. Drink now to 2027: the thiols will fade before the lees texture does, so early drinking is the commercial reality.

Sauvignon Blanc leads on citrus-tropical drive and brisk acidity; Sémillon, from seasoned oak, adds weight, fine phenolics and suppleness that Sauvignon alone could not supply at this modest alcohol. ## Wine 2 — c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good; benchmark estate level, AUD 30–40. Primary fruit indicates current release. Drink over three to four years; it will not gain. Premium supermarket and specialist retail in Australia, the UK and Asia, and a strong by-the-glass listing; competes with equivalently priced Bordeaux Blanc.

## Wine 3 — a) Identification (10 marks)

Chenin Blanc with Rhône white varieties, Swartland, South Africa. Warm medium-plus body, reading around 14%, mid-gold and viscous; quince, beeswax and a smoky reductive mineral note. ## Wine 3 — c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (7 marks)

## Wine 2

### a) Variety, country and region (8 marks)

## Wine 3

### a) Variety, country and region (8 marks)

Lemon-green, lighter-bodied, peach, apricot and citrus with only a trace of cut grass: Sauvignon Blanc, but with pyrazine suppressed. That excludes Marlborough, whose tropical-herbaceous intensity would dominate and which rarely carries lees weight of this kind, and the Loire, too cool for this stone-fruit ripeness and warmth. Ripe fruit plus umami lees depth and no oak points to Napa Valley, California — a producer deliberately working against the local norm of oaked, blended whites.

### b) Style and key winemaking decisions (9 marks)

Dry, medium-bodied, precise acidity; restraint is the story. Total absence of oak confirms stainless steel throughout. The umami richness indicates roughly seven months on fine lees with some stirring — unusual for New World Sauvignon and this wine's textural point of difference within the flight. ### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good, single-estate Napa white at $25–35. Fully dry with chalky schist minerality: Loire Valley, France. Outstanding, €30–45, in specialist on-trade and fine wine retail in France, the UK, Scandinavia and the USA where biodynamic Loire whites have a following. Sancerre was weighed and rejected: the subtle toast and creamy texture are inconsistent with the reductive unoaked Loire style, and the Sémillon component excludes it outright. Oak quality and length lift it above generic Bordeaux Blanc to the Graves/Pessac-Léognan tier.

**Wine 2** — Douro, Portugal; a field-style blend of indigenous whites (Rabigato, Códega, Arinto). Gold colour, medium-plus viscosity, flinty stone fruit with a piquant mineral finish. The almond paste and green-tea note match no mainstream international variety, and the retained juicy acidity rules out the low-acid whites of southern Iberia. Unlike Wine 1's citrus precision, this is schist-driven and savoury; the barrel influence and structure place it above Vinho Verde or Alentejo, in premium Douro Branco.

**Wine 3** — Swartland, South Africa. Chenin Blanc-dominant with Grenache Blanc and/or Clairette. Beeswax, lanolin and quince point to old-vine Chenin; orange blossom and dried citrus peel suggest a co-fermented Rhône-variety component. Loire Chenin was considered, but the light oxidative lift, chamomile and marshmallow texture do not belong to Vouvray or Savennières; dry-farmed old-vine Swartland with oxidative handling fits.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Fresh and precise but textured. Cool tank fermentation of the aromatic fraction preserved the grapefruit lift; the vanilla and brioche indicate barrique fermentation/maturation, perhaps 30–40% new given the restraint. The creamy roundness implies at least partial malolactic taming Sauvignon's acidity, and the saline length points to several months on lees.

**Wine 2** — Structured and restrained. Barrel fermentation with careful oxygen management gives the flinty, piquant finish; the almond-paste creaminess suggests older barrels or a small new-oak proportion rather than Wine 1's evident new wood. Full malolactic plus extended lees ageing explains the melting mid-palate while the varieties' natural acidity holds the line.

**Wine 3** — Textured and oxidatively inflected. Ambient-yeast fermentation with deliberate oxygen exposure at pressing, in older large-format wood or concrete, accounts for the nutty, waxy character; no new oak is detectable. Malolactic complete, giving the soft palate. Where Wines 1 and 2 protect fruit, this one trades primary purity for texture — the defining stylistic choice of the flight.

---

## c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding, at Cru Classé de Graves level, £45–65. Around three years old and delicious now, but the mineral spine suggests four to six years' further improvement, with primary citrus giving way to honeyed, toasty complexity, and a decade's holding. **Wine 2** — Very good, top of the Douro Branco hierarchy, £25–40. Young at three years; the firm mineral structure carries it four to five years further, then holds. Its market is the independent specialist and export on-trade — UK, Scandinavia, US — where Portuguese fine white is a growth category. Against white Rhône at the same price it is conspicuous value.

**Wine 3** — Good to very good, top of Swartland Chenin, £20–30. Drinking well now at three years and will hold four to six, but the oxidative handling means it will broaden rather than gain complexity. Its channel is the sommelier and natural-leaning independent trade in London, Copenhagen and New York, and its point of difference is precisely the textural, oxidative style set against the cleaner reductive Chenins of the Loire.

The saline, chalky finish and reductive stone-dominant mineral character place this in the Loire. The dry style with firm structure and restrained fruit narrows it to Saumur rather than Vouvray, which would show richer stone-fruit sweetness, or Savennières, which would show even greater phenolic grip.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Dry and reductive, with malolactic fermentation blocked, preserving Chenin's high natural acidity. Waxy, phenolic texture suggests whole-bunch pressing with extended skin contact at the press stage. Lees ageing contributes slight creamy mid-palate weight. Oak influence, if any, is old or large-format — no vanilla or toast is discernible.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, competing with mid-tier Savennières or Vouvray Sec. Retailing around €20–28 in export markets, the natural channel is independent specialists and fine-dining on-trade. The wine will improve over five to seven years as phenolic grip softens and tertiary honey and beeswax notes emerge.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Grape variety and origin (10 marks)

Welschriesling, Burgenland, Austria. Green apple, pear, chamomile, and wet-stone aromatics initially suggest Riesling, but the acidity here is broader rather than electric, and there is a waxy, herbal complexity — fennel and almond — inconsistent with true Riesling. Grüner Veltliner was considered: both share fresh herbal registers and Austrian origin, but Grüner's defining white-pepper spice is absent, and the saline-mineral finish points to a lakeside, reductive style. The quince, lemon-curd palate and long saline finish indicate a serious Burgenland bottling from the Neusiedlersee fringe rather than a lighter Steiermark example.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

A reductive, terroir-focused interpretation of a variety often dismissed as a workhorse grape. Protective cool fermentation in stainless steel accounts for the green-apple clarity. Lees ageing of perhaps six to nine months explains the textural complexity and almond character. Firm, linear acidity confirms no malolactic conversion. The saline minerality reflects calcareous and clay soils of the Neusiedlersee corridor.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality for the variety — clearly equivalent to a serious Erste Lage bottling. Retailing at approximately €25–40 in specialist outlets, it competes with premium Grüner Veltliner Smaragd on quality but faces a name-recognition ceiling internationally. For buyers who appreciate the chalky-saline tension of great Chablis, this wine punches well above its category price.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Grape variety and origin (10 marks)

Chardonnay, Carneros, California, USA. Ripe peach, white nectarine, and warm moderate-to-high perceived alcohol eliminate cool-climate Chardonnay immediately. Viognier was briefly considered given the stone-fruit intensity, but the absence of apricot-blossom perfume and glycerol weight rules it out. Within California, the measured rather than opulent style — ripe but not tropical fruit, present but restrained oak — points to Carneros rather than warmer Napa Valley floor sites. Carneros consistently shows ripe stone fruit with fresher acidity, a reflection of maritime cooling from San Pablo Bay.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Fermentation and ageing in French oak at approximately thirty to forty percent new for ten to twelve months is indicated by the toasty, lightly vanilla-inflected nose. Malolactic fermentation appears complete: the lactic, creamy texture and absence of sharp malic edges confirm full conversion. Lees ageing in barrel adds slight bready complexity. The result is a polished, modern-classic California Chardonnay that avoids the over-extraction and excessive new oak of earlier Napa styles.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, retailing at approximately USD 30–45, competing with Sonoma Coast or Russian River Valley Chardonnay at the same price. The style balances the richness sought domestically with the restraint increasingly demanded by export buyers. Premium supermarkets and fine-dining on-trade in the USA and UK are the most natural channels.

---

## Wine 4

### a) Grape variety and origin (10 marks)

Xarel·lo, Penedès, Spain. Toast, candied citrus, dried apricot, roasted nuts, and saline minerality on a dry, viscous palate initially suggest either an oxidatively aged white or a very concentrated style. White Rioja was eliminated because the fruit here is richer and more citrus-driven, without the dried-fruit and vanilla of barrel-aged Viura. Chenin Blanc with botrytis was briefly considered — the quince-paste register is present — but the palate is dry and the nut-and-saline axis is more characteristically Iberian. The saline minerality, concentrated candied-citrus core, and roasted-nut complexity all point to Xarel·lo from Penedès — a variety capable of extraordinary complexity when selected for concentration rather than Cava blending.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Deliberate barrel ageing in older wood with limited oxygen protection accounts for the roasted-nut complexity without full sherry-like oxidation. Very low yields are suggested by the high viscosity and concentration; dried-apricot character is consistent with some botrytis influence, but the dry finish and firm acid backbone confirm any affected fruit was integrated into an essentially dry wine.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality — among the most compelling expressions of a variety rarely seen outside its Cava blending role. Competing with serious white Rioja Gran Reserva in quality while remaining distinctive in style, it retails at approximately €35–60. US fine-wine specialists and UK independent merchants are the most receptive export markets. The wine will evolve beautifully over seven to ten years.

---

## Wine 5

### a) Grape variety and origin (10 marks)

Grüner Veltliner, Marlborough, New Zealand. White-pepper spice alongside green apple, lemon, and nectarine confirms Grüner Veltliner — white pepper is the variety's single most diagnostic marker, unreplicated by Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, or any other major white at this level of prominence. The question is origin. The palate here is lighter in extract and phenolic structure than a serious Austrian Grüner, and the finish is shorter than even a Federspiel of ambition. The clean-cut, relatively low-concentration fruit profile points to New World production. Marlborough, which has planted Grüner Veltliner in recent years, produces exactly this lighter, peppery, fruit-forward style at moderate perceived alcohol.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Clean, reductive, light-to-medium-bodied style points to stainless-steel fermentation, early bottling, and no oak. Malolactic fermentation appears blocked, maintaining fresh, zesty acidity. Minimal lees contact is suggested by the primary character without any creamy overlay. The wine's evident purpose is varietal freshness and early accessibility rather than structural complexity.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good quality — honest varietal expression at an accessible level, not a benchmark by Austrian Erste Lage standards. Retailing at approximately NZD 25–35 (around £15–20 in the UK), it suits premium supermarket shelves and wine-bar by-the-glass lists targeting consumers curious about varieties beyond Sauvignon Blanc. The novelty of Grüner Veltliner from Marlborough is itself a commercial asset in export markets. Drink within two to three years.

---

## Wine 6

### a) Grape variety and origin (10 marks)

Bukettraube, Cederberg, South Africa. Pronounced muscat-family aromatics — apricot blossom, lychee, floral muscat — with delicate residual sweetness immediately indicate a muscat-adjacent variety. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains was considered first, but the structure here is lighter and less unctuous than a classic Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise. Gewurztraminer was weighed — the floral and apricot register overlaps — but the characteristic rose-petal intensity of Gewurz is absent and the body is considerably lighter. Bukettraube, a South African muscat crossing rarely seen outside the Cape, precisely matches this profile: muscat aromatics at lower intensity, delicate off-dry palate, and a fresh-acid finish. Cederberg's altitude provides the cool nights that preserve the delicate florality.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Fermentation was arrested early to retain natural grape sugar. Cool stainless-steel fermentation protected the volatile muscat esters. No oak is evident. Crisp acidity provides structural balance against the sweetness, and early bottling maintains the light body and aromatic precision.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Acceptable to good quality — charming and honest, but the short-medium finish and light palate limit ambitions beyond entry-level aromatic white. Retailing at approximately ZAR 180–220 (around £8–12 in the UK), it suits by-the-glass programmes seeking an affordable aromatic alternative to Pinot Gris. Broader export penetration is constrained by near-total consumer unfamiliarity with the variety name. Drink within one to two years.

---

## a) Variety and origin (2 x 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Semillon, Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia.** Water-light body and markedly low warmth (around 11%) set against searing acidity, bone dry and entirely unoaked, is a combination almost no other variety delivers. Pronounced Meyer lemon and lemon curd over beeswax, toast and lamp oil indicate bottle development rather than wood. Aged Riesling was weighed — the lamp-oil note invites it — but the fruit is lemon curd, not lime, and the waxy breadth is Semillon's. Chardonnay is ruled out: no MLF, no oak, and it could not be picked this early.

**Wine 2 — Pinot Gris (Grauburgunder), Mosel, Germany.** Very low alcohol, around 8.5%, with high acidity and a clean dry finish points to a cool, northerly European origin. A Mosel Riesling Kabinett was my first call, but the fruit is ripe pear and quince rather than lime, there is no residual sugar, and a light almond-skin grip on the finish belongs to the Pinot family. Alsace is eliminated — more weight and warmth there. Slate-derived salinity with such low must weight narrows it to the Mosel.

## b) Style and the low alcohol (2 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Dry, taut, unoaked, austere on release and built for the cellar. The low alcohol is a picking decision: fruit taken at around 10.5–11 potential alcohol in early February ahead of subtropical rain, acidity still very high. Whole-bunch pressing, cool stainless ferment, no MLF — the malic line is intact — early bottling under screwcap, then years of reductive bottle age generating toast and honey without wood. The low alcohol is precisely what lets that acid line carry development rather than burn through it.

**Wine 2.** Light, dry, delicately fruity, drink-early. Here the low alcohol is climatic: marginal ripening on steep slate at modest must weight, harvested early with no enrichment, then fermented fully dry in stainless or neutral Fuder. Faint smoky reduction and textural grip suggest lees solids and brief skin contact rather than any wood.

## c) Quality, maturity, commercial position (2 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding — the reserve tier of its region, around AU$100 on delayed release. At eight or nine years it is only entering its plateau: improving 3–5 years, holding 10–15, gaining nutty, honeyed depth. Independent specialists and sommelier lists; a hand-sell, as low alcohol and no oak deter casual buyers, but cult status among UK and US collectors.

**Wine 2.** Very good, Gutswein/village level, around €18. Wholly primary and best now to three years — the acid will outlast the fruit rather than build complexity. Commercially the easier proposition: monopolies, premium supermarkets and by-the-glass, riding lower-alcohol demand against Alto Adige Pinot Grigio.

**Wine 2 — Grüner Veltliner; Kamptal, Austria.** Pale lemon-green, white pepper, lentil and pea-shoot, grapefruit pith and yellow apple; dry, high fresh acidity, medium-plus body, no oak, and a peppery dry extract that grips the finish at around 13%. **Wine 1.** Outstanding — top of the Anjou hierarchy, cru-level Savennières, £50–70. The telling decision is refusing the region's traditional sugar safety net: the acid line, not residual sugar, carries this level of ripeness. Independent specialists and fine dining; UK, US, Japan. **Wine 1 — Pinot Noir, Alsace, France.** Unusually for this flight, this is a red: clear medium ruby with no depth of extract, and a nose of fresh red cherry, raspberry and wild strawberry with a violet lift and a light forest-floor edge. Warmth is moderate at most — light-to-medium body, ~13% — with high, tart-cherry acidity, which points to a marginal northern European site. Burgundy village level was the obvious first call, but the fine mineral streak, the white-pepper spice and the leaner, more taut mid-palate without Burgundian flesh point further north-east, to a dry, rain-shadowed granitic origin: Alsace.

**Wine 2 — Pinot Gris, Willamette Valley, Oregon, USA.** Gold colour, quince, orange marmalade, lychee, almond and a fleshy, unctuous mouthfeel, yet bone dry with a medium(+) acid line and only moderate warmth (~13.5%). Alsace was weighed and rejected: an Alsace Pinot Gris of this ripeness would carry more residual sugar, more oiliness and higher alcohol. This freshness with New World fruit generosity, plus the deliberately golden hue, indicates a cool maritime West Coast origin — Willamette Valley, estate tier.

**Wine 3 — Friulano-led white, Collio DOC, Friuli, Italy.** Pale golden; dried thyme and tarragon over yellow apple, peach and white flowers, with a slight reductive struck note, orange zest, smoky minerality and a distinctly bitter-almond phenolic finish. **Wine 1.** A transparent, Burgundian-inflected style aiming at fruit purity, not power. Full destemming (no stalky green edge), a cool, gentle infusion-style maceration of a week or so, and maturation in older and larger French oak — the smoky oak note is barely visible, so little or no new wood, and no more than a year in barrel. Bottled with minimal fining to preserve lift.

**Wine 2.** Texture-driven and deliberately oxidative-leaning: the gold hue and phenolic flesh indicate several hours of skin contact before pressing. Fermentation cool in neutral vessel, malolactic evidently blocked to hold the acid line, then extended lees contact giving the almond and unctuous weight. No new oak.

**Wine 3.** Protectively handled — the struck-match reduction shows reductive, low-oxygen élevage — yet with a brief skin maceration for phenolic structure. Here is the tension worth resolving: gold colour and grip alongside undiminished acidity means the maker chased texture without oxidation, which is why this is bottled as one estate blend rather than three varietal cuvées. Lees ageing plus a fraction of large old wood.

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Very good quality, equivalent to a strong Burgundy Village; a benchmark for its appellation's red. Drinking now to six years. Around €30–35, Independent Specialists and sommelier lists, for drinkers of light, savoury Pinot.

**Wine 2.** Very good, estate tier — greater complexity and length than commercial Pinot Gris. Around US$28; US on-trade by-the-glass and specialist retail, a credible alternative to Alsace Pinot Gris at half the alcohol impact.

**Wine 3.** Very good, at the top of Collio DOC; €25–30. Sold through Italian fine-dining and export specialists in Germany, Austria and the USA; challenged by its unfamiliar variety and single-blend positioning.

Grüner Veltliner was considered but there is no white-pepper or lentil note, and the aromatic register is too citrus-and-honeyed. Mosel Riesling is ruled out by the alcohol and the absence of low-alcohol, sugar-balanced sweetness. The purity and the length narrow it to a top-quality Haut-Rhin site rather than generic AOC Alsace.

**b) Style and winemaking.** Intentionally a dry, texturally rich Riesling of clear ripeness — clean, reductive handling with no oak character and no diacetyl, so whole-cluster pressing, cool ferment in neutral vessel (old foudre or steel) and no malolactic. The honeycomb hints at a late, low-yield picking with a touch of noble rot in the blend; the fine textural weight indicates a slow indigenous ferment taken to near-dryness and several months on fine lees before bottling.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Outstanding quality, equivalent to Alsace Grand Cru or a top lieu-dit, retailing around £45–55. Sold through independent specialists and by the glass in serious restaurants; export markets in the US, Japan and Scandinavia. Competes with dry Rheingau Erstes Gewächs and Wachau Smaragd. Challenge: the residual-sugar confusion around Alsace still deters buyers who assume sweetness.

## Wine 2

**a) Chardonnay — Yarra Valley, Victoria, Australia.** White peach, grapefruit zest, Granny Smith, struck flint, brioche and cashew: barrel-fermented Chardonnay. Medium-plus acid, medium-plus body, moderate warmth (~13.5%). Meursault was seriously considered — the creamy lees and cedary oak fit — but the grapefruit-and-nectarine fruit is brighter and more citric than Burgundian hazelnut-and-orchard, and the saline finish reads New World cool-climate. Margaret River was the other option; that would show more melon and tropical breadth. The combination of struck-flint reduction, tight acid line and modest alcohol points to a cool Victorian site, and Yarra Valley over Adelaide Hills on the finer, less lime-driven fruit.

**b) Style and winemaking.** A restrained, Burgundian-modelled premium style. Whole-bunch pressed (no phenolic edge), fermented in barrel with indigenous yeast — the flint indicates deliberately reductive, low-sulphur handling and solids-inclusive ferment. Oak is fine-grained French, perhaps 25–30% new, in barriques for around 11 months; malolactic partial rather than full, since the crème brûlée note sits under a live acid line. Lees stirring modest, giving the sustained creamy mid-palate.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Very good to outstanding, an estate reserve tier at £30–35 — the second-order point is that the acid holds this level of ripeness and oak without the wine broadening, which is what separates it from the generic Australian Chardonnay category. Independents and premium on-trade; UK and Asian export.

## Wine 3

**a) Style first: a biologically aged fortified wine — Manzanilla, Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Andalucía, Spain, from Palomino.** Pale lemon-gold, low viscosity, spirit warmth around 15%, bone dry, with pronounced flor: sourdough, green olive brine, salted almond, chamomile and sea spray. Fino from Jerez was the alternative; the lighter, saltier, more delicate chamomile-and-iodine profile and the absence of any oxidative nuttiness point to Sanlúcar's cooler, humid cellars and thicker flor veil. No amontillado character, so the veil was unbroken.

**b) Winemaking.** Palomino pressed lightly, fully fermented dry, fortified to 15% — the minimum that still permits flor. Aged under veil in a criadera-solera of old butts, three-quarters full, roughly 4–5 years of average age, with regular sacas keeping the flor fed. Bottled with minimal filtration; freshness indicates recent release.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Very good quality at its category level, around £14–16 — not a VORS-level rarity but a fine, correct expression. Specialist retail, tapas and sherry-focused on-trade, by the glass. Challenge: the category's discount image and the need for fast rotation once opened.

## Wine 4

**a) Ribolla Gialla — Collio, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Italy.** Deep amber-gold with a slight haze, medium tannin and marked phenolic grip — a white made on skins. Dried apricot, orange peel, quince, beeswax, saffron, walnut skin; medium-plus acid and body, ~13%. Georgian Rkatsiteli qvevri wine was considered, and Slovenian Brda is essentially the same terroir; but the quince-and-beeswax core with saffron and that saline, resinous finish is the Ribolla signature, and Collio is the classic Italian home of this style.

**b) Winemaking.** Long skin maceration — several months, likely in buried amphora — with ambient ferment, no temperature control, no added sulphur and deliberate slight oxidative exposure. Aged in large old wood for years before an unfiltered, unfined bottling; the haze and tannin are intentional.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Outstanding within its niche, £70+; a benchmark rather than a commercial volume wine. Independent specialists and adventurous fine-dining lists; US, Japan, Scandinavia. Challenge: divisive texture and price limit the audience.

---

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 1 Question 2

## a) Identify the grape variety and country of origin (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough, New Zealand. Pronounced guava, pineapple and nectarine over grapefruit and lemon curd. Chenin Blanc was weighed and rejected: no wax, lanolin or quince, and the texture is too light. Viognier fits the apricot note but would be broader, oilier and lower in acid. Loire Sauvignon shows restrained gooseberry and smoke, not this guava exuberance; warmth in the mid-thirteens with searing acid confirms Marlborough.

**Wine 2** — Grüner Veltliner, Austria (Kamptal/Wagram). The diagnostic evidence is white pepper with crushed yarrow and a faint asparagus note over green apple and citrus on a linear, light-bodied palate. Riesling is the main alternative and shares the high-toned citrus drive, but offers lime, slate or petrol rather than peppery savouriness. Cooler perceived alcohol and the lithe frame point to continental Austria rather than Alsace.

**Wine 3** — Garganega, Soave Classico, Italy. Pale lemon, delicate white blossom, light citrus, and a bitter almond finish over chalky minerality. Pinot Grigio was considered for the light body and northern Italian frame but shows a copper-tinged phenolic edge and no almond/floral lift. Low alcohol and bright acid indicate volcanic hillside sites, not warmer flatland Soave DOC.

**Wine 4** — Chenin Blanc, South Africa. Deep gold; peach, nectarine, ginger, spiced citrus and honeyed almond over evident barrel texture, yet mouthwatering acid persists. Viognier would show lower acid and a broader, oilier finish. Toasted spice and almond, rather than the lanolin and wax of Loire Chenin, plus overt large-format oak and lees work on old-vine fruit, place it in the Cape.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Reductive and wholly primary. Pristine aromatics with no phenolic grip suggest whole-bunch pressing and cold settling; cool stainless-steel fermentation, malolactic blocked, minimal lees contact. Aromatic preservation is the sole objective.

**Wine 2** — Also unoaked steel, but the intent differs: here acid retention drives the picking decision, with early or selective harvest giving the low-thirteens alcohol. Short, unstirred lees contact leaves a clean rather than creamy texture, keeping the pepper and herb frame unblurred.

**Wine 3** — The most minimally handled wine of the four. Gentle whole-bunch pressing, cold settling, temperature-controlled tank fermentation, brief post-fermentation lees contact only. No oak, no MLF-derived breadth: the volcanic site, not the cellar, supplies the chalky texture.

**Wine 4** — The most interventionist. Seamless oak integration without sawdust or vanilla points to large-format (400L+) predominantly old French oak. The absence of diacetyl shows malolactic was blocked deliberately, retaining malic tension against the richness; a round mid-palate that stops short of flabby indicates lees stirring. Every decision is calibrated to build texture without softening acid.

---

## c) Quality and maturity (4 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; regional Marlborough tier, around £14–18. Aromatic intensity and a long, precise finish lift it above the entry level. One to two years old and at peak; will hold two to three more years but gains nothing, as primary fruit fades without replacement complexity. Drink now.

**Wine 2** — Good to very good; single-origin Ortswein level, £15–20. Vivid pepper typicity and clean persistence, but without the concentration of an Erste Lage. Drinking now at one to two years; holds three to four, complexity will not materially increase.

**Wine 3** — Good; Soave Classico DOC, £15–20. Honest hillside fruit with a defined mineral close, lacking the concentration of Superiore DOCG. Two to three years old, at early peak; may develop light nutty notes over two to three years, but drink within four of vintage.

**Wine 4** — Very good to outstanding, and the only cellar candidate here. Old-vine barrel-aged Cape Chenin, £30–45. Depth, seamless oak and the tension between richness and freshness put it well above regional average. At three to four years it is entering its window; expect five to seven years of improvement, gaining dried apricot, beeswax and savoury depth, then a five-year plateau.

---

## d) Relative commercial positions and principal export challenges (12 marks)

Wine 1 is the easiest sell — Marlborough Sauvignon moves through premium multiples, independents and by-the-glass lists in the UK, US and Asia — but sits in a saturated category where its relative restraint risks being outshouted by cheaper, more pungent examples; single-estate framing is essential.

Wine 2 has the steepest identity problem: Grüner remains unknown outside Austria and specialist circles, so it depends on sommelier advocacy and monopoly listings (Scandinavia, US East Coast) rather than shelf recognition. The challenge is consumer education, not quality.

Wine 3 must defend Classico credentials against the commodity reputation of generic Soave. Strong in Italian restaurants and specialist off-trade in Germany, the UK and US, its challenge is premiumisation: making the Classico designation and volcanic origin visible enough to justify the trade-up.

Wine 4 has the greatest long-term potential and the hardest immediate task. At £30–45 it competes with white Burgundy and Loire Chenin in specialist on-trade, undercutting both — which risks underselling the quality. Core markets are the UK and Belgium; the work is building collector and restaurant-list credibility for a category whose prestige narrative is still forming.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A hybrid of reductive and traditional handling. The majority fermented in steel, preserving citrus-floral lift; a portion in foudres or large older barrels with indigenous yeasts, showing as savoury textural weight rather than oak flavour — the barrel is being used for lees contact and micro-oxygenation, not aromatics. ## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good quality, around €20–28. It plays in the premium Loire Sauvignon bracket alongside upper-tier Sancerre but undercuts it — the commercial argument is value to a Sancerre drinker who knows the style. Northern Italian Chardonnay rather than Burgundy: the almond-savoury register and drier, more angular finish, without Côte de Beaune's citrus-and-lees polish. The Langhe DOC rather than the regional Piemonte designation signals site ambition.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Restrained Old World Chardonnay, fermented and briefly aged in older French or Slavonian wood rather than new barriques — integrated nuttiness with no vanilla or toast. Malolactic fermentation is probable given the rounded mid-palate, though the acid frame stays firm, suggesting partial suppression. Extended lees contact accounts for the creamy weight.

Very good quality, around €25–35. Premium on-trade is the natural home: fine dining in Milan and Turin, plus Germany, Japan and the US, where the region's red-wine reputation pulls consumers into white-wine curiosity purchases. Gewürztraminer, Bío-Bío Valley, Chile. Rose petal, lychee and honey with a smoky edge is diagnostic. The cool southerly Chilean valleys — Bío-Bío or Malleco — give exactly this combination of aromatic intensity and acidity, and it is lighter than warmer Maule fruit.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Fruit-forward and aromatic, for early drinking. Cool stainless-steel fermentation preserved the primary rose and lychee; no oak. Fermented dry, deliberately rejecting the off-dry Alsatian model, and the clean rather than textured finish indicates minimal lees work.

Good to very good, a Reserva-tier varietal white at USD 15–22. The obstacle is double: the variety is globally niche and Bío-Bío has none of Casablanca's or Maipo's recognition, so brand and Reserva designation must carry the price.

No oak influence and a lean palate confirm Village level rather than a richer Côte de Beaune Chardonnay.

**Wine 3 — Furmint, Tokaj, Hungary.** Lemon-gold, with apple, apricot, grape blossom and a stony-smoky mineral note that distinguishes it from every other wine in the flight. The palate is dry with crisp acidity and phenolic grip. Riesling was the first alternative — the smoky minerality and acidity fit — but the broader body, higher perceived alcohol and phenolic texture rule out German Riesling. Grüner Veltliner was eliminated by the absence of white pepper. The structured phenolic presence and stony terroir character point decisively to dry Furmint, Tokaj.

**Wine 4 — Riesling, Clare Valley, South Australia.** Lime, lavender, talc and a chalky mineral finish with moderate perceived alcohol and racy acidity are classic Riesling pointers. No RS-driven softness rules out Mosel; the absence of the broad, oily weight of Alsace Grand Cru rules that out too. The lime-juice focus, floral lift and bone-dry finish are characteristic of Clare Valley's diurnal-range-driven style.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1.** Fruit-forward and reductive. No oak, butter or lees-derived creaminess indicates stainless-steel fermentation and early bottling. No malolactic fermentation — acidity is crisp and linear, preserving thiol and pyrazine freshness.

**Wine 2.** Clean, unoaked, terroir-led. Cool stainless-steel fermentation preserves green apple and citrus purity; no toast or vanilla confirms no new oak. A subtle mid-palate roundness suggests brief lees contact, but no MLF — the acidity remains unmistakably malic and high-toned.

**Wine 3.** Textured and phenolically expressive. Broader body and slightly oily mid-palate suggest skin contact during pressing or a short maceration, consistent with Furmint's thick skins. Fermented to complete dryness; stony, reductive nose points to lees contact in a neutral vessel rather than new oak.

**Wine 4.** Reductive and tank-fermented. Pristine lime and talc without oxidative or yeast-derived notes indicate cold-settled juice in stainless steel. No MLF — acidity is vibrant and malic. Bottled early to preserve primary varietal character.

---

## c) Quality, maturity and drinking window (4 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1.** Good-to-very-good; above commodity level but without single-vineyard complexity. Very young, with fully primary tropical fruit showing no development. Drink now to 2–3 years; primary fruit will fade rather than evolve.

**Wine 2.** Very good, consistent with Village Chablis from a reliable producer. Balance of acidity, minerality and restrained fruit is admirable, though the palate lacks 1er Cru depth. Drink now to 4–5 years; no case for extended ageing.

**Wine 3.** Outstanding — the standout wine of the flight. Length, phenolic structure and smoky mineral depth signal capacity to develop waxy, complex bottle character even without botrytis involvement, a structural architecture that was uncommon in dry Tokaj a decade ago. Currently slightly closed. Drink from 2026; improve for 5–8 years, hold a further 5.

**Wine 4.** Very good; purity and chalky length are well above entry level. Very young with intensely primary lime. Drink from 2026–2027; will improve substantially over 5–8 years, developing petrol, toast and lanolin. Peak 2030–2033, holding to 2035+.

---

## d) Commercial positioning — all four wines (12 marks)

Wine 1 sits in the premium off-trade — independent merchants, premium supermarkets, online retail — targeting consumers seeking reliable fruit-forward dry white for everyday drinking. Key export markets are the UK, US and Australia; it competes at the entry tier below Cloudy Bay on a crowded shelf.

Wine 2 occupies the specialist-merchant and premium-restaurant channel at £15–20, a by-the-glass brasserie staple across Europe, the UK, Japan and the US. Its challenge is differentiation from négociant own-label Chablis at the same price.

Wine 3 is the most commercially interesting: dry Furmint occupies an underexploited sommelier-discovery niche at €25–40, competing with Grüner Veltliner GG and serious Alsace Riesling on fine-dining lists. Export to the UK, US and Scandinavian monopolies is growing. Consumer unfamiliarity with the dry style is the barrier; its quality-to-price ratio versus equivalent-quality Burgundy is the opportunity.

Wine 4 targets the specialist off-trade and fine-dining on-trade in Australia, the UK and the US at A$30–40, competing with Eden Valley Riesling and mid-tier Mosel GG. Ageability is its key commercial argument to collectors, while primary lime fruit makes it accessible on release.

---

Chenin Blanc, Loire Valley, France — Savennières. Wax, lanolin and quince with pronounced phenolic grip and racy acidity are decisive. ### b) Style and key winemaking decisions (8 marks)

A serious, age-worthy dry white made with minimal intervention. Phenolic texture and faint oxidative lift suggest fermentation in used barrels or demi-muids rather than steel — micro-oxygenation without new oak. No buttery overlay: malolactic was blocked or partial, preserving the taut acid line. Around 9–12 months on lees gives textural breadth without overt autolytic character.

### c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, top-tier Savennières level, €30–45. At perhaps 2–3 years old, primary quince and flint still dominate; it needs 5–8 years to build honeyed tertiary complexity and integrate the phenolics, then holds a decade. ### a) Variety, country and region (10 marks)

Grüner Veltliner, Austria, Wachau. White pepper, lentil and citrus pith over taut acidity and firm extract are unmistakable. ### b) Style and key winemaking decisions (8 marks)

Late-harvested at maximum permitted ripeness under Vinea Wachau rules. Unlike Wine 1, the aromatics are reductive and precise, indicating stainless steel or large neutral oak rather than barrel fermentation. Some 6–9 months on lees give creaminess beneath the pepper; no new oak is detectable, the wine resting entirely on fruit and mineral extract.

### c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (7 marks)

Very high quality at Smaragd level, €40–60. Youthful at around 2 years, primary pepper and citrus pith dominant; the window opens in 3–5 years as roasted hazelnut, honey and truffle emerge, holding 8–10 years thereafter. Sold through Austrian specialists and premium on-trade, with export to Germany, the USA and the UK, where Smaragd attracts growing collector interest.

Chenin Blanc, South Africa — most plausibly Swartland. Ripe peach and apricot over underlying wax give the variety; the warmer, more generous mid-palate and softer acid, with alcohol around 13% reading as ripeness rather than restraint, separate it from Wine 1's flinty, malic austerity. Carricante (or a Carricante-dominant blend), Etna Bianco, Sicily. Unwooded and minimally interventionist. Harvested at very low sugar levels, cold-settled, fermented in stainless steel, and bottled early. No oak, no MLF, no lees enrichment. ### a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough, New Zealand. Passionfruit, grapefruit, elderflower and lemongrass eliminate Chardonnay and Grüner Veltliner outright. The Loire is the real alternative: Sancerre would be smokier, tighter and lower in perceived alcohol, whereas here yellow peach and rock melon sit over a juicy, medium-plus body with warm alcohol — a warmer New World site. Ripe, dry, medium-plus body with racy acidity retained by cool fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel. Chalky mid-palate texture indicates extended lees contact; a fennel-like herbal note and dry textural finish suggest a small fraction in older neutral oak, adding complexity without wood flavour. Grüner Veltliner, Kamptal, Austria. Lemon balm, hay and apple: not pyrazine-driven, not petrol-accented, not tropical. The decisive marker is white pepper and spice on the palate. Pinot Gris matches the weight but cannot supply that spice or this lemon-herb freshness. Moderate alcohol, focused acidity and a supple rather than deeply extracted structure indicate village/Ortswein level; an Erste Lage would show greater concentration and a longer, saline finish.

### b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Dry, medium-light, fresh and spicy. Clean primary fruit with no oak or oxidative handling: cool stainless-steel fermentation. Supple mid-palate without creaminess points to brief lees contact, and the racy acidity to no MLF — an early-drinking build, unlike Wine 4's textural ambition.

Viognier offers the peach and florals but not this acid drive or grip. Richness plus persistent, racy acidity is the Assyrtiko signature.

### b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Full-bodied and dry from a ripe harvest; the high natural alcohol is typical of old ungrafted vines. Vanilla and nut indicate a modest proportion (roughly 15–20%) of new French barriques, contributing flavour without masking minerality; lees-derived weight suggests bâtonnage. Chenin Blanc from the Loire could offer comparable acidity but lacks this saline, almost volcanic character. The warmth of the mid-palate alongside that taut, linear acidity is consistent with volcanic island viticulture rather than a cool continental origin.

**Conclusion:** Assyrtiko, Santorini, Greece.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A dry, unoaked white handled reductively throughout. The struck-match-adjacent flinty quality is consistent with reductive fermentation in stainless steel at cool temperatures. The broad, almost creamy palate weight alongside searing acidity points to brief post-fermentation lees contact, adding texture without obscuring minerality. The concentration likely reflects ancient basket-trained Kouloura vines rather than any extraction technique.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good to outstanding — a benchmark single-estate Santorini PDO, retailing at approximately £25–40. The competitive set is premium unoaked whites globally — high-end Chablis 1er Cru, Pouilly-Fumé — and it holds its own on quality. Strong demand in the UK, US and Scandinavian markets from wine-savvy consumers seeking alternatives to Burgundy.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

The restrained white-fruit and citrus nose with a slate-like minerality, slight phenolic bitterness and lack of aromatic exuberance points to a cool-climate European white. Chardonnay was dismissed — the mineral-slate character and finish bitterness are untypical. The white-fruit austerity, crisp linear acidity and neutral aromatic profile, with oak-derived spice present but not dominant, point to Viura (Macabeo) as a modern barrel-aged Rioja Blanco Crianza. The moderate perceived warmth is consistent with Rioja's continental climate without the full ripeness of a warm-vintage southern expression.

**Conclusion:** Viura (Macabeo), Rioja, Spain — Blanco Crianza.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A dry, medium-bodied white with modest oak influence. Faint vanilla and spice without domination suggest ageing in a mix of new and used French oak for the Crianza minimum, rather than the prolonged oxidative approach of traditional white Rioja Gran Reserva. The absence of nutty, oxidative or amber characters confirms a modern reductive approach; MLF appears partially managed to retain freshness.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good quality, accurately positioned at Crianza level. Retailing at approximately £15–20, it competes with premium Mâconnais Chardonnay and Galician Albariño on the independent merchant shelf and restaurant list. Primary markets are Spain domestically and the UK, where modern white Rioja continues to grow in profile.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

The gold-tinged colour and complex aromatics — white peach, nectarine, grapefruit zest, brioche autolytic notes and a flinty struck-match reduction — immediately suggest serious Chardonnay. Pinot Gris was dismissed: it would not show this taut citrus spine or reductive lift. The diagnostic signal is the tension on the palate: peach concentration held by almost electric acidity. This is not Burgundy, where acidity tends toward tartaric firmness, nor California, which would show broader, fleshier fruit and less mineral definition. The saline, stony mineral quality and citrus-pith austerity, combined with the ripe-yet-tense structural profile, points to high-altitude New Zealand viticulture — most plausibly Central Otago, whose schist soils and wide diurnal range account precisely for this balance.

**Conclusion:** Chardonnay, Central Otago, New Zealand.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A dry, medium-full-bodied, barrel-fermented Chardonnay of considerable craft. Reductive handling and fermentation in a mix of new and used French oak barriques — perhaps 20–30% new — explains the restrained but real oak spice. Brioche and hazelnut notes indicate extended lees ageing, likely ten to twelve months with bâtonnage. MLF appears complete, softening acidity without losing saline freshness. Phenolic cleanliness implies whole-cluster pressing with no coarse extraction.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality — equivalent in ambition to a top Burgundy 1er Cru, retailing at approximately NZ$80–120 (£40–60). Site-specific saline minerality and structural tension place it well above regional appellation standard. Its market is serious Burgundy lovers exploring the Southern Hemisphere — UK specialist importers, premium restaurant lists and cellar-door direct sales. Currently approachable but with concentration and acidity to develop over five to eight years, evolving from primary stone fruit and reduction toward toasted nuts, dried citrus and integrated mineral depth.

modelAnswer:
## 1. Model Answer

#### Section A · For the flight as a whole

**d) Commercial positioning (6 marks)**

These three wines occupy distinct positions within the premium-but-accessible tier. Wine 1 is the most commercial: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc from a reserve sub-range, retailing around £14–18, sold through premium supermarkets and independents globally. Its competitive set is Sancerre at twice the price and commodity Marlborough at half. UK, US, and Scandinavian export markets absorb most of Marlborough's premium volume, making this a strong by-the-glass candidate in casual fine dining. Wine 2 targets a narrower audience, retailing around £18–24 through independent merchants and restaurant lists that know the Marche. Verdicchio competes with Greco di Tufo and Fiano for Italy-curious consumers; the variety name limits supermarket viability but creates a point of difference on curated lists. Wine 3 sits highest, retailing £25–35 through specialist importers, competing with Alsace Grand Cru for consumers seeking structured, cellarable European whites outside Burgundy. Wine 1 has the brand-recognition advantage; Wine 3 has the ageability argument.

---

#### Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1**

**a)** Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough, New Zealand. Passionfruit, pink grapefruit, blackcurrant leaf, and tomato vine rule out Chardonnay and Riesling immediately; the absence of wax and quince eliminates Chenin Blanc. Elevated tropical intensity and medium-plus body with salty mineral finish place this in Marlborough rather than Loire — Sancerre would show greater restraint and higher acidity with less tropical exuberance. The silky-creamy texture without oak suggests reserve-tier handling typical of the Wairau Valley.

**b)** Highly typical of premium Marlborough: vivid tropical aromatics, clean reductive winemaking, and a long saline finish. The sweet-fruited finish nuance is a hallmark of ripe Wairau fruit; the absence of oak is characteristic of the region's leading producers at this level.

**c)** Outstanding for the Marlborough Reserve tier. The 2024 vintage freshness means primary fruit is at its peak. It will hold through 2026–27 but gains little from cellaring; drink within 18 months for maximum aromatic expression.

---

**Wine 2**

**a)** Verdicchio, Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore, Marche, Italy. Pear, quince, beeswax, and blanched almond are Verdicchio's clearest fingerprints. Pinot Grigio was eliminated — it lacks this textural weight and bitter-almond finish. Fiano was plausible given the waxy character, but the tarragon and tangerine pith point away from Campania toward the Marche. Golden colour, medium-plus viscosity, and a honey note suggest two to three years' age with lees influence, consistent with Superiore production.

**b)** Highly typical of Classico Superiore Verdicchio: oily texture, pronounced bitter-almond nuttiness, and the herb-inflected nose reflect the variety's signature. The waxy, near-lanolin texture is a marker of extended lees contact characteristic of serious Castelli di Jesi producers.

**c)** Very good quality, Classico Superiore level, around £20. Bright acidity under the weight gives genuine cellaring potential. Drinking well now; will improve through 2026–28 as nutty complexity integrates, then hold through 2030.

---

**Wine 3**

**a)** Grüner Veltliner, Kamptal, Austria, Erste Lage. White pepper, lentil, and citrus-mineral profile with firm acidity and a saline, stony finish are definitive markers of Grüner Veltliner — white pepper alone rules out Chardonnay, Riesling, and Chenin Blanc. Wachau shares the spice-and-mineral character, but the Erste Lage structure and citrus-herb balance point to Kamptal's granite and gneiss soils, which confer a flinty tension absent from loess-dominated plots.

**b)** A textbook Kamptal Erste Lage expression. The tension between richness and precision is not a stylistic compromise but a site signature: the elevation ensures warmth accumulates slowly enough to preserve acid architecture, producing a wine that reads simultaneously ripe and taut in a way that loess-grown Grüner cannot replicate.

**c)** Outstanding quality, Erste Lage level, around £30–35. Firm acidity and mineral grip mean this will improve meaningfully over four to five years, peaking 2027–2029, then holding through 2032 before primary fruit yields to white truffle and preserved lemon.

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Pinot Gris, Alsace, France — Grand Cru level. Medium-deep gold with a hint of copper signals phenolic ripeness or partial skin contact. Ripe pear, dried apricot, candied ginger and a waxy lanolin quality distinguish this from Gewurztraminer — the closest alternative — which would show lychee and rose petal; the greater palate breadth and weight rule it out. Broad, almost viscous texture, warm generous body suggesting around 14%, and a long honeyed finish place this firmly in Alsace rather than Alto Adige (leaner, citrus-driven) or Oregon (lower alcohol, more linear). Concentration and length indicate Grand Cru selection.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Rich, dry to off-dry, with ripeness at or near Vendanges Tardives threshold. Colour depth and waxy texture suggest extended must settling; the seamless, integrated palate with no oak toast points to fermentation in large old foudres. Full or near-full malolactic conversion accounts for the round acid structure; extended lees ageing of at least twelve months explains the creamy mid-palate weight.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality, retailing around £45–60. Positioned in premium on-trade and specialist independents. Key export markets — UK, Germany, US — reward Alsace white among serious collectors. Low consumer awareness relative to Burgundy is the commercial challenge; growing appetite for complex, age-worthy dry whites is the opportunity.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Grüner Veltliner, New Zealand — North Canterbury or Wairarapa. White pepper on both nose and palate is the single most discriminating marker, ruling out Riesling (lime and slate, no pepper), Sauvignon Blanc (pyrazine-led) and Chardonnay (no pepper signature). Riesling from a cool New World site was considered given the lime zest and saline finish, but the white pepper, fennel and herbal character alongside an estimated 12.5% alcohol — lighter than classic Austrian GVL — and stony salinity shift origin to the Southern Hemisphere. Low-intervention character and cooler-climate weight narrow it further to New Zealand rather than Australia, where small biodynamic estates have trialled this variety.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Reductive, mineral and precise. No oak signature points to neutral vessel — stainless steel or old clay. Slight textural presence and phenolic zip suggest unfined and unfiltered handling. Malic acidity confirms no MLF. Controlled harvest at physiological rather than sugar ripeness, prioritising aromatic intensity over alcohol — the opposite of classic Austrian Grüner.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good quality, comparable in typicity to a Federspiel or lower-end Erste Lage; retailing around NZ$45–55 (£22–28). Consumer unfamiliarity limits shelf velocity, but specialist retailers, sommeliers and natural wine lists in the UK, Australia and major US cities will position it as a genuine conversation piece for adventurous drinkers.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Assyrtiko, Santorini, Greece. Searing acidity — the most pronounced in the flight — alongside medium-plus body, warmth suggesting around 13.5%, and a volcanic, chalky mineral finish point here before anywhere else. Vermentino lacks this acid precision; Albariño shares the saline quality but shows softer acidity and lower alcohol. The absence of aromatic flamboyance confirms Santorini over mainland Greece. Purity and length suggest Estate level.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Reductive and precise. Clean lemon, lime and mineral profile with no oxidative note indicates early harvest, temperature-controlled fermentation in stainless steel and careful SO₂ management. Early racking and young bottling preserve volcanic freshness; no lees-derived breadth is detectable. No MLF: malic acidity keeps the palate bright and linear. An unoaked, terroir-first expression relying on bush-vine kouloura viticulture and pumice soils for structure.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good to outstanding, Estate level, retailing around £25–35. Strong in the UK, Scandinavia and US on-trade, particularly seafood-oriented restaurants. Limited production constrains volume; the wine's unique volcanic salinity and electric acidity have no real substitute, which sustains premium pricing where consumer education is in place.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Riesling, Kamptal or Kremstal, Austria — likely a single-vineyard site. Lime, green apple, slate, white blossom and a hint of stone fruit confirm Riesling over Grüner Veltliner (already Wine 2), which would show white pepper and no floral lift. The structural contrast with Wine 2 is telling: greater extract, firmer acid backbone and warm body around 13% point to a dry, powerful Austrian expression rather than Mosel (lower alcohol, higher RS) or Alsace (broader, less taut). The combination of power and crystalline mineral precision is most consistent with a volcanic Kamptal Erste or Grosse Lage site such as Heiligenstein.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Bone dry, with no perceptible residual sweetness despite apparent fruit richness — a hallmark of great Austrian Riesling where phenolic maturity and racy acidity create an illusion of weight. Slight palate breadth beyond stainless steel but no new-oak imprint suggests large old wood or neutral vessel. Lees ageing of nine to twelve months provides creamy mid-palate integration. No MLF: tartaric sharpness and definition are fully intact. Harvest timing was judicious — stone-fruit richness balanced against searing acidity implies picking at the outer edge of physiological ripeness.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality, Grosse Lage equivalent, retailing around €35–50. Targets specialist retailers, fine-dining on-trade and auction in Germany, the UK, the US and Japan. Austrian Riesling still lives in the shadow of German and Alsatian equivalents for many consumers, but it delivers greater power and single-site precision than most Mosel expressions at the same price — a case educated sommeliers make readily.

---

**Sources consulted** — tier-1 references behind the production and appellation points above.

- [AWRI — Volatile Acidity](https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/s1982.pdf)

Gutedel (Chasselas), Markgräflerland, Baden, Germany. ## Wine 3 — a) Grape variety and origin (10 marks)

Viognier, Eden Valley, South Australia. Deep gold, high viscosity and pronounced apricot, orange blossom, ginger and marzipan with a lanolin texture: no other mainstream variety combines this perfume with that weight. Condrieu was the serious alternative, sharing the apricot-blossom signature, but the warm, round finish and candied citrus peel argue for a warmer origin. ## Section A · For the flight as a whole

**d) Commercial positions and target markets (12 marks)**

These three wines occupy distinct commercial niches. Wine 1, a Burgundy 1er Cru Chardonnay, sits in specialist on-trade and fine wine merchant channels, retailing around £40–55 in the UK. It targets the serious Burgundy collector and restaurant list buyer, competing with neighbouring 1er Cru Puligny or entry-level Meursault. Japan, the USA, and Scandinavia are active export markets. The principal challenge is price inflation, which pushes buyers toward top Mâconnais or premium New World Chardonnay.

Wine 2, a mature Hunter Valley Semillon at £25–35, builds its proposition on secondary development rather than fruit freshness, selling through specialist merchants and auction to experienced enthusiasts in Australia, the UK, and the US. The commercial challenge is that Hunter Valley Semillon remains poorly understood outside Australia — a communication problem, not a quality one — making it hard to command premium pricing relative to its complexity.

Wine 3, an off-dry Mosel Riesling Spätlese at £20–30, fits specialist merchants and food-focused by-the-glass programmes. The residual sugar remains the key barrier: consumers unfamiliar with the Prädikat system dismiss it as simply sweet. The wellness trend toward lower-alcohol drinking is a genuine opportunity, particularly in the UK and US.

---

## Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1**

*a) Style and method of production (9 marks)*

Dry, full-bodied, with citrus freshness, stony minerality, and nutty overtones. Fermentation in French oak barriques — likely 30–40% new — with 12–15 months on lees explains the toasty, almond complexity; the absence of vanilla confirms well-seasoned French rather than American oak. Full malolactic fermentation has softened naturally high acidity to a taut but round finish.

*b) Variety and origin (7 marks)*

Chardonnay is clear from the citrus and stone fruit core, subtle oak integration, and chalk-mineral thread. The firm, linear acidity rules out richer California or Mâconnais registers. Meursault was considered but lacks this wine's tightly wound structure and floral lift; those qualities are more consistent with Puligny-Montrachet. Length and complexity place this above village level: Puligny-Montrachet 1er Cru, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy.

*c) Maturity and drinking window (5 marks)*

Approximately 2–3 years old. Drinking well now, but firm acid architecture supports 4–6 further years of development — dried citrus, hazelnut, lanolin — then holding 10–12 years from harvest before risking oxidative flattening.

---

**Wine 2**

*a) Style and method of production (9 marks)*

Dry, medium-bodied, deeply developed — toasted brioche, beeswax, lemon curd, emerging petrol — yet with no evidence of oak. The waxy texture and intact linear acidity are entirely the product of extended bottle age on a wine fermented in stainless steel with no malolactic conversion. Time, not oak, has built all the complexity. Low perceived alcohol confirms deliberately early harvesting.

*b) Variety and origin (7 marks)*

Semillon. Beeswax, lanolin, and lemon curd with developing petrol, zero pyrazine (ruling out Sauvignon Blanc), and lean low-alcohol structure (ruling out oaked Bordeaux Semillon blends) point specifically to Hunter Valley. No other region produces dry Semillon with this secondary development and waxy transparency at this alcohol level. Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia.

*c) Maturity and drinking window (5 marks)*

Deep gold and pronounced secondary character indicate 7–8 years from harvest, at or near peak. Will hold a further 5–8 years, gaining tertiary depth, before fruit fades.

---

**Wine 3**

*a) Style and method of production (9 marks)*

Off-dry, light-bodied, crystalline — citrus, mandarin zest, honeysuckle, wet slate — with very low perceived alcohol and no warmth on the finish. Temperature-controlled stainless-steel fermentation halted before dryness preserved the natural residual sugar. No oak; no malolactic conversion: high, bright acidity remains fully malic, balancing the RS.

*b) Variety and origin (7 marks)*

Riesling: electric acidity, transparent fruit, and defining slate minerality preclude Chenin Blanc (broader, more phenolic) and Pinot Gris (less acid-defined). Very low alcohol and genuine RS narrow the call to Germany over Alsace (drier, higher alcohol) and Clare Valley (bone dry, lime-cordial character). Mandarin and crystalline finesse with wet-slate depth are consistent with Mosel Spätlese: Mosel, Germany.

*c) Maturity and drinking window (5 marks)*

Lemon-green colour and vibrant primary character suggest 2–3 years old, still in its youth. RS and taut acid indicate improvement over the next 5–8 years, developing petrol, lime marmalade, and beeswax, then holding a further 10–15 years before sweetness dominates.

**Wine 1:** picked early at low sugar to preserve acid, gently pressed, cool-fermented in stainless steel, no malolactic — the tartaric bite survives intact — no oak at any point, minimal lees, filtered and bottled young under screwcap. Complexity without a day in wood, bought by deliberately forgoing ripeness.

Chardonnay was the leading alternative — the taut, chalky austerity genuinely recalls Chablis — but Chardonnay would give broader citrus and a rounder mid-palate, not this pear/quince, white-flower and anise lift over a faintly waxy texture. Sauvignon is ruled out by the complete absence of pyrazine or thiol. Chenin's malic tension plus tuffeau-chalk minerality narrows to Anjou-Saumur; the fully dry finish argues Saumur rather than Vouvray.
