Fino was considered and eliminated: no spirit heat, no fortification. Oxidative white Rioja is ruled out by the lack of vanillin and by acidity this high and saline. Under the skin: six-plus years under voile has not flattened the wine — lemon curd and firm acid still run beneath the nuttiness, which points to Savagnin on Triassic marl at the top of the Jura hierarchy, not a *vin jaune*-styled Côtes du Jura.

## b) Style and key decisions (2 x 10 marks)

**Wine 1** is a protectively made, reductively handled dry white: whole-bunch pressing (no phenolic grip), cool fermentation, and no perceptible new oak — vanilla and toast are absent, so any wood is old and large. Malolactic has clearly been blocked, preserving the malic drive; the faint creaminess suggests lees ageing without stirring.

**Wine 2** is the opposite intention throughout. Late picking gives high natural sugar; after fermentation to dryness the barrels were deliberately left un-topped, allowing a film yeast to develop and the wine to age unracked in old 228-litre wood for several years. Evaporation without replenishment explains both the concentration and the sotolon.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 x 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — very good; top-of-appellation Saumur, around €22, competing with 1er Cru Chablis. Independent specialists and sommelier by-the-glass lists; the drinker who wants dry, unoaked wines with tension.

**Wine 2** — outstanding, Jura's flagship appellation, €70+, allocated. Fine dining and serious export specialists in the US, Japan and UK; the challenge is that this oxidative style polarises.

## Wine 1 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Savoury brioche depth and a creamy mid-palate over a lean frame indicate extended ageing on fine lees, well beyond the appellation minimum — plausibly Cru Communal duration. Fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel preserved the citrus and saline cut. MLF was blocked; that suppression is as deliberate a choice as its full deployment in Wine 2.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Maturity (5 marks)

Very good; Cru Communal level, around €18–22. Two to three years old, primary fruit still dominant. Drink now; will build waxy, savoury complexity over 4–5 years, plateau three more, then lose its saline drive.

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (9 marks)

Chardonnay, Margaret River. Deep gold, viscous, warm and fuller-bodied than Wine 1. White peach, lemon confit and honeysuckle over spicy French oak say Chardonnay; Viognier was considered for the peach-skin florals but would show lower acidity and no such acid backbone. Napa was rejected — the oak is too refined and the fruit too saline and restrained. Beeswax, lanolin and salted-nut complexity within a cushioned but defined palate point to Margaret River.

## Wine 2 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Barrel fermentation in French oak, perhaps 40–50% new given spice presence without dominance. Beeswax and lanolin indicate full MLF in barrel, softening acidity while keeping fruit definition. Pastry depth and silky mouthfeel suggest 10–12 months on fine lees with stirring; the absence of green phenolics implies whole-bunch pressing. Burgundian method applied to riper fruit.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Maturity (5 marks)

Outstanding, Premier Cru equivalent, AU$80–100. Two to three years old and not yet at peak: the oak needs 2–3 years to marry with the fruit, then holds 5–6 years before peach gives way to hazelnut, dried apricot and buttered toast.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (9 marks)

Riesling, Mittelmosel. Very low alcohol, electric acidity, lime and slate with incipient petrol fix the variety at once. Palpable residual sugar in tension with that acid excludes Alsace and Clare Valley, both dry at this tier, while the aromatic lift and filigreed weight argue against the Rheingau's firmer austerity. The sugar-to-acid ratio and low alcohol indicate Kabinett rather than Spätlese, which would show more extract.

## Wine 3 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Reductive purity and total absence of oak point to stainless steel or neutral vessels. Fermentation was arrested by chilling and sterile filtration, leaving roughly 20–30 g/L sugar. MLF avoided, protecting the racy malic frame. No lees influence: bottled early for primary aromatics, with conservative SO₂. Harvest at modest Kabinett must weights made partial fermentation possible without confecting the wine.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Maturity (5 marks)

Very good, Kabinett, €18–25. One to two years old with aromatics intact. Drinkable now, but the acid–sugar balance will carry it 8–10 years into petrol, dried lime and honey, then hold a further decade before the acid frame softens.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (9 marks)

Viura, Rioja Blanco Reserva. Deep gold with amber rim, medium-plus body, warmth. Peach, dried apricot, vanilla, toast and emerging walnut mark deliberate oxidative maturation — the opposite of the reductive handling in Wines 1 and 3. White Burgundy was weighed but would show crisper acidity, lees-creaminess rather than waxy walnut weight, and less oxidative development. The lower acidity with honey and lanolin confirms Viura aged to Reserva specification.

## Wine 4 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Vanilla warmth alongside finer spice suggests both American and French oak. Reserva demands two years' ageing with six months in cask; this exceeds that — perhaps 12–18 months in barrel plus bottle age. MLF complete, giving textural weight. The gentle walnut note is controlled oxygen ingress during barrel ageing, not a fault. Fermentation in stainless steel before transfer.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and Maturity (5 marks)

Very good, Reserva, €20–28. Around six years old and at peak, fruit now integrated with oxidative complexity. Drink over 3–4 years; longer risks the fruit fading behind oak, leaving an austere shell.

## d) Style Comparison and Commercial Position (12 marks)

Four philosophies: lees-driven restraint, Burgundian barrel work, arrested fermentation, and controlled oxidation. Wine 1 is the by-the-glass mineral white for seafood-led independents in France, the UK and the Netherlands, under €25. Wine 3 sits at the opposite end of the sweetness axis but shares that purity, selling through premium on-trade and specialists in Germany, the US and Japan, competing with entry Alsace Riesling and Grüner Veltliner on sommelier lists.

## a) Identify the grape variety and origin (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Savagnin, Jura, France, Arbois appellation. Roasted nuts, dried apricot, curry spice and a pronounced saline, nutty oxidative edge point toward an oxidatively aged white. Medium-plus alcohol — warm on the palate, around 14% — combined with high acidity and a waxy, phenolic texture narrows the variety. Chardonnay was considered but ruled out: the bitter almond, walnut-skin and savoury mineral profile is far more consistent with Savagnin, and this degree of oxidative handling would have stripped Chardonnay's fruit precision. The sous voile signature points unambiguously to the Jura; the concentration confirms Arbois rather than a lighter Côtes du Jura.

**Wine 2** — Chardonnay, Burgundy, France, Meursault. Honey, toasted hazelnut, wet rocks and a faint kerosene mineral edge, combined with creamy texture and chalky extract, point firmly to Chardonnay. Viognier was considered but lacks the structural acidity and chalky mineral backbone evident here. Reductive mineral tension alongside ripe fruit and discreet oak is characteristic of Burgundy; New World Chardonnay would show more overt oak and softer acidity. The hazelnut richness combined with mineral precision narrows origin to Meursault at village or premier cru level.

## b) Method of production (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Late harvest to achieve physiological maturity in Savagnin's high-acid frame. The defining decision is élevage sous voile — extended ageing under flor yeast in old porous barrels without topping up, minimum six years. This biological oxidation generates acetaldehyde-derived nuttiness, walnut, curry, dried fruit and the saline mineral edge. The wine was not ouillé, distinguishing it fundamentally from Wine 2.

**Wine 2** — Harvest at full physiological ripeness, consistent with the honey and ripe stone-fruit character. Barrel fermentation in French oak — likely 30–40% new — with full malolactic fermentation indicated by the rounded, creamy mouthfeel. Extended lees ageing with bâtonnage. Crucially, this élevage was entirely reductive — barrels kept topped up — preserving crystalline fruit purity and mineral freshness that contrasts directly with Wine 1's oxidative path.

## c) Style, quality and maturity (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Distinctive, dry white of very good quality, retailing around €30–45. The sous voile character is fully integrated; drink now to 2035, developing deeper nutty and dried citrus complexity over 8–10 years.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding quality at premier cru level, retailing around €50–70. Emerging kerosene and secondary hazelnut notes suggest 3–4 years into its window; it will improve for a further 5–7 years then hold for a decade, developing brioche and spiced-butter complexity. Drink 2026–2035.

## d) Commercial positioning (6 marks)

Wine 2 occupies familiar premium-Burgundy territory — sought after globally, suited to independent merchants, specialist retailers and fine-dining lists in Europe, the US and East Asia at €50–70, competing directly with other village and premier cru Meursault. Wine 1 targets a narrower specialist audience comfortable with oxidative style — those familiar with fino Sherry or aged white Burgundy — best placed through independent specialists and adventurous on-trade lists, with a growing audience in the UK, the US natural-wine scene and Japan. Its challenge is a polarising style; its opportunity is premiumisation built on a legally unique élevage story.

The combination of very high tartaric acidity, saline minerality, and warm-climate alcohol points firmly to Assyrtiko; Santorini's volcanic, basket-trained vineyards are the only origin that consistently produces this tension between extreme heat and extreme acid.

**Wine 2** — Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough, New Zealand. Pale lemon-green; lemon rind, green melon, orange blossom, and ripe stone fruit — thiols and pyrazines at the polished, riper end of the spectrum. Grüner Veltliner was briefly considered for the white pepper and citrus, but the structural weight and tropical tilt are inconsistent with that variety's lean frame. Sancerre was also in play, but the fruit generosity and juicy palate point to Marlborough rather than the Loire's more austere, flinty expression. Restrained tropical character rather than exuberant passionfruit suggests a cooler sub-region — Wairau Valley or Awatere.

**Wine 3** — Riesling, Rheinhessen (Westhofen), Germany. Crushed limestone, Amalfi lemon, lemon verbena, and flinty minerality; bone dry with no perceptible residual sugar rules out sweeter Prädikat styles. Power and concentration eliminate Mosel's lighter slate-driven profile and Alsace's broader, more phenolic expression. The chalky rather than slate minerality points to Rheinhessen's limestone-rich Westhofen plateau, making a Grosses Gewächs the logical tier.

**Wine 4** — Verdejo, Rueda, Spain. Lemon, green herbs, white pepper, pollen, and a slight smokiness, with a medium-minus bitter finish. Albariño was the obvious alternative but carries more saline extract and a rounder texture. Sauvignon Blanc was also considered, but the herbal register here is pithy and bitter rather than pyrazine-driven. The smoky finish and pollen-fennel character are typological for Verdejo; moderate weight and good ripeness are consistent with Rueda's high-altitude meseta vineyards.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Rich, textured, dry white with marked freshness. Discreet vanilla and nuttiness suggest roughly 15–20% new French oak at fermentation, with the balance in stainless steel to preserve mineral purity. Extended sur-lie contact (6–9 months) and bâtonnage build mid-palate weight. MLF appears suppressed: acidity retains a sharp tartaric character rather than the softer lactic quality MLF would produce — a deliberate choice to preserve volcanic minerality.

**Wine 2** — Fresh, aromatic, and polished. Reductive handling throughout — cold settling, cool-temperature fermentation in stainless steel — protects the thiols. No new oak is detectable; palate richness comes from ripe fruit and brief lees contact (3–4 months). MLF is absent: acidity is fresh and persistent, and primary varietal character fully intact. A deliberately reductive style at the premium end of the Marlborough category.

**Wine 3** — Concentrated, dry, mineral. No oak influence detectable; fermentation in large neutral oval casks (Stückfass) is plausible given slight textural breadth without toast. Extended lees contact (10–12 months) explains the silky, savoury complexity. MLF avoided: acidity is high, racy, and unbroadened. The chalky grip and extractive detail are preserved through light fining and filtration.

**Wine 4** — Light-to-medium body, fresh, unoaked. Stainless steel fermentation at low temperature preserves delicate herbal aromatics. No oak, MLF, or significant lees contact is evident; early bottling keeps the palate clean and linear. The slight bitter finish is intrinsic to Verdejo, not a winemaking artefact.

---

## c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good to outstanding; single-vineyard Santorini PDO, approximately €35–45. Currently 2–3 years old and drinking well; sufficient structure to develop over 5–7 years, gaining nutty and honeyed complexity. Suits premium on-trade and specialist independents in the US, UK, and Scandinavia.

**Wine 2** — Good to very good; upper-mid-tier Marlborough, approximately £18–22 in the UK. At 2–4 years old it is at or near peak; primary aromatics will fade within 2–3 years. Targets premium supermarket and independent specialist channels in the UK, US, and Australia.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding; Grosses Gewächs tier, approximately €40–60. At roughly 4 years old it is in primary-to-secondary transition — excellent now but will reward patience. High acidity and genuine extract suggest continued improvement over 8–12 years, fruit shifting from citrus to honey and petrol, holding well for 15–20 years from vintage. Fine-wine specialist channel; export to the US, UK, Japan, and Scandinavia.

**Wine 4** — Good commercial quality; mid-tier Rueda DO, approximately €10–14. Clean and varietally accurate, but the medium-minus finish signals no classification-ladder ambition. Best consumed at 1–2 years old; will lose primary herbal freshness beyond 3 years. Sits in premium supermarket and entry on-trade in the UK, Germany, and the US, where Verdejo is gaining ground as a fresh alternative to Pinot Grigio at a comparable price.

Currently around 3–4 years old and slightly closed; structure suggests 4–5 years of further development gaining savoury, spiced complexity, then a 5-year plateau. Strongest market among Grüner specialists in Germany, Scandinavia, and the UK fine wine trade, competing with top Chablis 1er Cru and Pfalz GG Riesling for the terroir-driven serious white wine enthusiast.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc, Martinborough, New Zealand. Sancerre was considered but the tropical fruit intensity and higher perceived alcohol rule out the Loire, where pyrazines dominate and body is lighter. The riper stone fruit, herbaceous undercurrent, and textural weight point to Martinborough rather than Marlborough: Martinborough Sauvignon Blanc carries greater structure and lower aromatics than the single-note passionfruit of the Wairau Valley.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Dry, medium-full bodied, and aromatic, with vivid primary fruit suggesting reductive winemaking — cool stainless-steel fermentation, early bottling, minimal lees contact. No oak influence is detectable. The balance between tropical fruit and green herb indicates careful picking timing: ripe enough for textural weight, early enough to retain freshness.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality, Maturity and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good quality, single-vineyard level, retailing around NZ$35–50 (approximately £18–25 UK). At its ideal drinking window now and over the next 2–3 years; primary character will fade beyond that and extended ageing is not indicated. Natural channels are premium on-trade by-the-glass and independent retail. Martinborough provenance supports a price premium over commodity Marlborough, with Sancerre as the aspirational competitive reference.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

A blend predominantly of Friulano with Pinot Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc, Friuli Colli Orientali, northeastern Italy. The almond bitterness and saline mineral finish are hallmarks of Friulano on ponca (flysch) soils; the floral-blossom character and fresh acidity are consistent with Pinot Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc rounding the blend. Alto Adige was considered for its Alpine freshness, but the palate weight and nutty, ponca-derived mineral character rule it out in favour of the Colli Orientali.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Full-bodied, dry, and structured. No vanilla or toast; textural richness and complex mid-palate point to fermentation and ageing in large neutral oak, preserving mineral and varietal character while adding integration. The slight oxidative development and long almond-inflected finish indicate low-intervention handling with careful SO₂ management, enabling slow evolution. Saline mineral persistence confirms low-yield viticulture on ponca soils as the primary quality driver.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality, Maturity and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality, benchmark Colli Orientali, retailing around €40–60 — comparable in complexity and longevity to premier cru white Burgundy. Around 3–4 years from harvest; approachable but early, with density and acidity to develop nutty, honeyed complexity for 5–7 years, then hold at plateau for a further 3–5. Specialist on-trade and fine wine merchant proposition in Italy, Germany, the US, and the UK, targeting Italian food-and-wine enthusiasts. Competes with premium white Burgundy and top Austrian Grüner, but the three-variety blend on ponca soils provides a distinctive collector's narrative.

## a) Identify the grape variety and origin for each wine (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Melon de Bourgogne, Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, Loire Valley, France.**

Pale lemon, low viscosity, and a medium-intensity nose of lemon, wet stone, and bitter citrus point to a cool-climate neutral variety. Racy acidity, lean body, and a saline finish confirm this. Chardonnay was considered — wet-stone minerality could suggest simple Chablis — but Chablis shows greater concentration and green-apple typicity; Atlantic freshness and citrus bitterness rule it out. Sauvignon Blanc was dismissed: no pyrazine, no herbaceous lift. Neutrality, lean phenolic texture, and ~12% perceived alcohol point decisively to Melon de Bourgogne. The absence of autolytic breadth suggests appellation rather than Cru Communaux level — Muscadet Sèvre et Maine.

**Wine 2 — Chardonnay, Margaret River, Western Australia.**

Deep gold, medium-plus viscosity, and a pronounced nose of stone fruit, nougat, toasted hazelnuts, and spiced butter indicate a warm-climate, barrel-fermented Chardonnay. Lemon-curd richness, creamy texture, flinty-saline mid-palate, long chalky finish, warm at ~13.5%. Burgundy was considered — the gunflint and chalky structure fit — but stone-fruit opulence and generous alcohol rule out Côte de Beaune. The glossy phenolic integration and salted-nut complexity are Margaret River's hallmark: Burgundian structure with New World fruit weight. California was eliminated; this wine lacks the tropical excess or overt American-oak vanilla of Napa.

---

## b) Compare and contrast style and winemaking — vessel choice, lees handling, MLF (20 marks)

Wine 1 shows no detectable oak: clean citrus aromas and a lean, direct palate point to stainless steel. Lees handling is restrained — mild phenolic grip suggests months of contact rather than the 12–24 months a Cru Communaux receives, with no autolytic breadth. MLF appears blocked entirely; acidity remains sharp and malic, preserving Atlantic freshness and linear terroir tension.

Wine 2 shows every hallmark of barrel fermentation in French oak, with well-assimilated toast and blonde tobacco suggesting significant new wood. Creamy texture and cashew-hazelnut richness are consistent with 10–12 months of lees ageing with bâtonnage. Full MLF is clearly indicated: lemon-curd creaminess and the absence of any malic edge confirm complete conversion. Where Wine 1 keeps acidity vivid as its structural anchor, Wine 2 uses MLF as the pivot — delivering roundness within a framework of firm natural acidity.

---

## c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (2 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1.** Very good quality, above standard Muscadet AOC, consistent with a producer-level bottling at €12–18. Primary character places this at 1–2 years old; the lean structure offers a 3–4 year window before fruit fades. Commercially this suits independent specialists and on-trade by-the-glass — shellfish pairing, strong appeal in the UK, Belgium, and Japan — competing with entry-level Chablis and Picpoul de Pinet.

**Wine 2.** Outstanding quality, equivalent in ambition to a Burgundy Premier Cru, retailing at AUD 80–120 (£45–65). Primary stone fruit still dominant but emerging hazelnut places this at 3–4 years from vintage. It will improve for a further 4–6 years — gaining dried citrus, toasted almond, and savoury depth — then hold for 5 more. It belongs on fine-wine specialist and high-end on-trade lists in Australia, the UK, Hong Kong, and the US, competing with premium Burgundy and offering compelling value at Burgundy-adjacent quality.

---

### a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Pale lemon-green, light-bodied, perceptibly low in alcohol (~12%). Restrained green apple, wet stone and a faint biscuity lees note; the palate is saline and iodic. Sauvignon Blanc would give pyrazine herbaceousness; Riesling, electric lime acidity and greater aromatic lift. This neutrality plus salinity is Melon de Bourgogne. ### b) Method of Production (8 marks)

Whole-bunch pressed, then cool-fermented in stainless steel on neutral or indigenous yeasts — no oak character, and the reductive freshness supports tank. The biscuit tone and creamy texture indicate extended fine-lees ageing sur lie, at least eighteen months as the cru rules require. Malolactic was blocked: no butter or roundness. Dry, no residual sugar.

### c) Style, Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good quality; cru-level Muscadet at €20–35. At about three years the lees are integrated and it is entering its peak, holding four to six years while gaining honeyed weight. Unlike Wines 2 and 3, it sells on austerity rather than richness: independent merchants and seafood-led on-trade, with export traction in Scandinavia and Japan. Its competitive set is Sancerre, which it undercuts.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Medium-plus viscosity, warm, ~13.5%. Lemon pith, pineapple, pastry, flint and a mushroomy savouriness; full, firm, pithy, long. Viognier is ruled out by the absence of apricot and floral perfume, and by the high acidity. Burgundy would be narrower and less tropical; Barossa less structured. Tropical citrus with maritime acid retention indicates Chardonnay from Margaret River, Western Australia.

### b) Method of Production (8 marks)

The savoury, umami depth suggests wild-yeast fermentation, conducted in French oak barriques — sweet pastry and vanilla point to roughly 30–50% new wood, well matched to the fruit weight. Partial malolactic: creaminess is present but acidity stays firm; full MLF would broaden it. Around nine months on lees in barrel builds the mid-palate. Bottled dry.

### c) Style, Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding, premier cru Burgundy in standard, around AUD 80–110 (£45–65 export). At two to three years the reductive flint is still closed; expect three to five years' improvement, then five to eight holding, moving to cashew and toasted hazelnut. This is the flight's cellar wine on oak-derived structure, where Wine 3 ages on acid and sugar. Premium independents and fine dining; buyers who want Meursault complexity below Meursault money in the UK, US and Asia.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Very light, low perceived alcohol (~8%), searing acidity against clear residual sugar. Lime blossom, white peach, crushed slate. Gewürztraminer is excluded by the lack of lychee or rose and by the acid level; nothing warm-climate could carry this tension. This is Riesling from the Mosel, Germany. The concentration and long slate-driven finish suggest a single-site Spätlese from the middle Mosel rather than Kabinett or Gutswein.

### b) Method of Production (8 marks)

Cool, slow fermentation in stainless steel or large neutral cask on indigenous yeasts, arrested by chilling and racking off the yeast so that natural grape sugar is retained — not süssreserve. No new oak; light lees contact for freshness only. Malolactic avoided, since the malic acidity is the structural counterweight to the sweetness.

### c) Style, Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding; classified-site Spätlese, €30–50 in Germany, £35–55 in UK specialist. At two years it is primary and slightly closed, improving five to eight years into petrol, wax and lanolin, then holding ten to fifteen. Specialist merchants, Riesling-led lists and top on-trade; Germany, UK independents, Japan and the US fine-wine channel, where low alcohol is now an asset rather than an apology.

Fresh, light-bodied and dry, vinified for immediate accessibility. Viognier. The pronounced white peach, apricot and violet perfume, broad generous palate and relatively low acidity are hallmark. Full-bodied, dry and expressively aromatic. The soft, integrated palate suggests moderate-temperature fermentation in stainless steel with short-term lees contact adding mid-palate roundness. Very good quality for a varietal Eden Valley Viognier, approximately AUD 25–35. Primary aromatics place this at one to two years of age and at its expressive peak. Viognier does not improve significantly with age; consume over the next two to three years before freshness fades.

Very good quality for a premium California Rhône-style white, approximately $45–60. Gold colour and developing aromatic complexity suggest two to three years of age. **Wine 1** — a fruit-forward, early-drinking village style. Whole-bunch pressed, cool-fermented largely in tank or well-used wood; the toasted-nut note and rounded mid-palate indicate several months on fine lees with partial malolactic. The near-absence of vanilla or toast shows new oak was deliberately withheld to keep apple/pear primary. Bottled young for immediate sale.

**Wine 2** — a mineral, ageworthy grand-vin style. Barrel-fermented, full malolactic (butterscotch, creamy texture), roughly 18 months' élevage with lees contact, but modest new oak — perhaps a fifth — since toast never surfaces. That restraint is the tell: a grower with this fruit concentration suppresses new wood so the site's oyster-shell salinity carries the finish. That confidence is itself evidence of Premier Cru material, not négociant village.

## c) Quality and commercial position (18 marks)

Wine 1 is very good quality at village level — balanced and correctly fruited, but intensity and length stop at medium(+). Wine 2 is outstanding: greater complexity, mineral definition and a genuinely long finish; textbook Premier Cru, with 10+ years ahead.

Wine 1 is the volume proposition at £22–28, premium supermarket and high-street specialist, by-the-glass in mid-market on-trade, competing with St-Véran and premier cru Chablis for drinkers wanting the Burgundy name affordably. Wine 2 is allocated at £150+, sold ex-cellar to fine-wine merchants, Michelin lists and US/Asian collectors, against top Chassagne; its challenge is price inflation and residual premox anxiety, not demand.

# Mock answer — Paper 1 Question 1

## a) Identify the grape variety (60 marks)

Chardonnay, from France, and specifically from Burgundy.

The variety call rests first on structure rather than aroma. All six are dry, tannin-free, and sit in a narrow alcohol band — the lightest (Wine 6) reads around 12.5% with only medium-minus weight, the richest (Wines 2, 4 and 5) around 13.5% with medium-plus body and a discernible glycerol slide. Acidity ranges from high and racy (Wine 1) to medium-plus and rounded (Wines 2, 4, 6), and in the rounder examples there is a soft, lactic, yoghurt-and-butter edge (clearest in Wine 6) that indicates a variety routinely put through full malolactic conversion. A grape that tolerates that acid loss and still reads balanced must start with substantial malic acid and moderate pH — Chardonnay.

Second, all six show the same relationship with oak and lees. Vanilla and hazelnut in Wine 6, brioche and smoke in Wine 1, patisserie and toasted hazelnut in Wine 5, a struck-match reductive edge in Wine 4: this is a neutral-to-subtly-fruited variety that is barrel-fermented and lees-aged as a matter of course, and which absorbs oak without the oak taking over. An aromatic variety would fight it.

Third, the fruit spectrum. Green apple, lemon and grapefruit at the cool end; white peach, nectarine and yellow plum in the middle; baked apple and dried fruit at the ripe end — with acacia and honeysuckle floral lift, and no terpenes, no pyrazine, no muscat grapiness anywhere.

Alternatives weighed. **Chenin Blanc** was the strongest rival, given the chalk, honey and almond of Wines 2 and 5 — but Chenin would show wax, lanolin and quince, a sharper, more angular malic acid line, and it does not take malolactic and new oak with this ease; ruled out. **Semillon** would give the lanolin and the gold colour but not the citrus definition or the acid retention of Wine 1; ruled out. **Pinot Gris/Pinot Blanc** would be broader and duller-fruited, with a phenolic bitterness on the finish that is absent throughout.

Country: the flight is unified by wet-chalk and crushed-stone minerality, restrained rather than tropical ripeness, moderate alcohols, and a house style of barrel-and-lees handling in mostly used French oak. That is Burgundy, and the flight is plainly a vertical of its quality ladder — regional, Mâconnais, village, 1er Cru and Grand Cru.

## b) Origin, and how quality is reflected in style and winemaking (6 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Chablis Grand Cru.** The killer evidence is the pairing of high, racy, almost saline acidity with pronounced flint and oyster-shell reduction — Kimmeridgian marl, not Côte de Beaune limestone. Against that cool signature sits a genuinely rich, fleshy, glycerol-coated mid-palate and smoky toast, which rules out village Chablis or Petit Chablis; the wine has been barrel-fermented with a proportion of new wood and given extended lees contact, an investment only made for a top slope. The orange-zest and lily-of-the-valley lift plus the long, mineral-driven finish take it beyond most 1er Crus. Outstanding for its appellation: Grand Cru.

**Wine 2 — Puligny-Montrachet 1er Cru.** Gold colour with honey, honeysuckle, fresh almond and emerging dried fruit and spice signals both a warmer vintage and a Côte de Beaune address. Meursault was considered, but this has a firmer, more citrus-and-floral backbone and lacks Meursault's buttered-hazelnut breadth — Puligny. The velvety texture over a firm mineral spine indicates barrel fermentation, full malolactic and around a year on fine lees in perhaps 20–30% new oak. That combination of length and tension is 1er Cru, above village but short of Grand Cru concentration.

**Wine 4 — Meursault 1er Cru.** Distinctly reductive, lightly spiced, with ample weight and ripe apple over grapefruit, and a long but currently closed finish. The reduction is a deliberate modern choice — minimal bâtonnage, low-oxygen barrel handling — made to build ageability. The sheer palate weight is Meursault's, but the fine-boned mineral line and citrus rather than butterscotch suggest the Puligny-facing crus of the Genevrières/Charmes side. 1er Cru, currently under-delivering against its potential.

**Wine 5 — Corton-Charlemagne Grand Cru.** The flight's finest wine, and the one that repays a second thought. It shows unmistakably generous, warm-vintage ripeness — baked apple, white peach, patisserie, creamy lees, toasted hazelnut from roughly 20–25% new oak — yet it carries a wet-chalk, flinty, saline spine of an intensity you would otherwise associate with Chablis. A Meursault at this ripeness would have gone flabby. Ripeness held by that much tension points not to heat but to elevation and a cool, north-westerly aspect on deep limestone: the Corton hill. Outstanding, Grand Cru, and the only wine here with 15+ years in front of it.

**Wine 3 — Mâconnais, named village.** Lemon-green, medium-plus intensity, grapefruit, nectarine and gooseberry with a fine leesy texture and only a whisper of oak; medium body, medium-plus finish. The riper stone-fruit profile and lower acid than the Côte d'Or wines place it south, in the Mâconnais; the saline edge, fine lees work and clarity of fruit lift it above generic Mâcon-Villages to a named commune. Quality reflected in restraint: no new oak, because the fruit could not carry it.

**Wine 6 — Bourgogne Blanc.** Pale gold, medium intensity, pear and apricot with vanilla and hazelnut sitting on top rather than integrated, a buttery, yoghurty malolactic character, medium-minus body and a short finish. Dilution and a lack of mineral drive place this at regional level — high-yielding vineyard land, tank fermentation with a portion of older barrel, full malo to soften, early bottling.

## c) Commercial position (6 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1:** Independent fine-wine specialists and seafood-led restaurant lists, around £70 a bottle — a credible alternative to Côte de Beaune 1er Cru at lower cost. Strong in the UK and Japan.

**Wine 2:** Allocated through the négociant chain to private clients and Michelin-level lists at £90–120; competitive set is 1er Cru Chassagne and top Meursault.

**Wine 4:** A cellaring purchase at £110–150, likely bought en primeur by collectors who want reduction and tension over richness. Needs 4–5 years before it shows on a list.

**Wine 5:** £180–250, auction and top-end collector demand, concentrated in the US and Asia; its challenge is that Grand Cru white Burgundy pricing now outruns much of its traditional restaurant trade.

**Wine 3:** The value engine — independent merchants and premium by-the-glass at £22–28, aimed at the drinker who wants real Burgundy without Côte d'Or pricing.

**Wine 6:** Premium supermarket and multiple retail at £15–18, targeting the consumer trading up from branded Pays d'Oc Chardonnay; sells on the word "Bourgogne" rather than on what is in the glass.

# Mock answer — Paper 1, two dry whites, same country, same variety

## a) Grape variety and country (10 marks)

Chardonnay, France. Both glasses share a lemon-and-orchard-apple core with no terpene lift, no lychee, no pyrazine — the aromatic varieties are out. Both carry high, tartaric-edged acidity with medium-plus body, a creamy lees texture and discreet barrel spice: the classic neutral-but-transmissive profile of Chardonnay. Chenin Blanc was the serious alternative, but neither wine shows quince, wet wool or that scouring malic bite, and both have a broader mid-palate than Chenin at this ripeness. For Wine 1 I also weighed Savagnin, given a nutty edge; the total absence of fenugreek/curry and the presence of soft yellow-apple fruit rules it out. Restraint over tropical fruit, savoury mineral finishes and warmth suggesting only around 13–13.5% in both point to a cool, continental European origin — France rather than the New World.

## b) Region and growing conditions (2 x 13 marks)

**Wine 1 — Jura (Arbois/Côtes du Jura).** Medium lemon-gold, yellow apple, crushed hazelnut, a struck-match reduction and a distinctly saline, almost bitter-almond finish. Burgundy was the first thought, but the phenolic grip, that iodine-saline signature and the oxidative nuttiness held inside bright fruit take me east to the Jura. Here is the interesting tension: the nutty note without any fenugreek tells me this is *not* sous voile — the barrels were topped up (ouillé) and the wine kept reductive, a Burgundian idiom deliberately applied in a region famed for the opposite. Cool continental climate with a long, late-ripening autumn gives ripeness with acidity intact; Jurassic grey marl over limestone at 250–400m, plus frost- and hail-reduced yields, explain the density and mineral salinity that lift this above appellation norm.

**Wine 2 — Mâconnais, village level (a named-commune Mâcon).** Pale lemon, white peach, citrus pith, subtle toast and a chalky, gently creamy close. Softer, rounder acid line and riper stone fruit than Wine 1 — warmer, southerly Burgundy on clay-limestone, east/south-facing slopes with early Mediterranean influence bringing earlier, fuller ripening. Not Côte de Beaune: it lacks that depth of chalky extract and length.

## c) Quality, maturity, commerce (2 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding for its appellation, performing at good Côte de Beaune 1er Cru level; around £35–45. Three to four years old, drinking now, will improve 4–5 years and hold 8–10, gaining hazelnut and dried apple. Independent specialists and sommelier-led lists; the biodynamic-curious drinker; UK, US, Japan, Scandinavia.

**Wine 2** — Very good, at the top of the village Mâcon hierarchy, competing with Saint-Véran; £22–28. Two to three years old, drink now to five years, no great gain from cellaring. Premium supermarket fine-wine aisle and by-the-glass in bistros; consumers wanting real Burgundy pedigree below Côte d'Or pricing.

## Wine 1 — a) Grape variety and region (10 marks)

Chenin Blanc, Vouvray, Loire Valley. Gold colour with high viscosity points to weight and extract uncommon in northern Loire whites. Ripe quince, honeyed apple, beeswax, lanolin — waxy phenolic grip is signature Chenin Blanc, immediately ruling out Sauvignon Blanc or Chardonnay. High acidity alongside medium-plus warmth eliminates Muscadet. The chalky, quince-driven texture and dry concentrated mid-palate narrow to Vouvray Sec rather than Savennières, which is more austere and phenolically severe in youth.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Pronounced intensity and textural density suggest low yields and manual harvesting. Whole-bunch pressing is indicated by the clean but phenolic palate. Fermentation in old large-format oak — no new wood detectable — accounts for texture without vanilla. Extended lees contact of at least six months explains the creamy mid-palate. Dry fermentation, neutral large oak and extended lees are purposeful decisions that express site character rather than mask it.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality, equivalent to a single-vineyard Vouvray Sec, retailing around €25–35. Demand is strongest in Parisian on-trade and UK and Japanese independents. Vouvray Sec remains undervalued against Sancerre or Pouilly-Fumé, limiting mainstream placement. Its age-worthiness — improving five to seven years, then holding a decade, developing honey and dried apricot — is the strongest argument for sommeliers championing cellarable Loire whites.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Grape variety and region (10 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc, Sancerre, Loire Valley. Pronounced grapefruit zest, flint and gunflint smoke narrow to Loire Sauvignon immediately. The absence of tropical passionfruit and the presence of chalk and saline minerality rule out Marlborough. Partial-barrel roundness on the mid-palate rules out lighter Touraine Sauvignon. Pouilly-Fumé was considered but eliminated: the chalky rather than smoky-flinty finish and slightly fuller body favour Sancerre, where fumé character is less dominant.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Medium-to-full body results from partial barrel fermentation in older demi-muids — subtle roundness with no vanilla or toast. Cold settling and temperature control preserved thiol purity. The absence of phenolic bitterness indicates careful SO₂ management at press. Partial malolactic fermentation is plausible given the broad but restrained acidity. Barrel fermentation is the key human intervention, adding textural complexity without blunting primary freshness.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, upper Village Sancerre approaching single-vineyard complexity, retailing around €25–30. Sancerre has strong placement in premium supermarkets, upscale on-trade, and export to the USA, UK, and Switzerland, positioning it as the reference alternative to Burgundy without Premier Cru pricing. The main competitive pressure is Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc at €12–15 for less price-sensitive buyers.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Grape variety and region (10 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc-dominant blend with Menu Pineau, Cheverny, Loire Valley. Lemon-green colour and medium-minus body place this in a cooler, neutral style. Gooseberry, fresh lime and chalk are classic Loire Sauvignon markers, but subtle waxy texture on the palate indicates a Menu Pineau component, characteristic of Cheverny's permitted blend. The saline minerality and waxy mid-palate distinguish it from pure Touraine Sauvignon, while lighter weight and herbal finish rule out Sancerre's silex-driven concentration.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Clean, reductive aromatics and bright citrus purity indicate cold fermentation in stainless steel around 14–16°C. No oak is detectable. Mild lees contact of three to four months adds light texture without building weight. Human input is deliberately minimal: no oak, no malolactic fermentation, prioritising freshness and varietal transparency.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good quality, entry-to-mid Cheverny AOC, retailing around €12–18. More affordable than Sancerre while sharing Loire minerality, making it well suited to by-the-glass positioning in bistros and wine-bar channels. Consumer recognition is low, requiring sommelier education. Export is largely through specialist Loire importers in the UK, Belgium, and the USA. Drinks well now and over two to three further years.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Grape variety and region (10 marks)

Chenin Blanc, Anjou (Coteaux du Layon), Loire Valley — moelleux style. Deep gold with high viscosity signals rich, sweet white with considerable extract. Botrytis honey, quince and an unusual red-fruit register — cherry, blackberry — with very high acidity against full sweetness narrow sharply to Loire sweet Chenin; no other Loire variety holds acidity at this sugar level. Sauternes was eliminated: Sémillon's lanolin richness and Sauvignon's pungency are both absent, and the red-fruit aromatic register is specific to fully botrytised Chenin Blanc in Anjou.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Concentrated sweetness and pronounced botrytis indicate selective hand-harvesting in multiple tries successives, gathering only the most botrytised berries at each pass. This labour-intensive intervention separates moelleux of this depth from simple late-harvest style. Slow fermentation in old oak was halted naturally by high sugar concentration; no new oak is detectable. High acidity was preserved without acidification. The winemaking is entirely patient rather than interventionist — the cellar adds time, not flavour.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality, Coteaux du Layon Villages level, retailing around €25–45 per half-bottle. Sweet Loire Chenin improves for fifteen to twenty years, developing dried apricot, quince-paste and saline complexity — compelling value versus Sauternes. The commercial challenge is structural: sweet wine faces global consumer hesitation. Strongest channels are French fine-dining by-the-glass with dessert, Japanese and US sommelier-driven on-trade, and UK independents positioning on relative value against Sauternes.

---

## Wine 5 — a) Grape variety and region (10 marks)

Melon de Bourgogne, Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie, Loire Valley. Low viscosity, low-to-medium body, green apple, oyster shell, sea spray and subtle yeasty autolysis are diagnostic. Saline, iodine minerality with light brioche from extended lees contact narrows to Muscadet sur lie well beyond the statutory minimum. Cheverny was eliminated by the complete absence of Sauvignon's herbal character and by the profound marine minerality specific to Atlantic-influenced Muscadet. The tensile, stony mineral quality points to granite-dominant soils within Sèvre et Maine, confirming a Clos-level single-parcel bottling.

## Wine 5 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Extended sur lie ageing — indicated by light brioche and textural weight beyond what unassisted Melon delivers — is the defining human intervention, consistent with 18–24 months rather than the statutory nine-month minimum. No oak. Whole-bunch pressing is implied by the phenolic-free palate. Stainless steel, no fining and late bottling preserve both varietal neutrality and site mineral expressiveness. The winemaker's contribution is patience: extended autolysis contact with no additions to inflate beyond what the site delivers.

## Wine 5 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, Clos-level Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie, retailing around €15–22 against generic Muscadet at €8–12. The strongest competitive positioning is against Chablis Village: comparable salinity and minerality at a lower price, with added lees texture. Premium on-trade with shellfish menus and independents in the UK, USA, and Scandinavia are the key channels. Drinks well now, improving over three to four years before primary freshness fades.

---

## Wine 6 — a) Grape variety and region (10 marks)

Gamay, Touraine, Loire Valley. Ruby with purple hues and low viscosity signal a young, light-to-medium red. Raspberry, red cherry, white pepper and crushed stone with high acidity and low tannin rule out Cabernet Franc (more tannin, capsicum, firmer structure) and Côt (deeper colour, more extract). Pineau d'Aunis was briefly considered — the white pepper is consistent — but red-berry juiciness points more firmly to Gamay, which at the Loire's northern limit produces precisely this pepper, crushed-stone, raspberry character in an unoaked style at around 12.5% perceived alcohol.

## Wine 6 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

The juicy, fruit-forward palate indicates short maceration of five to seven days at low temperatures, possibly with partial whole-cluster or carbonic maceration to maximise primary fruit and minimise phenolic extraction. No oak: raised entirely in stainless steel or cement. Early picking — evidenced by retained freshness and absent over-ripeness — reflects a deliberate choice to capture Gamay's primary register before alcohol accumulates. Very low tannin confirms no post-fermentation extended maceration.

## Wine 6 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good quality, entry-to-mid Touraine AOC red, retailing around €10–15, competing directly with Beaujolais-Villages in the fresh, fruit-forward category. The principal opportunity is volume on-trade by-the-glass and carafe listings. The key challenge is differentiation: Touraine carries little consumer recognition and buyers default to Beaujolais at this price. ## b) Sub-region, appellation, and grape variety (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, Melon de Bourgogne. Iodic salinity, oyster shell and a faint brioche from extended lees contact, at low perceived alcohol: no other French appellation combines autolytic texture with this degree of salinity.

**Wine 3** — Saumur Blanc, Chenin Blanc. Straight citrus-and-pear palate, white flowers, chalky tufa grip, medium body with warmth around 13%. Neither the waxy opulence of Savennières nor the residual-sugar honey of Vouvray, so a dry Saumur.

**Wine 4** — Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, Chenin Blanc. Deep gold, viscous, pronounced honeyed botrytis with praline, toasted peach and a white pepper lift. Coteaux du Layon was the alternative, but the concentration, length and purity exceed it; the carboniferous phthanite bedrock supplies the saline freshness that stops the sugar cloying.

## c) Quality assessment — winemaking and site (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; top of the Muscadet hierarchy, a single-vineyard Sèvre et Maine sur lie, €15–20. Lees autolysis has built texture well beyond generic Muscadet, and the marriage of salinity to creaminess is deliberate. Still a wine of moderate concentration rather than depth.

**Wine 2** — Good only; appellation-level Touraine at €12–15, the weakest here by a clear margin. Purity and absence of phenolic grip indicate whole-bunch pressing and reductive handling; the site gives chalky tension but not concentration. Aromatic clarity, not complexity, is what it sells.

**Wine 3** — Very good; serious village-level Saumur. The tension implies low yields and hand picking to protect acidity, and the finish argues for a well-exposed tufa slope. #### Section A · For the flight as a whole

## a) Variety and Region (9 marks)

All three are lemon-green, bone dry, with high tartaric-driven acidity that is linear rather than broad, and perceived alcohol in a restrained cool-climate range (~12.5%). Citrus, white stone fruit, oyster shell and flint recur across the flight: Chardonnay. Origin narrows to Chablis. The flinty-smoky, briny oyster-shell signature over taut acidity is unlike Mâconnais Chardonnay, which is rounder and more orchard-fruited with less mineral drive, and unlike the Côte de Beaune, which carries greater body and a different oak-integration pattern at equivalent tiers. The iodine-inflected finish common to all three is the Kimmeridgian marker.

**Conclusion:** Chardonnay, Chablis, northern Burgundy.

---

#### Section B · For each wine individually

## b) Quality and Ranking (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 3 — Grand Cru (1st).** Outstanding. Pronounced intensity, tropical and stone fruit layered over a mineral core, oak evident but well placed, and exceptional tension between ripe fruit and driving acid. Length is exceptional and the mid-palate has real depth. £60–90.

**Wine 2 — 1er Cru (2nd).** Very good. Medium-plus intensity, ripe citrus with honeyed-floral lift and a smoky silex finish — a clear step up from Village in concentration and site expression, but without Wine 3's depth. £30–45.

**Wine 1 — Petit Chablis (3rd).** Good, correct for entry tier. Lime and grapefruit freshness with genuine salinity, but lighter-bodied, shorter and less complex than the others. £12–18.

## c) Winemaking (3 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1.** Clean primary citrus, no buttery or vanilla note: stainless steel throughout, malolactic blocked to protect the racy acid. Absence of breadth indicates minimal lees contact and early bottling — the correct economics for the tier.

**Wine 2.** Toast and lemon-curd richness alongside retained mineral precision points to partial barrel fermentation in used French oak rather than new, so the site is not buried. Broader texture suggests six to nine months on lees; acid remains taut, so malolactic is limited at most.

**Wine 3.** Greater textural depth, toffee-apple richness and a faintly phenolic grip on the finish indicate full barrel fermentation and maturation with a higher proportion of new oak than Wine 2, plus twelve months or more on lees. Under the skin: malolactic appears suppressed, so the ripeness reads as terroir power rather than warm-vintage softness — the tension is a deliberate stylistic decision, not simply site.

## d) Style, Maturity and Commercial Position (3 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1.** Primary, unoaked, drink-now at one to two years. Will hold two to three years but gains nothing; fruit then fades. Premium supermarket and independent off-trade, £12–18, for consumers wanting a crisp food-friendly white, competing with entry Mâcon and New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc.

**Wine 2.** Structured and layered at around three years, with oak still integrating. Will improve three to four years as the silex intensifies and the mid-palate fills, holding to eight to ten years from vintage. Independent specialists and mid-tier on-trade, £30–45: more site specificity than Mâcon, cheaper than Village Puligny-Montrachet.

**Wine 3.** Powerful and still relatively closed at four years. Should improve seven to ten years, gaining honeyed and saline tertiary complexity, then hold five more. Fine dining, serious merchants and collectors, £60–90 plus. It competes on quality with top Chassagne-Montrachet 1er Cru, but the iodine austerity makes it irreplaceable rather than substitutable.

Both wines share the defining Chablis signature — saline iodine-and-oyster minerality on a lean, high-acid Chardonnay framework — but the contrast in weight and presence is pronounced. Wine 1 is precise and refreshing, with primary citrus and white fruit and a clean linear finish. Wine 2 shares those cool-climate bones but offers far greater extract and tension. Barrel use adds structure; the primary driver is the vineyard — a south-east-facing Grand Cru slope of Kimmeridgian limestone producing naturally higher sugar accumulation and phenolic ripeness. Both share the Grüner Veltliner signature — white pepper, herb, mineral freshness — but diverge sharply in weight. Wine 4 is a step above: richer palate, stone-fruit generosity and crystalline mineral persistence reflect a great single vineyard — primary rock and loess-over-gneiss soils at Smaragd ripeness. ## Section B · For each wine individually

### Wine 1

**b) Sub-region / appellation**

The rounder, more voluminous texture distinguishes it from a Grand Cru, which would show greater concentration and a more imposing mineral architecture.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Predominantly reductive winemaking in stainless steel or neutral vessels, preserving iodine and primary fruit. The fleshy texture and nutty note suggest limited lees contact — six to nine months on fine lees in tank or older oak. The absence of new-oak vanilla points to neutral maturation. **d) Quality and maturity**
Very good quality, firmly Premier Cru — the length and volume exceed Village Chablis, but the wine lacks the structural density of a Grand Cru site. Retail around €30–45. **b) Sub-region / appellation**
Chassagne-Montrachet, Premier Cru. The citrus-mineral axis, slight bitterness on the finish, and focused power distinguish this from Chablis' saline iodine character, while the herbal aromatic nuance and tight structure are more consistent with Chassagne than the broader opulence of Puligny.

Fermentation and maturation in French barriques, likely 20–30% new oak for approximately twelve months. The silky texture and density indicate full malolactic fermentation in barrel and regular bâtonnage. Slight petrol-like reduction suggests reductive handling early, with careful sulphur management.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Outstanding quality at the top of Premier Cru level. The tight, coiled structure suggests this is currently slightly closed at two to three years old; a further two to three years of cellaring would be rewarding, peaking around 2027–2029 and holding to 2032. ### Wine 3

**b) Sub-region / appellation**

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Almond-nougat character suggests some older barrel influence, but primary freshness remains dominant, indicating restrained oak. **b) Sub-region / appellation**
Corton-Charlemagne, Grand Cru. The pronounced aromatic intensity, toasted oak, chalk-and-flint minerality, saline finish, and — most tellingly — the concentration and creamy lees texture with underlying honeyed richness signal the top of Burgundy's white hierarchy. No Premier Cru delivers this combination of power, complexity, and length simultaneously. The anise nuance and honeysuckle are consistent with Corton-Charlemagne's calcareous, iron-rich soils.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Fermented and matured in French barriques with approximately 40–50% new oak for twelve to eighteen months. Full malolactic fermentation in barrel with sustained bâtonnage contributes the creamy lees texture. Careful oxidative handling during racking promotes hazelnut and honeyed complexity. The saline mineral finish is a structural correlate of the site's chalk substrates.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Exceptional — unambiguously Grand Cru, one of Burgundy's greatest white wine expressions. Retail around €150–250. The underlying honeyed richness signals a warm vintage, yet firm acidity holds the wine in tension — ripeness disciplined by the hillside's elevation and drainage. At approximately four years old, still relatively closed, with toast and oak currently dominating fruit. Will benefit substantially from five to seven further years of cellaring, peaking around 2032–2035 with complex hazelnut, white truffle, and candied citrus, holding at peak for a decade beyond that.

### Wine 5

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Santenay Blanc, Village level. The ripe peach-and-nectarine nose, light toasted hazelnut, and chalky mineral note are consistent with the southernmost Côte de Beaune commune producing white wine of genuine character. **c) Style and key winemaking**
Ripe peach alongside light vanilla and brioche indicates barrel fermentation with perhaps 20–25% new French oak, followed by full malolactic fermentation. Approximately ten to twelve months maturation with moderate lees contact produces the almond note and accessible, fruit-forward style.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Very good quality at Village level — above the generic Bourgogne tier, comparable to a well-made Saint-Aubin Blanc. Retail around €25–40. Bright primary fruit suggests two years from vintage. Drinking well now; hold for a further two to three years at most. Drink through 2027.

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Mâconnais — a named-village Mâcon appellation. The ripe, slightly exotic character — yellow plum, mango, citrus blossom, melon — and the medium-minus finish point to the warmer, less structured wines of southern Burgundy. The absence of any serious mineral spine or oak complexity rules out Pouilly-Fuissé Premier Cru.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Cool fermentation in stainless steel with no or minimal oak contact, producing the clean, neutral background and soft, juicy texture. The absence of buttery creaminess indicates either no or carefully managed partial malolactic fermentation. Light lees contact softens the mouthfeel. A deliberately accessible, early-drinking style.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Good quality for the appellation — a well-made Mâcon-Villages, retailing around €15–22, sitting at the entry tier of the Burgundian hierarchy. The vibrant ripe fruit indicates one year from vintage. No structural case for ageing: drink through 2026 before tropical fruit softens and freshness fades.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 1 Practice Question (France Flight)

## a) Country and Regional Origin (4 × 8 marks)

The country is **France**. The spread of styles — chalky mineral, reductive aromatic, waxy and phenolic, heady floral — with consistently firm acid spines and no residual sugar fits France better than Germany (Prädikat gradations would give varied sweetness and lower alcohol) or Italy (more phenolic bite, different acid shape).

**Wine 1 — Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru (Côte de Beaune).** Pale lemon-green, concentrated citrus and white peach, creamy texture, high acid and a chalky finish: cool-climate barrel-fermented Chardonnay. Chablis would be leaner and more reductive with little oak texture; Meursault broader and nuttier. The vertical drive and mineral length exceed Village level but lack Grand Cru power, so Premier Cru.

**Wine 2 — Sancerre (Loire).** Pale lemon, stony flint over restrained pyrazine, high racy acid with saline persistence: Loire Sauvignon Blanc. Marlborough is ruled out by the absence of pungent tropical aromatics and by the harder acid line. Pouilly-Fumé is the near miss; the muscular chalky mid-palate points to Sancerre's limestone-silex.

**Wine 3 — Alsace Grand Cru, Haut-Rhin.** Bone-dry, phenolic grip, pronounced petrol and lime with a gunflint edge, warming alcohol around 14%: mature Alsace Riesling. Dryness rules out German Kabinett/Spätlese; the extract and density rule out generic Alsace. Sustained mineral finish and structural authority indicate a Grand Cru site.

**Wine 4 — Condrieu (Northern Rhône).** Deep gold, peach blossom, apricot and white flowers, generous body, warm alcohol, only moderate acidity: Viognier from a warm site. New World Viognier would show overt tropical fruit and less textural precision; Château-Grillet is stylistically close but tiny in volume. Youthful aromatic lift confirms a recent vintage of Condrieu.

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Structured, oak-influenced dry Chardonnay made for freshness. Whole-bunch pressing explains the phenolic-free purity; barrique fermentation with perhaps 30–40% new oak gives integrated vanilla and spice as texture rather than flavour. Full malolactic accounts for the creamy mid-palate and absence of malic bite; a year or more on lees supplies the bready savouriness.

**Wine 2.** Pure, unoaked, reductive Sauvignon: cold settling, cool stainless-steel fermentation, early bottling to hold primary aromatics. Unlike Wine 1 there is no autolytic or oak character at all. The rounded yet muscular texture suggests slightly extended skin contact at pressing rather than pure free-run juice.

**Wine 3.** Dry, powerful, age-worthy — the antithesis of off-dry aromatic Alsace. Petrol and lime intensity with phenolic grip indicate late harvesting at full ripeness. No new-oak signature, so large neutral foudres or steel, with mildly oxidative cellar handling adding complexity. Malolactic avoided, preserving the malic tension that carries the ageing structure.

**Wine 4.** Opulent and aromatic. Picking at full physiological ripeness captures Viognier's floral peak; the waxy mid-palate and soft acid line point to partial barrel fermentation or short lees contact, but the florality is too pure for new oak. Fermented fully dry, with the alcohol rather than acidity providing drive — the opposite balancing act to Wine 2.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding; Premier Cru Puligny at roughly €80–120. Above Village level in concentration and drive, below Grand Cru in power. Fine dining and specialist retail in France, the UK, US and Japan; competitive set is top Meursault Premier Cru. At 2–3 years it will improve for 5–8 more, peak around 2030–32 and hold a further decade as the citrus turns to hazelnut and honey.

**Wine 2.** Very good; top Sancerre, effectively a lieu-dit bottling, €35–55. Mineral complexity and textural muscle lift it above generic Sancerre without approaching Wine 1's ambition. A benchmark premium by-the-glass and short-list restaurant wine, strongest in the UK, US and Scandinavia where Loire Sauvignon holds a premium over Marlborough. Drinking now at 1–2 years, holding 3–5; it will not reward cellaring.

**Wine 3.** Outstanding; Alsace Grand Cru, €60–100. Density, petrol complexity and phenolic precision place it far above regional Riesling at €10–20. Specialist retail and fine dining, with export strength in Germany, the UK, US and Asian markets now buying dry age-worthy Alsace. Not yet at plateau: improving 5–7 years, holding 15–20, gaining dried apricot depth. The commercial catch is that consumers still expect sweetness from Alsace Riesling, so this wine has to be sold by the sommelier rather than the shelf.

**Wine 4.** Very good to outstanding; single-vineyard-level Condrieu, €45–70, prices supported by minuscule appellation volume. Aromatic intensity and texture are exemplary, but unlike Wines 1 and 3 the acid cannot sustain long evolution. Fine dining and specialist retail in France, the US and UK, and a compelling premium pour on distinctiveness alone — few global comparators. It will not suit drinkers seeking restraint. Drink within 2–4 years; it fades rather than develops.

Wines 2 and 3 show progressively warmer, riper expressions, yet tannin quality remains fine-grained and acidity retains freshness, ruling out Syrah (coarser tannin, peppery savouriness) and Grenache (lower acid, broader texture). Cabernet Franc was briefly considered for Wine 1 given the violet note and leafy earth, but the absence of pyrazine and the silk of the tannin eliminate it. The graduation in weight and ripeness across the three wines is consistent with Pinot Noir spanning a cool continental European origin, a coastal Californian site, and a high-altitude Southern Hemisphere region.

---

## b) Region of origin

**Wine 1 — Côte de Nuits, Burgundy.** Sour-cherry-and-mushroom lift, faintly saline finish, and very high racy acidity at moderate body point to a cool continental Burgundian origin. The truffle-and-leather complexity and silky tannin indicate premier cru level rather than village.

**Wine 2 — Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California.** Deeper ruby, violet and rose florality alongside riper Bing cherry and boysenberry, with warm generous body and cedar-pipe tobacco complexity. Oregon shares the floral register but rarely achieves this fruit density; the combination of richness and fog-cooled freshness narrows the call to Russian River Valley over warmer Sonoma sites.

**Wine 3 — Central Otago, New Zealand.** Dense dark cherry, mulberry, and blood plum with exotic spice and raw cocoa. Perceived warmth is high yet acidity remains genuinely fresh — tension that points to altitude rather than maritime cooling, distinguishing Central Otago from Marlborough or Martinborough.

## c) Style and winemaking

**Wine 1.** Restrained and terroir-expressive. The purity of sour cherry and integration of truffle suggest whole-bunch inclusion lifting aromatic tension without adding green tannin. The silky texture and saline finish indicate extended lees contact in older Burgundian pièces; the absence of vanilla confirms minimal new oak.

**Wine 2.** Richer and more generously textured. Cedar and toast point to French oak ageing, perhaps 30–40% new, yet the rose and violet florality is retained — suggesting a short maceration preserving aromatic lift, supplemented by cold-soak pre-fermentation to build colour without extracting coarse tannin.

**Wine 3.** Concentrated yet polished. Layers of dark fruit and spice alongside fine integrated tannin suggest around 13 months in French oak with moderate new oak (~25%). The raw cocoa finish indicates ripe tannins managed through temperature-controlled fermentation and gentle pump-overs rather than aggressive extraction.

## d) Quality, maturity and commercial position

**Wine 1.** Outstanding quality at premier cru Côte de Nuits level, retailing around £80–120. Complexity, persistence, and saline-mineral finish place it above village Burgundy. Currently 3–4 years old and rewarding now; will improve over 5–6 years as truffle and sous-bois deepen, then hold a further 8–10. Best placed with independent specialist retailers and fine dining on-trade in the UK, US, and Japan, where premier cru provenance commands strong collector demand.

**Wine 2.** Very good quality, comparable to a top-tier Russian River Valley estate bottling at $60–80. Ready to drink now with well-integrated oak; will hold at this plateau for 4–5 years. Target market is premium US restaurant lists and West Coast specialist retailers, with export potential to the UK and Scandinavia where the floral, approachable style suits on-trade by-the-glass positioning.

**Wine 3.** Very good to outstanding, benchmark Central Otago level at NZ$80–120 (approximately £40–60). Still youthful — 2–3 years from its optimal window — and will develop spice and undergrowth complexity over 5–7 years, holding for a further 5. Priority export channels are the UK, US, and Asian fine wine markets; the principal commercial challenge is price competition from premier cru Burgundy at similar retail points, where French provenance narrative retains the advantage.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety (25 marks)

The grape variety is Pinot Noir. Across all five wines the structural fingerprint is consistent: translucent to mid ruby colour, medium body, high and racy acidity, fine-grained silky tannins, and moderate warmth suggesting roughly 13–13.5% perceived alcohol. This eliminates the main alternatives. Syrah would show deeper purple-black colour with black olive, smoked meat and pepper aromatics alongside coarser tannin. Gamay shares the translucency and juicy acidity but its tannins are softer and more carbonic, and it lacks the forest floor and sous bois complexity visible here. Nebbiolo presents similarly pale, evolved garnet but with punishing, drying tannin and rose-tar aromatics absent in this flight. Sangiovese shares the sour-cherry register of several wines but always delivers firmer, more angular tannin and a dried-herb and leather frame.

The clinching evidence is the coherence of red and dark cherry, violet, forest floor and earthy minerality across five wines spanning three continents — a profile expressing Pinot Noir's thin skin, low anthocyanins, and site-sensitive character. The variation in fruit weight, earthy depth and oak integration confirms rather than undermines the call: no other grape simultaneously produces Burgundian earthiness (Wine 1), New World juiciness (Wines 2 and 3), cranberry delicacy (Wine 4) and limestone-graphite grip (Wine 5). **Variety: Pinot Noir.**

---

**Wine 1**

**b)** Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France — village appellation level.

**c)** Dark plum, sour cherry and forest floor underscored by truffle, porcini and game. This depth of secondary character, combined with restrained warmth and a saline finish, points to a cool continental climate where Pinot Noir ripens slowly and retains acidity. Silky tannins and a light structural grip suggest partial whole-cluster inclusion rather than fully destemmed fruit. Integrated spice implies a moderate proportion of new French oak without overt vanilla. Quality is very good — a well-sited Morey-Saint-Denis village approaching premier cru complexity.

**d)** Priced $60–90 retail, this sits in the independent specialist and fine-wine merchant channel. Export to the USA, Japan and UK is its natural home, targeting serious Burgundy enthusiasts who value terroir over approachability. Competition from Gevrey-Chambertin and Chambolle-Musigny village wines at comparable prices is intense; early secondary character gives it an advantage on premium restaurant lists.

---

**Wine 2**

**b)** Geelong, Victoria, Australia.

**c)** Strawberry and raspberry dominate over dark fruit, with five-spice, dried herb and cedar from French oak barriques. The sous bois character grounds this in a cool maritime climate — Geelong's proximity to Port Phillip Bay moderates temperatures and extends the growing season, producing Pinot Noir with vibrancy but without Burgundian brooding earthiness. The palate is more fruit-forward and generous than Wine 1, with mulberry and blackcurrant adding mid-palate weight. Quality is very good, equivalent to a single-vineyard cool-climate Australian Pinot Noir at upper premium tier.

**d)** Retail AUD 60–90 / £45–65, targeting independent merchants and premium on-trade in Australia and the UK. Export to the US and Japan should be prioritised, where Australian Pinot Noir is gaining recognition as a credible alternative to New Zealand. The challenge is communicating Geelong's identity distinctly from the better-known Yarra Valley.

---

**Wine 3**

**b)** Marlborough, New Zealand.

**c)** The most intense fruit concentration in the flight: blackberry, black cherry, liquorice and earthy loam with fennel seed on the palate. This darker profile is striking for Marlborough; the long finish and crisp acidity point to the Wairau or Awatere sub-valleys, where limestone soils and southerly winds produce firmer, darker Pinot Noir than Martinborough. Well-judged new French oak delivers sweet spice without heaviness. Unlike Wine 2, the fruit register is darker and more primary; unlike Wine 1, there is minimal tertiary development. Quality is good to very good, at the top of New Zealand's export tier.

**d)** Retail NZD 50–70 / £35–50. The UK and US on-trade offer strong opportunities, where New Zealand Pinot Noir holds genuine shelf presence. The key challenge is differentiating Marlborough as a Pinot Noir origin against entrenched Central Otago perceptions.

---

**Wine 4**

**b)** Eola-Amity Hills AVA, Willamette Valley, Oregon, USA.

**c)** The most restrained, pale-fruited wine in the flight: red cherry, cranberry, blood orange and pomegranate with dried rose petal and savory herb. The Eola-Amity Hills sit at elevation with significant marine influence from the Van Duzer Corridor, driving acidity and holding perceived alcohol in check. Light oak integration and red-fruited transparency suggest partial whole-cluster fermentation with limited new oak — a structural choice as much as a climatic one. Compared with Wine 5's limestone-graphite minerality or Wine 1's earthy depth, this wine is defined by delicacy and transparency. Quality is very good, equivalent to a single-vineyard Eola-Amity Hills at premium Oregon level.

**d)** Retail USD 50–80, with primary placement on restaurant lists in New York, Chicago and San Francisco. Export opportunity exists in Japan and the UK among consumers seeking restrained, food-friendly Pinot Noir. Competition is intense from other Willamette AVAs and from Burgundy at this price point.

---

**Wine 5**

**b)** Baden, Germany — Kaiserstuhl sub-region, Grosses Gewächs classification.

**c)** The most structured and mineral wine of the flight. Graphite, earthy minerality and fine limestone-driven tannin grip are the single most diagnostic features: this is an argument about terroir before winemaking. Kaiserstuhl's volcanic loess overlying limestone delivers the unique saline-mineral tension alongside kirsch and red plum. New French oak is better integrated than in Wine 2 — vanilla and cedar present but subordinate to the mineral core, suggesting 12–18 months in barrique with controlled new wood proportion. Quality is outstanding within the German Spätburgunder canon, equivalent to premier cru Burgundy in ambition. Warmth from a riper vintage has added length without sacrificing the site's acid spine.

**d)** Retail €55–85 in Germany; £70–100 in the UK. The domestic fine-wine market is the anchor, but export demand is growing as international awareness of Grosses Gewächs Spätburgunder rises. Independent specialists and auction houses are the correct channels. The key challenge is consumer unfamiliarity — most buyers associate Germany with white wines — but the opportunity is significant for merchants able to position this as a serious Burgundy alternative at comparable quality and slightly lower price.

## b) Origin (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Saint-Émilion, Bordeaux, France.** Dark cherry, mocha, aniseed and crushed stone, with medium-minus acidity and polished medium-plus tannins, point to the Right Bank. The floral lift and stony minerality distinguish this from Pomerol, where the profile tends toward rounder, earthier plushness. Structure and aromatic complexity are consistent with grand cru classé level.

**Wine 2 — Napa Valley, California, USA.** Candied black cherry, red liquorice and sweet baking spice, with a lush full body and marked sweet oak, are characteristic of a warm continental origin. The opulent texture and prominent vanilla-mocha overlay from new French oak point firmly to California over cooler Stellenbosch or Washington State.

**Wine 3 — Stellenbosch, South Africa.** The most restrained of the three: medium body, medium acidity and medium tannin suggest a cooler origin than Napa, yet warm-climate ripeness in the plum-and-spice profile rules out a cooler European source. The absence of sweet-oak opulence seen in wine 2 is consistent with Stellenbosch.

## c) Style and winemaking (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Structured yet refined — a classic Merlot-dominated Right Bank style with contemporary polish. Full physiological ripeness at harvest is suggested by the ripe dark fruit; the silky tannin and integrated cedar-mocha notes indicate French barrique maturation with a measured proportion of new oak. The menthol freshness and crushed-stone minerality point to minimal reductive handling and careful extraction to preserve elegance.

**Wine 2.** Opulent and fruit-forward, with the candied fruit and sweet spice indicating harvest at high Brix. Pronounced vanilla, mocha and baking-spice overlay suggests extended maturation in a high proportion of new French oak — 15 months or more. The lush texture implies minimal fining or filtration, prioritising mouthfeel over austerity.

**Wine 3.** Straightforward and fruit-driven. The plum-and-spice profile without obvious oak overlay suggests neutral or older vessels, preserving primary varietal character. Medium-plus body and medium tannin are consistent with moderate maceration and temperature-controlled fermentation — clean and varietally expressive, without the layered complexity of wines 1 and 2.

## d) Quality and commercial position (3 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1.** Very good quality, Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé level, retailing around €40–60. Aromatic complexity and structural refinement place it clearly above generic Saint-Émilion. **Wine 2.** Very good to outstanding quality, upper-premium Napa Merlot tier, retailing around $50–70. The full, generous style competes directly with top Napa Cabernet blends for American fine-dining and collector markets. Asian and UK export potential is strong on brand recognition; the challenge is justifying price against Napa Cabernet at the same level.

**Wine 3.** Good quality, mid-tier Stellenbosch Merlot, retailing around $15–20. Well-placed for premium supermarkets and by-the-glass on-trade in the UK and Nordic monopolies. The key commercial challenge is differentiation in a segment crowded by Chilean and Argentine alternatives at similar price points.

#### Section B · For each wine individually

---

**Wine 1**

## b) Region of origin

Northern Rhône, France — Crozes-Hermitage.

Green peppercorn, dried herb and savoury mineral dominate over primary fruit — a reductive, cool-climate frame that points to France rather than the New World. The palate is medium-bodied with taut acidity and only moderate warmth. Within the Northern Rhône, the medium-plus finish and comparatively lighter mid-palate indicate the Crozes plateau rather than a Hermitage hillside; Côte-Rôtie is ruled out by the absence of lifted violet perfume and bacon-fat Viognier character.

Classically made and reductive: fermentation kept cool enough to protect the peppery-savoury aromatics, with no vanilla or toast, implying old large-format demi-muids or foudres rather than new barriques.
