# Mock answer — Paper 2, six wines / six countries / six varieties

## a) Grape variety and region of origin (6 x 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Cabernet Sauvignon-led Bordeaux blend, Haut-Médoc, northern Médoc.** The blackcurrant fruit sitting alongside blackcurrant leaf, mint, cedar and cigar-wrapper tobacco is the Cabernet Sauvignon signature, and the high, fine-grained but genuinely firm tannin with medium(+) acidity and a full, warm frame (~13.5%) points to a maritime European origin working Cabernet on deep gravel. Cabernet from Napa or Coonawarra was considered, but the leafy-mint lift over savoury tobacco, and the fact the tannin outweighs the fruit sweetness, are Left Bank rather than New World. Within Bordeaux, the mineral austerity beneath a fat, creamy finish and the sheer tannin volume argue for the northern Médoc rather than plush Right Bank Merlot — Saint-Estèphe in character, so Haut-Médoc on its northern boundary.

**Wine 2 — Carménère, Colchagua Valley (Apalta), Chile.** Deep ruby-purple with ripe dark plum and black cherry, yet an insistent green bell-pepper pyrazine and dried thyme that persist right through the palate — that combination of full ripeness *and* unresolved methoxypyrazine, at generous ~14% warmth with soft, fine-grained tannin, is Carménère's fingerprint. Cabernet Franc was weighed and rejected: Loire Franc would show higher acid, lower alcohol and raspberry rather than plum, and would not carry mocha oak. Merlot was rejected because pyrazine this overt with tannin this ripe is not Merlot's habit. The graphite and earthy clay-loam undertone with cocoa-toned oak narrow it to Colchagua's Apalta amphitheatre.

**Wine 3 — Frappato, Vittoria, south-eastern Sicily.** Light ruby, low viscosity, medium(-) finish: a light-bodied Mediterranean red. Violets, lavender, wildflowers and raspberry with orange-peel citrus lift, dusty red fruit and a faint spritz. Pinot Noir was the obvious alternative but there is no forest floor or mushroom, and the floral-citrus register with a saline, oceanic edge is southern Italian, not Burgundian; Gamay is ruled out by the sweet-spice and orange-peel tone rather than banana and boiled sweet. This aromatic, pale, low-tannin profile with high-toned florals is Frappato — the Vittoria zone.

**Wine 4 — Shiraz, Barossa Valley, South Australia.** Pronounced blackberry compote, blood plum, licorice, cola and menthol over black pepper, with a deep purple core, high viscosity and obvious alcoholic warmth (~14.5%) against only medium acidity — a warm-climate Syrah. Northern Rhône was eliminated: Hermitage or Côte-Rôtie would show olive, smoked meat and a firmer acid spine, not compote and butterscotch. The mocha-vanilla and cedar of American and French oak, plus that menthol-eucalypt lift, are unmistakably Australian; the sheer fruit sweetness held by a tight firming core says Barossa Valley rather than cooler Heathcote.

**Wine 5 — Blaufränkisch, Moravia, Czech Republic.** Modest ruby with a slight haze, medium(-) body, high acid, medium tannin and only moderate warmth (~12.5%): a cool-continental red. Black plum and red cherry with plum pit, white pepper, purple flowers and a stalky green-stem note. Gamay was considered and rejected — the peppery, blue-fruited spice and firmer tannin are not carbonic Beaujolais. St Laurent and Zweigelt were also weighed; the peppery austerity and pit-fruit sourness favour Blaufränkisch. Burgenland is the default home, but the leaner build and lower ripeness point further north-east into Moravia.

**Wine 6 — Cabernet Sauvignon, Stellenbosch, South Africa.** Blackcurrant and dark plum with pencil lead, tobacco, undergrowth and a gravelly mineral edge; ruby with garnet at the rim, medium(+) acid, medium seamless tannin, medium(+) body. Cabernet again, but a wholly different expression from Wine 1 — no leaf-mint herbaceousness, warmer alcohol yet more restrained weight. Bordeaux is excluded here because Wine 1 already occupies that country and, more usefully, because the fruit is purer and rounder with an earthy undergrowth rather than cedar-and-graphite austerity. The gravel-and-earth signature over ripe, unforced blackcurrant is Stellenbosch, likely the Helderberg foothills.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (6 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** A classical, structured claret built for the cellar. The density and flesh suggest a long cuvaison of three weeks-plus with post-ferment maceration to build that high tannin, then 12-18 months in French barriques, perhaps 40-50% new — the cedar and cigar-box read as oak, not fruit. Full malolactic in barrel accounts for the creamy, fat finish.

**Wine 2.** Modern, fruit-forward but savoury. Retention of pyrazine indicates picking for physiological rather than maximum sugar ripeness, avoiding over-extraction; pumping over rather than punching down given the supple mid-palate; roughly 12 months in French barriques, largely used, giving cedary integration rather than sawn-oak sweetness.

**Wine 3.** Deliberately unmanipulated. No oak character at all, spontaneous ferment, likely amphora or cement for maturation, minimal sulphur, no fining or filtration — hence the faint carbonic spritz. Short, cool maceration to preserve florals and keep tannin light.

**Wine 4.** An overt, generous commercial style. Late picking for compote ripeness, warm ferment with vigorous extraction, then 12-15 months in a mix of French and American hogsheads, some new, giving butterscotch and mocha. Alcohol left high rather than adjusted.

**Wine 5.** Low-intervention: haze indicates no filtration and minimal sulphur; the stalky note suggests a portion of whole bunch; ferment in neutral vessel or old wood with no new oak, bottled early to keep the energetic lift.

**Wine 6.** Restrained, terroir-first estate winemaking. Gentle extraction — tannin is medium and seamless, not extracted — with 18 months in mostly seasoned French oak; the pencil-lead is fruit-derived, not toast.

## c) Quality and commercial position (6 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding, over-performing its appellation — the concentration, tannin volume and length match a Cru Classé rather than a typical Haut-Médoc, and the ripeness suggests a warm, dry recent vintage. Around £35-45, independent specialists and fine-wine lists; drink from five years, hold 15-20.

**Wine 2.** Very good, icon-tier Chilean at roughly £18-22 — premium supermarket and on-trade by-the-bottle, strong in the UK, USA and Japan. Competes with Reserva-level Rioja; the pyrazine polarises consumers.

**Wine 3.** Very good for its light, low-tannin category, though short. Around £25-30, a natural-wine specialist and wine-bar listing, sold on personality; challenged by its price-to-weight ratio.

**Wine 4.** Very good commercial quality, mid-tier of a large branded range, £16-20; off-trade and chain on-trade, USA and Canada the core markets. Drink now to eight years.

**Wine 5.** Good quality, small-volume artisanal, £22-26, independent and by-the-glass in urban wine bars. Challenge: an unfamiliar variety and country need hand-selling.

**Wine 6.** Very good, upper-estate tier at £25-30; independents, hotel lists and export to the UK, USA and Netherlands. Drink now to ten years, developing cigar-box tertiaries.

**Wine 4** — Xinomavro, Naoussa PDO, Macedonia, Greece. Garnet, with rose, dried tomato, tobacco and black tea — an aged Nebbiolo profile, and Barolo/Barbaresco was the leading alternative. It is ruled out by black olive, gunpowder and liquorice, outside Nebbiolo's canon, and by tannins that are robust but rounder. Agiorgitiko would be softer and more fruit-forward, lacking this tomato-leaf and dried-herb savouriness. Naoussa is the benchmark for premium Xinomavro; the rounded mouthfeel indicates a Reserva-tier release.

---

## b) Style and winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Light, fresh, unoaked and built for early drinking. The absence of vanilla or toast points to stainless steel or large neutral vessels; the chalky, undemanding tannin to a short maceration of roughly 8–12 days, taking colour without grip. Picked at phenolic ripeness but before over-maturity — essential on cool tuffeau — with malolactic completed, giving the broad, clean acid line.

**Wine 2** — Richer and oak-shaped, with clove and nutmeg over blackberry. Warmth and generous body indicate a riper harvest in the sun-exposed Alba zone. The spice is integrated rather than assertive, suggesting 10–14 months in mixed formats with a high proportion of used wood. Malolactic has softened what would otherwise be a searing natural acidity — here oak and malolactic are doing corrective work, not decorative work, which is the reverse of Wine 1's hands-off approach.

**Wine 3** — Deliberately interventionist, tempering Pinotage's rustic tendencies. Vanilla, cedar and roasted coffee indicate 12 months or more in French oak with some new wood; the ripe, firm but unaggressive tannin suggests pump-overs rather than punch-downs. The faint reduction implies a low-oxygen élevage protecting the dark fruit core.

**Wine 4** — Structured and age-intended, working with rather than against the variety's acid and tannin. Extended maceration built the backbone; ageing in mixed French and American oak of varying sizes has rounded the mouthfeel and added tobacco and leather without stripping the dried-tomato and olive character intrinsic to Xinomavro.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Good. Entry-level Chinon AOC, £12–16. Primary fruit and a medium-minus finish keep it below the single-vineyard tier. Premium supermarket and independent off-trade, against Anjou Rouge and entry Saumur-Champigny; Scandinavia, UK and Benelux are natural markets. The obstacle is Cabernet Franc's weak varietal recognition outside Bordeaux.

**Wine 2** — Very good. Barbera d'Alba Superiore, £20–28. Concentration, length and oak integration lift it above basic DOC. Independent specialist trade in the UK, US and Northern Europe, competing with Dolcetto d'Alba and Barbera d'Asti Superiore. Its ceiling is capped by Barbera's status as Barolo's understudy rather than by anything in the glass.

**Wine 3** — Very good for the appellation. Premium Stellenbosch varietal red, £15–22. Structure and oak integration exceed commodity Pinotage. Independent off-trade and mid-range on-trade in the UK, Netherlands and domestic market, with growing German and Scandinavian demand for premium Cape reds. The variety's reputation, set by its cheapest examples, remains the brake on price.

**Wine 4** — Very good to outstanding. Reserva-level Naoussa PDO, £22–35. Savoury complexity, length and fine oak sit well above the appellation floor. A specialist wine: independent merchants, Greek on-trade, destination retailers in the UK, Germany and US. Low recognition is the challenge, but the opportunity is precisely the Nebbiolo confusion noted above — an undervalued analogue to premium northern Italian reds at half the price.

---

## a) Identification — grape variety and country/region of origin (6 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend, Haut-Médoc, Bordeaux, France**

Cassis, cedar and graphite over a leafy herbal edge, with firm fine-grained tannin and medium-plus acidity, indicate dominant Cabernet Sauvignon. Merlot was weighed — plum is present — but the structural firmness and cedar-and-leaf register rule out a Merlot-dominant right-bank wine. Cigar-box cedar signals new French oak typical of the Left Bank; the fruit is classical, not overripe, confirming Haut-Médoc rather than a warmer inland appellation. Mid-palate weight suggests Cru Bourgeois Supérieur or Classified Growth level.

**Wine 2 — Tempranillo, Rioja DOCa, Spain**

Ripe black fruit, dark spice, liquorice and a firm mineral backbone point to Tempranillo. Garnacha was considered given the opulence, but the earthy register, firmer tannin and absence of lifted warm-strawberry fruit rule it out. Concentrated cassis and coffee with high freshness suggest a modern-school wine raised in French rather than American oak; the weight exceeds Crianza tier.

**Wine 3 — Shiraz, Barossa Valley, South Australia**

Deep colour, full body, blackberry, chocolate and sweet oak spice: warm-climate Shiraz. Northern Rhône Syrah was the alternative, but the alcohol reads generous, the fruit is jammy rather than savoury-olive, and the oak is overt where the Rhône would be tighter and more reductive. The near-viscous palate and dried-fruit intensity pinpoint Barossa; Eden Valley or McLaren Vale would show higher acidity and more violet lift.

**Wine 4 — Pinot Noir, Alsace, France**

Bright red cherry and raspberry, taut high acidity and light-to-medium tannin give Pinot Noir. Burgundy was the first alternative: the acidity fits, but the texture is broader and open-knit, lacking the mineral focus of even village Côte de Beaune. German Spätburgunder was also weighed, but lacks the exotic, forward fruit here. That generous ripeness without a firm spine indicates Alsace in a warm vintage.

**Wine 5 — Malbec, Cahors, France**

Sour cherry, black olive, laurel, violet and a smoky tannic grip give Old World Malbec. Argentine Malbec was considered on the dark fruit and floral lift, but the bitter black-olive and black-tea character, drying tannin and absence of plush Mendoza ripeness rule it out. Smoke, iris and wild-berry savour are diagnostic of Cahors.

**Wine 6 — Tannat, Maldonado, Uruguay**

Deep, viscous, with blackberry, dried fig and kirsch, dense but noticeably softer tannin than classic Madiran, and a saline lift suggesting a maritime climate. Pinotage was considered on the jammy dark fruit, but no rubber or acetone note appears and the tannin is cleaner. Ripe fruit, moderate oak and Atlantic freshness point to Uruguay's Maldonado.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (6 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — A structured Médoc built for ageing. Cedar, toast and espresso indicate new French barriques, perhaps 60–70% new over 18 months. Creamy tannin points to gentle pump-over extraction; the rounded mid-palate suggests malolactic in barrel.

**Wine 2** — Modern, internationally styled Rioja. Subtle vanilla with prominent dark spice and coffee indicates French rather than American wood. Concentration points to extended maceration and 18–24 months in oak, placing this at Reserva tier or above.

**Wine 3** — Full-extraction warm-climate Shiraz. Sweet chocolate and vanilla suggest American hogsheads or an American/French mix with significant new wood. The near-syrupy texture indicates long maceration with extended post-fermentation contact; the total absence of green notes confirms late harvesting.

**Wine 4** — Fruit-forward with restrained oak. No toast or vanilla: neutral vessel, old oak or stainless. Light tannin and high acidity indicate short maceration, and the wine reads as bottled early, at 10–12 months.

**Wine 5** — Traditional Cahors built for longevity. Smoky, cedar and bitter-herb complexity over dark fruit points to new and one-use French barriques for 18 months or more. Dusty, firm tannin suggests minimal fining.

**Wine 6** — Deliberately approachable Tannat. Absence of toast points to large-format neutral casks, preserving primary fruit and kirsch. Tannin firm but without Madiran's aggression, suggesting shorter maceration or micro-oxygenation.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (6 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; Cru Bourgeois Supérieur or low Classified Growth equivalent. Concentration and finish exceed simple Haut-Médoc. At €30–45 it sits with fine wine merchants in France, the UK and Asia, competing with top Cru Bourgeois on complexity. At 6–7 years, primary fruit still dominant; another 8–10 years of improvement, holding 15–20, developing tobacco and leather.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding, at Gran Reserva or prestige cuvée level. Fine oak integration and a very long finish support €40–70, competing with premium Ribera del Duero. Export to the USA, UK, Germany and Scandinavia is the natural channel. At 3–4 years it is tightly wound; needs 5–8 more, will hold 15–20.

**Wine 3** — Very good for the Barossa premium tier: above commodity Shiraz, below icon single-vineyard bottlings. At AUD 35–55 it belongs in premium supermarket and independent channels in Australia, the UK and the USA, where Barossa carries strong brand recognition. Ripe tannin makes it appealing now; it will hold 8–10 years but lacks the complexity to improve much beyond.

**Wine 4** — Good, village-equivalent Alsace Pinot Noir, a niche category within its appellation. At €18–28 it competes with entry-level Burgundy and is best placed domestically and in Germany and Switzerland, where Spätburgunder familiarity aids recognition. Drink now to 3–4 years; longer cellaring loses the primary fruit that is its main appeal.

**Wine 5** — Very good, top-tier Cahors. Structural depth and finish exceed basic appellation wine. At €25–45 it reaches independent specialists and fine-dining on-trade in France, the UK and the USA, offering a savoury alternative to Argentine Malbec at the same price. At 5–6 years it is beginning to open; 5–8 further years of improvement, holding 15, gaining leather and dried berry.

**Wine 6** — Good, Reserva-level Tannat, creditable within an emerging fine-wine category. Ripe fruit and moderate oak give it appeal beyond specialists. At USD 18–28 the opportunity is the USA and Brazil, where Uruguay is gaining traction as a South American alternative to Malbec. The commercial constraint is category awareness rather than quality: Tannat remains unfamiliar to most consumers, limiting shelf velocity outside specialist channels, which is precisely why the winemaking has been softened towards accessibility. Drink now to 5 years.

The darker plum and blackberry notes, spice and long gravelly finish exclude a simple carbonic Beaujolais-Villages and point to a cru — Moulin-à-Vent, whose granite and manganese soils give structure and fruit density absent in Fleurie or Chiroubles.

**Wine 1** — Colour depth, spice and finish length rule out full carbonic maceration; semi-carbonic or conventional fermentation has preserved structure alongside fruit. # Mock Answer — Practice Paper 2 (Chinon / Carménère / Lagrein)

## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (3 × 11 marks)

**Wine 1** — Cabernet Franc, Chinon, Loire Valley. Translucent ruby, raspberry, dried herb and violet suggest Pinot Noir first, but the tannin rules it out: fine and powdery yet angular, firmer than Pinot's silk, and the dried-herb/liquorice register is wrong for Pinot. Syrah is dismissed by the absence of pepper, smoked meat and weight. Paprika-edged fruit over pure cassis with a long, precise finish confirms Cabernet Franc. Within that, the cool linearity, chalky-powdery tannin and layered mid-palate favour Chinon over the softer, fruitier Saumur-Champigny or Bourgueil; warmth is restrained, consistent with a cool continental site.

**Wine 2** — Carménère, Maipo Valley, Chile. Deeper, more violet-edged than Wine 1. Roasted capsicum and paprika over cassis and spiced mulberry raise Cabernet Sauvignon, which is the serious alternative — but the tannins are dusty and supple with a juicy finish rather than Cabernet's graphite-and-cedar architecture, and the bramble/pomegranate fruit is too soft-edged. The green-spice-over-ripe-fruit duality with medium-plus length is Carménère's signature. Generous warmth and full body place it in a warm New World origin; Chile dominates the variety, and Maipo's heat with Andean diurnal swing explains ripe fruit retaining freshness.

**Wine 3** — Lagrein, Alto Adige. Opaque purple-ruby, far deeper than either preceding wine; dark plum, bitter chocolate, violet and alpine herb. Nebbiolo matches on tannin intensity but not on colour or fruit richness. Syrah is plausible on violet and dark fruit but lacks the bitter-chocolate grip and mountain freshness. Firm, mouthcoating, faintly bitter tannin with high acidity points to Lagrein, the indigenous variety of Alto Adige, at Riserva level given the structural completeness.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Precise and pure. No vanilla, toast or coconut: no new oak, with concrete or old wood preserving herbal purity and fruit definition. The powdery textural grip on the finish suggests the wine went unfined and unfiltered; the aromatic lift is consistent with indigenous-yeast, low-intervention fermentation.

**Wine 2** — Built for approachability. Soft, dusty tannin and juicy finish indicate a shorter maceration than Wine 3, with cool, controlled fermentation protecting fresh fruit; the absence of pronounced wood spice points to neutral oak or tank. Positioned for near-term drinking, not cellaring.

**Wine 3** — The opposite decision: extended maceration to build the opaque colour and mouthcoating tannin. Integrated wood spice without overt vanilla suggests large botti or older barrique, leaving bitter chocolate and dark plum reading as varietal rather than oak-derived. Riserva implies a minimum two years' ageing, including cask.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding; a single-vineyard or vieilles vignes tier above village Chinon, roughly €25–35. Seamless precision and layered length lift it well clear of generic Touraine Cabernet Franc. Aimed at the engaged fine-wine buyer using Loire red as a cheaper alternative to mid-range Burgundy or Bordeaux; specialist merchants and fine-dining lists in the UK, USA and Scandinavia. Constraint: Chinon's weak name recognition outside that circle.

**Wine 2** — Good quality, Reserva tier, around $12–16. Sound commercial winemaking; competes directly with Chilean Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon Reserva at the same shelf price. Supermarket off-trade in the UK, USA and northern Europe. The variety's unfamiliarity is the obstacle, but it is also the point of difference against yet another Cabernet.

**Wine 3** — Very good to outstanding, Alto Adige DOC Lagrein Riserva, €25–40. Depth and structure match the best of the variety. Sold through specialist Italian lists and fine-dining on-trade in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and the USA, where the region carries premium recognition. Invisible in mainstream retail, but its higher-order commercial value lies in having no New World analogue — a deeply coloured, structured Italian red that gives sommeliers genuine distinctiveness on a premium by-the-glass programme.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 2 Question 1

## Wine 1 — a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Grenache-led, blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre. Sweet cherry and ripe plum, violet lift and baking spice over concentrated but melted tannins at warm, full-bodied weight point to the Southern Rhône; roasted meat and cocoa suggest Mourvèdre, the blue fruit and backbone a Syrah component. Châteauneuf-du-Pape was weighed — the concentration and tannin integration fit — but the finish, though long and fresh, lacks the breadth and complexity of top CdP. Lirac AOC, Southern Rhône.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Traditional and terroir-driven rather than internationally extracted. Harvest at full phenolic maturity; melted, rounded tannins indicate whole-berry fermentation with moderate extraction. Cocoa and baking spice without toast point to older large-format wood — foudres or demi-muids — not new barriques. The long, fresh finish shows fruit concentration held alongside elevated but integrated alcohol.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, upper-tier Lirac at roughly €25–35, competing with mid-level Châteauneuf-du-Pape and outperforming much of it. The commercial argument is value against CdP: equally serious, more accessible. Specialist independents and premium on-trade; exports to the USA, UK and Scandinavia. Drink now to 2030–2033.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Barbera. Deep ruby, brisk tartaric acidity, cherry and redcurrant with bitter chocolate and coffee, and — decisively — low, soft tannin. Nebbiolo is excluded by the absence of savage tannin and by the depth of colour; Nero d'Avola and Montepulciano cannot deliver this acid–fruit cut at this alcohol. The complexity and oak integration indicate a Superiore/DOCG-tier wine: Barbera d'Asti, Piedmont, plausibly Nizza.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

An ambitious rather than everyday Barbera: dense, round palate from low yields and full ripeness. Bitter chocolate, coffee and spice indicate barrique or tonneau ageing with some new oak, well integrated. Where Wine 1 uses old foudres to soften, here oak is purposeful and signals international ambition. No green tartness — malolactic complete. Length comes from both extract and acid.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good to outstanding, DOCG tier, around €22–35. Barbera remains undervalued beside Barolo, which is both the obstacle and the opening: strong quality-to-price returns for Italian specialists and restaurants with deep Italian lists in the USA, UK, Switzerland and Germany. Unsuited to volume supermarket channels. Drink now to 2028–2030.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Malbec. Near-opaque garnet-purple, rose and violet florals, ripe plum and blackberry with a balsamic thread — a saturation and floral lift Cahors does not reach. Body is full, yet the finish is bracingly fresh, and this is the telling detail: lower-altitude Mendoza at this ripeness turns plush and unchallenged. The acid tension implies a high-elevation Uco Valley sub-zone such as Gualtallary or Altamira. Argentina, Mendoza, Uco Valley.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

A premium single-vineyard wine from above 1,000 metres, where cool nights preserve the acidity behind that lift. Soft vanilla only: French barriques, largely second and third fill, since new oak would bury the florals. Plush texture points to moderate maceration and gentle, gravity-fed handling to protect aromatics; tobacco and leather show bottle development. Against Wine 1's warm traditionalism, this is precision winemaking with a deliberately light oak footprint.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, benchmark single-vineyard tier, USD 80–130 — the top of the Argentine fine wine market, priced against Premier Cru Burgundy. The story is named high-altitude provenance, which resonates with US, UK, Brazilian and Chinese fine wine buyers. Specialist importers and fine wine channels; by-the-glass is uneconomic here. The real challenge is winning cellar space from Old World benchmarks at the same price. Drink now to 2035+.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Medium purple-red, lighter than Wines 1 and 3, so a lightly pigmented variety despite evident ripeness. Red berries, dried herbs, oregano, sundried tomato and leather with rounded tannins and balanced acidity: diagnostic of Xinomavro. Nebbiolo shares the tomato-leather and high acid register but would show far more aggressive tannin and paler colour at this stage; Sangiovese and Tempranillo do not give the oregano–sundried tomato combination. Amyndeon PDO, Macedonia, Greece.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

A modern, polished Xinomavro with its habitual angularity smoothed — either longer hang time for tannin polymerisation or extended, temperature-controlled maceration extracting fine-grained rather than green tannin. Vanilla and spice from older or moderately new French oak, well integrated. Uniquely in this flight, the winemaking goal is legibility: bridging a difficult indigenous variety to an international palate without erasing its herbal signature.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good, single-vineyard PDO tier, €20–30. Xinomavro's low recognition abroad is the obstacle and the opportunity, as Greek fine wine expands in the UK, US and Germany among buyers seeking original varieties. Specialist independents and adventurous on-trade; position it at Nebbiolo-curious drinkers wanting that aromatic register more cheaply. Drink now to 2029–2032.

**Wine 1** — Syrah, Crozes-Hermitage, Northern Rhône, France. Black raspberry, dark cherry, pepper, spearmint, and crushed rock point immediately to Syrah. The taut, spice-driven freshness rules out warm-climate Shiraz, which would show jammy fruit and sweeter oak. Grenache was briefly considered but eliminated: the tannin here is more linear and the pepper character distinctively northern rather than the warm strawberry of a southern Rhône wine. The moderate-plus body and mineral precision sit within the Northern Rhône; the wine lacks the sheer density of Hermitage or Cornas, consistent with Crozes-Hermitage's broader, more accessible style.

**Wine 2** — Barbera, Barbera d'Alba DOC, Piedmont, Italy. Crushed berries, plum, blackberry, and violet with high natural acidity and deep colour suggest an Italian red. Dolcetto was eliminated because the tannins here are fuller and the fruit richer. Sangiovese was considered but the absence of sour cherry and the softer tannin structure, combined with the floral violet note, points away from Tuscany. The warm, generous body and elevated alcohol warmth are consistent with ripe Barbera d'Alba, where lower yields produce greater concentration.

**Wine 3** — Tempranillo (with Mazuelo and Graciano), Rioja DOCa, Spain. Cocoa, coffee, lavender, black cherry, cloves, cinnamon, and vanilla cream confirm extended oak maturation. The combination of American-oak vanilla alongside dark fruit and warm spice is the signature of long-matured Tempranillo. Brunello and Barolo were briefly considered for the structural depth, but the vanillin sweetness, the warming spice, and the orange zest note are distinctly Iberian. The depth of development and complexity indicate Gran Reserva level, consistent with a minimum of five years' ageing before release.

**Wine 4** — Malbec, Uco Valley, Mendoza, Argentina. Vivid violet-red colour with fresh red fruit, flowers, herbs, mint, and spice point to high-altitude Malbec. Lower-elevation Mendoza would show riper, jammier fruit. Cahors Malbec was briefly considered but eliminated: the aromatic lift and warmer body point decisively to the New World. Within Argentina, the mineral freshness and mid-weight structure are hallmarks of the Uco Valley rather than the more opulent Luján de Cuyo style.

---

## b) Style and winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, medium-full-bodied, with a long, fresh finish. The purity of fruit and absence of obvious new oak suggest fermentation in stainless steel or neutral vessel, with texture shaped by moderate maceration. The pepper and mineral notes point to minimal intervention and likely modest time in old oak or large vessel before early bottling — a style prioritising terroir expression over wood.

**Wine 2** — Dry, full-bodied, with a creamy texture and ripe, generous fruit. The smooth mouthfeel suggests controlled-temperature fermentation to preserve aromatics, followed by ageing in a portion of French barriques that adds structure without dominating the fruit. Careful extraction management accounts for the absence of harsh tannin. Concentrated palate consistent with low-yielding Alba vineyards.

**Wine 3** — Dry, full-bodied, shaped profoundly by extended oak maturation. Vanilla, cream, and coconut alongside cocoa and coffee point strongly to extended ageing in American oak, consistent with Gran Reserva regulations requiring two years in oak and three in bottle. The remarkable integration of wood suggests the wine has been cellared well beyond the minimum. Fresh fruit and floral notes on the finish confirm the wine retains vitality despite considerable development.

**Wine 4** — Dry, medium-full-bodied, with vivid fruit and notable freshness. The lack of obvious new-oak sweetness suggests large-format used French oak or concrete, which adds slight structure without imparting vanilla or toast. The herbal, floral, and mint character points to cool fermentation preserving primary aromatics — an approach prioritising varietal purity and terroir over extraction or wood.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, mid-tier Crozes-Hermitage: above the appellation's average but below top single-vineyard expressions. Retailing around €20–25, it suits independent merchants and premium on-trade lists, competing directly with serious Crozes-Hermitage and entry-level Saint-Joseph. Primary export markets are the UK, USA, and Japan; the challenge is the appellation's relative obscurity compared to Hermitage, requiring active communication of provenance.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality, upper end of Barbera d'Alba DOC — well above simple Barbera d'Asti but below a prestige single-vineyard Barolo. Retailing around €18–22, it fits specialist retailers and Italian restaurant by-the-glass programmes. Export opportunities are strongest in the USA, Switzerland, and Germany. The challenge is that Barbera remains overshadowed by Barolo and Barbaresco in prestige terms.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding quality, Gran Reserva level from one of Rioja's most respected traditional houses. Retailing €30–45, it belongs on specialist merchant lists and high-end on-trade rather than supermarkets. Its maturity makes it appealing to consumers seeking aged, ready-to-drink fine wine. Strong opportunities in the UK, Germany, and the USA; the challenge is persuading younger consumers that the American-oak style remains relevant alongside modern French-oak-influenced Riojas.

**Wine 4** — Good to very good quality, upper-mid tier Uco Valley Malbec — above generic Mendoza but below top single-vineyard expressions. Retailing around US$20–28, it targets specialist off-trade and premium by-the-glass programmes, competing with Chilean Carménère and Luján de Cuyo Malbec at similar prices. Export strength lies in the USA, UK, and Brazil. The primary challenge is differentiating Uco Valley provenance in markets where all Malbec is labelled simply "Mendoza."

## Wine 1

### a) Variety and region (10 marks)

Deep ruby-purple, pronounced dark plum and violets with a smoky-earthy edge; firm, dusty, chunky tannin and high acidity signal a cool mountain climate. This is **Lagrein from Alto Adige**. Syrah was weighed — it shares violet and dark plum — but the tannin is broader than the Northern Rhône's sleek frame and there is no cracked black pepper. Sangiovese is ruled out by colour depth and the absence of sour cherry. The fruit concentration points specifically to the **Bolzano basin** rather than lighter, higher-altitude sites.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

A structured red built for ageing. Dense, drying tannin suggests extended maceration of 15–20 days at controlled temperature. Dark chocolate and vanilla indicate **French oak barrique**, perhaps 20–30% new for 24 months, supportive rather than dominant. No green tannin despite the firm structure: well-managed ripeness on the basin's sun-trap sites.

### c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, at Riserva DOC level. At 3–4 years it is young; it should improve 5–7 years and hold 10–12 as tannin softens and fruit turns to leather and dried herb. Suited to **specialist merchants and premium on-trade** in Germany, Switzerland and Austria at €30–50; the obstacle is low recognition of Lagrein beyond its home market.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Variety and region (10 marks)

Ripe red cherry and blackberry with a **smoky, rubbery undertone**; juicy fruit, slightly coarse tannin and warmth suggesting mid-14% alcohol. This is **Pinotage from Stellenbosch**. Shiraz shares the dark fruit and smoke but would bring black pepper and sleeker tannin; Malbec would show cedary depth rather than light vanilla. The coarse tannin texture plus cherry lift inside dark fruit is Pinotage's fingerprint, and the oak polish argues Stellenbosch over the more rustic Swartland.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

A **modern, fruit-forward style** deliberately suppressing the variety's acetone character. Clean primary fruit implies cool fermentation around 20–22°C to limit volatile acidity. Light vanilla and chocolate suggest roughly 12 months in a mix of new and older French oak — measured, not the American oak sweetness of older Cape reds. The mid-palate weight hints at old-vine fruit.

### c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good, at reserve tier, around €18–25 export. At 2–3 years it drinks well now and will hold 3–5 more, gaining savoury leather, but gains nothing from long cellaring. Best in **specialist off-trade and Cape-focused on-trade** in the UK, Netherlands and Scandinavia; the opportunity is accessible food-friendliness at mid-market prices, the challenge Pinotage's lingering image problem.

Wine 4 is conversation-driven: USD 35–45 to sommeliers in the USA and Brazil looking past Malbec, a natural grilled-meat match, though its tannin mass rules out glass pours.

#### Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1 — Variety and origin (10 marks)**

Pale-to-medium ruby with a translucent rim; violets, wet leaves, forest floor, red currant and a clear white-pepper edge; medium body, fine but gripping tannin, mouthwatering acidity, moderate perceived alcohol. Cabernet Franc: no other major variety combines violet-and-pepper lift, red currant, herbal savour and fine-grained tannin. Pinot Noir was weighed on the translucency and red fruit but is excluded by the pepper note and firmer tannin grip; Gamay lacks both the aromatic complexity and this structure. Warm-climate Cabernet Franc (Saint-Émilion, Napa) is ruled out by the lack of ripeness and the herbal edge — this is Loire, and the forest floor, root bitters and violet suggest Chinon or Bourgueil.

**Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Vivid primary aromatics indicate early bottling, within about a year. Gentle, whole-berry-inclined extraction explains why tannin is present but never bitter. No vanilla, toast or spice: stainless steel or large neutral vessel, a deliberate choice for purity over structural build-up, with reductive handling shown by the clean, unoxidised palate.

**Quality and maturity (5 marks)**

Very good, village appellation level, around £20. At peak now on primary fruit; will not improve, and should be drunk within two to three years.

---

**Wine 2 — Variety and origin (10 marks)**

Medium-deep garnet; cranberry, red currant, cherry, chocolate and fine tobacco; mineral freshness, firm integrated tannin, long finish, medium-plus warmth checked by acidity — freshness from elevation rather than latitude. Lagrein: the swing between cranberry brightness and dark chocolate over a mineral spine is its signature. Sangiovese was considered on the cherry but shows dried herb and sour-cherry acidity, not chocolate; Merlot offers the softness but neither the mineral grip nor the tobacco. Alto Adige — Dolomitic soils and wide diurnal range.

**Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Fine, fully integrated tannin without extractive dryness suggests a controlled maceration of roughly fifteen to twenty days. The long, oak-integrated finish points to eighteen to twenty-four months in large Slavonian casks with some barrique, consistent with the Riserva minimum. Retained freshness implies tight fermentation temperature control.

**Quality and maturity (5 marks)**

Outstanding at single-vineyard Riserva DOC level, €40–50. Developing but still fresh, approaching peak; will hold four to six years, gaining savoury complexity.

---

**Wine 3 — Variety and origin (10 marks)**

Near-opaque dark crimson; cranberry, black cherry, spicy raspberry, violet, vanilla and a distinct musk; generous alcohol, yet energetic acidity within a full frame — that tension is the interpretive key. Pinotage: musk-and-candy over cranberry and dark fruit is diagnostic, and the freshness indicates a cool, likely elevated Stellenbosch site rather than commodity warm-region fruit. Zinfandel was rejected for the absence of jammy overripeness and the non-Zinfandel musk; Shiraz for a different fruit and tannin texture.

**Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Spice and structural lift beyond typical Pinotage suggest partial whole-cluster fermentation. Vanilla without toast or woody extraction indicates short time in older or large-format French oak. Crucially, no rubber or acetone: precise temperature control and tight SO₂ management, the discipline that separates this from the variety's reputation.

**Quality and maturity (5 marks)**

Very good, single-vineyard Stellenbosch, £20–25 export. Drinking well now, holding fruit for three to four years; no meaningful improvement expected.

---

**Wine 4 — Variety and origin (10 marks)**

Deep garnet, viscous; pronounced black fruit, mulberry, cassis, raisin, black olive, tomato leaf, violet and smoke; chalky, dense tannin with real freshness and a long finish, perceived alcohol around fourteen percent without heat. Tannat: the phenolic density here exceeds anything Malbec shows, which is why Malbec — otherwise plausible on the dark fruit — is out; Petit Verdot is eliminated by the tomato-leaf typicity. Uruguay, Atlantic-influenced coastal vineyards near Montevideo, where full ripeness coexists with more freshness than Madiran.

**Style and winemaking (8 marks)**

Tannin mass on this scale implies maceration of twenty days or more. Integration and sweet spice point to twelve to fifteen months in French oak with an American component supplying the vanilla behind the smoke. The raisin note shows very ripe fruit at harvest, yet acidity survived — early-morning picking or cool nights.

**Quality and maturity (5 marks)**

Very good to outstanding, Uruguayan Reserva level, USD 35–45. Youthful and still austere; three to five years to integrate the tannin, then a decade of holding.

Thymiopoulos, Young Vines, 2022. Naoussa, Greece. (13%)
Diemersdal Estate Pinotage, 2022. Durbanville, South Africa. (14%)
Casa Silva, Los Lingues Gran Reserva Carmenere, 2021. Colchagua Valley, Chile. (14%)

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Cabernet Franc, Chinon, Loire Valley. Medium-depth garnet with morello cherry, roasted pepper and wet earth points to a cool-climate European red. The pyrazine-driven cigar-leaf note, medium-plus acidity and moderately grippy tannins confirm Cabernet Franc over Cabernet Sauvignon, which would show denser cassis and firmer structure. Pinot Noir was ruled out by the herbaceous edge and tannin grip — Pinot at this weight would be silky and green-free. The bone-mineral quality anchors this in Chinon's tuffeau rather than warmer Cabernet Franc from Stellenbosch or Saumur-Champigny.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Traditional and terroir-expressive: dry, medium-bodied, varietal character over intervention. Pure fruit and restrained extraction suggest temperature-controlled fermentation with moderate maceration of 15–18 days. No evident new oak — the earthy spice is varietal, pointing to used foudre or large old vessels. The slight brett is typical of Chinon cellar culture and adds complexity.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good, equivalent to a mid-tier Chinon Vieilles Vignes at €20–25. Suits independent merchants and specialist on-trade seeking Burgundy-red alternatives; the UK, Belgium and US all show demand for Loire reds. Typicity and honest pricing are the commercial assets; the brett may deter modern-style accounts.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Xinomavro, Naoussa, Greece. Dried cranberry, dried herbs and smoky forest floor with firm tannins and genuinely high acidity are the structural anchors. Nebbiolo was the most compelling alternative — the dried red fruit and firm tannin overlap substantially — but the pronounced herbaceous quality, absence of rose-petal and tar, lighter body and less savage grip rule out Barolo or Langhe. Sangiovese was eliminated by the drier, more austere tannin texture versus Chianti's sour-cherry freshness. Dried-fruit intensity with smoky, vegetal character and a long firm finish is consistent with Naoussa.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A modern, fruit-forward style deliberately softening Xinomavro's austere edge. Fresh red fruit and accessible tannins suggest moderate maceration of 10–14 days, preserving primary aromatics rather than maximising extraction. Maturation in old oak or stainless steel presents structure without adding tannin — approachability on release, unusual for this variety.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good to very good, village-level Naoussa PDO, around €15–18. Sits in the fashionable "alternative European reds" category with real sommelier traction; the UK, US and Scandinavia are receptive at this tier. Consumer unfamiliarity is the challenge; the opportunity is on-trade positioning as a terroir-driven discovery.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Pinotage, South Africa. Blueberry, violets and red berry with savoury spice over a velvety, concentrated palate narrow the field. Syrah was considered — spice and violet overlap — but Syrah at this weight would show black olive and smoked meat rather than this bright red-berry register, with firmer tannin. Malbec shares the violet-plum character but would carry more chocolate weight and less red-berry energy. Pinotage, a Pinot Noir × Cinsault crossing, explains the floral lift alongside concentrated, faintly rubbery spice. The clean, unforced fruit fits Durbanville, where Atlantic influence moderates the climate relative to hotter inland sites.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Contemporary and fruit-forward, moving away from the variety's older acetate-tinged reputation. Clean floral dark fruit with soft tannins points to temperature-controlled fermentation and gentle extraction — pump-overs rather than aggressive punch-downs. Medium-plus concentration suggests second-fill French barrique, adding spice integration without overwhelming fruit.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good quality, single-estate Durbanville WO at Reserve level, around R300–400 (£13–16). Fits premium supermarket shelves and mid-market on-trade in the UK, Netherlands and domestically. The variety's image problem persists in some markets; the opportunity lies with buyers who understand how far the style has evolved.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Carménère, Colchagua Valley, Chile. Deep colour with cassis, spiced mulberry and a roasted bell-pepper herbaceousness distinct from Loire raw pyrazine. Cabernet Sauvignon was the obvious alternative given the cassis density, but the softer, more supple tannin and the roasted rather than raw green note confirm the switch; Cabernet at this ripeness would grip harder. Malbec was eliminated by the absence of violet-floral weight and chocolate richness. Warm, generous palate at around 14% perceived alcohol yet with retained freshness points to a cooler altitude site — the Los Lingues sub-zone, where cold nights preserve acidity, explaining why a generous wine reads balanced rather than extracted.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A polished Gran Reserva style balancing ripeness with freshness. Colour depth and concentration suggest hand-harvesting at full phenolic ripeness with maceration of 18–21 days. Spice-framed oak — mulberry and spice rather than overt vanilla — points to 14–18 months in French barrique with a moderate new-wood proportion. Dusty, supple tannins confirm careful sorting and de-stemming to minimise green-tannin extraction.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good, Gran Reserva tier, £15–20 / US$18–24. Principal markets are the UK, US, Brazil and China, where Chilean reds at this price-quality ratio have strong on- and off-trade presence, and the Gran Reserva designation adds shelf stand-out in premium supermarkets. The challenge is differentiating Carménère from familiar varieties at this price; the opportunity is a flavour profile increasingly recognised as a genuine South American original.

# Mock Answer — Three Countries, Three Varieties (Cornas / Barolo / Cederberg Cabernet)

## Wine 1 — a) Variety, Region, Country (8 marks)

Syrah, Northern Rhône, France — most probably Cornas. Dark cherry, blueberry, cured meat and a lifted rose-petal note are the fingerprint of cool-climate Syrah; Grenache was weighed and rejected for its lack of savoury, meaty depth and its higher perceived alcohol. The silky texture with pronounced mineral grip and a medium-plus finish indicates a terroir-driven wine rather than New World Shiraz, which would bring sweeter oak, jammier fruit and more weight. Within the Northern Rhône, the density of fruit allied to that stony grip favours Cornas over Saint-Joseph or Crozes-Hermitage, both lighter-bodied and shorter at this level.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Cool granitic soils and a wind-moderated continental climate concentrate flavour while preserving the linear character in the glass. No vanilla or toast suggests whole-cluster fermentation and little or no new oak — ageing in older or large-format wood. The silky texture and integrated tannin point to short maceration and gentle extraction. Elegance rather than power.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Very good to outstanding, consistent with €40–60 retail. Cornas remains commercially overshadowed by Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie, so offers genuine relative value. Independent specialists and on-trade in France, the UK, North America, plus Japan and Scandinavia; the constraint is small volume and low appellation recognition beyond enthusiasts.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety, Region, Country (8 marks)

Nebbiolo, Barolo DOCG, Piedmont, Italy. Red cherry, spicy plum, violet, liquorice and a raw-beef note over a firm, austere palate with bright acidity and a long finish is diagnostic. Sangiovese was considered but gives a more translucent, lighter wine without this density; Pinot Noir was excluded on the scale of the tannin and the higher perceived alcohol. Within Piedmont, the power, lifted violet and evident oak favour Barolo over Barbaresco, which shows finer, softer tannin.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Langhe warm days and cool nights build the phenolic ripeness Nebbiolo demands; calcareous clay lends the chalky tannin grip. Spice and aromatic complexity suggest French oak, a mix of new and used, in a modern-leaning style that does not bury the fruit. Barolo's 38-month minimum ageing allows tannin polymerisation; this wine feels close to that minimum — tannins are developing but not yet resolved, and will reward five to ten years, when the meaty, truffled tertiary layer emerges.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Outstanding, €50–80, competing with leading single-vineyard bottlings globally. It demands patience, which rules out by-the-glass listings, but commands fine-wine specialist and auction attention in Italy, the USA and the UK.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety, Region, Country (8 marks)

Cabernet Sauvignon, high-altitude South Africa — almost certainly Cederberg, Western Cape. Black pastilles, ripe plum and pencil shavings over firm, chalky tannin is classic Cabernet; Shiraz would have shown pepper and cured meat, Merlot would lack this tannin frame. Warmth and plump fruit indicate a warm season, yet the bright, linear finish signals altitude cooling rather than a coastal or valley site. Napa was weighed and rejected: the tannin is chalky, not plush, and there is no sweet American oak.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Cederberg's vineyards above 1,000 metres give a diurnal range that holds acidity at full phenolic ripeness — the key insight is that what first reads as generous warmth is anchored by structure that altitude, not cool climate, explains. Cedar and pencil shavings indicate French oak with a moderate new proportion; the silky mouthfeel over chalky tannin suggests extended but controlled maceration.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Very good to outstanding, performing above its regional standing at €30–50 and competing with premium Stellenbosch Cabernet. Cederberg is unfamiliar to most consumers; the counterweight is a legitimate altitude-freshness story. Best placed with independent specialists and premium restaurant lists in the UK, USA and Germany, where the South African fine-wine narrative has traction.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (4 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Cabernet Franc, Chinon, Loire Valley, France. Red berries, violet, green pepper and graphite, with silky tannins and moderate alcohol (~13%), point to a cool-climate red of modest structure. Syrah was considered — graphite and violet could fit — but Syrah shows smoked-meat character, deeper colour and firmer tannin. Pinot Noir was weighed for translucency and red fruit, but green pepper and anise are diagnostic of Cabernet Franc. Within the Loire, graphite minerality rather than the chalkier profile of Saumur-Champigny points to Chinon on tufa and gravel soils.

**Wine 2** — Lagrein, Alto Adige, Italy. Deep ruby-violet, morello cherry, dark chocolate, plum and cocoa nibs show real complexity. Barbera was considered for deep colour and dark cherry, but lacks this chocolatey richness and shows tartly higher acidity. Blaufrankisch was another candidate — violet and dark fruit fit — but the velvety tannin and cocoa depth, in a distinctly Italian mineral register, point firmly to Lagrein. The sheltered valley floor delivers ripeness and concentration while Alpine soils contribute lift — a paradox no lowland Italian red replicates.

**Wine 3** — Pinotage, Coastal Region, South Africa. Black cherry, mulberry, smoked meat, truffle and sweet oak spice, with an earthy, rubbery undertone, point to this variety. Syrah was initially considered, but South African Shiraz shows more pepper and olive; mulberry and the rubbery register are diagnostic of Pinotage. The broad Coastal Region designation is consistent with quality-focused but commercially positioned producers.

**Wine 4** — Malbec, Uco Valley, Mendoza, Argentina. Pronounced floral aromatics, sweet entry, wide mid-palate and integrated French oak are hallmarks of a high-altitude, cool-diurnal site. Carmenère was considered — both share deep colour and floral notes — but Carmenère shows green pyrazine character and angular structure absent here. Floral purity combined with freshness at full ripeness points specifically to Uco Valley above 1,000 m, distinguishing it from rounder, lower-acid Luján de Cuyo Malbec.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Fresh and fruit-forward. Fermentation in stainless steel, short maceration (~10–15 days) and completed malolactic fermentation explain the silky mouthfeel. The absence of toasty character confirms early bottling within 12 months, without barrel contact.

**Wine 2** — A structured Riserva approach. Extended maceration of three to four weeks built the dense tannin frame. Maturation in French oak barriques — around 40–50% new, for at least 18 months — contributes vanilla and cocoa overlay. Full malolactic fermentation smoothed Lagrein's naturally firm tannins, and pre-release bottle ageing has knitted the layers together.

**Wine 3** — Basket pressing signals deliberate low-intervention extraction, avoiding the coarse tannin Pinotage can show under harder pressing. Ageing in French barriques for 12–18 months with a moderate proportion of new oak (~25–30%) adds sweet spice. Oxidative handling during barrel ageing accounts for the smoked-meat and truffle development rather than primary fruit alone.

**Wine 4** — Cold-soak extracted vivid colour and floral aromatics before alcohol built. Fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel, followed by ~12 months in French oak with modest new oak (~20–30%), delivers integrated spice. High-altitude natural acidity removed any need for acidification, preserving the freshness that defines Uco Valley Malbec.

---

## c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Good quality, mid-tier Chinon AC. At two to three years old it is ready now and will hold for a further three to four years as red fruit shifts toward savoury, tobacco-inflected notes. Retails around €15–20 through independent specialists and mid-range on-trade, competing with entry-level Saumur-Champigny and lighter Bourgueil. Strongest in France, Benelux and the UK.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding quality, comfortably at Riserva DOC level. At three to four years the tannins retain a firm core; this will develop over five to seven more years, adding dried fruit, leather and tar while shedding primary chocolate and plum, holding for 12–15 years from vintage. Retails around €35–50 through specialist on-trade and fine-wine retail, competing with premium Blaufrankisch Riserva from Burgenland. Italy is the primary market; secondary opportunity in Germany, Switzerland and the UK.

**Wine 3** — Very good quality, premium Coastal Region Pinotage, above entry-level but below top single-vineyard Stellenbosch expressions. At three to four years old it is at or near its peak, holding for a further three to five years as smoked-meat and truffle deepen. Retails around €18–25 export in the premium off-trade and on-trade by-the-glass segment. Export strength in the UK, Netherlands and Germany; basket-press positioning helps counter residual consumer prejudice against the variety.

**Wine 4** — Very good quality, Reserva-level Uco Valley Malbec, clearly above commodity but below top single-vineyard expressions. At two to three years it is drinking well now and will improve modestly for three to four further years as florals integrate and fruit deepens toward dried violet and dark plum. Retails around USD 18–25 in premium supermarket and mid-range restaurant channels, competing with Chilean Carmenère and mid-range Californian Cabernet Sauvignon. The altitude and Uco Valley provenance narrative provides clear differentiation across the USA, UK, Brazil and China.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 2 Question 1

## Wine 1 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Barbera, Barbera d'Asti DOCG, Piedmont. Vivid purple-ruby: high anthocyanin, no Cabernet opacity. Sour cherry, blackberry, violet and bitter almond — the almond note is Piedmontese Barbera's fingerprint. Decisively, pronounced mouthwatering acidity sits above unusually light tannin, a combination almost unique among Italian reds. Nebbiolo ruled out: it would deliver far higher, drying tannin, rose and tar, and a paler garnet rim. Asti over Alba on the brighter, less structured, more overtly fruited profile.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A modern, fruit-forward Barbera, not an old-style oxidative one. Freshness and violet lift suggest whole-berry fermentation with gentle extraction. Vanilla and tobacco are discreet: large format or a small share of new barriques, since extended new oak would smother the acidity. MLF is complete — the mid-palate is rounded — yet primary sour cherry survives, indicating bottling at around twelve months. Clean, reductive handling; no VA or brett.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good; Superiore-level Barbera d'Asti, £18–24. Two to three years old, drinking well now, holding three to four more before prune notes emerge and acidity dominates. Independent merchants and mid-market Italian restaurants in the UK, Germany and USA, where appetite is growing for structured but approachable Italian reds beyond Tuscany.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Pinotage, Stellenbosch, South Africa. Opaque ruby, high viscosity. Black plum and cedar wrapped in smoke, with a tarry, faintly rubbery undertow that is Pinotage's calling card. Shiraz is the plausible alternative — dark fruit plus smoke — but Syrah gives pepper and a firmer, finer tannin spine, not this broad, dense, slightly acetone-edged palate. Warm coastal origin from the ripe weight and high-moderate perceived alcohol. Stellenbosch over Swartland: cedar-framed new oak and polish rather than Swartland's whole-bunch, sauvage handling.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Reserve tier, deliberately internationalised. Colour and extract imply ten to fourteen days on skins with active cap management. Cedar and sweet spice suggest French barriques, perhaps thirty percent new, over twelve to sixteen months. Tannins are polished rather than rustic, so extraction was temperature-controlled with gentle pump-overs; full MLF gives the creamy mid-palate. Crucially, none of the burnt-rubber reduction that afflicts cheap Pinotage — this is clean, ripe-fruit-driven fruit selection.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good, £20–28. Three to four years old and harmonious; a further four to five years before the fruit dries and oak asserts. Premium South African specialists, fine-wine retail in the UK, Scandinavia and the Netherlands, and on-trade seeking an alternative to same-price Malbec or Shiraz. The Reserve positioning is the point: it separates the wine from the commodity Pinotage that damaged the variety's name.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Blaufränkisch, Eisenberg DAC, Südburgenland, Austria. Dark cherry and blackcurrant carry an alpine herbal signature — bay leaf, hibiscus, black olive, liquorice — over a flinty, iron-like mineral base. Tannins are fine-grained and lacy; acidity linear and fresh. Zweigelt was weighed and rejected: it gives softer, rounder tannin and lacks this earthy, saline grip. Pinot Noir is excluded by colour depth and the blackcurrant-olive-liquorice register. Eisenberg rather than Mittelburgenland on that ferrous minerality and the leaner, less upholstered frame.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Restraint is the defining choice here, and it separates this wine from every other in the flight. No new-oak toast: fine tannin and pure primary fruit point to older or large-format barrels, possibly acacia, adding structure without flavour. A faint smoky reduction on the finish indicates low-oxygen, minimal-intervention handling. Gentle extraction in open-top vessels explains delicate tannin at this fruit concentration, and the vertical acidity argues for partial rather than full MLF.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding — top-tier Eisenberg DAC, £25–35. Three to four years old, just opening, with six to eight years of development ahead towards leather, dried herb and greater mineral complexity. A sommelier's wine: Austrian-focused independents, Scandinavian monopolies, and lists rewarding lesser-known European reds with site identity. It matches serious Nebbiolo and northern Rhône on quality and beats them on price.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Carménère, Colchagua Valley, Chile. Deep red-violet; cassis and spiced mulberry lifted by roasted green pepper — partially resolved pyrazine, Carménère's signature. Merlot is the real alternative, sharing plush tannin and dark fruit, and the two were historically confused in Chile; but ripe Merlot does not give the roasted capsicum note or the pomegranate-toned red-fruit layer found here. Dusty, supple tannins and medium-plus length indicate a warm but moderated site — the higher-altitude eastern Colchagua, where diurnal range preserves that pyrazine lift alongside full phenolic ripeness.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Gran Reserva-tier modern Chile. Juicy fruit and soft tannin imply a restrained eight to twelve day maceration under temperature control to protect aromatics. Oak supports rather than leads: medium-toast French, mixed new and used, around twelve months. Most tellingly, the tannins are ripe and dust-fine despite the herbaceous nose — harvest was timed for tannin ripeness, with the pyrazine retained as a house style rather than avoided as a fault.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality, Maturity, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good, £15–22. About three years old and at peak; three to four years further, though the green note will grow as fruit fades. Premium supermarket and specialist retail in the UK and Germany, plus casual-dining on-trade. Its competitive set is Argentine Malbec at the same price, against which its varietal distinctiveness is the selling point; USA and Japan are secondary export targets.

---

## Wine 5 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Touriga Nacional, Dão, Portugal. Deep ruby-garnet, pronounced intensity; violet and pine needle over red fruit, chocolate and oak — only Touriga combines that florality with this structural weight. Tannins are assertive and mouthcoating, matched by fruit concentration: a variety built for ageing. Douro was the serious alternative and would show darker, denser fruit and greater alcoholic warmth; the mineral precision, cooler red-fruit register and elegant rather than opulent body point to Dão's granite and altitude. The flight's finest wine.

## Wine 5 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

A varietal bottling of a grape usually blended — itself a quality statement. Preserved florals alongside chocolate spice indicate cool, controlled fermentation before oak. The firm astringency reflects a long maceration, fourteen to eighteen days, exploiting thick skins. Chocolate and vanilla depth suggests French barriques with perhaps forty to fifty percent new wood for eighteen months — a level of oak the fruit absorbs without strain. MLF complete; no malic edge under the structure.

At two to three years it is still primary, tannins firm and fruit unintegrated; it should improve markedly for five to seven years, gaining dried meat and black olive, then hold a further five. £35–50 through independent merchants, destination restaurant lists and collectors, with UK, USA, Japan and Switzerland the premium markets. Malbec, Uco Valley, Mendoza. Dense purple, viscous, with plum, blackberry and vivid violet. Cabernet Sauvignon is excluded by the silky rather than angular tannin and by plum in place of cassis; Petit Verdot shares the floral lift but would grip harder. Polished and modern, concentrated but not overworked. The silky texture points to a controlled two- to three-week maceration with gentle pump-overs, building structure without harshness. **Wine 1 — Grenache-led blend, Priorat DOQ, Spain**

Rioja Garnacha is eliminated by the mineral precision and density here — llicorella schist, steep slopes and old vines give exactly this translucency with savoury length.

**Wine 2 — Grenache, McLaren Vale, South Australia**

Deeper ruby-purple, broader and more opulent, with black and blue fruit and greater perceived warmth (~14.5%+); tannins coat more widely though still soft. Warm-climate Grenache. Barossa was the alternative, but Barossa examples run heavier and jammier; the defined fruit profile and firmer acid line point to McLaren Vale.

**Wine 3 — Pinot Noir, Nahe, Germany**

Pale-medium translucent ruby, red cherry, violet, light forest floor, silky fine tannin, high acidity — Pinot Noir. Burgundy was the obvious call, but the flinty, near-volcanic minerality and sun-kissed, polished fruit read German rather than Côte de Nuits earthiness. Pfalz was rejected as richer and lower in acid at this ripeness; the Nahe's volcanic and slate soils explain the flint.

**Wine 4 — Nerello Mascalese, Etna DOC, Sicily**

The pale, Burgundian silhouette invites a Pinot call, but pronounced volcanic smoke, graphite, tart wild strawberry and rose florality are not Burgundian. High acidity, fine-medium tannin, saline iron palate. Nebbiolo was considered on colour and tannin but is ruled out by the floral vibrancy and absence of tar. Benchmark Etna Rosso.

---

## b) Style and winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Priorat**

No vanilla or toast: neutral or large-format maturation rather than new barriques. Gentle traditional maceration has preserved aromatic lift and given fine tannin despite the warm origin. Deliberately site-expressive rather than a modern extractive blockbuster.

**Wine 2 — McLaren Vale**

Built on ripe fruit and palate weight. Extended maceration explains the mouthcoating tannin and colour depth; the absence of overt new oak alongside that density indicates older barriques or large vessels adding texture, not flavour. Hedonistic where Wine 1 is restrained.

**Wine 3 — Nahe Spätburgunder**

Destemmed, gentle fermentation with a short controlled maceration — hence the polished tannin and pure fruit rather than whole-bunch stalkiness. Neutral vessels (old barriques or foudres) leave the flinty minerality unmasked. A reductive, Burgundy-influenced philosophy transplanted to Germany.

**Wine 4 — Etna Rosso**

Large old botti: aromatic freshness retained, slow oxidative evolution, no wood flavour imposed. The saline iron note and sweet-sour fruit tension are terroir, not intervention; the clarity of finish suggests minimal fining and filtration. Southern concentration in a Burgundian frame.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1 — Priorat**

Outstanding; a top-tier Priorat DOQ bottling at roughly €35–55 cellar door, more in export. Competes with premium Rhône and Spanish fine wine through independent specialists and fine-wine on-trade in the US, UK, Germany and Scandinavia. The constraint is recognition: Priorat still trades in Rioja's shadow, capping volume even where quality-to-price is compelling.

**Wine 2 — McLaren Vale**

Very good to outstanding old-vine Grenache, around AUD $80–120 domestically, aimed at the premium Grenache bracket against Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Priorat in the US and UK. Opportunity: rising interest in terroir-driven Australian Grenache. Challenge: persuading markets that see Australia as Shiraz country to accept Grenache at this price.

**Wine 3 — Nahe Spätburgunder**

Very good, Grosse-Lage equivalent, around €30–45. Sits against Baden and Pfalz domestically and entry Burgundy Village internationally — arguably outperforming the latter. The commercial argument is precisely that undervaluation relative to Burgundy, which suits independent specialists and premium on-trade in the UK, US and Japan; German red still lacks broad consumer recognition.

**Wine 4 — Etna Rosso**

Outstanding, benchmark for the DOC, €40–70 export. Competes with Burgundy Village and Premier Cru on style rather than imitation, and belongs in fine-wine specialists and Michelin-level lists, especially the US and UK where volcanic terroir has become a fine-wine category in its own right. The higher-order point across the flight: three of these four wines — Priorat, McLaren Vale, Etna — succeed commercially by borrowing Burgundy's or the Rhône's reference points while offering translucent, low-extraction styles from hot climates, a repositioning of warm-region red wine away from weight toward transparency. Etna's remaining obstacle is convincing buyers that Sicily sustains Grand-Cru-adjacent pricing.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 2 Question 1

## a) Grape variety and country/region of origin (6 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Syrah, Northern Rhône, France (Côte-Rôtie). Deep ruby, pronounced roasted dark cherry, smoked meat, black olive, pepper, dried violet and truffle: the savoury-smoky Syrah fingerprint. Warmth is restrained (~13.5%), pointing to a moderate European origin. Barossa Shiraz was the main alternative — same grape, but it would show sweeter American-oak coconut, jammier fruit and more heat. The floral lift, savouriness and cedar oak rule it out. Within the Northern Rhône, the perfumed violet top note and body lighter than Hermitage place it in Côte-Rôtie rather than Crozes.

**Wine 2** — Grenache (Cannonau), Sardinia, Italy. Deep ruby with garnet rim, warm (~14.5%), ripe black cherry, cranberry, hibiscus, dried fig and dried herbs — a hot Mediterranean red. Grenache over Syrah because there is no pepper or smoked meat, and the cranberry/hibiscus red-fruit register is Garnacha's. Primitivo and Nero d'Avola were weighed: both fit the heat, but neither gives dried cranberry with leather and tobacco over velvety rather than grippy tannin. Cannonau di Sardegna at riserva ripeness.

**Wine 3** — Tempranillo, Navarra DO, Spain. The most restrained wine here: medium ruby, red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, cedar, red liquorice, medium finish. Warm spice with red fruit and cedar, lacking Syrah's smoke or Grenache's herbal-cranberry lift, says Tempranillo. Rioja was the competing call and is ruled out by the lighter body, the absence of the dill-coconut American-oak signature and the lack of Reserva structure; the herbaceous lift suits Navarra's cooler northeast. Navarra Garnacha was dismissed — insufficient breadth and alcohol.

**Wine 4** — Cabernet Sauvignon, Stellenbosch, South Africa. Cassis intensity, minty lift, chewy grippy tannin, long finish. Bordeaux would give more graphite and restraint; Napa would be plusher and warmer. Coonawarra also shows mint and cassis, but the tannin weight and gravelly, earthy depth read as the Simonsberg/Helderberg foothills, where altitude preserves aromatic freshness in a moderately warm climate.

**Wine 5** — Cinsault-Syrah-Cabernet blend, Bekaa Valley, Lebanon. Deep purple, medium-plus intensity, strawberry, cherry, violet, mango, earthy depth, peppery finish — no single variety resolves it. Strawberry-violet suggests Cinsault, the pepper Syrah, the frame Cabernet; oak is absent entirely. Southern France uses the same varieties but would show firmer extraction and more structured tannin. The Bekaa is the established fine-wine region where these three co-exist at this modest warmth and aromatic register.

**Wine 6** — Pinot Noir, Patagonia, Argentina. Pale ruby, medium-minus viscosity, light plum, glacé cherry, white pepper, pink musk, cocoa; juicy berry and cardamom on the palate — young, primary, cool-climate Pinot. Burgundy fits the grape but the fruit is riper and lacks forest-floor depth. Central Otago shares ripe cherry and spice, but the glacé-cherry sweetness and musk read South American. Patagonia's cool, high, windswept sites give exactly this bright register without Mendoza's warmth.

---

## b) Style and winemaking (6 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Full-bodied, savoury, mostly primary with tertiary development beginning. Pure fruit and no phenolic edge suggest careful extraction; the vanilla, cedar and dark chocolate indicate French barriques, around 30% new, for 18–22 months. The smoked-meat and truffle complexity points to partial whole-cluster fermentation, the Northern Rhône signature. Polished tannins imply a ripe vintage.

**Wine 2** — Where Wine 1 uses stems for lift, this wine's shaping decision is extended maceration in a hot vintage, giving dense but velvety tannin alongside dried fig and leather. The integrated, non-intrusive vanilla and spice suggest large neutral botti rather than new barriques. Fully dry despite high sugar at harvest.

**Wine 3** — Medium-bodied, fruit-forward, made for early drinking. No toast, vanilla or coconut: fermentation and maturation in inert vessel or neutral wood, preserving primary cherry and raspberry. Minimal intervention, clean and technically sound, built for accessibility rather than ageing.

**Wine 4** — Structured yet fruit-forward. Pronounced cassis and firm, chewy tannin indicate a longer, temperature-controlled maceration; cedar and dark chocolate suggest 40–50% new French oak for 14–18 months. Unlike Wine 1, the freshness here is viticultural rather than stem-derived — cool-site fruit retaining mint. Built for medium-term ageing.

**Wine 5** — Light to medium-bodied, aromatic, entirely unoaked. Stainless steel, restrained skin contact and early bottling preserve the vivid strawberry-cherry-violet. The blend is assembled for aromatic expressiveness rather than structure, and the refusal of wood is the defining stylistic decision.

**Wine 6** — Bright and primary. Glacé cherry and musk with no tertiary development show a young wine, gently handled: short cool maceration of roughly a week, possibly some whole berries given the juicy brightness, matured in older wood or inert vessel with no detectable new oak.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (6 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; village-level Côte-Rôtie, around €40–55. Complexity, length and integration place it clearly above Crozes-Hermitage. Specialist off-trade and fine-dining on-trade in the USA, UK and Scandinavia. It is drinking well now and will gain meat and truffle depth over 8–12 years. The commercial challenge is justifying the premium over cheaper Northern Rhône appellations.

**Wine 2** — Good to very good, Cannonau di Sardegna riserva level, roughly €15–22. Velvet texture and length are notable for the DOC. It undercuts Châteauneuf-du-Pape on a similar flavour profile — its clearest selling argument — with Germany, Switzerland and the USA the natural markets. Drink over five years; the low international profile of Sardinia versus mainland Italy is the obstacle.

**Wine 3** — Acceptable to good DO Navarra Tempranillo, €8–12. Everyday drinking without the structure to face Rioja Reserva; drink within two years. Supermarket and casual by-the-glass listings, competing with Rioja Joven and entry Ribera. Price-quality is favourable but differentiation in a saturated entry-level Spanish category is the difficulty.

**Wine 4** — Very good, upper-tier estate Stellenbosch Cabernet without single-vineyard status, about $25–35. Concentration and tannin structure lift it above commodity Cape Cabernet; it will improve for 6–10 years as the mint softens into cedar. USA, UK and Asian fine-wine channels, positioned as a serious Napa alternative at two-thirds the price. The story to tell is altitude-driven freshness.

**Wine 5** — Good for an entry-level Bekaa red, around $15–20. Fresh and aromatically appealing but not age-worthy; drink within three years. Its market is the appetite for under-represented origins — specialist independents, natural-wine-adjacent retail and diaspora communities in the USA and UK. Political instability and fragmented supply chains undermine on-trade listing confidence.

**Wine 6** — Good varietal Patagonian Pinot Noir, $18–25. Clean and competent but lacking the site definition of Central Otago or the depth of Village Burgundy, against which it competes by the glass. Value is its weapon: recognisable Pinot character below New Zealand pricing. USA, UK and Brazil. Drink within three years; the task is establishing Patagonia as a distinct premium origin separate from Mendoza.

Under the skin, the flight is a study in how much of a red wine's identity is decided by oak: Wines 1 and 4 are shaped by new French barriques into age-worthy statements, Wine 2 by neutral cask into texture, and Wines 3, 5 and 6 by the deliberate absence of wood into immediacy — three different price arguments made with the same varietal raw material.
