**Wine 2 — Nebbiolo, Barolo DOCG, Piedmont, Italy.** Garnet with a bricking rim; rose petal, clove and tar over taut, savage tannin. Sangiovese was the alternative — shared high acid and tannin, but no rose-and-tar register and less phenolic austerity. Warmth (~14.5%) fits a warm recent vintage; the lean, focused rather than plush palate suggests a single vineyard on the Serralunga axis.

**Wine 3 — Pinot Noir, Marlborough, New Zealand.** Translucent, no purple density. Primary cherry and plum with Earl Grey, fennel seed and loam — riper and more primary than Burgundy's forest-floor restraint, which ruled that out. Gamay lacks this fruit weight and structural depth. Perceived alcohol ~13.5%, integrated, fits Marlborough's high sunshine with cool nights; the tea-and-loam character separates it from Central Otago's darker, denser style.

**Wine 4 — Tinta de Toro (Tempranillo), Toro DO, Castilla y León, Spain.** Ruby-purple, violet rim, high viscosity: young, concentrated, hot inland origin. Tempranillo was the hypothesis, but fruit density and warmth (~14.5%) exceed Rioja Reserva. Wild blackberry over raspberry and thick palate weight indicate Toro rather than Ribera del Duero's more polished fruit.

---

## b) Style and winemaking, with particular reference to oak maturation (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** is full-bodied, dry, reductive and single-varietal. Silky tannin alongside pepper spice suggests partial whole-bunch inclusion. Cedar and spice within, not over, the fruit indicate French barrique for 12–18 months at perhaps 20–30% new — oak for structure, not flavour.

**Wine 2** is traditional in build. Taut, firm tannin with no vanillin sweetness points to large-format Slavonian oak rather than new barriques; the tar and spice are varietal. Predominantly neutral vessels allowed slow oxidative development without wood flavour, leaving a wine far tighter and less approachable than Wine 1.

**Wine 3** prioritises fruit expression. Earl Grey and fennel imply some whole-cluster fermentation, adding aromatic complexity without tannin density. Oak is moderate — a mix of old and new French, roughly 20–25% new for 10–12 months — so cherry and loam lead. The reverse of Wine 4, where wood speaks first.

**Wine 4** carries the flight's most overt oak: vanilla sweetness from American oak with French-derived dried spice. Its short maturation, likely 3–6 months at Roble level, imparts flavour without building the structural complexity of a Crianza or Reserva — a deliberately approachable commercial construction.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** is outstanding, at single-vineyard Cornas level, around €60–90. Independent merchants and high-end restaurant lists in the UK, USA and Japan. Cornas's lower profile beside Hermitage caps volume but gives value-focused buyers comparable quality for less money.

**Wine 2** is exceptional, benchmarked at single-vineyard Barolo, €80–120 upwards, competing with top Burgundy and Bordeaux through auction, specialist retail and premium on-trade. The strong vintage supports pricing, but 10–15 years' cellaring is required — a real commercial obstacle among consumers used to New World drinkability.

**Wine 3** is very good, upper-tier Marlborough Pinot at roughly €25–40, competing with premium Willamette Valley and Burgundy village wines. Freshness and accessibility suit premium by-the-glass and independent specialists in the UK, USA and Scandinavia; it lacks the concentration for fine-wine positioning against Central Otago's top single vineyards.

**Wine 4** is good — honest, fruit-driven, below the Crianza and Reserva tier where Toro's serious wines sit. At €8–15 it belongs on premium supermarket shelves and in independent off-trade in Spain, Germany and the UK. Bold fruit and visible oak deliver flavour at everyday prices, but insufficient complexity and length to threaten wines above €20.

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; a single-domaine Saumur-Champigny at €18–25, clearly above generic appellation level on aromatic finesse and finish length. Premium independent specialists and sommelier lists in the UK, USA and Japan, where Loire Cabernet Franc has a committed following. Drink now to 2028; it will hold but not deepen materially.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding; Grosses Gewächs level, the top dry-red tier of the VDP classification, at €50–80. Competes with premier cru Burgundy on quality and undercuts it on price. Specialist importers and fine-dining lists in Germany, the USA and Scandinavia. Will improve five to eight years, gaining dried fruit, tobacco and earth, then hold a further five.

**Wine 3** — Good to very good; premium single-vineyard Mendoza Malbec at USD 25–40, competing with Luján de Cuyo and Uco single-vineyard bottlings. Approachable without losing identity: premium off-trade and by-the-glass in the USA, UK and Brazil, where Malbec has ready consumer recognition. Drink now to 2027.

**Wine 4** — Very good; Ried (single-vineyard) Blaufränkisch, the apex of the Südburgenland DAC hierarchy, at €25–40. Austrian domestic market plus independent specialists in Germany, Switzerland, the USA and UK. The commercial obstacle is name recognition, which makes it a sommelier's recommendation rather than a shelf purchase — its peppery freshness and structure sell it as a Burgundy alternative by the glass. Drink now to 2030, improving over three to four years.

Under the skin, three of these four wines are cool-climate reds built on acid and fine tannin rather than extract, and each earns its price from site articulation; the outlier, Wine 3, sells on varietal recognition instead — which is precisely why it is the cheapest per unit of quality and the easiest to place.

# Mock answer — Paper 2, four-wine quality-hierarchy question

## a) Identify the grape variety (20 marks)

Nebbiolo. All four are pale-to-medium garnet with a watery, already-bricking rim despite obviously youthful fruit — a thin-skinned, low-anthocyanin variety. Aromatically: dried rose petal, sour cherry, tar and liquorice, gaining truffle and dried orange peel as one moves up the flight. The palate is the killer evidence: searing tartaric acidity sitting alongside very high, fine-grained but drying tannin, carried on a warm, medium-full frame I would read at 13.5–14.5%. That double severity of acid *and* tannin at such pale colour is diagnostic. Sangiovese was weighed — it shares the pale hue and high acid, but its tannin is markedly softer and its markers are dried herb and tomato leaf, not rose and tar. Pinot Noir matches the colour but could never carry this tannin load. Xinomavro is the nearest mimic, yet shows more olive and volatile lift and lacks this sweet, resinous tar.

## b) Region and level in the hierarchy (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Piedmont, Langhe DOC: the entry tier. Least warmth of the flight, bright primary cherry, shallower tannin, short finish — younger vines or declassified fruit, released early.

**Wine 2** — Barolo DOCG, a multi-commune "classico" blend; village-equivalent. Warmth to ~14.5%, tar and truffle emerging, tannin more architectural, but the mid-palate broadens rather than narrowing to one site.

**Wine 3** — Barolo DOCG, single MGA on the cooler western rim, Novello/Ravera side. Taut, saline, vertical, near-austere tannin: elevation plus Sant'Agata marl.

**Wine 4** — Barolo DOCG, single cru, Castiglione Falletto — a Rocche-type sandy marl. Perfume is the tell: greater florality, tannin powdery rather than vertical.

## c) Style and winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** Fruit-forward, oak invisible. Destemmed, 10–14 days' maceration, gentle pump-overs, malolactic done, a year in large old botti — tannin softened, no toast. Bottled early.

**Wine 2** More serious, still approachable: three weeks on skins, submerged cap, then roughly two years split between barrique (a little new — faint cedar) and botti. Blending across communes buys consistency.

**Wine 3** Longer, cooler maceration around 30 days and 30-plus months in large casks; extraction has been pushed because the site's acid can carry it.

**Wine 4** Infusion, not extraction — minimal working of the cap to protect aromatics, then extended élevage in neutral wood. Here is the tension: 14.5% of warmth with rose petal wholly intact. That is not an over-ripe hot year; it is picking on aromatic ripeness on free-draining sand, where sugar accrues faster than perfume is lost.

## d) Commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** ~US$28, independents and by-the-glass; the gateway Nebbiolo against Ripasso and Chianti Classico. Challenge: tannin unfamiliar to entry drinkers.

**Wine 2** ~US$70, specialist retail and premium supermarket fine-wine bays; competes with village Burgundy and Brunello annata. Volume backbone of the estate.

**Wine 3** ~US$130, allocated, fine-wine merchants, US/Japan/Scandinavian monopolies. Needs eight years — capital tied up.

**Wine 4** ~US$220+, Michelin lists and auction; collector demand secure, but priced against Grand Cru Burgundy, its scarcity both defence and constraint.

# Mock answer — Paper 2, six wines / six countries

## Wine 1

**a) Grenache-dominant Southern Rhône blend — Lirac.** Deep garnet, medium(+) viscosity; broad, warm and generous on the palate with alcohol assessed around 14.5% but carried without burn, moderate acidity and ripe, grippy tannin. The pronounced garrigue — thyme, rosemary, lavender — laid over ripe black cherry and black olive tapenade is the signature of Grenache on stony Mediterranean soils, with peppery dark fruit and a leathery edge indicating Syrah and Mourvèdre in support. Châteauneuf-du-Pape was weighed first, but the frame is narrower and fresher than a Châteauneuf, with an iron-graphite mineral line rather than that appellation's kirsch breadth and sweeter alcohol; Gigondas would give cooler blue fruit and a firmer acid line from altitude. Châteauneuf ripeness on a slightly leaner build points across the river to **Lirac**.

**b)** Old vines are implied by the concentration at moderate yields. The dark fruit purity with no stalky green edge suggests destemming of the Syrah and Mourvèdre, with a long maceration of around three to four weeks to build that tannin. Oak reads as cedar and cocoa dusting rather than vanilla or coconut — older large-format demi-muids, no new barriques, roughly 12–18 months — a deliberately non-interventionist élevage intended to frame fruit and site.

**c)** Very good to outstanding, sitting at the very top of its appellation and matching lower-tier Châteauneuf. Retailing around £30–35, Independent Specialists and serious on-trade lists, offering Châteauneuf character at a discount to consumers who track appellation value. Drink now to eight years.

## Wine 2

**a) Pinot Noir — Nahe, Germany.** Translucent medium ruby, medium body, high fresh acidity, silky fine-grained tannin and modest warmth assessed near 13% — the lightest structural build in the flight. Red cherry, wild strawberry, rose petal and violet with a faint forest-floor savoury note confirm Pinot Noir. A Côte de Beaune village wine (Volnay) was the obvious alternative, but the higher-toned red fruit, the smoky-stony minerality rather than Burgundian sous-bois, and the near-absent new oak point instead to Germany; Baden would be riper and broader. The taut acid line and chalky slate grip narrow this to the **Nahe**, single-vineyard level.

**b)** Careful sorting and gentle handling — no extraction excess. Largely destemmed with cool fermentation and hand plunging to keep tannin fine; oak is neutral, older barrels for roughly 12 months, giving integration rather than flavour, the restraint itself being the key decision. Malolactic completed in barrel, giving the silky texture without any buttery overlay.

**c)** Very good quality, equivalent to a good Erste Lage / GG-level Spätburgunder and to Village-plus Burgundy, around €40–45. Sells to sommeliers and Burgundy-literate collectors in Germany, the UK and Scandinavia; the challenge remains persuading buyers to pay Burgundy money for German Pinot. Drink now, improving three to five years, holding ten.

## Wine 3

**a) Cabernet Sauvignon — Maipo Valley, Chile (Puente Alto).** Deep ruby with high viscosity, full-bodied, dry, medium(+) acidity, medium(+) firm tannin and warmth around 14%. Blackcurrant, plum and cedar over a distinctive tarragon-and-basil herbal lift is Cabernet. Napa was considered and rejected: this has more energy, brighter cranberry acidity and less sweet-oak plushness. Bordeaux was rejected for the fruit ripeness and viscosity. The **under-the-skin marker** is that full ripeness held taut by medium(+) acid and a juicy, lifted finish — that combination reads as diurnal shift on the Andean alluvial foothills, not as heat; a warm-flat site would have given the same ripeness with flabby acid.

**b)** Hand-harvested, fully destemmed, fermented warm with regular pump-overs for gentle but complete extraction; extended post-ferment maceration explains the firm yet resolved tannin. Cedar and dark chocolate without coconut indicate French barriques, perhaps 60–80% new, for 18–20 months, with the oak already knitted in.

**c)** Outstanding, a genuine world-class Cabernet — Chile's icon tier, benchmarking with First Growths and Napa cults at $150–300. Fine-wine merchants, auction and collector channels in Asia, the US and UK. Its challenge is that Chile's price ceiling is imposed by reputation, not liquid.

## Wine 4

**a) Frappato — Vittoria, south-east Sicily.** Light ruby, low viscosity, light body, low tannin, medium(-) acidity, moderate alcohol, with a faint prickle of CO2 and a medium(-) finish. Violets, lavender, wildflowers, raspberry and orange peel over a saline undertone. Gamay was the strongest alternative, but Beaujolais would show tarter granitic acidity and more crunch; Cinsault was possible, though the wildflower perfume and citrus-peel lift are more specific. The soft acidity is atypically low for the variety and reads as a warm vintage in a Mediterranean maritime site — **Frappato from Vittoria**.

**b)** Picked early to hold alcohol down; a substantial whole-bunch fraction with very short, cool maceration to keep extraction minimal. No oak flavour at all — inert vessels, likely concrete or terracotta amphora. The spritz and the absence of hard edges point to minimal SO2 and no filtration.

**c)** Good quality at DOC Vittoria level, around £22–25. Sells through Independent Specialists and natural-leaning by-the-glass programmes in London, New York and Copenhagen, competing with chillable light reds; drink within two years, served cool.

## Wine 5

**a) Syrah-dominant blend — Yarra Valley, Victoria.** Medium-full body, fine but firm tannin, fresh acidity and warmth around 13.5%. Violet, cranberry and plum with fragrant five-spice, cigar-box and cardamom; a savoury-sweet interplay and a faint apricot floral lift suggesting a white co-ferment. Côte-Rôtie was the leading alternative given the violet and the co-fermentation signature, but the absence of reductive bacon fat and the sweeter, polished spice and brighter cranberry point to the New World. Hawke's Bay would be leaner; this is **Yarra Valley**.

**b)** Co-fermentation with a small white fraction, plus Mourvèdre, is deduced from that perfumed lift and savoury tail. Whole-bunch inclusion explains the spice and tannin tension; open-top fermentation, foot-treading, ageing in older French barriques for around 18 months — oak as structure, not seasoning.

**c)** Outstanding, benchmark Australian Syrah, A$100+, comparable to Northern Rhône cru wines. Fine-wine retail and premium restaurants in Australia, plus UK and Asian export. Improving five to eight years, holding fifteen.

## Wine 6

**a) Chenin Blanc — Swartland, South Africa.** Gold, medium(+) viscosity, dry, with pronounced dried apricot, quince, candied orange, beeswax, lanolin, roasted nuts and light rancio over persistent saline stoniness; alcohol reads modest, near 12%. Mature Loire Chenin was considered but the acid line is less searing and the fynbos herbaceousness and salinity are not Loire; Jura Savagnin was rejected because sous-voile character would dominate over this quince-and-apricot fruit weight. Old dryland bush vines on granite — **Swartland**.

**b)** Early picking for freshness; whole-bunch pressed, wild-fermented, no MLF given the tight acid; long élevage in old foudres on full lees with deliberately permissive oxygen exposure producing the rancio, minimal SO2 and no filtration.

**c)** Outstanding, at the summit of the Cape white hierarchy, £55–65, sold to sommeliers and collectors in the UK, US and Scandinavia. Will improve a decade.

**Wine 2 — Gattinara Riserva DOCG, Piedmont**
In contrast, this shows a ruby with notable orange rim alongside a more open nose of red cherry, strawberry, rose, and leather — markers of greater evolution. The palate is mineral and spiced, with a lighter frame and more accessible tannins than Wine 1. The cooler aromatic register and lower perceived weight suggest northern Piedmont's higher-altitude granite soils. Distinguished from Barolo by its lighter, more ethereal style; the evolved tannins confirm *Riserva* level.

## c) Style and winemaking

**Wine 1**
Concentrated dark fruit and broad tannin texture indicate a traditional approach: extended maceration in large Slavonian oak *botti grandi*, yielding tannic mass and oxidative development without overt vanilla. No new oak character is perceptible, and integration suggests minimum five years' ageing before release, consistent with Barolo Riserva requirements.

**Wine 2**
Brighter red fruit, floral lift, and mineral edge point to shorter extraction preserving freshness on granite terroir. Subtle vanilla hints suggest brief small-oak contact, though primary character remains intact. The transparent style reflects northern Piedmont terroir and a winemaking approach prioritising aromatic delicacy over tannic weight.

## d) Commercial position

**Wine 1**
Outstanding quality at the top of the Barolo DOCG hierarchy — Riserva, single-vineyard — retailing around £80–120 through specialist independents and fine dining. Principal markets are Italy, the US, and the UK, targeting consumers seeking serious, ageworthy Nebbiolo.

**Wine 2**
Very good quality, Gattinara Riserva DOCG, retailing around £35–55. An under-the-radar alternative to Barolo for the MW-literate consumer, positioned in specialist independents. Competes with Ghemme and Lessona, offering compelling value within the northern Piedmont hierarchy.

# Mock answer — Paper 2 Question 1

## Wine 1

**a) Cabernet Sauvignon, Mediterranean southern France — the Alpilles/Provence hinterland (IGP or equivalent, not Bordeaux).** Clear ruby of only medium depth with medium-plus viscosity, and a nose of Morello cherry and raspberry over cocoa, roasted hazelnut, menthol and dried aromatic herbs. Structurally: medium-plus acidity, only medium tannin, full body but moderate warmth on the finish, ~13.5%. Syrah was the first alternative, but the pepper here is a Timut-like lift rather than the crushed-black-pepper/violet core of Syrah, and the cool menthol-cedar edge with a graphite-free, sinewy tannin is Cabernet's signature. Bordeaux was eliminated: no gravelly austerity, and the pronounced garrigue herb and warm cherry fruit point south. The combination of Cabernet ripeness with garrigue and only medium tannin narrows to a warm, dry, stony Provençal site farmed for freshness.

**b) Style and winemaking.** A deliberately restrained, savoury, terroir-first style rather than an extract-driven one. The silky, un-drying tannin indicates gentle, long maceration with infusion rather than heavy pumping-over, and destemming (no stalky green edge). Vanilla and toast are subtle and secondary to fruit — consistent with maturation in older, large-format neutral oak, perhaps 18–24 months, with minimal new wood. Low intervention: no acidification evident, and the vibrant freshness suggests early picking by southern-French standards.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Outstanding quality, comparable to a Cru Classé Graves in complexity but idiosyncratic in style; the long, spiced, cool-herb finish confirms top-tier fruit. Retails around €70–90 despite the modest appellation tier — a collector's wine sold through Independent Specialists and fine-dining lists in Paris, London, New York and Tokyo. Challenge: the humble appellation name makes the price hard to justify to a supermarket shopper.

## Wine 2

**a) Nero d'Avola, western Sicily (Contessa Entellina area).** Deep ruby, high viscosity, pronounced blackberry and blackcurrant with balsamic hints, black pepper and sweet toast; medium-plus acidity, medium-plus velvety tannin, full body, and clear warmth on the finish — ~14%. Merlot was considered for the flesh and blackcurrant, but the marked sapid, almost saline grip and balsamic top note are Sicilian rather than Bordelais. Primitivo would show riper, jammier confiture and lower acid. The retention of medium-plus acidity at this ripeness level indicates a high-altitude inland Sicilian site rather than the coastal plain.

**b) Style and winemaking.** A polished, internationally styled *cru* — ripe but not raisined, so a careful picking window. Sweet toast and coconut-free vanilla suggest around 12–14 months in French barriques, a proportion new, with malolactic in barrel giving the velvety mouthfeel. Fermentation warm with extended post-ferment maceration for the tannin volume, then fining/filtration for the polished clarity.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Very good to outstanding, the estate's flagship DOC tier rather than generic Sicilia DOC; around €50. Sold through premium restaurant lists and specialists in Germany, the US and Japan; competes with Etna Rosso *contrade* and Tuscan IGT reds. Opportunity: Sicily's rising fine-wine credibility; challenge: consumer unfamiliarity with the DOC name.

## Wine 3

**a) Pinot Noir, coastal Chile — San Antonio/Leyda.** Colour is deeper than classic Pinot, but the medium body, medium tannin, medium-plus acidity and modest ~13.5% warmth, with sour cherry, strawberry, thyme, white pepper and a reductive smoky-cedar note, are Pinot. Syrah was ruled out by the lack of tannic frame and the red-fruited, translucent-textured palate. Burgundy was eliminated: no forest floor, and the sesame/smoke reduction plus dried Mediterranean herb reads New World coastal. The cool ocean-driven acid line with ripe fruit points to Chile's coastal ranges over Central Otago, which would give greater thyme-free purity and higher acid still.

**b) Style and winemaking.** Modern, fruit-forward but savoury. The reduction indicates minimal SO₂ handling and lees contact; some whole bunch is possible given the peppery lift, but there is no stalkiness. Cold soak for colour, then ferment in open vessels; well-integrated oak suggests ~10 months in used French barrels.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Very good quality — an estate/single-vineyard tier, around $25–30, well above generic Chilean Pinot but short of Burgundy Village depth. Independent retail and by-the-glass in the UK, US and Brazil; competes with entry Central Otago and Sonoma Coast Pinot on value.

## Wine 4

**a) Syrah/Shiraz, Eden Valley, South Australia.** Deep crimson, pronounced spiced plum, blue and black cherry, sage, bay, anise, crushed black pepper and cedar; medium-plus acidity, medium-plus fine velvety tannin, full body, generous warmth ~14.5%. Cabernet was excluded by the absence of cassis/graphite and by the fleshy blue-fruit core; Grenache by the depth of colour and tannin. **The tension here is the giveaway: this ripeness of plum and this alcohol should flatten the acid, yet the line stays taut and the pepper survives — that combination is diurnal-swing altitude, not simply heat, which places it on the Eden Valley hills rather than the Barossa floor.**

**b) Style and winemaking.** Old-vine, single-site expression: concentration comes from low yields rather than extraction. Fully destemmed, warm ferment with heading-down for tannin ripeness, MLF in barrel, then ~18 months in French hogsheads with modest new wood — cedar not coconut, so French rather than American oak.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Outstanding; a benchmark Australian single-vineyard red equivalent in standing to a top *cru* Hermitage, around A$150–200. Fine-wine merchants, allocation lists, auction interest; strongest in Australia, UK, US and Asia. Challenge: Shiraz's commodity image caps discovery at this price.

## Wine 5

**a) Garnacha, Priorat DOQ, Spain.** Deep ruby, high viscosity, high firm tannin, medium-plus acidity, full body and pronounced warmth — ~15% — with black cherry, plum, graphite, garrigue, orange peel, black tea and spicy oak over a stony, licorice-inflected core. Syrah was considered but the tannin is more mouthcoating-schistose than peppery-fine; Tempranillo would show American-oak vanilla and less mineral grip. The graphite-and-schist signature with orange-peel lift at this alcohol confirms llicorella slate rather than Montsant or Jumilla.

**b) Style and winemaking.** Powerful but not over-extracted: old low-yielding bush vines, hand harvest, destemmed, long maceration, then ~14–18 months in French barriques with a portion new — the wood is fine-grained and spicy rather than sweet. Youthful, unevolved, so recently bottled with minimal filtration.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Outstanding, a Vi de Vila/single-estate top tier, around €70–100. Specialist retail and Michelin-level lists in Spain, the US and Northern Europe; competes with Ribera del Duero *reserva* and Châteauneuf. Needs 3–5 years to shed its tannic youth.

## Wine 6

**a) Carignan, Swartland, South Africa.** Medium-depth ruby, medium body, medium fine-grained tannin, medium-plus acidity, ~14% — red berry, blueberry, anise, black pepper, baked clay, graphite and cedar, with a striking blood-orange note. Syrah was weighed but the fruit is redder and the frame lighter; Cinsault would be paler and softer still. The dry-farmed, sun-baked clay character with high acid retention and savoury sapidity points to bush-vine Carignan on Swartland's decomposed granite and schist near the coast.

**b) Style and winemaking.** Deliberately old-school and low-intervention: whole-bunch component giving the peppery lift, natural yeasts, gentle foot-treading, then maturation in large old foudres — no discernible new oak, only faint cedar. No fining, minimal sulphur.

**c) Quality and commercial.** Outstanding for South Africa and world-class in its idiom, around R900/£60; allocated through specialists and sommelier lists in the UK, Scandinavia and the US. Competes with Northern Rhône and Swartland peers; challenge is convincing buyers to pay Rhône money for a Cape red.

## Wine 1

### a) Variety and region (12 marks)

Deep purple, pronounced blackberry and dark plum with liquorice, graphite and dried herbs, wrapped in smoky vanilla-cedar oak: **Tempranillo**. Full-bodied, warm (mid-14%), medium-plus acidity. Garnacha was weighed and rejected — the colour is far too deep and the tannin too dense and firm; Syrah too, since the peppery Northern-Rhône signature is absent and the coconut-vanilla oak points elsewhere. The mix of American and French oak, balsamic herbal lift and ripe structure place it in **Rioja**, at single-vineyard or Gran Reserva level rather than Crianza, given the graphite depth and length.

### b) Style and key winemaking (6 marks)

Concentrated, modern-classical. Extended maceration explains the dense colour and grippy tannin; the coconut-vanilla is American oak, the graphite and cedar French — a blend of barrel types, and fully integrated, implying at least 18–24 months in wood before a dry finish.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, Gran Reserva equivalent, €40–60 — the apex of Rioja's Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva ladder. Suits fine wine retail and top on-trade in the UK, USA, Germany and Japan, competing with flagship Ribera del Duero and Priorat for collectors of age-worthy Iberian reds. Drinking now; will gain for five to eight years as the oak recedes and the balsamic notes turn savoury.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Variety and region (12 marks)

Translucent ruby, wild strawberry and raspberry with curry leaf, roasted herbs and smoky granite; medium body, high acidity, fine powdery tannin. This is **Garnacha**. Tempranillo, the obvious same-country alternative, is ruled out by the pallor, the acid level and the fine-grained rather than angular tannin; Syrah by the lifted red perfume and absence of pepper.

Crucially, this freshness is inconsistent with warm, low-altitude Garnacha from Priorat or the south. The granite minerality, earthy undertone and restrained warmth (~13.5%) indicate high-altitude, decomposed-granite soils: **Sierra de Gredos**, where old vines yield tension and smoky precision rather than sun-baked sweetness. The granitic cut is the tell.

### b) Style and key winemaking (6 marks)

Reductive and low-intervention. Whole-cluster or partial destemming, fermented in neutral vessel — concrete or old oak — accounts for the pure fruit and negligible oak imprint. Chalky tannin and high natural acidity suggest native yeast and no correction; the smokiness is textural, not barrel-derived. Bottled early, hence the primary fruit.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good to outstanding, €25–40. Gredos is prestigious but still developing, lacking Rioja's formal classification — so quality here exceeds what the label tier implies. Suits specialist independents, natural wine bars and progressive on-trade in the UK, Scandinavia, USA and Japan, positioned against artisan Priorat Garnacha and village Burgundy for drinkers buying terroir and rarity. Limited volume and low regional awareness remain the constraint.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 2 Question 1

## Wine 1 — Rosé, France

### a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Pale salmon, dry, light-bodied, with medium-plus acidity and strawberry/white flower aromatics. Grenache-led rather than Syrah-led: no peppery or meaty character, and the palate is rounder and fruit-sweeter than Cinsault alone would give, which would be lighter-framed still. Weight and acidity are too low for Tavel and lack Bandol's structure, placing this in the high-volume Provençal idiom.

**Conclusion:** Grenache-dominant rosé, IGP Var / IGP Méditerranée, Provence, France.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

The very pale colour and absence of phenolic grip indicate direct pressing rather than saignée. Cool stainless-steel fermentation with cultured yeast gives pure primary fruit; a faint vanilla lift suggests staves or chips rather than barrel work. Malolactic blocked — the lemony acid line is intact — and early bottling to protect freshness.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good quality, IGP tier, £12–15. Competes with entry-level Côtes de Provence AOP in premium supermarkets and by-the-glass programmes in the UK, Scandinavia and North America. The category is crowded; the pale-and-dry Provençal cue is what sells it. Drink now.

---

## Wine 2 — Malbec, Argentina

### a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Deep ruby-purple, medium-plus body, with raspberry, blueberry, violet and a white-pepper edge. Syrah was the serious alternative — shared dark fruit and floral lift — but ruled out by the absence of bacon fat or olive and by the polished, medium-minus tannin rather than Syrah's angularity. Pinotage dismissed: the fruit is far too clean. Cola, eucalyptus and nutmeg over juicy black cherry, plus warmth and integrated French oak, point to Mendoza; the concentration and length argue for a named sub-region rather than generic Mendoza.

**Conclusion:** Malbec, Luján de Cuyo / Uco Valley, Mendoza, Argentina.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Low yields and a warm season behind the density. Pump-overs during fermentation have given ripe but non-aggressive extraction. Around 12 months in French barriques — praline and spice, not the coconut of American oak. Malolactic complete, giving the round mid-palate. Reserva-level élevage aimed at polish rather than power alone.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, Reserva tier, £18–22. Distinguished from Wine 5 by fruit-forward accessibility rather than structural ambition. Specialist off-trade and steakhouse on-trade in the UK, USA, Brazil and Canada. The Reserva tier is now crowded; the Malbec name still carries it. Drink over 5–7 years.

---

## Wine 3 — Cabernet Sauvignon blend, Lebanon

### a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Deep purple, medium-plus tannin and body, long finish. Blackcurrant, plum, bell pepper, tobacco and earth: the pyrazine lift over cassis is diagnostic of Cabernet Sauvignon, and rules out Syrah, which would offer olive and pepper instead. The medium acidity — not the tartaric bite of cool-climate Cabernet — combined with warm body, game and dried-earth complexity, indicates a hot continental Levantine site at altitude where Cabernet ripens fully yet keeps herbal lift.

**Conclusion:** Cabernet Sauvignon (predominant), Bekaa Valley, Lebanon.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Cold soak of several days to gain colour without harsh tannin, then extended post-ferment maceration to explain the tannin volume and its integration. Around 30–40% new French barriques for 12–18 months adds cedar without covering the fruit. Malolactic complete. Unlike Wine 5, oak here supports an older, more traditional Bordeaux-modelled style.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality; top Bekaa tier, £20–28. Sold through specialist importers in the UK and US, diaspora restaurant trade, and sommelier lists seeking a point of difference. Consumer unfamiliarity is the obstacle; scarcity and regional story are the lever. Drinking well now, developing 5–8 years.

---

## Wine 4 — Nerello Mascalese, Sicily

### a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Translucent ruby, medium-minus body, high acidity, fine tannins — pale for its evident structural seriousness. Cherry, strawberry, balsamic, dried herbs and leather. Sangiovese was the closest call, but the dusty tannin and dried-tomato note of Tuscany are absent and the mid-palate carries a saline-volcanic tension instead. Pinot Noir ruled out by that same balsamic warmth and herbal spice, foreign to cool-climate Pinot.

**Conclusion:** Nerello Mascalese, Etna Rosso DOC, Sicily, Italy.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Gentle whole-berry fermentation with minimal extraction — Nerello punishes hard handling. Roughly 12 months in old oak or chestnut botti, giving leather and balsamic without vanilla. Acidity suggests malolactic was partial at most. The philosophy is transparency: the site, not the cellar, is doing the work — the opposite of Wine 5's cellar-shaped build.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, Etna Rosso DOC, £20–28. Sells to fine-wine specialists and volcanic-terroir-literate sommeliers in Italy, the UK and the USA. The market for lighter, high-acid warm-climate reds is expanding; the challenge is that the variety name means nothing to most consumers, so the appellation must carry it. Drink now to 6–8 years, improving.

---

## Wine 5 — Cabernet Sauvignon, South Africa

### a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

Inky and opaque, the deepest wine here. Pronounced black pastille, black cherry, cedar and pencil shavings — graphite and cedar are structurally Cabernet, not Syrah's smoked meat and olive; Merlot is far too soft for this density. Chalky tannin, warm medium-plus body suggesting around 14.5%, yet a vibrant acid line beneath. That paradox — full phenolic ripeness with mountain freshness — is the higher-order point: it indicates an elevated, cool site within a warm country, not a warm valley floor, which would give softer acid and rounder tannin.

**Conclusion:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Cederberg, Western Cape, South Africa.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Extended maceration of 20–30 days with regular pump-overs explains both colour and the chalky, polymerised tannin. Around 30–40% new French oak for 18 months, restrained relative to the fruit weight. Malolactic complete. Cellar work calibrated to longevity rather than early appeal — the distinguishing decision against Wine 3's more immediate oak sweetness.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality; benchmark Western Cape Cabernet, £30–40, competing with top Stellenbosch reserve bottlings and entry Napa. Fine-wine specialist retail and premium on-trade in the UK, USA, Netherlands and Germany. A mountain appellation still building recognition is the constraint; competition results and critical scores are the route through. Cellar 10–15 years.

---

## Wine 6 — Pinot Noir, Australia

### a) Variety and origin (10 marks)

The lightest colour in the flight, medium-minus body, medium-plus acidity, medium-minus fine tannin. Dark cherry, cranberry, pomegranate, orange rind, wildflowers and a green stemmy spice. Gamay was weighed and rejected: it lacks this aromatic layering and savoury undertow. Burgundy at this quality would show more forest floor and less overt fruit sweetness; the ripe cherry core with whole-bunch lift and gentle alcohol warmth reads New World maritime cool-climate.

**Conclusion:** Pinot Noir, Mornington Peninsula, Victoria, Australia.

### b) Style and winemaking (8 marks)

Partial whole-bunch inclusion — the stemmy spice and reductive lift are deliberate, not faulty. Predominantly older French oak, barrique and larger format, with minimal new wood, keeping fruit transparent. Short, gentle maceration suited to Pinot's tannin. Malolactic complete. Where Wine 4 achieves lightness through site, this achieves it through restraint in the cellar.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality, premium single-region rather than prestige cuvée, £25–35. Competes with mid-tier Central Otago and cool-climate Sonoma. Fine-wine specialist retail and premium on-trade in the UK, USA and Asia. Opportunity: cool-climate Australian Pinot as a credible Burgundy alternative; challenge: New Zealand undercuts it on price. Drink now to 5–8 years, gaining savoury complexity.

That coconut points to American oak, and American oak allied to medium tannin, medium(+) acidity and only gentle warmth (a moderate 13.5% band) is a Rioja fingerprint. Sangiovese was weighed — sour cherry overlaps — but its tarter acid line and drying, austere tannin are absent here. Ribera del Duero was the closer alternative and is ruled out: I would expect deeper colour, more muscular tannin, higher perceived alcohol and French rather than American wood.

**Wine 2 — Rioja Alta/Alavesa, same Tempranillo base.** Garnet throughout, sour cherry, laurel leaf and a distinctly brackish, iodine savouriness. Fuller than Wine 1 — medium(+) tannin, body and warmth (nearer 14%) — yet the acid holds a juicy tension that no warm Rioja Baja site would retain at that ripeness; that combination reads as high-altitude limestone-clay, not heat. Crucially, the oak here has been absorbed into structure rather than flavour: long ageing in *old* casks, not new ones, which is why a wine with obvious bottle age shows no sweet vanilla at all.

## b) Style and key winemaking/maturation decisions (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** is a fruit-forward, early-drinking style. Destemmed, temperature-controlled stainless-steel ferment with restrained extraction (hence medium tannin), full malolactic, then around twelve months in older American barriques — vanilla and coconut present but no toast or grip — and early bottling to protect primary fruit.

**Wine 2** is traditional and oxidatively handled. Riper selected fruit, longer maceration for the firmer tannin, then roughly two years in old American casks with repeated rackings; that slow air contact explains the laurel/iodine and garnet, followed by extended bottle age before release. No new-oak masking, minimal filtration.

## c) Official category and maturity (2 × 4 marks)

**Wine 1** — Crianza. Ready now, at 3–4 years old; will hold 3–4 years but gain nothing.
**Wine 2** — Gran Reserva. Around 8–9 years old, fully mature, drinking beautifully; the acid and tannin will carry it 6–8 more years before the fruit dries.

## d) Commercial position (2 × 3 marks)

**Wine 1** — a premium-supermarket and high-street workhorse at £11–14, a reliable Rioja for everyday buyers; competes with Côtes du Rhône and Chilean Merlot.
**Wine 2** — Independent specialists and by-the-bottle restaurant lists at £35–45, sold to collectors in the UK, US and Switzerland who want mature wine without paying classed-growth prices.

A flight containing a Cabernet-dominant blend, a Pinot Noir, and a garrigue-and-cassis southern red sits uniquely within France, which produces benchmark examples of all three in distinct zones.

## b) Region and variety (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Pauillac, Bordeaux. Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant blend.**
Blackcurrant, graphite, cedar, tobacco, and iris on the nose; chalk, mint, and firm fine-grained tannins on the palate. Left Bank Bordeaux is clear. St-Estèphe lacks the iris and graphite purity; Margaux shows softer, more fragrant tannins. The sweet cherry roundness mid-palate confirms a Merlot component in the classic Pauillac proportion.

**Wine 2 — Gevrey-Chambertin, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy. Pinot Noir.**
Translucent ruby; red berry, cherry, tobacco, and cedar with a saline, vibrant palate. High acidity and fine tannin rule out Gamay and Cabernet Franc. The tobacco complexity and saline mineral thread point to the Côte de Nuits over the Côte de Beaune; the structured length and Premier Cru concentration suggest Gevrey-Chambertin rather than Vosne-Romanée, which would show more silk and less grip.

**Wine 3 — Pays de l'Hérault, Languedoc. Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant blend.**
Garrigue, cassis, crushed violets, cardamom, and cocoa — medium-plus acid, medium-minus tannin. The cassis and structured mid-palate point to a Cabernet Sauvignon lead, unusual in the region and implying a terroir-focused estate. Warmth of spice and dried herbs is consistent with the Hérault rather than the more structured appellations of Roussillon.

## c) Style and winemaking (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Structured, age-worthy. Creamy mid-palate texture alongside graphite and espresso indicates French oak barrique maturation with a significant proportion of new wood. Fine chalky tannins and length suggest extended maceration. Full malolactic fermentation is evident from the roundness behind the firm frame.

**Wine 2** — Restrained, terroir-expressive. No overt oak vanilla or toast; old or neutral oak, possibly larger vessels, allows the saline mineral thread and red fruit purity to lead. Whole-cluster inclusion or minimal destemming is likely, adding tobacco and cedar spice. The bright acidity retained suggests partial malolactic fermentation.

**Wine 3** — Richer and Mediterranean-influenced despite moderate tannin. Cocoa, mocha, and vanilla point to French barriques with moderate new oak. Garrigue and cassis purity suggest careful sorting and longer maceration to build colour and aromatic depth without over-extraction — consistent with the medium-minus tannin given the evident fruit concentration.

## d) Quality and commercial position (3 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding quality; Second Growth Pauillac level. Concentration, complexity, and length indicate classified growth status, retailing at £80–120. Best placed with fine-wine specialists and premium restaurant lists in the US, UK, Hong Kong, and China.

**Wine 3** — Very good; well above generic IGP Pays de l'Hérault, equivalent to a high-performing artisan Languedoc estate. Both wines display the structural fingerprint of Sangiovese — sour cherry, dried herb, high acidity, firm chalky tannin, and savouriness. **Wine 2** — Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG. Deeper garnet, pronounced dark fruit, citrus peel, moss and sweet spice, compact grippy tannin, and notably higher viscosity point to the appellation's apex designation. Vibrant acidity holds the concentration together, consistent with a single-vineyard site.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Fruit-forward and approachable. Ripe cherry and integrated spice suggest fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel, then around 18 months in a mix of large Slavonian casks and some barriques. Well-managed maceration avoids harsh tannin; the wine is made for medium-term enjoyment rather than extended cellaring.

**Wine 2** — Concentrated and structured for ageing. Compact tannin and pronounced dark fruit indicate longer skin maceration for greater phenolic depth. Approximately 25% new French oak barriques followed by large-cask maturation deliver complexity without aggressive wood. Dried mushroom and savoury notes signal partial tertiary development already underway, underpinned by single-vineyard fruit and careful picking.

## c) Quality and maturity (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, ~€20–30. Approximately two to three years old. Primary and secondary characters are well-integrated; drink now to 2030 without meaningful further improvement.

## d) Commercial positioning (8 marks)

Wine 1 competes in the premium off-trade and casual on-trade — independent specialists and mid-range restaurant lists in Italy, the UK and Northern Europe — alongside Riserva-level Chianti Classico and entry-level Barolo. Wine 2 targets the fine-wine channel exclusively: specialist merchants, high-end restaurant lists, and auction, competing with Brunello, Barolo Riserva and top Super-Tuscans. The US, Switzerland and Japan are primary export opportunities. ## a) Country and Region of Origin (3 × 8 marks)

All three are **Italian**: high firm acidity throughout, tannin present in every wine, and savoury, restrained fruit rather than the plusher New World register. The aromatic continuum — dried rose and tar, sour cherry and dried herb, wild berry and spice — is Italian, not French or Iberian.

**Wine 3 — Calabria, Cirò DOC.** Cranberry, wild berry and plum with supple tannin and a fresh finish indicate a warm south, yet the acidity stays bright — **Gaglioppo** in **Cirò**. Primitivo was ruled out: it would show jammier fruit and higher perceived alcohol. Monastrell was dismissed for the absence of lavender-herbal lift.

---

## b) Style and Winemaking (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** Traditionally made: clean, precise fruit suggesting whole-berry ferment, then extended maceration for the fine, firm tannin. No vanilla or sweet toast — large neutral botti, not barrique. Dry, medium-plus body, very high acidity, long savoury finish.

**Wine 2.** Medium maceration in steel or cement, preserving vibrancy. Density beyond basic Chianti suggests old vines and fruit selection; a discreet cedar-spice overlay indicates some French barrique, polishing rather than masking the variety. Structured for mid-term development.

**Wine 3.** Short, temperature-controlled maceration to avoid over-extracting a grape that turns tannic in heat, giving supple texture. Large or neutral vessels, no toast or vanilla. Clean, medium-bodied, immediately expressive.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding, unequivocally DOCG level: aromatic precision and length place it above village Langhe and among better single-vineyard bottlings, short of the finest Riservas. Approximately £35–55, fine-wine independents and premium on-trade; US, UK, Germany and Japan. Category awareness is the issue — Barbaresco still trades commercially in Barolo's shadow at equal quality.

**Wine 2.** Very good, Riserva or Gran Selezione tier, clearly outperforming annata in concentration. Around £20–30, independent specialist and restaurant channel, undercutting Brunello while offering real cellar-worthiness. A crowded appellation makes differentiation hard without producer recognition; the opportunity is growing demand for food-friendly, terroir-driven Italian reds under £30.

**Wine 3.** Good quality — honest, characterful and varietally typical, a solid DOC expression rather than a fine-wine statement. Around £10–15, for independent merchants and progressive supermarkets seeking value alternatives to Sicilian and Puglian reds. Neither grape nor appellation is recognised outside Italy, so the realistic route is positioning as a discovery wine for adventurous buyers.

The flight's underlying lesson is that Italian tannin quality, not fruit weight, tracks the hierarchy here: fine and dusty at the top, firm and structural in the middle, deliberately softened at the bottom — each the product of a maceration decision calibrated to the market the wine is built for.

Translucent ruby colour, red cherry and strawberry fruit, high but refined acidity and fine-grained tannin at moderate perceived alcohol point decisively to Pinot Noir. Gamay was weighed — it shares the pallor and red fruit — but the structural depth and tannin presence in both wines exceed it. Nebbiolo has the acidity but would bring deeper colour, tar and far more savage tannin; absent here.

France is equally clear: an earthy, mineral undertow, restrained rather than sweet fruit, and no confected cherry or overt vanilla of New Zealand or Oregon. German Spätburgunder was considered and rejected — the vinous weight and earth-and-spice architecture here are more Gallic than the lighter, higher-toned German register.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions

**Wine 1 — Alsace Pinot Noir**
Medium-plus intensity: strawberry, red cherry, orange zest, fennel seed, over a lively minerally palate with delicate tannins. The sappy tannin quality suggests partial whole-cluster; oak is limited to faint wood and caramel, so older Burgundian barrels, not new. A short maceration of ten to fourteen days, cool fermentation and early bottling have preserved fragrance. Freshness, not extraction, is the goal.

**Wine 2 — Côte de Nuits Grand Cru**
A different register. Pronounced rose petal, violet, lavender, sandalwood and soy; a muscular, focused palate building slowly to a long, austere finish. Despite that density, oak sits well behind the fruit — perhaps 20–30% new, fully integrated. The austere, slow-building tannin indicates extended maceration of around twenty to twenty-five days with gentle pigeage, extracting depth without hardness. The higher-order point: Wine 2's concentration comes from site and low yields, and the winemaking is therefore subtractive, while Wine 1's charm is actively built in the cellar.

## c) Quality and commercial position

**Wine 1**
Very good quality, comparable to a well-made Village Burgundy, at €25–40. Alsace Pinot Noir is underexplored by consumers who read the region as white-only: a differentiation opportunity on independent merchant and on-trade lists, but a category with little pull. Switzerland, Germany and Belgium are natural export homes; UK and US specialists would buy the story.

**Wine 2**
Outstanding, Grand Cru level, several thousand euros at release and more at auction. Distribution is self-selecting — négociant allocations, auction, top restaurant cellars — and the only commercial issue is scarcity. A benchmark for collectors in Asia, the US and Europe.

## a) Country of Origin and Grape Variety (4 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — France, Cabernet Sauvignon-led Bordeaux blend.** Blackcurrant and damson with sooty, graphite minerality over firm, polished medium-plus tannin and pronounced acidity gives a classic Left Bank structure. Body is medium — conspicuously lighter than Wines 1 and 4 — with medium-plus acidity. Napa and Australia were considered, but that eucalypt-menthol/dill signature over a lighter frame is Chilean rather than either. Warmth suggesting around fourteen percent alcohol implies a sunny yet elevated, coastally influenced site — Aconcagua rather than the broader Central Valley.

**Wine 3 — Germany, Pinot Noir.** Translucent ruby, medium-minus body, red cherry, raspberry and violet, silky fine-grained tannin, medium-plus acidity. Burgundy was the main alternative and village Côte de Nuits would fit the fruit and restraint; however the wet slate and graphite, the perceptibly lower alcohol than the Cabernets here, and the smoky-mineral finish point to Rheingau Spätburgunder, riper and more mineral than Ahr or Baden.

**Wine 4 — Australia, Cabernet Sauvignon.** Full-bodied, pronounced cassis with black olive, cedar and dried bay, and the warmest palate in the flight (~14%), over firm but fine medium-plus tannin. Napa overlaps on cedar and graphite, but Napa's plush oak-sweetness and softer acid line are absent; the olive, herb and earthy grip read as Margaret River, whose maritime cooling explains structural restraint unusual for warm-climate Australia.

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Sooty, spicy oak fully wrapped into the fruit indicates a high proportion of new French barriques, perhaps 80%, over sixteen to eighteen months. Polished tannin without astringency suggests gentle pump-overs rather than aggressive extraction; the retained citrus tension implies rigorous sorting and acid adjustment in a warm year.

**Wine 2.** Unlike Wine 1, oak here is partly American — the dill and sweet vanillin — used to flesh out a lighter frame; conventional fermentation with controlled pump-overs, no carbonic character. The plushness beneath the Cabernet spine suggests a Malbec component, with Carmenère contributing the herbal note: an assemblage built for texture and freshness rather than mass.

**Wine 3.** Aromatic lift and silky texture without green tannin point to whole-berry or partial whole-bunch fermentation and gentle infusion-style handling. Oak is a supporting frame only — perhaps 20–30% new barriques for twelve months — and the preserved slate/graphite lift indicates reductive élevage.

**Wine 4.** Depth of cassis with fine tannin suggests extended maceration of roughly three to four weeks for structure without coarseness. Oak is deliberately more restrained than Wine 1's — around 30–40% new French for eighteen months — the choice of a producer wanting site character, not barrel character, to carry the wine.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding; classified Saint-Julien Cru Classé level, £60–80 retail. Independent specialists and fine-dining on-trade; UK, US, Hong Kong and Japan. Competes with the second wines of neighbouring classified estates.

**Wine 3.** Very good; GG-level Spätburgunder from a top slate site, £45–65. Independent merchants and ambitious on-trade in Germany, the UK and US. Its competitive set is village Burgundy at the same money, against which it offers comparable structure and better value — the barrier is consumer disbelief in Rheingau red.

**Wine 4.** Outstanding; flagship Margaret River Cabernet, £70–100. Domestic Australian fine-wine channel, UK specialists and Asian export. Its Bordeaux-like restraint separates it from Barossa and McLaren Vale icons, positioning it as Australia's Left Bank analogue.

Under the skin, the flight is a study in how Cabernet's structure is inherited from site rather than added by cellar: Bordeaux and Margaret River arrive at the same architecture from opposite hemispheres, Chile trades weight for aromatic lift, and the German Pinot proves that slate minerality, not oak, is the most reliable marker of a cool origin.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 2 Question 1

## Wine 1 — Malbec, Mendoza, Argentina

**a) Variety and origin**

Deep ruby-purple, viscous, with pronounced plum, blue fruit and violet over a mineral undertow: Malbec. Cabernet Sauvignon was weighed — cassis and oak spice fit — but there is no cedar or graphite and the tannin is plush rather than angular. Cool-climate Syrah was set aside: the florality is violet, not black pepper. Warmth of fruit with mineral lift and mountain herb indicates altitude moderating a continental climate — Mendoza, most plausibly Luján de Cuyo or the Uco Valley.

**b) Style and quality**

Long sunny days build the dark-fruit concentration; diurnal range preserves the acidity that holds it in tension. Silky tannin and mocha-spice integration suggest French barriques, perhaps 30–40% new, for 12–14 months, with restrained extraction. Outstanding quality, Reserva/Gran Reserva level, around USD 35–50 — well beyond appellation-level Mendoza. The distinguishing feature is that the ripeness reads as site rather than heat.

**c) Commercial position**

Premium independents and fine-casual on-trade in the US, UK and Northern Europe, where Argentine Malbec has ready recognition. Competitive set: benchmark Luján de Cuyo and Uco bottlings at USD 40. The altitude story sells it to buyers wanting an accessible but serious New World red.

---

## Wine 2 — Cabernet Franc, Chinon, Loire Valley, France

**a) Variety and origin**

Medium ruby, moderate weight; cracked pepper, blackcurrant leaf, raspberry and dried bark — the pyrazine-inflected leafiness against ripe cherry is diagnostic of Cabernet Franc. Pinot Noir was considered for the red-fruit register but is inconsistent with the peppery spice and powdery tannin. Merlot lacks the herbaceous lift and has fleshier plum weight. Medium-plus acidity and moderate alcohol place this in the Loire; the dark-fruit depth and firm structure favour Chinon over lighter Bourgueil or Saumur-Champigny.

**b) Style and quality**

A cool, marginal Atlantic climate delivers high natural acidity and moderate alcohol, preserving fresh fruit without jammy overripeness. Powdery tannin and textural depth point to gentle extraction and ageing in old foudres or large barrels — there is no vanilla or toast, only structural support. Very good quality, at serious Vieilles Vignes level, EUR 20–30. The refusal of new oak is itself the statement: nothing cosmetic between the variety and the site.

**c) Commercial position**

Specialist on-trade and independent retail in the UK, US and Scandinavia, where Loire Cabernet Franc trades as an alternative to Burgundy and Bordeaux at accessible money. Weakness: appellation recognition beyond educated consumers. Strength: the shift toward lighter, terroir-driven reds.

---

## Wine 3 — Negroamaro, Salento IGT, Puglia, Italy

**a) Variety and origin**

Deep ruby, viscous; balsamic notes with sour cherry, mulberry, violet, liquorice and oriental spice — a southern Italian register, and the balsamic-plus-sour-cherry combination points to Negroamaro. Primitivo was considered for the Puglian weight but shows jammier, raisined sweetness without this savoury undertow. Aglianico fits the tannic mass but finishes more austere and iron-driven, with higher acidity than the soft close here. Salento IGT.

**b) Style and quality**

A hot, dry Mediterranean climate supplies the concentration and warmth. The soft entry and elegant tannin indicate shortened maceration or gentler extraction to avoid coarseness at this ripeness, with tonneaux ageing giving chocolate and clove without dominance. Very good quality, Riserva-equivalent, EUR 18–28. Achieving tannins this fine at this alcohol in so hot an appellation is the winemaking achievement.

**c) Commercial position**

Italian specialist on-trade and premium independents in the UK, Germany and the US. Price-to-quality is genuinely competitive, but with no appellation prestige the wine must trade on producer and varietal curiosity — helped by current buyer appetite for southern Italian varieties.

---

## Wine 4 — Cabernet Sauvignon, Galilee, Israel

**a) Variety and origin**

Concentrated cassis, dark cherry, tobacco, herb and chocolate over firm, gritty tannin: Cabernet Sauvignon in a warm climate. Syrah was considered on the anise and spice, but the cassis-tobacco core and tannic architecture rule it out. Generous ripeness with an herbal, earthy undertow implies heat tempered by diurnal swing; the freshness alongside the concentration and the fine French oak point to the Galilee, plausibly the elevated basalt soils of the Golan Heights.

**b) Style and quality**

Mocha and tobacco suggest 12–18 months in French barriques, roughly 30–50% new, absorbed without smothering fruit. Structured tannin and a long finish indicate a wine built to age. Outstanding quality, comparable in position to a classified Napa estate or Stellenbosch flagship, USD 40–60. What separates it from Wine 1's altitude freshness is that the balance here comes from cool nights working against Mediterranean sun rather than elevation alone.

**c) Commercial position**

Premium on-trade and specialist retail in the US, UK and Western Europe; kosher certification widens the addressable market without narrowing general appeal. It competes in a crowded USD 40–60 band against Napa, Stellenbosch and Bordeaux, where the Golan terroir story is the differentiator.

---

## Wine 5 — Grenache, Campo de Borja, Spain

**a) Variety and origin**

Ruby, medium viscosity; ripe cherry, violet, raisin and a peppery lift, with bright sour cherry on the palate — Grenache. Tempranillo shares the cherry and violet but would bring leather, tobacco and more evident oak framing; the raisin-and-sour-cherry combination reads as old-vine Garnacha. Warm, semi-arid Spanish origin: Campo de Borja in Aragón. Priorat was rejected — its Garnacha carries far greater mineral density and structure than this approachable profile.

**b) Style and quality**

Old vines on a hot, continental site give concentration at restrained yields. Soft tannin and a fruit-forward, unoaked character indicate stainless-steel fermentation with ageing in neutral or older vessels, preserving varietal purity. Very good quality, Viñas Viejas level, EUR 12–20 — the value proposition of the flight.

**c) Commercial position**

Off-trade specialists and premium supermarket listings in the UK, US and Scandinavia. With low appellation recognition, it sells on the varietal name and the "old vine" claim rather than DO prestige, shelved against Australian and Rhône Grenache.

---

## Wine 6 — Syrah, Franschhoek, Western Cape, South Africa

**a) Variety and origin**

Deep ruby, viscous; plum, violet, black liquorice and anise, then blueberry, pepper, sweet tobacco, black cardamom and a charry iron/tar finish — savouriness plus iron and pepper is the mark of serious Syrah. Northern Rhône was considered for exactly that register but cannot account for the blueberry generosity and charry sweet spice, which read New World. Barossa was then set aside: it would give jammier fruit and coconut-vanilla oak, not this anise-and-cardamom savouriness. That savoury, ferrous profile points to South Africa; the concentration and structural ambition support Franschhoek.

**b) Style and quality**

Atlantic influence moderates the valley heat, allowing dark-fruit depth alongside savoury structure. The charry edge and sweet tobacco suggest French barriques with perhaps 20–30% new oak, framing rather than masking the intrinsic spice. Outstanding quality, flagship single-vineyard level, USD/GBP 40–60. The under-the-skin point: the iron and cardamom are not a warm-climate imitation of Rhône aromatics but a granite-and-sandstone mineral texture that distinguishes the wine from both its New World peers and the archetype it references.

**c) Commercial position**

Fine-dining lists and premium off-trade in the UK, US and Northern Europe, aimed at drinkers seeking terroir-driven Syrah outside the Northern Rhône. It undercuts Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph on price; the constraint is that South African Syrah still lacks benchmark-category recognition, so it depends on specialist importers and advised buyers.

## Pair 1: Wines 1 & 2 (Italy)

### Wine 1 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Pale translucent garnet, lifted raspberry, fresh cherry and violet, high acidity and medium-plus chalky tannin. Pinot Noir was weighed and rejected: the acid is higher and the tannin firmer and more chalky than that variety gives at this weight of fruit. Grenache is excluded by the grippy tannin and the absence of warmth — this reads at around 13.5%, medium-bodied. Floral lift over firm tannin at low colour density is Nebbiolo. The crunchy fruit and orange-zest finish, without the density of a DOCG bottling, indicate Langhe Nebbiolo DOC from Piedmont.

### Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Fresh and primary, built for early drinking. Purity of red cherry with no secondary development suggests a short maceration of roughly 10–15 days — enough for moderate tannin, stopping short of the severity of extended skin contact. No vanilla or sweet toast means large older Slavonian oak or stainless steel, and aromatic brightness points to bottling 12–18 months after harvest.

### Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Deeper garnet, pronounced black cherry, tobacco, dried rose and liquorice, with tar and orange peel on a full-bodied palate carrying high but fully ripe tannin. Sangiovese was dismissed: no sour-cherry or herbal edge, and the tannin is grippier and finer-grained. Tar and rose over this tannic scale is Nebbiolo at DOCG level. The density of dark fruit and full architecture, rather than the marginally lighter frame typical of Barbaresco, point to Barolo DOCG.

### Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Traditionally styled and age-worthy. The tannic mass implies an extended maceration of 20–30 days. Integration of tar, dried rose and tobacco without any sweet vanilla marker indicates large-format Slavonian botti — concentration prioritised over polish. Structure and length suggest at least 36 months' total ageing, most likely a single-vineyard standard release rather than a Riserva.

### Pair 1 — c) Relative Quality, Maturity, and Commercial Position (2 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1** is very good for its tier — Langhe Nebbiolo DOC, around €15–20. At roughly 2–3 years old it is at peak and will hold 2–3 years before fresh fruit fades; it will not improve. Its home is the independent specialist and premium by-the-glass list, offering Nebbiolo character to drinkers unwilling to pay Barolo prices.

**Wine 2** is outstanding — single-vineyard Barolo DOCG at €55–80. At 5–6 years old it is approachable but far from resolved: expect 8–12 years of further development, tar and rose giving way to truffle and dried fruit. The insight is that high acidity, not ripeness, enables that arc; altitude and calcareous Langhe marl deliver acid retention at full phenolic ripeness. It competes with Right Bank Bordeaux and Gran Selezione Chianti Classico on fine-wine lists.

---

## Pair 2: Wines 3 & 4 (Spain)

### Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Clear ruby; medium-intensity ripe cherry, raspberry and plum over vanilla and sweet toast; medium body, medium-plus acidity, soft tannin. Garnacha is ruled out by the modest perceived alcohol and absence of jammy warm fruit; Mencía by the lack of herbal, lighter-framed structure and the coconut-vanilla oak signature. Ripe red fruit plus American-oak vanilla on soft tannin is Tempranillo in Rioja, and the short oak signature and medium finish place it at Crianza level, Rioja DOCa.

### Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Fruit-forward, shaped by limited oak contact: coconut-tinged vanilla and light toast indicate American oak, mostly used barrels with a small new component, for close to the 12-month Crianza minimum. Maceration was moderate, perhaps 10–14 days, and the rounded mouthfeel confirms full malolactic conversion.

### Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Ruby-garnet with violet rim; pronounced black cherry, balsamic and fine cedar; full body, concentrated but polished tannin. Again Tempranillo — Garnacha was reconsidered and rejected because the tannin is too structured and fine-grained for that variety at this body weight. Balsamic and cedar in place of raw vanilla signal long cask and bottle age: Rioja Gran Reserva DOCa, showing the development of a wine of 7–10 years.

### Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

A longer maceration of 20 days or more on selected fruit. Cedar and balsamic rather than primary oak sweetness indicate extended ageing across both French and American casks, consistent with Gran Reserva minima of 18 months in wood and 36 in bottle. Tannin is fully resolved — carefully managed, largely older cooperage.

### Pair 2 — c) Relative Quality, Maturity, and Commercial Position (2 x 7 marks)

**Wine 3** is good to very good; mid-tier Rioja Crianza at €12–18. At 3–4 years old it is at peak, will not gain, and should be drunk within 2–3 years. It belongs on premium supermarket shelves and mid-range on-trade lists, against entry Côtes du Rhône and Chilean Cabernet.

**Wine 4** is very good to outstanding; Gran Reserva at €40–60. At 8–9 years old it is on its plateau and will hold 5–8 years, gaining leather and dried fig. Its route is independent specialists and fine dining, UK and US export, competing with premium Ribera del Duero Reserva and mid-tier classified Bordeaux. The key point is that the buyer is purchasing bottle age the producer has financed — the price gap over Wine 3 is largely carrying cost, not fruit cost.

---

## Pair 3: Wines 5 & 6 (USA)

### Wine 5 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Ruby; medium-plus red cherry, wild strawberry, dried rose and violet with spice and light forest floor; medium body, medium-plus acidity, medium tannin, modest warmth around 13%. Syrah is excluded by the pale colour and absent pepper; Grenache by the low perceived alcohol and lack of warm sweet fruit. This is Pinot Noir. Cardamom and dried-herb stem character points to New World whole-bunch practice, and the combination of that spice with bright fruit and restrained body indicates cool-climate Oregon — Eola-Amity Hills in the Willamette Valley, where marine influence through the Van Duzer corridor gives higher acid and a lighter frame than the warmer Dundee Hills.

### Wine 5 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Partial whole-cluster inclusion supplies spice and stem tannin while keeping freshness. Light vanilla and fine toast indicate French barriques with perhaps 20–30% new. A cool ferment of around 12–15 days with restrained extraction has preserved aromatic precision; full malolactic conversion softens the mid-palate.

### Wine 6 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

The same ruby and Pinot Noir fruit spectrum — wild strawberry, spiced cherry, dried herb, a touch of leather — but higher acidity and a clear iron and saline note. Gamay was weighed and rejected: it rarely shows this iron-driven minerality or length of structured finish. What separates this from Wine 5 is definition rather than fruit: tighter acid, longer finish, mineral grip. This is a single-vineyard bottling from the same Eola-Amity Hills zone — the iron edge points to Jory-type basaltic soils on hillside sites rather than alluvial valley floor.

### Wine 6 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

More site-driven and structured. Dried rose, baking spice and integrated cedar suggest a comparable French oak regime to Wine 5, but firmer tannin implies a higher whole-cluster proportion or longer post-ferment maceration. The mineral finish is not oak-derived; winemaking has been deliberately restrained to let the site speak. Emerging leather indicates one vintage more age.

### Pair 3 — c) Relative Quality, Maturity, and Commercial Position (2 x 7 marks)

**Wine 5** is very good — Willamette Valley AVA level, $35–50. At about 3 years old it drinks well now and will add texture over 3–5 years before plateauing. It suits premium on-trade and specialist retail in the USA with export to the UK and Japan, positioned as an elegant alternative to Burgundy Premier Cru.

**Wine 6** is outstanding — single-vineyard, $55–75. At around 4 years it is opening out and will develop 5–8 years towards dried fruit, forest floor and leather, holding a further five. Mineral precision and structural definition place it clearly above Wine 5. It belongs on fine-dining lists competing with Burgundy Village and lower Premier Cru for buyers who want visible terroir in Pinot Noir.

modelAnswer:
## a) Region and Grape Variety (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — The light body, green-tinged lemon-gold colour, and racy malic-edged acidity point to a cool-climate white at low apparent alcohol. The nose of white peach, Meyer lemon, tangerine blossom, and a pronounced blue-slate mineral lift narrows decisively to Riesling. Gewürztraminer was considered but its oily body and rose-lychee aromatics are absent; Grüner Veltliner lacks the slate character and apricot florals present here. The blue-slate minerality and precision of the finish indicate a classified south-facing Mittelmosel site. **Riesling Spätlese, Mosel, Germany.**

**Wine 2** — Deep gold, high viscosity, and a nose of dried apricot, orange peel, honey, and saffron-tobacco confirm botrytised sweetness at moderate alcohol. Furmint anchors the wine through its high acidity and waxy texture; softer honeyed notes alongside suggest Hárslevelű in the blend. The puttonyos-style concentration balanced by fresh citrus and delicate oak points to **Tokaji Aszú, Tokaj, Hungary** — Furmint and Hárslevelű (possibly with Sárgamuskotály).

**Wine 3** — Mahogany-edged colour, pronounced spirit warmth, and an intense nose of rose petal, raisins, dates, candied orange rind, caramel, and rancio-like oxidative richness immediately route this to the fortified category. The floral top notes rule out Tawny Port, whose dried-fruit profile lacks this rose-blossom lift. **Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (Brown Muscat), Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia.**

**Wine 4** — Brilliant gold, thick glycerol tears, and a clean nose of ripe peach, tropical mango, and candied citrus with a petrol lift at low apparent alcohol. The acidity is laser-sharp and entirely free of botrytis character — confirming freeze-concentration rather than noble rot. The limestone-influenced mineral tension places this on the lakeshore. **Riesling Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada.**

**Wine 5** — High viscosity, intensely floral nose of ripe citrus, pear, and orchard fruit with mineral depth, and a velvety yet electrically acidic palate unique to ripe Chenin Blanc. Viognier was considered but lacks this acidity; Roussanne lacks the precision. The mineral density and fruit-acid tension narrow the origin to **Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, Anjou, Loire Valley, France — Chenin Blanc.**

---

## b) Mechanism of Sweetness (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — **Arrested fermentation at Spätlese level.** Grapes are harvested late with naturally elevated sugar, then fermentation is halted by chilling or sterile filtration before all sugar is converted, leaving roughly 60–90 g/L residual sugar at low alcohol. No fortification, botrytis, or freezing is involved.

**Wine 2** — **Noble rot (Botrytis cinerea) and traditional aszú maceration.** Individually harvested botrytised berries are mashed into a paste and macerated with base wine for 24–48 hours before pressing. The 5 puttonyos designation indicates five baskets (~100 kg) of aszú paste per 136-litre Gönc barrel, yielding minimum 120 g/L residual sugar. Fermentation is slow and arrested when the desired balance is reached.

**Wine 3** — **Fortification during fermentation, followed by long oxidative solera-style maturation.** Spirit is added to arrest fermentation while substantial sugar remains (typically 200 g/L+). Younger fortified parcels are blended progressively into older stock over decades, building the rancio concentration and caramel complexity evident here.

**Wine 4** — **Natural cryoextraction (freeze-concentration).** Grapes remain on the vine until temperatures drop to −8°C or below, freezing the water in the berry. The unfrozen, sugar-concentrated juice is pressed at sub-zero temperatures, yielding tiny volumes of intensely sweet, clean must. The absence of any botrytis character confirms freeze-concentration.

**Wine 5** — **Noble rot, with possible passerillage contribution.** Morning mists from the Layon river encourage Botrytis cinerea to colonise Chenin Blanc skins, concentrating sugars to 150–250 g/L RS while increasing glycerol — explaining the velvety texture. Multiple selective harvest passes (tries) are essential. Fermentation halts naturally under the wine's own sugar load, balanced by Chenin's high tartaric acidity.

---

## c) Style, Quality, and Commercial Position (5 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Delicate and precise: low apparent alcohol, racy acidity, medium-minus body, and stone-fruit sweetness threaded through with blue-slate minerality. Outstanding quality at single-vineyard Mosel Spätlese level, retailing around £30–45 in the UK. Appeals to consumers seeking complexity without weight; works as aperitif or at table. Strong export markets in Germany, the UK fine-wine trade, Japan, and the USA. The site-specific mineral identity differentiates it from generic Mosel off-dry Riesling; the commercial challenge is overcoming the persistent perception that Mosel Riesling is simply sweet and simple.

**Wine 2** — Richly textured and opulent, with dried apricot, honey, and tobacco balanced by bright citrus acidity and a long complex finish. Outstanding quality at 5 Puttonyos level (minimum 120 g/L RS), retailing £40–70 in UK specialist channels. Positioned alongside Sauternes as a classic world sweet wine, with a commercial advantage in its distinctive orange-peel-and-tobacco identity. Principal export markets are Germany, the UK fine-wine trade, and the USA. The challenge remains low consumer awareness outside traditional markets.

**Wine 3** — Extraordinary concentration of raisin, date, caramel, and rose petal in a seamless, velvety whole. This is the **Museum Reserve** tier — the highest level within the Rutherglen Muscat classification — retailing around AUD 60–90 per 375 ml. Sold through specialist fine wine and premium on-trade; exported to the UK and USA where Australian fortifieds are gaining renewed interest. The opportunity is unsurpassed value relative to old Tawny or Vintage Port at comparable quality; the challenge is limited category awareness globally and a format suited to glass or half-bottle service.

**Wine 4** — Pure and crystalline: frozen-fruit-nectar intensity of peach and mango held by searing acidity. Outstanding quality at VQA Icewine level, retailing around CAD 80–120 per 375 ml. Canada's primary export calling card, with its strongest markets in China, Japan, and South Korea where gift-giving culture drives volume, plus the USA and Europe. Positioned in premium gifting and fine-dining lists. The challenge is tiny production volumes, cold-chain logistics, and competition from botrytised styles at lower price points for consumers who prioritise sweetness over provenance.

**Wine 5** — Opulent yet precise: honeyed stone fruit and floral concentration held in tension by Chenin's vibrant acidity — rich without heaviness, sweet without cloying. Outstanding quality at Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru level, retailing around €35–70 per 375 ml from specialist importers. Demand is concentrated among UK fine-wine merchants, Belgian and US sommeliers. Competes with Sauternes in the premium sweet white space, with the advantage of a distinctive floral-mineral character and remarkable ageability over 20–40 years. Very low production and limited global recognition outside knowledgeable trade buyers remain the principal commercial constraints.
