# Mock answer — Paper 3, Wines 1 & 2

## a) Grape variety and region (2 × 10 marks)

**Savagnin, Arbois (Jura, France).** Wine 1 is the door-opener: deep gold, viscous, and dominated by walnut, curry, green olive and parmesan rind — a classic sotolon/rancio signature from ageing under a yeast veil. Fino or Amontillado was the obvious alternative, but there is no spirit heat: the warmth reads generous and seamless, an estimated 14–15% reached by fermentation alone, not by fortification, and the fruit is dried apricot and preserved lemon rather than Palomino's saline chalk. That rules out Jerez and points to unfortified *sous voile* ageing, which in practice means the Jura.

Wine 2 confirms the variety by stripping the veil away. Same yellow-plum and citrus-peel core, a nutty echo, but bright lemon and green apple over searing, tartaric-edged acidity at a moderate 13%-ish weight. Chardonnay was weighed — it shares the region — but its texture would be broader and rounder with softer acid; this taut, slightly bitter-phenolic line with a saline finish is Savagnin. Within Jura, Château-Chalon produces only the veiled style, so a region yielding both wines narrows to Arbois.

The telling detail on Wine 1: it is bone dry yet unusually concentrated. Evaporative loss through years of ullage has built extract, not sugar — the mark of a genuine long veil, not a briefly oxidised wine.

## b) Method of production (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — late-picked for high potential alcohol, fermented dry in old wood, then deliberately *not* topped up. A film yeast established over the ullage, and the wine sat undisturbed in neutral 228-litre barrels for at least six years; the absence of any vanilla or toast confirms no new oak. ## a) Identify the grape variety (20 marks)

Malvasia was also considered but shows nuts and a bitter twist rather than this floral purity. Negligible tannin, moderate acidity and the variety's ability to hold aroma through sparkling, fortified and dried styles are diagnostic. Wines 1 and 2 read as small-berried Petits Grains; Wine 3's rose-and-toffee mahogany suggests the red-berried mutation; Wine 4's coarser candied-citrus musk points to Muscat of Alexandria.

## b) Method of production and style (4 × 15 marks)

**Wine 1** — Pale lemon, a delicate low-pressure bead, barely 5–6% warmth, around 120 g/L sugar, pear-drop grapiness. Tank method: chilled must fermented under pressure in a single sealed vessel and arrested at roughly half-completion by chilling and sterile filtration, retaining both natural CO2 and sugar. The pure primary aroma indicates protective, reductive handling with no lees or malolactic. Style: a sweet, low-alcohol, lightly sparkling aperitif made for immediate drinking.

**Wine 2** — Pale gold, still, clear spirit warmth at roughly 15%, sugar near 110 g/L, orange peel and lime blossom with no oxidative edge. This is mutage: neutral grape spirit added at about 5–6% alcohol to halt fermentation and fix the sugar, then brief inert-vessel élevage and early bottling. Style: reductive fortified sweet wine where fruit purity, not maturation, is the whole intention.

**Wine 3** — Deep mahogany with an olive rim, thick staining tears, hot 17–18% spirit, intensely sweet, with rancio, toffee, walnut and cold tea. Fortified on the same principle but then aged oxidatively in old wood under warm conditions and blended across vintages toward a house average — a non-vintage style constructed by blending rather than expressing a single season.

**Wine 4** — Deep amber, yet no spirit heat at all behind roughly 14.5% warmth and 190 g/L sugar. That combination can only come from grapes dried to raisins: sun-drying on racks, the dried fruit then steeped into fermenting must for extract. ## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good for its DOCG category, at the top of a mostly commodity field; around £15–18, independent specialists and by-the-glass dessert listings; competes with Brachetto and premium Prosecco. Challenge: category price perception.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, four-wine single-variety sweet flight

## a) Grape variety (28 marks)

Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. The thread running through all four glasses is an overtly grapey, musky perfume married to orange blossom and rose petal — a varietal signature no other white shares in this combination. Wine 1 shows it in its purest primary form (rose, ginger, ripe peach, honeysuckle) at a barely-warming, watery-light alcohol; Wine 4 carries the same floral-and-stone-fruit core at moderate warmth; Wine 2's orange-blossom and white-peach lift survives fortification intact; and even in Wine 3, buried under raisin, rancio and treacle, the dried orange peel and beeswax betray the same grape. Structurally the family holds: moderate-plus rather than racy acidity throughout, no tannin, no phenolic bitterness.

Gewurztraminer was the leading alternative — it shares rose and lychee-adjacent perfume — but its characteristically low acidity, broad oily phenolic grip and high natural alcohol are absent here, and it is not a fortified-wine grape in any established tradition. Riesling was eliminated on structure: none of these wines shows the searing tartaric line, lime-and-slate register or petrol development a Riesling of this sweetness would carry. Muscat of Alexandria is plausible for Wine 4 but the fine-boned floral precision across the flight favours Petits Grains.

## b) Origin (4 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Asti, Piedmont; Moscato d'Asti DOCG. A gentle frizzante bead, pale lemon colour, wholly primary fruit and an alcohol so low it barely registers as warmth is a legally-defined profile made in one place at this quality.

**Wine 2** — Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, southern Rhône. Gold, viscous, obvious spirit warmth around 15%, yet reductively made with no oxidative colour or nuttiness. That combination of fortified sweetness and preserved primary fruit is the classic French VDN model; Rivesaltes or Frontignan were considered, but the fresh white-peach delicacy over aggressive raisin points north to Beaumes-de-Venise.

**Wine 3** — Rutherglen, Victoria. Tawny-brown with an olive-green rim, spirit warmth near 18%, rancio, espresso and Christmas cake. Only the hot-store, extended-oxidative Australian tradition produces this; a very old Tawny Port was weighed and rejected — the intense grapey-orange peel core and treacle viscosity are Muscat, not Touriga.

**Wine 4** — Navarra, Spain. Pale gold, unfortified, moderate warmth around 12%, sweet but with a slightly syrupy edge and no botrytis markers. A dry-climate late-harvest style; the fresher tangerine lift and quince place it in northern Spain rather than Valencia's heavier Moscatel.

## c) Production and how sweetness was achieved (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Whole-bunch pressed, cold-settled must held chilled, then a single fermentation in pressurised tank taken only to about 5.5% before being arrested by rapid chilling and sterile filtration off the yeast. Sweetness is therefore *unfermented* must sugar, roughly 120 g/l, and the light bead is the same ferment's own CO₂ retained under a modest 1–1.5 bar. No lees ageing, no malolactic — the absence of any autolytic or buttery note confirms both.

**Wine 2** — *Mutage*: neutral grape spirit at high strength added mid-ferment to kill the yeast, leaving around 110 g/l sugar at 15%. Everything about the wine argues protective handling — inert vessels, no wood, cool storage, early bottling — because the fruit is still primary.

**Wine 3** — Late-picked, partly shrivelled fruit fortified early to retain very high sugar, near 300 g/l, then decades in small old oak in hot conditions. Evaporative concentration explains the viscosity; oxygen ingress explains the rancio and the olive rim; blending younger aged material into an old base explains the seamlessness. Here is the wine's real trick: the "acidity" holding 300 g/l from cloying is not tartaric freshness but the volatile lift that old-wood hot-store maturation generates — that balance places it in the Rare tier, above Grand.

**Wine 4** — Sugar concentrated by passerillage on the vine, not noble rot (no saffron or botrytis funk). Fermented cool in tank and stopped short by chilling, sulfur and filtration at around 12%, leaving roughly 100 g/l — a partly-fermented rather than naturally-arrested wine, hence the faintly syrupy rather than cut finish.

## d) Style and commercial position (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality DOCG, drink within 12 months. A low-alcohol aperitif and brunch style, ~£14 in premium supermarkets and independents; huge in the USA. Challenge: freshness is perishable.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality AOP VDN, half-bottle format, ~£18. On-trade dessert-by-the-glass, France and Benelux; a cheaper foil to Sauternes.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding, Rare classification, ~£130 per 375ml. Specialist merchants and fine-dining lists; UK and USA collectors. Tiny volumes are the constraint, not demand.

**Wine 4** — Good quality regional late-harvest, ~£11. Domestic Spanish off-trade and export supermarkets, competing with Moscatel de Valencia in a shrinking sweet category.

Acetaldehyde-driven olive, apple and hay with autolytic lift points to a continuous yeast film in old, part-filled butts. The seamless, ages-averaged character with no vintage definition confirms fractional blending through a solera. No new oak — the wood is old and passive.

**Wine 2** — an unfortified, wholly oxidative dry white of real concentration. The generous but unspirity warmth, around 14.5%, is natural alcohol from late picking and full fermentation to dryness. # Mock answer — Paper 3, Question 1

## a) Identify the grape variety, with reference to each wine (30 marks)

**Chardonnay.** All six are traditional-method sparkling wines with a citrus/green-apple fruit core, no terpenes, no phenolic grip and no varietal aromatic signature — the classic neutral-but-transparent canvas.

Wine 1 gives the clearest evidence: lemon-gold with grapefruit and candied lemon carrying brioche and cocoa butter, a combination only Chardonnay sustains over long lees ageing. Wine 5 confirms it — greengage, lemon oil and a chalk-driven, saline mid-palate with a creamy texture that shows the variety's affinity for malolactic and barrel work. Wine 2 shows the same lemon and baked-apple core stretched over a very high, malic-tasting acid line, and Wine 3 shows Chardonnay at the ripe end — pineapple, tangerine, white peach — proving the variety's cool-to-warm range within one flight.

Riesling was seriously considered for Wines 2 and 6, but there is no lime blossom, no kerosene, and no residual-sugar/acid tension; the lees-derived nuttiness of Wine 4 would also sit oddly on Riesling. Grüner Veltliner is the honest alternative for Wines 4 and 6, whose white pepper, ginger and numbing spice are atypical; but there is no lentil or radish note, the fruit remains apple/citrus pith, and the creamy autolytic mid-palate is Chardonnay-shaped. I read that pepper as cool continental site and reductive handling rather than a second variety.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (6 x 15 marks)

**Wine 1** — A serious vintage-dated Blanc de Blancs built for gastronomy. The lemon-gold depth, dried nuts and cocoa butter against still-vibrant acidity point to a wine bottled from a single harvest and left on lees for seven to nine years, then disgorged one to two years ago. Purity of citrus with no phenolic bitterness indicates whole-bunch pressing at low yield of free-run juice; the rounded, buttery breadth of the mid-palate indicates full malolactic in stainless steel rather than oak, since there is no vanilla or toast beyond patisserie. Mousse is fine and persistent, dosage around 7–8 g/l — brut, sufficient to gloss the acidity without reading sweet.

**Wine 2** — Cooler, leaner and more taut: an aperitif-styled vintage traditional method. The searing, apple-skin acidity and absence of buttery breadth suggest malolactic was blocked or only partial, a deliberate choice to preserve tension. Autolysis is present as toasted sourdough but subordinate to fruit, consistent with four to five years on lees. Critically, the palate is noticeably rounder than the acid figures would predict, which tells me dosage has been pushed to around 9–10 g/l — the winemaker cushioning a marginal-climate malic line rather than chasing fashionably low sugar.

**Wine 3** — The most fruit-forward and commercially generous of the six. Pineapple, tangerine and white peach indicate a distinctly riper harvest at higher potential alcohol before tirage, and the medium-plus rather than long finish suggests a shorter tirage of two to three years — autolysis reads as brioche but does not dominate. Hints of vanilla chiffon and a soft, broad texture point to a proportion of barrel-fermented reserve wine plus full malolactic. Dosage around 9 g/l brut. The intent is approachability on release, not a decade in bottle.

**Wine 4** — A non-vintage reserve blend of real ambition. Toasted hazelnut and almond paste alongside a creamy lees texture, yet without any single-harvest precision, points to a multi-vintage assemblage with a meaningful reserve component and at least three years on lees. Whole-bunch pressing again (citrus pith, no bitterness), partial malolactic to keep the chalky line intact, and a restrained dosage at the extra brut/low brut boundary — the ginger and white currant would be smothered by more sugar. Cool continental fruit gives the chalky, high-acid spine.

**Wine 5** — The most terroir-transparent wine here and the most interesting decision-set. Zero dosage is evident: the finish is bone dry, stony, almost cistern-like. Yet it is not austere, and that is the point — full malolactic, long ageing on fine lees and fermentation in seasoned wood (smoke, patisserie, medium-plus body) have been used as textural substitutes for sugar. Working back, a grower only omits dosage entirely when the fruit arrives fully ripe from old vines on deep chalk and late-picked; the ripe apricot behind the greengage is that ripeness, and the acid holds it. Natural yeasts and low sulphur explain the reductive smoke.

**Wine 6** — Deliberately primary, vintage-dated and unmistakably reductive. Pronounced Szechuan pepper, black lava-salt salinity and numbing spice with no nutty autolysis point to stainless-steel fermentation, no malolactic (hence the electric line), and a short tirage of roughly 18–24 months. Dosage is nil to 3 g/l — the salinity would be dulled otherwise. The style prioritises site salinity and aromatic lift over autolytic complexity: a modern, low-intervention Sekt idiom rather than a Champagne pastiche.

## c) Quality and commercial position within category (6 x 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding for its category; a vintage Grand Cru–sourced Blanc de Blancs. Retailing around £75, sold through Independent Specialists and Michelin-level lists; competes with vintage Blanc de Blancs from major houses. Drink now to 12 years.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality, top-tier English sparkling and the equal of good non-vintage Champagne, though the dosage betrays a cooler margin. Around £50–55, UK premium off-trade and domestic on-trade; nationally led export to the US and Scandinavia.

**Wine 3** — Very good quality at the top of its domestic category, if not classic-region depth. Around $45, US premium supermarkets, cellar door and by-the-glass programmes; competes with Champagne NV on price, which is its challenge.

**Wine 4** — Very good quality; a benchmark Sekt at the region's highest tier, comparable to good grower Champagne NV. Around €30, Austrian and German on-trade plus specialist export; sells on regional identity rather than price.

**Wine 5** — Outstanding; Grand Cru grower Champagne, allocated. £90–110 through specialists and sommelier lists. Its risk is that zero dosage divides consumers — a proposition wine for those who prize salinity over generosity.

**Wine 6** — Good quality, a step below Wine 4 in complexity but distinctive. Around €25, independent merchants and natural-leaning wine bars in Vienna, Copenhagen and New York; drink now to three years, while the aromatics last.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, two fortified Muscats

## a) Grape variety (10 marks)

Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. Wine 1 is the open door: pronounced orange blossom, rose petal and fresh apricot over candied citrus zest — the unmistakable grapey/terpene signature, and no other variety carries floral musk with that purity. Gewürztraminer was weighed for the lychee and rose, but it lacks Muscat's citrus-zest lift and would show a soft, low-acid, faintly bitter phenolic finish rather than this taut line. Wine 2 is raisined and rancio-dominated, yet beneath the fig and toffee sit orange marmalade and a musky floral lift that survive oxidation — consistent with Muscat, not with Pedro Ximénez, which gives molasses and fig without any floral trace.

## b) Style and winemaking (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1.** A reductively-made, youthful sweet fortified wine. Gold colour with heavy tears, luscious apricot-jam sweetness held by fresh natural acidity, and only moderate spirit warmth — perhaps 15% — showing clean, unobtrusive integration. Sweetness was achieved by mutage: neutral grape spirit added to fermenting must so ferment arrested early, retaining roughly 110–125 g/L sugar while keeping alcohol low. The absence of oak, oxidative or nutty notes points to a short élevage in inert vessels under protective handling and early bottling. The telling decision is restraint in the spirit: a coarser, hotter mutage would smother the terpenes, and preserving them is the whole point of the style. Southern Rhône — Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise.

**Wine 2.** An oxidatively matured, blended non-vintage fortified Muscat. Tawny colour, viscous, luscious, with noticeable spirit heat — around 18% — plus burnt toffee, walnut and true rancio. Here fortification was to a higher strength early in ferment, then years in old wood in a hot climate, where evaporative concentration builds sugar and viscosity beyond what raisining alone gives; a fractional blending regime explains the NV consistency. Crucially the acidity remains high beneath the sugar, so the base fruit was picked fresh and fortified, not dried to flabbiness. Rutherglen, Australia.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1.** Very good quality, top of the Vin Doux Naturel appellation tier; retails around €20–25. Independent specialists, French on-trade as an aperitif, and dessert-by-the-glass listings; competes with Muscat de Rivesaltes and premium Moscato.

**Wine 2.** Excellent quality at Classic tier — the rancio depth exceeds entry Rutherglen but lacks the treacly concentration of Rare. Around AU$45 per 500ml, specialist retail and export to the UK and USA.

Chardonnay, in all three wines. Each shows pale lemon-green to gold colour, a fine persistent mousse, and a fruit spectrum running from green apple and preserved lemon to stone fruit and toasted hazelnut, over high, taut acidity — the firm acid backbone Chardonnay retains in cool sites. Autolytic brioche and biscuit across the flight indicates extended lees contact in traditional-method wines.

Pinot Noir was weighed and rejected: none shows the red-fruited lift, broader mid-palate or coarser bead of a blanc de noirs. Meunier is ruled out by the finesse and structural length here, which exceed what that variety delivers. These are blanc de blancs.

## b) Region of origin (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Côte des Blancs, Champagne.** Palest in the flight, with the finest, most persistent mousse and a pronounced chalk-and-flint register. Acidity is racy and linear rather than merely high, the dosage restrained, and the finish tense rather than broad — a cool, northern-continental origin. The combination of chalk minerality, lemon curd and pronounced autolysis narrows it to Grand or Premier Cru Côte des Blancs rather than the Montagne or the Aube.

**Wine 2 — Pipers River, Tasmania.** The oyster-shell minerality suggests Europe, but white peach and white blossom over a rounder texture betray the New World. What separates it from Wine 1 is fruit generosity held against equally high acidity — a maritime southern-hemisphere signature rather than a continental one. Tasmania's northern coastal sites (Pipers River, Tamar Valley) supply that acid at that ripeness; mainland Australia would not.

**Wine 3 — Carneros, California.** Deepest gold, with gardenia, citrus rind and cardamom pastry over lychee and poached pear — riper and broader than either of the others. English sparkling and Crémant were considered and eliminated: neither reaches this tropical breadth. Yet acidity survives, which points to a warm region cooled by fog — Carneros, on San Pablo Bay.

## c) Style, production and dosage (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Traditional method, almost certainly a single vintage. The very fine bead and pronounced brioche, cream and toasted almond imply three to four years minimum on lees. Bone-dry, with piercing acidity unbuffered by sugar: Extra Brut to low Brut, 0–6 g/L, letting chalk and lemon curd dominate.

**Wine 2** — Traditional method with meaningful autolysis (hazelnut, biscuit), but primary peach and floral fruit still leads, implying a shorter lees regime of roughly two to three years. A gentle sweetness cushions the acidity without being perceptible as sugar: Brut, around 6–8 g/L.

**Wine 3** — Traditional method, confirmed by persistent bead and pastry-hazelnut autolysis, but the generous, riper palate suggests shorter lees contact than Wine 1 and warmer base-wine conditions. Brut, 6–9 g/L, the dosage well concealed by the wine's own richness.

## d) Quality and commercial position (3 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding. Precision, mineral tension and length place it at the top of the blanc de blancs category, £60–100+ retail. Fine wine specialists and Champagne-led on-trade; Asia and North America are the natural export channels.

**Wine 2** — Very good; prestige-cuvée tier for Australia, AUD $50–80. Domestic fine wine buyers first, with export traction in the UK, Scandinavia and Asia as cool-climate Australia gains profile.

**Wine 3** — Very good to outstanding for a Californian blanc de blancs, around USD $60–80. North American fine dining and lifestyle buyers seeking a Champagne alternative with provenance; its competitive set is prestige Californian sparkling and top Crémant, and its floral, fog-shaped personality is the point of difference.

The flight's real lesson is that autolysis is a stylistic choice, not a regional one: what actually separates these three is how much primary fruit each site allows to survive under it.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 2

## Wine 1 — Australia

**a) Country and region (8 marks)**

Grenache: pronounced strawberry and rose petal, dried herb, and fine sandy tannin. Warm, medium-full, perceived alcohol 14–15%, yet the fruit is lifted rather than jammy. That purity argues against southern France, where the style is richer and more rustic, and against Spain, where American oak and denser fruit would show (as in Wine 2). The fragrant expression with dusty, sand-derived tannin points to McLaren Vale, South Australia, the maritime influence tempering the warmth beneath a generous mid-palate.

**b) Style and winemaking (9 marks)**

Dry, perfumed, built on purity rather than extraction. No vanilla or toast: large-format or seasoned oak, if any. The dusty tannin and herbal lift suggest gentle maceration with whole-berry or partial whole-bunch fermentation.

**c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (8 marks)**

Outstanding for the region; A$50–80. At 2–3 years it drinks well now and will gain complexity over 5–8 years as the red fruit dries towards spice. Specialist fine-wine retail and premium on-trade domestically, with growing UK, US and Scandinavian export, where old-vine Grenache is pitched to Burgundy drinkers priced out of the Côte d'Or.

---

## Wine 2 — Spain

**a) Country and region (8 marks)**

The same variety, but denser and oak-driven: vanilla, sandalwood, chocolate, tar over dark fruit. Perceived alcohol 15%+, with loamy earthy depth. Southern France and the New World are ruled out by the American-oak signature and sheer fruit mass; Priorat is ruled out because schist would give sharper, more linear minerality and tannin. High-altitude Aragón — Campo de Borja or Cariñena — fits: old-vine Garnacha, Moncayo altitude holding acidity against the alcohol, and generous new oak at this level.

**b) Style and winemaking (9 marks)**

Extended maceration in large tanks explains the colour depth and tannin mass. A high proportion of new barrels for 12–18 months — American for the coconut-vanilla, French for chocolate and spice — with malolactic in barrel integrating the richness.

**c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (8 marks)**

Very good, Reserva-equivalent, €25–45. At 4–5 years it is approachable, will integrate over 2–3 more and hold 8–10, moving towards dried fruit and rancio. Specialist importers and premium on-trade in the US, UK and Germany, undercutting southern Rhône Grenache blends of similar weight.

---

## Wine 3 — France

**a) Country and region (8 marks)**

Fortified Grenache Noir: spirit warmth, viscous texture, blackberry jam, prune, fig and orange marmalade, made by mutage — spirit added mid-fermentation to retain grape sugar. Port was weighed: the dark fruit could suggest the Douro, but Touriga-based Vintage Port is fuller-bodied and firmer in tannin, and would not show these violet florals or this fresh blackberry lift. This is Banyuls, Roussillon, in Rimage style — bottled young, so no tawny rancio — with a mineral finish consistent with the schist terraces of the Côte Vermeille.

**b) Style and winemaking (9 marks)**

Fermentation arrested at roughly 5–7% alcohol, leaving around 80–100g/L residual sugar, then brief tank or old-wood ageing and early bottling to protect primary fruit. Unlike the oxidative traditional style, nothing nutty intrudes. The silky texture indicates restrained extraction.

**c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (8 marks)**

Very good appellation-level Rimage, €20–35. At 3–4 years it is at peak; this style is not for cellaring and the primary fruit will attenuate within 5–7 years. Independent merchants and specialist on-trade, sold against the chocolate dessert course, with niche export to the UK, US and Japan. Its commercial obstacle is recognition rather than quality: it must be sold by staff or shelf-talker, since the consumer reaches for Port by name.

## 1. Model Answer

#### Section A · For the flight as a whole

**a) Grape variety (15 marks)**

The variety is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. The call rests on a consistent fingerprint — orange blossom, rose petal, fresh and dried apricot, and a distinctly grapey floral lift — that survives radical shifts in sweetness, alcohol and production method. Riesling was weighed for its ability to span dry, sparkling and sweet styles, but its defining lime/petrol/slate signature is absent throughout. Gewürztraminer shares rose and lychee yet lacks the grapey, apricot core and is not made in fortified form here. The pronounced aromatic intensity of Wines 1, 2, 3 and 5 alongside the delicate frothing Wine 4 confirms Muscat's unmatched stylistic range.

---

#### Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1 — b) Method of production and style (15 marks)**

Deep gold, viscous, sweet and floral: a Vin Doux Naturel from the southern Rhône. Production is by mutage — grape spirit added mid-fermentation to arrest the yeasts and retain natural sugar — with perceived alcohol moderately warm at around 15%. Absence of oak and the freshness of orange blossom and peach indicate early bottling and reductive handling, in sharp contrast to the oxidative Wines 2 and 3. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise in style.

**Wine 1 — c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (7 marks)**

Very good at VDN appellation level; pronounced aromatics and a long, balanced finish. Wholly primary fruit suggests 1–3 years old and at peak; aromatics fade within 2–3 years, no gain from cellaring. Around £14–18 per half-bottle for specialist merchants, premium supermarkets and restaurant dessert lists in the UK and North America.

---

**Wine 2 — b) Method of production and style (15 marks)**

Deep amber with orange rim and high viscosity signal extended oxidative ageing after fortification. Mutage again underpins it, but what separates Wine 2 is maturation in partially filled casks over several years. Caramelised walnut, dried fruit and honey layered over the grape base point to Samos Nectar PDO, where sun-drying (passerillage) concentrates the sugars before fortification. The result is deeper and nuttier than Wine 1 and darker than Wine 5.

**Wine 2 — c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (7 marks)**

Very good at PDO Samos Nectar level; layered complexity clearly exceeds the simpler VDNs. Amber colour and dried-fruit dominance suggest 5–8 years old, drinking well, holding a further 3–4 years without improving. Around €15–20 through independent merchants and on-trade in the UK, Germany and Australia.

---

**Wine 3 — b) Method of production and style (15 marks)**

The most opulent wine here. Amber-gold with copper tints, very high viscosity, raisin, toffee, fig and cardamom over rose water: Rutherglen Muscat. Very ripe or sunned fruit is fortified mid-ferment, then aged in a fractional blending system akin to a solera, younger material continuously refreshed with parcels decades old and concentrated by evaporation in hot sheds. Alcohol reads hotter than Wines 1 and 5, near 17–18%. No single-vintage fortified achieves this rancio depth; the lift on the finish that stops it cloying is the signature of younger spirit cutting extreme concentration.

**Wine 3 — c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (7 marks)**

Outstanding at Rutherglen Muscat classification level. Vintage dating is impossible under fractional blending, but oxidative depth implies an average age of 8–15 years; it will hold indefinitely. Around AUD 25–35 per 375ml domestically, with specialist and on-trade export to the UK and USA and strong by-the-glass potential on cheese courses.

---

**Wine 4 — b) Method of production and style (15 marks)**

The radical outlier: pale straw, gently sparkling, and weightless on the palate with almost no warmth, reading at 5–6%. This is Moscato d'Asti DOCG by the Asti method — partially fermented must chilled to halt fermentation, then refermented in sealed autoclave to capture CO₂ and stopped again at low alcohol. No fortification, no oak, no lees work: everything is directed at primary aromatic capture. Sage, mint, white flower and peach confirm Moscato Bianco. Alone in the flight, the grape appears unmediated by spirit or oxidation.

**Wine 4 — c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (7 marks)**

Very good at DOCG level, with an aromatic precision above generic Asti Spumante. Bright straw and purely primary nose indicate 1–2 years; drink now, as mousse and aromatics fall away quickly. Around £12–16 per 750ml via premium supermarkets, specialists and Italian restaurants, with strong demand in the USA, UK and Asian markets for low-alcohol sweet sparkling.

---

**Wine 5 — b) Method of production and style (15 marks)**

Wine 5 shares Wine 1's VDN basis — mutage of fermenting Muscat must — but is more austere. Gold, with orange blossom and apricot, yet cut by a bracing citrus-mineral line that is the diagnostic marker for Muscat de Saint-Jean-de-Minervois, a small high-altitude Languedoc appellation on limestone. Against Wine 1's rounder, more luscious profile, this is tighter, with acidity giving genuine tension against the sugar and greater food versatility.

**Wine 5 — c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (7 marks)**

Very good at VDN appellation level, and arguably the most gastronomic of the four fortified wines. Pale gold and primary; 1–3 years old, drink now, fading within three. Around £12–16 per half-bottle through specialist merchants and dessert lists. It competes head-on with Wine 1, but its mineral structure gives a clear point of difference for by-the-glass listing in modern wine bars.

## a) Identify the region of origin and the grape variety for each wine (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 — Tokaj, Hungary; Furmint.** Bone dry, very high racy acidity, warm medium-plus body, with flinty, saline sapidity and subtle vanilla from older oak. Riesling was weighed — the lime and flint overlap — but the broader texture and lower aromatic intensity rule it out; Chenin Blanc fails on the absence of quince and waxy honey. Volcanic minerality plus dry, textured weight is Furmint's signature.

**Wine 2 — Tokaj, Hungary; Furmint (likely with Hárslevelű).** Deep gold, thick tears, prominent viscous sweetness held by high tartaric acidity, alcohol modest and body derived from sugar rather than extract. Citrus-led rather than tropical, clean rather than raisined: this excludes Sauternes (marmalade, higher alcohol) and German TBA (lower alcohol still, petrol notes). Botrytis-affected Aszú.

---

## b) Compare the methods of production, with reference to residual sugar and alcohol (18 marks)

**Wine 1** is a dry table wine: Furmint picked at phenolic ripeness in October with acidity deliberately preserved, fermented to dryness (RS below 4 g/L). Subtle toast indicates fermentation and ageing in older barriques, building texture without oak flavour. Malolactic appears suppressed — the sharp, malic-edged finish confirms it. Perceived alcohol is warm and generous, around 13.5%, from a ripe continental vintage.

**Wine 2** follows the Aszú method. Individually hand-picked botrytised berries, their water degraded and sugars concentrated, are macerated as paste in base wine or must for 12–48 hours. The intensity of sweetness reads at roughly 120–150 g/L, consistent with 5 Puttonyos. Fermentation is slow and cool under osmotic stress and is arrested by chilling and filtration at around 10% perceived alcohol, which the light palate weight confirms. No oak is detectable; the intent is to protect citrus and honeyed botrytis. The logics are opposed: Wine 1 removes sugar entirely, Wine 2 is built around preserving it at the deliberate cost of complete fermentation.

---

## c) Style, quality, and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — dry, mineral, sapid; very good quality, single-vineyard estate level, €20–35. Competes with premium Grüner Veltliner and Burgundy Village whites through independent specialists and premium on-trade in Germany, the UK and US. Low varietal awareness remains the brake on the category.

**Wine 2** — outstanding, a 5 Puttonyos equivalent at €50–100 per 500ml, sold via fine wine merchants, restaurant lists and auction. Its comparators are Sauternes and Beerenauslese, and it often outranks them. Markets: UK, US, Japan, increasingly China. Sweet wine's ageing demographic is the risk; heritage and cellaring potential are the offset.

## a) Grape variety (6 marks)

Chardonnay. All three show a fine, persistent mousse and pale lemon-gold colour consistent with traditional-method sparkling from a neutral, high-acid variety. Across the flight the aromatics run citrus zest, white peach, acacia and fresh almond, with varying autolytic brioche. Structurally, each has crisp to medium-plus acidity and a lean frame that carries autolysis without weight, with moderate perceived alcohol pointing to cool-to-moderate climates. Pinot Noir was weighed — the autolysis and mousse would fit — but the total absence of red fruit, copper tone or rosé inflection rules it out. Riesling Sekt was also considered, given that variety's cross-style reach, but the brioche depth of Wine 1 and the almond-pastry complexity of Wine 3 exceed Riesling's steely, citrus-driven profile, and no petrol or lime-blossom lift appears. A consistent Blanc de Blancs character across all three confirms a single white grape: Chardonnay.

## b) Region of origin (3 × 13 marks)

**Wine 1 — Champagne, Grand Cru (France).** Extremely fine, persistent mousse and a luminous lemon-green colour signal a prestige traditional-method appellation. The nose is restrained but precise: fresh brioche, lemon, white flowers, saline chalk. The chalky, meringue-like texture and lime-driven tension on the palate point to the Côte des Blancs. Crémant de Bourgogne was ruled out — mousse quality, salinity and length are too refined — and a California Blanc de Blancs would lack this acid tension. Integration of dosage and exceptional finish confirm Grand Cru Champagne.

**Wine 2 — North Coast, California (USA).** Deeper lemon-gold than Wine 1, with generous peach and ripe citrus in place of salinity, a rounder acid line and a marginally softer bead. English sparkling was the main alternative: its searing acidity and green-apple austerity are absent here, and the fruit ripeness and warmer body eliminate it. The mid-palate breadth places this in a warm-climate site, while retaining enough cool-site acidity to avoid flatness — North Coast.

**Wine 3 — Rheinhessen, Germany (Sekt).** The richest of the three: lemon curd, baked apple, toasted hazelnut and almond pastry indicate extended lees ageing in a warm vintage. Chalky minerality and a honeyed mid-palate sit on broad, medium-plus acidity — less racy than Wine 1, which separates it from Champagne and from English sparkling. Cava is excluded by the autolytic depth and the absence of that appellation's earthy, rooty character. Rheinhessen Sekt fits precisely.

## c) Style, production and quality (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Non-vintage Blanc de Blancs, zero or very low dosage given the purity of fruit. Fermentation and ageing in stainless steel or neutral vessel explains the absence of oak; long lees ageing supplies the brioche. Outstanding quality, Grand Cru Champagne tier, around £80–100 retail through specialist merchants and fine-dining lists. Drinking now, will hold 5–7 years, gaining honeyed and toasty weight.

**Wine 2.** Vintage Blanc de Blancs, traditional method with extended tirage. The rounder palate suggests partial barrel or tank fermentation and short post-disgorgement rest. Best now to three to five years; unlikely to gain further complexity.

**Wine 3.** Winzersekt: extended lees contact behind the hazelnut and almond pastry, with dosage judged to balance the broad mid-palate, and a gentle oxidative note from post-disgorgement development. The creamy, textural mid-palate indicates malolactic fermentation was carried out, producing a rounder, more approachable style. A clove note hints at possible short-term oak on the base wine. A vintage date was likely declared, reflecting riper, more consistent fruit than the NV approach of Wine 1.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, equivalent to non-vintage Grande Marque Champagne, retailing around £40–50. Balance, length and textural elegance place it above entry-level NV. It suits the independent specialist and premium on-trade across the UK, USA and East Asia, competing directly with other major-house Blanc de Blancs expressions.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality for Australian sparkling, retailing around AUD$60–75 at the top of the domestic premium tier. It targets consumers who have outgrown entry-level NV Prosecco and seek autolytic complexity with a riper fruit profile. Export potential to the UK and USA is real, though competition from Champagne at a similar price remains the principal commercial challenge.

Domaine des Forges Savennières Clos du Papillon, 2022. Loire Valley, France. (13.5%)

modelAnswer:
## a) Grape variety and region of origin (2 × 10 marks)

Both wines are Chenin Blanc from the Loire Valley. The case rests on a convergence across two very different styles: floral jasmine and citrus blossom over stone fruit, and above all the very high, tartaric-driven acidity that is Chenin's diagnostic signature — cutting the sweetness of Wine 1 and lending Wine 2 its steely finish. Riesling was weighed and ruled out: its acidity is more electric and petrol-edged than the rounder, lanolin-inflected quality here. Viognier offers aromatic overlap but lacks the structural austerity.

**Wine 1** is Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, Anjou. Deep amber, viscous, with confit pear, mango and a clear botrytis signature of powdery white peach and browned sugar. The taut acidity beneath the opulence rules out simple late-harvest and confirms a Grand Cru site capable of richness and precision together, distinguishing it from broader Coteaux du Layon.

**Wine 2** is Savennières. Dry, stone-fruit-driven, with steely acidity and a long mineral finish. The absence of residual sugar and the stony, citrus-blossom character confirm Savennières over Vouvray sec, which shows rounder, apple-driven fruit.

---

## b) Methods of production (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** relies on selective harvesting of botrytis-affected grapes across multiple tris. Barrel fermentation is likely given the integrated texture and nutty notes, halted at low alcohol to retain high residual sugar; extended lees contact adds richness without masking the botrytis.

**Wine 2** comes from late but fully ripe harvesting, fermented in tank or old oak — no new barrel influence is detectable — preserving stony purity. Malolactic appears blocked, retaining malic-edged, linear freshness. Mid-palate weight suggests some lees contact, though the wine stays precise.

---

## c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding, around €50–80. The balance of concentrated sweetness against energising acidity, and the very long, dense finish, mark it among the Loire's finest sweet wines. At 8–10 years it drinks beautifully now and has the acid backbone for another 15–20 years, gaining beeswax and dried apricot. Specialist merchants, fine dining and auction — UK, US, Japan — competing with Premier Cru Sauternes and top Tokaji.

**Wine 2** — Very good, around €20–30. At 2–3 years it drinks well now but will reward 5–8 years' cellaring, developing waxy lanolin and quince. Independent specialists and premium on-trade in the UK and Scandinavia, competing with top Vouvray sec for the consumer seeking mineral, food-friendly dry whites.

For each wine:

Domaine des Forges, Coteaux du Layon Saint-Aubin, 2019. Loire Valley, France. (11.5%)
Konrad Salwey, Oberrotweiler Henkenberg Gewürztraminer Auslese, 2020. Baden, Germany. (10%)
Peller Estates, Vidal Icewine, 2021. Niagara Peninsula, Canada. (7.5%)
Donnafugata, Ben Ryé Passito di Pantelleria, 2021. Sicily, Italy. (14.5%)
Bodegas Gutiérrez Colosía, Pedro Ximénez, NV. Jerez, Spain. (17%)

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1

### a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Riesling, Mosel, Germany. Lime, green apple, white peach and pineapple with no herbaceous cut immediately rule out Sauvignon Blanc. The perceived alcohol is barely warming — light-bodied, filigree — which eliminates Alsace Riesling (more weight, ~12–13% warmth) and Rheingau (firmer structure). The racy tartaric acidity and slate-tinged minerality are diagnostic of Mosel Spätlese.

### b) Sweetness Method (8 marks)

Sweetness is achieved by arresting fermentation before all sugar converts, preserving naturally ripe grape sugars. Grapes were harvested at Spätlese ripeness and fermentation halted by chilling. The fruit is pristine and primary — no botrytis or drying markers — confirming late picking rather than selective noble-rot harvest.

### c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Delicate, off-dry and racy, sweetness acting as counterpoint to pronounced acidity. Very good quality, equivalent to a classic Spätlese from a named Einzellage, retailing around £20–28 at independent specialists. Drink now or hold 5–10 years, when petrol and honey complexity will emerge. Key export markets: UK, USA, Japan, Scandinavia.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Chenin Blanc, Coteaux du Layon, Loire Valley, France. Deep gold, high viscosity, and a nose of lemon meringue, barley sugar, apricot and quince point clearly to Chenin Blanc. Semillon was considered — shared honeyed, waxy texture — but the pronounced tartaric freshness and confit-lemon precision cut through the richness in a way Semillon's softer, lanolin character does not. Riesling was eliminated immediately by body weight and the absence of lime or slate. The quince-and-barley-sugar richness with high acidity confirms the Loire; the fully sweet, unbotrytised freshness narrows the origin to Coteaux du Layon village level.

### b) Sweetness Method (8 marks)

Sweetness comes from selective harvesting of very ripe, lightly concentrated Chenin Blanc followed by arrested fermentation. The absence of heavy botrytis markers — no dominant saffron, ginger or oxidative notes — suggests moelleux-level ripeness from late picking rather than fully botrytised passerillage. Fermentation is halted by chilling or filtration to preserve natural sugars.

### c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Rich and texturally generous but lively — sweetness with genuine cut. Good to very good quality, village-level Coteaux du Layon, below the Chaume 1er Cru tier, retailing around €18–25 through on-trade and independent specialists. Will gain waxy honeycomb and dried quince over 10–15 years. Key export markets: UK and Belgium.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Gewürztraminer, Baden, Germany. Rose petal, lychee, Turkish delight, ginger and white pepper confirm Gewürztraminer beyond doubt. Muscat was considered given the floral intensity, but Muscat lacks the rose-and-lychee precision and ginger-pepper spice. Alsace Vendanges Tardives was the primary origin alternative, but the firmer acid structure and lower perceived alcohol — lighter-bodied, less broad — point to a cooler German origin. Baden's Kaiserstuhl produces Gewürztraminer with more tension than the riper Alsace examples; the Auslese designation confirms the German classification framework.

### b) Sweetness Method (8 marks)

Sweetness is achieved through Auslese-level harvesting: individually selected, very ripe bunches at minimum 83–100° Oechsle, with fermentation arrested before completion. No heavy botrytis is evident — the fruit remains aromatic and primary rather than showing saffron or oxidative character — indicating selection of super-ripe rather than botrytis-affected fruit.

### c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Opulently aromatic yet fresh enough to avoid Gewürztraminer's tendency toward flabbiness — the defining tension of the wine. Outstanding quality for a named-Einzellage Auslese, retailing around €25–40 at specialist retailers. Drink now through 10 years, developing dried rose and marmalade complexity. Limited production constrains export; principal markets are Germany, Switzerland and the UK.

---

## Wine 4

### a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Vidal, Niagara Peninsula, Canada. Syrupy viscosity combined with barely-warming perceived alcohol against extreme sweetness is the structural signature of Icewine. Riesling Eiswein was the primary alternative — both share intense sweetness and low alcohol — but the broader, rounder tropical-fruit profile (mango, tangerine, candied citrus) and the absence of Riesling's crystalline lime-zest precision confirm Vidal, a hybrid variety bred for Canadian winters that delivers riper, softer fruit than Riesling Icewine. The Niagara Peninsula is the principal Icewine region.

### b) Sweetness Method (8 marks)

Sweetness is achieved through freezing concentration on the vine. Vidal grapes are left until temperatures reach −8°C to −12°C; the water in the berries freezes and only the concentrated, unfrozen juice — extremely high in sugar, acid and flavour — flows from the press. Residual sugar typically reaches 180–250 g/L. No artificial freezing is permitted under Canadian Icewine regulations; concentration is entirely physical, not by botrytis or fermentation arrest.

### c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Intensely sweet and tropical with honeyed depth, though the finish is slightly shorter than the finest Niagara Riesling Icewines — competent rather than exceptional. Good to very good quality, estate-level, priced around CAD 50–80 per 200ml. Sold primarily through airport duty-free, hotel on-trade and gift retail targeting international tourists, particularly from Japan, China, South Korea and the USA.

---

## Wine 5

### a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria), Pantelleria, Sicily, Italy. Amber-gold, high viscosity, and a nose of candied orange peel, dried apricot, mango and Mediterranean scrub suggest a passito from a hot island origin. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains was considered, but the broader, rounder profile, the candied orange and papaya, and the absence of delicate neroli-and-lime precision of Muscat Blanc point to Zibibbo, the larger-berried variant. The Mediterranean herb note is a terroir signature of Pantelleria's volcanic soils. Perceived alcohol is warming and generous but without fortification heat, confirming a passito style consistent with Passito di Pantelleria DOC.

### b) Sweetness Method (8 marks)

Sweetness is achieved through passerillage: harvested Zibibbo grapes are sun-dried on mats (*girapoggio*) for two to four weeks in the intense Pantellerian sun and wind, concentrating sugars, acids and flavour compounds by evaporation. Fermentation then stops naturally at a high residual sugar level. Unlike botrytis wines, the profile shows dried and candied fruit rather than saffron or oxidative markers. No oak is detectable, preserving the aromatic purity of the grape.

### c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Rich, intensely aromatic and warm, with dried apricot and candied orange lifted by Mediterranean herb complexity — genuine typicity and place. Very good to outstanding quality, retailing around €30–50 per 375ml. The textural concentration suggests 5–10 further years of development. Positioned in fine-dining on-trade and independent specialists; key export markets are Germany, Switzerland, the USA and Japan.

---

## Wine 6

### a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Pedro Ximénez, Jerez, Spain. Dark mahogany with very high viscosity is immediately diagnostic. Caramelised raisins, molasses, dried fig and patisserie on the nose, with a creamy, intensely sweet palate, place this conclusively as PX Sherry. Old Tawny Port was the only serious alternative — shared mahogany colour and dried-fruit intensity — but Tawny shows more obvious spirit heat and rancio nuttiness with red-fruit dried-fruit character (prune, fig), whereas this wine's profile is dominated by pure raisin, molasses and creamy liqueur sweetness without fiery spirit presence. Perceived alcohol is medium-plus but not burning, confirming Sherry-level fortification rather than Port's higher spirit level.

### b) Sweetness Method (8 marks)

PX grapes are spread on esparto mats (*asoleo*) for 10–21 days under the Andalusian sun, losing up to 70% of their water and concentrating sugar to 400–500 g/L in the must. The must is lightly pressed and fermentation halted by fortification with grape spirit, preserving concentrated residual sugar — regularly exceeding 400 g/L in the finished wine. Subsequent ageing in a solera system adds caramel and rancio depth without diminishing the fundamental sweetness.

### c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Massively sweet and viscous, held together by raisin-and-molasses complexity that lifts it beyond simple confection. Good to very good quality, commercially accessible NV PX below the VORS tier, retailing around £15–22 per 50cl in both on-trade dessert lists and independent specialists. PX does not decline; serve now or hold indefinitely. Key export markets: UK, USA, Germany and the Netherlands.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

---

## 1. Model Answer

#### Section A · For the flight as a whole

**a) Grape variety — Riesling (4 marks)**

All four wines share the same high-toned aromatic signature — citrus blossom and lime — over a backbone of searing, precise acidity that carries very different sugar levels without ever feeling heavy. The floral lift (elderflower in Wine 1, honeysuckle in Wine 4) sits alongside a flinty slate character in Wines 1 and 2. Gewürztraminer is ruled out by the complete absence of phenolic grip; Chenin Blanc at comparable sweetness would show broader honeyed wax rather than this laser citrus tension, and would not give the petrol notes developing in Wines 2 and 3. Muscat was considered for Wine 1's grapey floral register but the lime-dominant citrus and petrol development across the flight confirm Riesling. The decisive structural proof is the variety's retention of electric acidity at extreme ripeness — visible even in the most concentrated glasses.

---

#### Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1 — b) Germany, Mosel; c) Sweetness; d) Alcohol; e) Style, quality, commercial**

Pale lemon-green, light-bodied, with a faint natural spritz: a cool-climate wine picked ripe but very low in alcohol. Lime blossom and elderflower over a flinty slate backbone point to the Mosel. Perceived warmth is very low — around 7–9% — and high acidity with light body fits Auslese harvesting where natural concentration, not fungal influence, dominates. Sweetness therefore comes from selective picking of late-harvested, naturally concentrated fruit; the purity and total lack of honeyed, fungal complexity rule out botrytis, while the low alcohol and absence of any freeze-concentration density rule out Eiswein. Outstanding quality at Auslese Prädikat level, around €35–55 retail. Specialist retail and fine-dining on-trade in the UK, USA and Japan; the challenge is consumer resistance to sweetness at low alcohol, the opportunity the sommelier advocacy of Riesling for food matching.

**Wine 2 — b) Alsace, France; c) Sweetness; d) Alcohol; e) Style, quality, commercial**

Deep gold, viscous and markedly fuller than Wine 1. The nose is more developed — honey, apricot, girolle mushroom and emerging petrol — indicating higher ripeness with partial botrytisation. Sweetness is achieved by Vendange Tardive: late harvest at very high natural sugars, here with some noble rot involvement, but well short of the full infection and dried-fruit concentration of an SGN. Perceived alcohol is medium, around 12%, reflecting drier autumn conditions than the Mosel and separating this wine from Wine 1 as much as the colour does. Very good to outstanding, equivalent to grand cru-sited VT, around €40–65. On-trade fine dining in France, Germany and Benelux, with export growth in Asia for rich whites; the constraint is that VT Alsace lacks the brand recognition of Sauternes.

**Wine 3 — b) Niagara Peninsula, Canada; c) Sweetness; d) Alcohol; e) Style, quality, commercial**

Gold, extremely viscous, yet the acidity is the most electric in the flight — sharp and malic — with pure unoxidised mango, peach nectar and mandarin. That combination of massive sugar with wholly clean fruit is diagnostic of freeze-concentration rather than botrytis, which would have brought marmalade, saffron and dried apricot. Sweetness comes from Icewine: grapes pressed frozen at or below −8°C so that water remains as ice and only sugar-rich juice runs, giving very high residual sugar at low alcohol — around 9–10%. Very good to outstanding, benchmarked against top Niagara Icewine at roughly CAD 80–120 per 200ml. This is Canada's signature category, positioned in East Asian luxury gifting (China, South Korea, Japan) and domestic cellar-door tourism; tiny yields and half-bottle formats limit mainstream off-trade viability.

**Wine 4 — b) Clare Valley, Australia; c) Sweetness; d) Alcohol; e) Style, quality, commercial**

Gold and viscous, but the aromatic register is lime curd, kumquat and candied citrus over honeysuckle — a warm-climate Riesling at high ripeness. The palate separates it clearly from the other three: sweet and round with a velvety texture, no fungal complexity, no petrol development, and none of Wine 3's freeze-driven acid shock. This is Cordon Cut: canes severed before harvest so water and nutrient flow to the bunches stops and sugars concentrate passively on the vine over several weeks. Perceived alcohol is around 12–13%, consistent with the Clare's warm continental growing season. Very good quality, premium varietal Riesling at regional best, around AUD 35–50. Sold to Australian domestic consumers seeking premium sweet whites and to UK and US specialist retail, where the named production method gives a genuine point of difference against Sauternes and Mosel on the same shelf.

The flight's higher-order lesson is that Riesling's fixed acid structure allows four entirely different routes to sugar — passive over-ripeness, noble rot, ice, and vine-severance dehydration — to be read off the palate, because each leaves a distinct signature in what accompanies the sweetness rather than in the sweetness itself.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (2 × 9 marks)

Both wines share elevated perceived alcohol, saline-spicy minerality and persistent oxidative character pointing decisively to Savagnin from the Jura. Chardonnay was briefly considered — it can adopt oxidative styles here — but the pronounced saline, herbal intensity with lemon pith and bitters on Wine 1, and the curry-leaf, farmyard, aniseed complexity of Wine 2, are more diagnostic of Savagnin's phenolic grip. Chenin Blanc was considered for Wine 1's apple and meadow-herb profile but ruled out by the absence of honeyed waxy richness and the shared regional origin confirmed by Wine 2.

**Wine 1 — Côtes du Jura.** Fresher, more primary character — lemony citrus, meadow herbs, flake salt, subtle oxidation — places this in the broader Côtes du Jura appellation. Restrained barrel influence and lighter body point away from full sous voile ageing.

**Wine 2 — Château-Chalon.** Profound oxidative complexity — walnut, curry leaf, flor — combined with dense texture and extraordinary length confirms full sous voile ageing. This is consistent with the appellation's minimum six-year voile requirement, the markers that separate it decisively from Wine 1.

## b) Compare the maturation regimes and their impact on style (16 marks)

Wine 1 shows controlled oxidative exposure: subtle toffee, burnt lemon and spicy mineral edge suggest used-oak ageing with limited topping-up but no dominant flor influence. Retained lemon-core freshness indicates an ouillé or semi-ouillé approach, where oxidation enhances complexity without erasing primary varietal character.

Wine 2 exhibits the complete sous voile signature. Flor yeast consuming oxygen has generated acetaldehyde, producing walnut, curry leaf and sour-flor notes; all primary fruit has been replaced by oxidised apple, aniseed and mineral intensity. Prolonged ageing in old, non-topped barrels has built exceptional density and length entirely unlike the partial exposure in Wine 1.

## c) Quality and state of maturity (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality for Côtes du Jura, around €20–30. The balance between primary character and oxidative complexity is well-handled. At peak now, consistent with roughly three to four years of age; will hold a further four to five years as citrus lift gradually yields to textural weight.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding quality at Château-Chalon's appellation ceiling, around €80–120+. Approximately eight years old, fully mature but far from decline: walnut and curry are precisely integrated and the finish exceptional. Will continue developing for ten to fifteen years, deepening in nutty complexity and saline intensity.

## d) Compare the commercial positioning (6 marks)

Wine 1 is an entry point to Jura's oxidative tradition: specialist independents, premium on-trade by-the-glass, and natural-wine retailers in France, Switzerland, and urban UK and US markets, competing around €25.

Wine 2 is a connoisseur's purchase sold through allocation lists, specialist importers and fine-dining lists in France, Japan and the US. Tiny production limits volume; Château-Chalon has no true equivalent anywhere, commanding strong pricing and fierce loyalty among enthusiasts.

## a) Region of origin (3 × 9 marks)

All three are Riesling. The common thread is a bone-dry acid skeleton — tartaric, racy, mouthwatering — carrying high sugar without heaviness, with lime, citrus peel and floral blossom, no oak and a faint petrol lift on the two riper wines. Chenin Blanc was the main alternative but would give quince, wool and a broader, softer acid line; Muscat is ruled out by the absence of grapey terpene sweetness.

**Wine 1 — Middle Mosel, Germany; Piesport/Bernkastel sector, Auslese.** The killer evidence is structural: barely any warmth on the finish, feather-light body, a lifting natural spritz, and acid that outruns the sugar. Only the Mosel makes sweet Riesling at this alcohol. Lime blossom, green apple and a crushed-slate, saline undertow narrow it to a Devonian slate site rather than the Rheingau, which would be broader and rounder.

**Wine 2 — Niagara Peninsula, Canada.** Gold, thick-legged, pronounced, with concentrated peach nectar, mandarin and candied citrus, yet no honeyed saffron or botrytis funk — the fruit is pure and unbotrytised. That purity at this sugar level points to freeze concentration rather than noble rot: Icewine. Perceived alcohol is low, around 9–10%, ruling out Sauternes-style botrytis. German Eiswein was weighed, but the mango-tinged tropical ripeness and limestone-edged tension read as Beamsville Bench, Niagara, not Mosel.

**Wine 3 — Clare Valley, South Australia.** Lime flesh and lemon curd sit under honey, sherbet and kumquat; the fruit is raisined-sweet but not rotten, and there is faint white pepper. Alcohol is a touch warmer than Wine 2, medium body, and no oak. That combination — intense lime, dried-fruit concentration without botrytis, and high acid held at moderate alcohol — is Clare Valley cane-cut Riesling.

## b) Style and winemaking (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1:** Late-picked healthy fruit with a little botrytis at most; whole-bunch pressed gently, cool ferment in stainless or old Fuder, stopped by chilling and sterile filtration to retain sugar and CO₂. No malolactic — the malic zest is intact. The under-the-skin point: at this ripeness the estate could have chased higher must weight, but held picking so acid outran sugar, which is why a wine this sweet drinks weightless.

**Wine 2:** Netted fruit left to freeze on the vine and pressed below −8°C, the ice retained in the press so only concentrated juice runs. Long, sluggish cool ferment arrested at low alcohol; no oak, no malolactic, protective handling to keep the fruit primary.

**Wine 3:** Different mechanism again — canes severed on the vine and fruit dehydrated in situ (passerillage), concentrating sugar and acid without rot. Pressed, cool-fermented in stainless steel, ferment stopped by chilling/filtration; velvety texture from glycerol, not lees or wood.

## c) Quality, maturity, commercial (3 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1:** Outstanding, top-Auslese/Einzellage level, around €45. Youthful, 5–6 years old; will improve 10 years and hold 25+, gaining honey and kerosene. Independent specialists and fine-dining lists.

**Wine 2:** Very good; Canada's flagship export tier, ~CAD 70/375ml. Drink now to 8 years. Duty-free, gifting and Asian export markets; challenged by price and sweet-wine decline.

**Wine 3:** Very good, benchmark for its niche, ~AUD 40/375ml. Drink now to 6 years. Independents and by-the-glass dessert pours domestically.

## d) Residual sugar (3 × 2 marks)

Wine 1: 85 g/L. Wine 2: 220 g/L. Wine 3: 130 g/L.

Acidity is medium-plus rather than racy, the mousse softer; perceived alcohol low, around 11–11.5%, consistent with early harvest. Residual sugar is low brut, 9–12 g/L. Lees contact will have been shorter, perhaps 12–18 months, after in-bottle fermentation. Chardonnay here is fruit-forward rather than complexity-driven.

Acceptable to good quality, equivalent to a competent Cava Reserva at £10–15. Suits off-trade multiples and casual by-the-glass lists, competing with Prosecco Superiore DOCG but offering more structure; differentiation in a crowded entry-level segment is the commercial challenge.

**Wine 2 — Anderson Valley, California, USA (Brut NV)**

Deeper lemon-gold from riper fruit: white nectarine, apricot, toast, creamy texture. Acidity is refreshing but broader and less linear than the European wines; perceived alcohol moderate, around 12%, adding body. Residual sugar is low brut, though fruit ripeness gives an impression of richness. Extended lees ageing, likely 24–36 months, explains the pastry-like palate, while partial malolactic fermentation in the base wine has softened the acid line and cool nights preserved freshness.

Very good quality, equivalent to mid-tier California prestige sparkling at £25–40. Suits independent merchants and premium restaurant lists, with export appeal in the UK and Scandinavia for credible New World alternatives to Champagne; pricing above many export Champagnes demands a confident consumer narrative.

**Wine 3 — Blanc de Blancs Brut, Champagne, France (Vintage 2016)**

The most complex wine in the flight. Pale gold; abundant, fine, creamy mousse indicating four or more years on lees. Powerful and precise: ripe pear, honeysuckle, beeswax, brioche, mandarin oil. The palate is rich yet defined by high, racy acidity — quince, candied citrus, exceptional length. Perceived alcohol 12–12.5%, well integrated; dosage low, around 8 g/L. Stainless-steel base fermentation has preserved citrus precision; no new oak detectable.

The key insight: the combination of generous ripeness with sustained racy acidity reads not as warmth but as vintage quality. The 2016 harvest delivered exceptional natural ripeness allied to the region's acidity — Chardonnay fully expressive yet precisely framed.

Outstanding quality — benchmark vintage Blanc de Blancs Grande Marque at £60–90. Independent specialists, fine dining and gifting, with strong export to Japan and Hong Kong. Will improve for five to eight years, developing toast, dried flowers and almond paste.

**Wine 4 — Blanc de Blancs, West Sussex, England (Vintage 2018)**

Lemon-green with a finer, more persistent bead than Wine 1. Lemon, lime, baked apple, brioche and a delicate pastry note: autolytic complexity is clearly present, but the fruit retains a tensile quality distinct from Wine 3's rounder generosity. Very high, linear acidity is the defining feature, with a chalky, saline finish that separates this wine from the rest of the flight. Perceived alcohol around 12%; residual sugar low brut, 8–10 g/L, barely perceptible against the acidity. Traditional method with 36–48 months on lees; reductive, cool base-wine handling has kept primary citrus alongside developed autolysis.

Very good quality, equivalent to non-vintage Grande Marque Champagne at £45–65. The primary market is the UK on-trade, where aspirational restaurants position English sparkling as the premium domestic alternative; export to the USA and Scandinavia is growing, though communicating value at or above Champagne pricing remains the central challenge. Will gain complexity over three to five years while retaining its defining acid freshness.

modelAnswer:
## a) Country and Region of Origin (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Champagne, France (Côte des Blancs, 1er Cru)**
Singed bread, toasted almond, lemon curd and chalky wet-asphalt minerality point to Champagne. Crémant de Bourgogne shares Chardonnay and lees character but lacks this flinty mineral tension; English sparkling has a leaner green-apple register distinct from the riper lemon-curd weight here. Chalky soils and cool-fruit intensity narrow the origin to the Côte des Blancs; the complexity is above Village level, consistent with 1er Cru.

**Wine 2 — Franciacorta, Lombardy, Italy**
Same lemon-green appearance as Wine 1 but a softer, pillowy mousse — yellow apple, fresh apricot, rye bread, orange blossom — with less mineral tension. The reduced-pressure effervescence identifies this as Satèn, a subtype unique to Franciacorta. Cava was considered but would show savoury almond-skin aromatics from Xarel-lo; Prosecco was eliminated given the clear autolytic contribution. Warm-climate apricot fruit combined with traditional-method structure places this in northern Italy; the Satèn mousse confirms Franciacorta.

**Wine 3 — Kent, England**
Green apple, lemon peel, struck flint, white flowers and a not-yet-integrated brioche note. The palate is the leanest in the flight — very high acidity, slightly angular finish — and autolytic depth is shallower than Wine 1. Champagne was the obvious comparison, but the crisper green-apple register and undeveloped autolysis point to a younger wine in primary-to-secondary transition, consistent with a 2018 vintage Blanc de Blancs. Struck-flint reduction over green fruit is a signature of Kent and Sussex chalk.

**Wine 4 — Tasmania, Australia**
The most evolved wine: brioche, nougat, beeswax, saline, yet the palate retains very high acidity and crisp apple. New World weight and beeswax complexity point to Australia; Margaret River and Hunter Valley are eliminated by the very high natural acidity and cool-climate restraint. Tasmania's cold coastal sites produce exactly this combination of power and salinity, and the 2014 vintage is consistent with seven or more years on lees.

**Wine 5 — Robertson, South Africa**
Subtle toast, pear, white peach, ripe apple. Genuine traditional-method structure is present, but autolytic depth is the shallowest in the flight. The riper stone-fruit register excludes Europe; the less-developed profile compared to Wine 4 indicates shorter lees contact. Robertson's limestone-influenced inland valley delivers riper fruit than coastal Elgin while retaining genuine acidity — consistent with what is in the glass.

---

## b) Key Winemaking Decisions (5 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Whole-bunch pressing inferred from the clean, phenolic-free palate. Stainless steel fermentation preserves primary citrus fruit. Extended lees ageing of three or more years accounts for the singed-bread complexity. No significant oak. Minimal dosage inferred from the taut, linear finish.

**Wine 2** — Bottling at approximately 4.5 atmospheres rather than the standard 6 confirms the Satèn style. Stainless steel fermentation preserves fresh primary fruit. Lees ageing of 18–24 months accounts for the rye-bread breadiness, though shorter contact than Wine 1 explains the reduced autolytic depth. Bone-dry finish indicates low or zero dosage.

**Wine 3** — Reductive handling accounts for the struck-flint character alongside still-developing brioche. The angular palate structure indicates partial or no MLF, a deliberate choice to preserve the racy natural acidity of this cool site. The 2018 vintage with recent disgorgement is consistent with lees notes not yet fully integrated.

**Wine 4** — Completed MLF is evident from the rounder texture alongside very high acidity; without it the wine would be searingly sharp. Extended lees ageing of seven or more years produces the beeswax and nougat complexity. Whole-bunch pressing explains the clean palate. Low dosage of approximately 3 g/L deliberately foregrounds natural acidity and autolytic depth.

**Wine 5** — Shorter lees contact than the rest of the flight, consistent with meeting MCC minimum requirements, explains the restrained autolytic character. Stainless steel fermentation produces the clean primary fruit profile. Dosage around 6–8 g/L is consistent with an accessible Brut style.

---

## c) Quality and Maturity (5 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding at 1er Cru level, approximately £35–45. At or near peak now, with capacity to hold a further 3–4 years before gentle decline.

**Wine 2** — Very good, NV Franciacorta Satèn DOCG, approximately €20–30. Creamy mousse and stone-fruit purity are well-executed; mineral depth is limited. Drink now; will hold 2–3 years without meaningful improvement.

**Wine 3** — Very good to outstanding for English sparkling, approximately £40–55. Still developing — will improve over 2–4 years as autolytic notes integrate, then hold a further 3–5 years.

**Wine 4** — Outstanding, among the finest New World traditional-method examples, approximately AUD 80–100 (£45–55). Preserving freshness and saline tension across a decade is remarkable. At or just past peak; drink within 2–3 years before fruit fades.

**Wine 5** — Good at mid-tier MCC level, approximately ZAR 350–450 (£15–20). Clean and well-made but lacking the autolytic complexity of the rest of the flight. Drink now; consume within 1–2 years.

---

## d) Commercial Position (5 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Independent merchants and premium on-trade in France, the UK, the US and Japan at £35–45. Competes with other Côte des Blancs 1er Cru grower Blanc de Blancs. The opportunity is continued premiumisation of grower Champagne globally; the challenge is educating consumers beyond major house brands.

**Wine 2** — Premium Italian restaurants and specialist independents in Italy and Germany at €20–30. The opportunity is positioning Franciacorta as Italy's Blanc de Blancs alternative below Champagne pricing; the challenge is low awareness outside Italy against the dominance of Prosecco internationally.

**Wine 3** — Premium specialist merchants and fine-dining on-trade in the UK at £40–55, with growing export potential in Scandinavia and the US. The vintage Blanc de Blancs format suits the quality-conscious consumer seeking a Champagne alternative with a strong provenance story. The challenge is limited production volume.

**Wine 4** — Fine-dining on-trade and specialist retailers in Australia, the UK and Hong Kong at AUD 80–100. Competes with top-tier Blanc de Blancs Champagne at a comparable price. The opportunity is Australia's growing reputation for cool-climate sparkling; the challenge is communicating the Tasmania terroir story to export markets.

**Wine 5** — Mid-market on-trade and specialist off-trade in South Africa, with export potential to the UK and the Netherlands, at £15–20 domestically. Competes with entry-level Champagne and Crémant. The opportunity is positioning MCC as a premium alternative to Prosecco and Cava; the challenge is limited international recognition for South African sparkling.

#### Section A · For the flight as a whole

**a) Grape variety (15 marks)**

Riesling. All three wines span radically different sweetness levels and climates yet share lime and citrus fruit, pronounced floral lift, and a high, characteristically taut acidity that cuts through sweetness rather than being overwhelmed by it. Wines 1 and 2 both carry late-harvest tropical and honeyed fruit with preserved-citrus concentration; Wine 3 shows a bone-dry register — lime juice, green apple, herbal and saline edges — yet the same acid signature is immediately recognisable. **Wine 1 — Alsace Vendanges Tardives**

**b) Sweetness and style (13 marks)**

Sweetness arises from selective late harvesting of botrytis-affected and overripe grapes, concentrated through water loss rather than arrested fermentation. The wine reads as medium-sweet, with residual sugar supported by sufficient acidity to prevent a cloying finish. Unctuous texture points to genuine grape concentration; aromas of candied tropical fruit, lychee, and delicate spice suggest partial botrytis rather than pure passerillage. Alcohol feels barely perceptible — consistent with fermentation stopping before full dryness. Style: rich and aromatic, opulent yet lifted, with the paradoxical freshness that distinguishes Alsace VT from heavier dessert styles.

**c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)**

Outstanding quality, equivalent to Alsace Vendanges Tardives AOC — a legally defined tier requiring minimum must weights substantially above table wine. Retail around £45–65 per half bottle through specialist merchants and top-end restaurant lists in the UK, Germany, and Japan. Competes with Mosel Spätlese/Auslese but offers more aromatic exuberance. Will develop over 10–15 years.

---

**Wine 2 — Mosel Auslese**

**b) Sweetness and style (13 marks)**

Sweetness derives from selective harvesting of botrytis-affected berries — individual bunches showing noble rot removed by hand from partially healthy clusters. Alcohol is barely perceptible, pointing to very low final ABV and substantial residual sugar retained through early cold stabilisation. The acidity is electric and racy — a steely, tartrate-dominant structure providing extraordinary tension against the honeyed sweetness. Aromatically: apricot, saffron, beeswax alongside clean lime zest. Compared with Wine 1, the body is lighter and the profile more mineral and precise, where Wine 1 reads more opulent and spiced — the key distinction within the flight.

**c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)**

Very high quality, Auslese Prädikat — legally requiring 83–100° Oechsle in the Mosel. Retailing around £35–55 per half bottle from a recognised single-vineyard estate through specialist merchants and fine-dining restaurants in Germany, the US, and East Asia. **Wine 3 — Eden Valley Dry Riesling**

**b) Sweetness and style (13 marks)**

No sweetness mechanism is at work: the wine is bone dry, fermented fully to dryness with no deliberate arrest or late-harvest concentration — the defining difference from Wines 1 and 2. Any impression of fruit sweetness comes from ripe lime, green apple, and white peach held against very high, mouthwatering acidity from high-altitude fruit grown above 400 m. The herbal, minerally-saline edge and white pepper note are distinctive regional markers absent from the European wines in this flight. Style: linear and intense, vibrant dryness at the serious end of Australian Riesling.

**c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)**

Very good quality, Museum Reserve tier — extended cellaring before release demonstrating confidence in ageability.
