## 1. Model Answer

#### Section A · For the flight as a whole

**a) Grape variety and origins**

Both wines are sweet with fresh acidity and stone-fruit, honeyed aromatics, making Sémillon and Riesling the principal candidates. Muscat and Chenin Blanc were weighed and rejected: no grapey terpene lift, no quince or wet-wool.

The split is structural. Wine 1 is broad, warm and viscous, deep amber-gold, with pronounced honeyed botrytis and glycerol-rich weight — richer and rounder than Riesling delivers at any sugar level. This indicates **Sémillon**, and the combination of botrytis concentration and body places it in **Sauternes, Bordeaux**, at classed-growth level.

Wine 2 is tighter and more lifted — dried apricot, frangipani, piercing acidity holding the sugar in check for a fresh rather than cloying finish. That acid architecture and mineral tension is **Riesling**, and the cool-climate signature points to **Elgin, Western Cape, South Africa**.

---

#### Section B · For each wine individually

**b) Methods of achieving sweetness**

Wine 1 relies on **botrytis cinerea**, desiccating Sémillon on the vine and concentrating sugar, acid and glycerol while adding honeyed complexity. Selection is by *tries successives*, several passes taking only fully botrytised berries. Fermentation stops naturally as rising alcohol overwhelms the yeast, leaving high residual sugar.

Wine 2 is a **noble late harvest**: botrytis contributes, but on Riesling's thinner skins it gives cleaner, more delineated concentration rather than glycerol-rich unctuousness, and *passerillage* on the vine shares the work. Fermentation is arrested deliberately — chilling and sterile filtration — at a chosen sweetness, protecting the racy acid.

**c) Style and quality**

**Wine 1** — Opulent, fully botrytised, viscous and deeply concentrated. Outstanding quality, consistent with Premier Grand Cru Classé Sauternes at £60–80 per 375ml. Drinking well now, it will hold and deepen toward marmalade and toffee over fifteen years or more.

**d) Commercial position**

**Wine 1** — Fine wine merchants and top on-trade; established collectors; export to Asia and North America.

**Wine 2** — Independent specialists and premium off-trade; by-the-glass dessert listings; Nordic and UK export.

**e) Residual sugar, Wine 1** — approximately 120 g/L.

**f) Residual sugar, Wine 2** — approximately 80 g/L.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, Wines 1 & 2

## a) Region and grape variety (2 × 8 marks)

Both wines: **Jura, France; Savagnin.**

Wine 2 opens the flight. Deep gold, high viscosity, and pronounced walnut kernel, curry powder, dried apricot and rancio point to prolonged ageing under a film yeast. Fino/Amontillado was the obvious alternative, but there is no spirit heat: the warmth reads unfortified, around 14.5%, and the acid line is high and lemony rather than the bone-dry saline austerity of Palomino. Oxidative white Rioja was also weighed and rejected — no coconut/American oak. Curry powder plus preserved lemon on an unfortified base is the *sotolon* signature of Vin Jaune; the concentration and textural depth indicate Château-Chalon rather than a generic Côtes du Jura bottling.

Wine 1 sits in the same house. Gold, medium(+) viscosity, star fruit, silex, apple and wheat/fresh bread, with only a whisper of oxidative lift and very fine phenolic grip; warmth is moderate, ~13%. **Wine 1** — a dry, taut, fresh-fruited style deliberately made in the modern topped-up idiom. Whole-bunch pressing is suggested by the purity and absence of coarse phenolics; indigenous ferment and ageing in older large casks, regularly topped, explain the trace of oxidation without any voile character. **Wine 2** — the antithesis: barrels deliberately left unfilled, a *voile* allowed to form, and a minimum six years and three months in cask before bottling in clavelin. Evaporation concentrates everything; the aldehydic drive comes from the veil, not from oak, which is neutral throughout.

Under the skin: the richness here outruns the aldehyde frame, suggesting a generous vintage and a producer whose veil stayed intact — rancio complexity without volatile acidity or bruised-apple collapse.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, Wines 1 & 2 (same region)

## a) Region and grape variety (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 2** opens the door. Deep gold, high viscosity, pronounced walnut, curry, mushroom, dried grasses and resin over saline citrus — yet the finish carries weight (~14.5%) without any spirit warmth. That absence of fortification rules out Amontillado and dry Sercial Madeira, the two obvious look-alikes; Madeira would also show volatile lift and a baked, caramelised edge that is not here. Unfortified, flor-derived curry (sotolon) with bruised-apple and hazelnut, held by searing acidity, points to **Savagnin aged sous voile in the Jura**. The depth, salinity and persistence argue for **Château-Chalon** rather than a generic Côtes du Jura Vin Jaune.

**Wine 1** shares the silex, star fruit and saline signature but with only a whisper of oxidation and less weight: **Savagnin, Côtes du Jura, ouillé**. Jura Chardonnay was the alternative, but its broader orchard-cream breadth is absent — the fine phenolic grip and flinty, star-fruit line indicate Savagnin.

## b) Methods of production compared (20 marks)

Neither shows vanilla or toast, so both were raised in old, neutral wood after whole-cluster pressing and indigenous ferment.

Wine 1 was then **topped up (ouillé)** — barrels kept full, roughly a year, malolactic at most partial given the firm acid line, minimal bâtonnage, early bottling. Style: protective, primary-leaning, taut and mineral, with the faint oxidative trace betraying deliberate tolerance of a little ullage rather than a reductive regime.

Wine 2 was **left unfilled and never racked or topped**, developing a voile of yeast across the surface for a minimum of six years and three months. Under the skin: the voile is thin and discontinuous in Jura's cold, swinging cellars, so ageing is biological *and* slowly oxidative at once — that is why sotolon-curry sits beside walnut without volatile spoilage, and why evaporative concentration yields the viscosity and alcoholic weight from a base picked at modest ripeness. Bottled in the 620ml clavelin.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

Wine 1: very good, at the top of the Côtes du Jura appellation, around €30. Independent specialists and by-the-glass in Paris and London bistronomie; competes with premium Chablis 1er Cru. Drink now to eight years.

Wine 2: outstanding — the Jura's grand-cru-equivalent AOC, €80–100, allocated through fine-wine merchants to the US, Japan and Scandinavia. Niche: its oxidative register limits volume appeal, but scarcity sustains price. Will improve fifteen years, hold thirty.

## a) Grape variety and origin (4 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Vespaiolo, Breganze, Veneto, Italy.** Deep gold, thick slow tears, and pronounced dried apricot, fig, barley sugar and marzipan against only a marginal rot note: the sweetness mechanism is dried grapes (appassimento) with incidental botrytis, not rot-led. Tokaji Aszú was weighed — Furmint gives smokier orange peel and a rot-derived bitter grip absent here — as was Recioto di Soave, but Garganega shows softer acid and almond blossom. **The telling point:** the acid line is still tartaric and cleansing beneath 180–200 g/L of sugar, and only a very late-ripening, acid-retentive native grape survives months on drying racks into midwinter without going flabby. That marriage of raisin concentration and searing acid is the Breganze idiom.

**Wine 2 — Petit Manseng, Jurançon, south-west France.** Also deep gold and sweet, but the fruit is fresher and more exotic: apricot nectar, pineapple, passion fruit, grapefruit and lime leaf, with fresh grape rather than raisin. That points to passerillage — thick-skinned berries shrivelling on the vine — not botrytis. Sauternes was considered and rejected: no lanolin, no rot funk, and the acid is medium-plus and pithy rather than Sémillon-broad. Warmth is noticeably higher than Wine 1, around 14%, with a full, glyceric body — consistent with grapes hanging into November in the Pyrenean foothills.

**Wine 3 — Grüner Veltliner, Heiligenstein, Kamptal, Austria.** Lemon-green, dry, and defined by prominent white pepper with green herb, lemon zest and a chalky, faintly saline texture. Alcohol is modest, around 12%, with high acid — a cool continental site. Sauvignon Blanc was considered but there is no pungent thiol or nettle; Riesling would give lime and stone rather than pepper and lentil. The mineral cut and pepper together narrow to a single-vineyard Kamptal or Wachau site.

**Wine 4 — Pinot Noir, Martinborough, Wairarapa, New Zealand.** Medium ruby with a bright crimson rim, translucent, silky layered fine tannin — the only red in the flight, and unmistakably Pinot in weight and texture. Smoke and flint, floral lift, dark cherry, cola and a meaty base with medium-plus alcohol around 13.5%. Burgundy was considered, but the fruit purity and cola-chocolate sweetness read New World; Central Otago would be denser and more plum-driven. The savoury, herb-edged spine points to Martinborough.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 x 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** Harvested ripe, then whole bunches hung to dry for several months, concentrating sugar and acid alike. Pressing raisined fruit gives low yields; the slow, incomplete ferment stops naturally as alcohol climbs, leaving high residual sugar. The integrated vanilla and light toast, plus crème brûlée and hazelnut, indicate a long ferment and maturation in small barrels, mostly used. Malolactic clearly avoided — the acid is razor-sharp.

**Wine 2.** A different route to sugar: multiple tries through late autumn on the vine. Whole-bunch pressed, then fermented cool and slowly in barrel, the ferment arrested by chilling and sulphur once balance is reached. Creamy vanilla and gentle toast suggest 10–12 months in barriques, a minority new, with lees stirring for the full, rounded mouthfeel. No malolactic; the citrus is preserved.

**Wine 3.** Deliberately reductive and transparent. Whole-bunch pressed, cool-fermented in stainless steel or large neutral oak, no oak flavour whatsoever, no malolactic, brief lees contact for the chalky grip, bottled early with a light CO2 spritz. The modest alcohol suggests picking held back to protect acidity rather than chasing botrytis-free super-ripeness.

**Wine 4.** Mostly destemmed with a portion whole bunch, giving the floral-smoky lift; cold soak, wild-yeast ferment and gentle punchdowns rather than hard extraction — hence medium colour with fine, layered tannin. Full malolactic, then 10–12 months in French oak, perhaps 20–30% new: chocolate and cola without overt vanilla. Unfined and unfiltered on the evidence of the brilliant but not stripped appearance.

**Wine 2.** Very good quality, the top cuvée tier within its appellation and superb value beside Sauternes at twice the price. €20–25 for a full bottle; UK and Dutch independents, French on-trade, US export. Drink now to ten years.

## a) Region and grape variety (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Pedro Ximénez, Montilla-Moriles, Spain; very old solera.** Opaque brown-black, treacle-slow tears; the palate is near-syrupy, RS clearly above 400 g/L, yet the warmth is only gentle and rounded — an estimated 16%, low for a fortified — with soft, low acidity and a faint volatile lift. Raisin, date, molasses, espresso, walnut. Málaga was weighed (same grape) but the absence of Moscatel florality and arrope roast argues against it; sweet Malmsey Madeira is excluded by the missing searing acid line and estufagem caramel bite.

**Wine 2 — Savagnin, Jura; Château-Chalon.** Deep gold, limpid, no spirit heat at all but generous warmth around 14.5%. Walnut, green apple, bruised apple, curry/fenugreek, dried ginger, saline. Bone dry, very high acid, prolonged. Amontillado was the obvious alternative and is ruled out by the absence of fortification heat and of Palomino's chalky salinity; oxidative Rioja Viura is ruled out by the lack of oak vanillin and the pronounced sotolon. Within Jura, this intensity and length point to Château-Chalon rather than a Côtes du Jura vin jaune.

**Wine 3 — Barossa Valley, South Australia; Grenache with Shiraz/Mataro.** Mahogany with an olive rim, viscous. Rancio, dried fig, toffee, coffee, orange peel; sweet at roughly 110–130 g/L with marked spirit warmth, ~20%. Tawny Port was considered but lacks this raisined, drier, brandy-spirit signature and shows a fresher red-fruit seam; Rutherglen Muscat is excluded by the absence of grapey, rose-petal aromatics. Average age around 20 years.

## b) Style and winemaking, role of oxidation (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1.** Grapes sun-dried on mats (asoleo) to raisin, giving a must too concentrated to ferment far; fortification arrests it almost immediately, hence high sugar with modest alcohol. Decades in a static/solera cask system under deliberate oxidation and evaporative concentration produced the black colour and rancio-coffee depth; oxidation here builds sweetness and viscosity rather than nuttiness.

**Wine 2.** Late-picked, unchaptalised, fermented dry, then racked to old barrel and deliberately not topped up for over six years, allowing a *voile* of film yeast. This is biological, not oxidative, ageing — acetaldehyde and sotolon under the veil, with only limited ingress of air. The higher-order point: unfortified flor survives only in a narrow alcohol/acid window, and that this wine retains a bright green-apple core rather than maderising after six years sous voile indicates cool marl slopes and a producer confident enough to leave the veil undisturbed.

**Wine 3.** Fermentation stopped by neutral spirit with sugar retained, then long maturation in small, old, warm-loft barrels with ullage and evaporation — a true fractional-blending house style. Oxidation here drives rancio and colour loss toward mahogany.

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding; Gran Reserva tier, ~£70/50cl. Independent specialists and dessert lists; a foil to blue cheese-driven lists in the UK and Japan.

**Wine 2.** Outstanding, top of its AOC, ~£85/62cl. Sommelier-driven, Comté-adjacent; tiny volumes limit reach.

**Wine 3.** Very good–excellent, 21-year age-statement tier, ~£60. Australian off-trade fine wine plus UK/US collectors; challenge is a shrinking fortified category.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, four wines from one country

The flight is unlocked by Wine 3: dark olive-brown with a green rim, liqueur-sweet and raisined, is a signature no other origin produces. That fixes the country as Australia, and the other three then read as the pillars of that country's fortified and sweet tradition.

## Wine 1

**a) Palomino, Barossa Valley, South Australia — an aged Apera in Amontillado style.** Deep amber, high viscosity, still, with integrated spirit warmth suggesting around 18% and a dry-to-just-off-dry palate. Bready, yeasty notes sit beneath roasted nut, orange peel and mixed spice — evidence of flor ageing followed by oxidative ageing. Andalusian Amontillado was the obvious alternative but the softer acid line, rounder mid-palate and candied, almost honeyed citrus lack the searing salinity and bone-dry rasp of Jerez. Madeira is ruled out: no volatile lift, no curry note, and the acidity is nowhere near electric. The complete absence of varietal aromatic imprint points to a neutral grape — Palomino, planted for exactly this purpose.

**b)** Neutral base picked at modest ripeness and fermented dry, fortified to around 15% and rested under a flor veil for some years, giving the yeasty, saline undertone. A second fortification to ~18% killed the veil, after which long ageing in old seasoned casks in a warm store produced the amber colour, viscosity and nutty rancio through evaporative concentration. The delicate honey suggests a small sweetening addition before bottling.

**c)** Outstanding within its category — the equivalent of a VOS Amontillado, and worth around AUD 50–70. Sold in tiny volume through independent specialists and sommelier lists. The challenge is a structurally declining fortified-white category; the opportunity lies in the aperitif and cheese-course by-the-glass revival in the UK and US on-trade.

## Wine 2

**a) Shiraz, McLaren Vale, South Australia — sparkling red.** Ruby with a fine persistent bead, full-bodied, medium tannin, medium acid, medium-dry, with warmth around 13.5%. Plum, blackberry and licorice are overlaid by fruit cake, brickdust, leather and cedar. Only Australia takes this category seriously, so Lambrusco falls away immediately — it would be lighter, tarter, lower in tannin and free of oak. Within Australia, the plush warm-climate plum and softer acid argue McLaren Vale rather than the Grampians, which would give firmer acid and more black pepper.

**b)** A full red table wine first: skin-fermented dry, matured with a modest oak component for the cedar. The brickdust and leather show a blend built on mature reserve wines. Secondary fermentation in bottle with extended lees contact gives the fine bead and creamy texture — a tank ferment could not; then disgorgement with a sweet red dosage of roughly 20–30 g/L, which is what softens the tannin into velvet.

**c)** Very good to outstanding, the reference tier of a small category, around AUD 70. Domestic on-trade and cellar-door driven, a winter and festive-season seller; export interest is curiosity-led and hard to scale.

## Wine 3

**a) Muscat à Petits Grains Rouges, Rutherglen, Victoria — Rare classification.** Virtually opaque olive-brown with a green rim, staining the glass; liqueur-sweet, viscous, spirit fully integrated at around 17–18%. Raisin, molasses, treacle, Christmas pudding, sandalwood and rancio. PX was considered and rejected: this has grapey, marmalade-lifted perfume PX never shows, and PX lacks the green rim.

The insight is the balance: enormous sugar carried by a lemony acid line and a trace of drying tannin. That tannin can only come from decades in very old wood, while the freshness indicates the house is blending its oldest solera fractions into younger, brighter material rather than bottling old wine straight — which is precisely how the Rare tier achieves complexity without becoming cloying.

**b)** Muscat left to raisin on the vine, fermented briefly, then arrested by neutral grape spirit at high residual sugar. Decades of ageing in old seasoned casks in hot tin sheds drives evaporative concentration; a modified solera blends across generations.

**c)** Iconic quality, world-class, AUD 100+ per half bottle. Sold through fine-wine specialists and Michelin-level lists globally; the challenge is that sweet fortifieds are bought by the few, so scarcity pricing rather than volume is the model.

## Wine 4

**a) Semillon, Riverina, New South Wales — botrytis sweet, oxidatively aged.** Deep amber and viscous but with no spirit warmth at all and light alcohol around 10%, so this is unfortified. Marmalade, honey, grilled stone fruit with campfire smoke and nutty nougat: botrytis concentration plus deliberate oxidative maturation.

**b)** Late-picked botrytised fruit from a warm irrigated inland region, pressed hard, fermented in barrel until arrested by sugar and alcohol, then held for years in old casks with generous ullage — the source of the smoke and cashew.

**c)** Excellent, well above standard commercial botrytis Semillon, around AUD 40 per half. A specialist-retail and dessert-list wine; the challenge is convincing consumers a sweet white can taste this savoury.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Country and Region of Origin (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — France, Sauternes (Bordeaux). Deep gold, viscous, with candied citrus, beeswax and apricot: a botrytis wine. The warm, generous body (~14%) and savoury vanillin oak place it in a warm-climate, barrel-fermented tradition. Tokaji is ruled out — no orange-peel-and-ginger Furmint signature, and the acid is firm rather than searing. German BA/TBA would show far lower alcohol and no oak. The tropical opulence over crystallised grapefruit bitterness reads Sémillon-dominant, at Cru Classé concentration.

**Wine 2** — Germany, Mosel. Pale, featherlight, apparent alcohol barely 8%, with piercing lime acidity and slate. Alsace equivalents carry more weight and spice; Austrian Riesling is firmer and drier-framed. The combination of extreme lightness with substantial sugar masked by acidity is Mosel-specific, and the sugar/acid balance indicates Auslese rather than BA — there is no botrytis viscosity or dried-fruit depth.

**Wine 3** — South Africa, Constantia. Light gold and viscous, with white peach, lychee, rose petal and mango: Muscat, unmistakably. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is excluded by the absence of spirit heat and by the oak-derived ginger and nutmeg; the mango-guava ripeness and integrated new wood point New World, consistent with Constantia's Muscat de Frontignan tradition.

---

## b) Method by which sweetness has been achieved (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Botrytis cinerea. Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc, picked in successive *tries* as noble rot spreads unevenly. The fungus desiccates berries, concentrating sugar, glycerol and acid while generating the honey and beeswax compounds on the nose. Slow barrique fermentation stalls naturally near 14%, leaving high residual sugar — the sugar is a by-product of concentration, not of intervention.

**Wine 2** — Arrested fermentation of selectively harvested overripe and lightly botrytised bunches meeting the Auslese must-weight minimum. Fermentation is halted early by chilling and SO₂ — hence the very low alcohol — retaining both sugar and the racy acidity that carries it. Unlike Wine 1, sweetness here comes from stopping the ferment rather than exhausting the yeast.

**Wine 3** — Passerillage: on-vine over-ripening and partial raisining without botrytis. The aromatics are clean, floral and pure, with none of the honeyed rot funk of Wine 1. Fermentation runs to roughly 14% before arrest; extended new oak followed by foudre adds spice and grip without smothering the Muscat aromatics.

---

## c) Quality, style and commercial position (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding; Cru Classé Sauternes standard, £60–90. Opulent, layered, with a long finish and clear ageing capacity. Specialist merchants and fine-dining on-trade in Hong Kong, the US and France. The challenge is the shrinking luxury sweet-wine category; the opportunity is undercutting the handful of first-rank names while matching their concentration.

**Wine 2** — Very good to outstanding single-vineyard Auslese, £35–55 per half-bottle. Ethereal, contemplative, with a decade or more ahead as the lime turns to petrol and honey. Its 8% alcohol makes it unusually relevant to health-conscious premium buyers — a genuine point of difference from the other two, both of which are 14% wines. Sold via specialist merchants and auction in Germany, the UK, Japan and the US; the barrier is consumer confusion over Prädikat sweetness, the asset is site prestige and collectability.

**Wine 3** — Very good; premium still sweet wine, £40–60. Richly aromatic and oak-complexed, which separates it from the fresh, unwooded Muscats it competes against. Constantia's historic reputation supports the price and gives sommeliers a story, driving listings in specialist on-trade and fine independent retail in the UK, the Netherlands and the US. The constraint is low awareness of South African sweet wine above £30 — heritage, not varietal, is what sells this bottle.

## Wine 1 — a) Variety and Region (8 marks)

Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Douro, Portugal. Deep gold, viscous, with pronounced orange blossom and rose petal — an aromatic Muscat signature. Torrontés was weighed for the same floral register but ruled out by the spirit warmth, candied orange peel and evident sweetness: this is fortified, not a still table wine. Setúbal was the other candidate; the richer dried-fruit depth and warm, tightly knit spirit point instead to mountain-grown Douro Moscatel.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Method of Production (9 marks)

Naturally sweet fortified white made by mutage: fermentation of ripe Moscatel arrested by grape spirit at around 77% abv, retaining substantial residual sugar and vivid primary floral character. The dried citrus peel and honey suggest some post-fortification time in large wood, but the rose and orange blossom survive intact — short ageing in inert vessel or old wood rather than new barrel, which would have flattened the aromatics.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Very good; a premium Moscatel do Douro, €15–22. Sits in specialist off-trade and better on-trade as an aperitif alternative to Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, with export traction in the Nordic monopolies and UK specialists.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Region (8 marks)

A blend of native Douro varieties led by Touriga Nacional and Tinta Roriz — a Garrafeira Tawny, Douro. Tawny-amber with a brick rim confirms long oxidative ageing; dried fig, walnut, orange peel and rancio place it firmly in the Port family, with moderate spirit warmth, high sugar cut by an oxidative dry finish and fine tannin. A 20-year-old Tawny was the alternative, but the greater structural depth, silkier texture and layered tertiary detail indicate the bottle-aged Garrafeira style rather than pure cask ageing.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Method of Production (9 marks)

Extended initial ageing in small seasoned oak (300–600L) delivering the walnut, dried orange peel and rancio, followed by prolonged reductive ageing in glass demijohn or bottle. The spirit is fully absorbed, implying decades of maturation. Where a wood-aged Tawny finishes broad and nutty, the Garrafeira's glass phase yields the linear, detailed, almost silky structure shown here.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Outstanding; prestige Garrafeira Tawny at £40–70 through specialist retail and the fine-wine on-trade, aimed at collectors and fortified enthusiasts. Strong in the UK, USA and Japan, though volumes are tiny and consumer awareness of the Garrafeira category outside Portugal remains the commercial constraint.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Region (8 marks)

Malvasia (Malmsey), Madeira, Portugal. Amber-gold with a green-flecked rim, volatile lift and a curry-leaf, dried-fruit profile separate this from both Port and Sherry. The decisive marker is structural: searing acidity held against high residual sugar and spirit warmth — a tension only Madeira achieves. Sercial and Verdelho were considered and rejected on sweetness and weight; the dried fig, caramel and toffee sit well above their drier range. Depth and integration suggest a 10-year age indication.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Method of Production (9 marks)

Sweet fortified wine, fortified early to retain sugar, then aged oxidatively under heat. For a ten-year single-variety Malmsey, canteiro — cask ageing under warm warehouse eaves — is more likely than estufagem tank heating, given the finesse of the volatile lift and the absence of any cooked, caramelised coarseness. Malvasia's high natural acidity is preserved and sharpened by the heat, and evaporative concentration over the decade explains the rich texture.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Very good to outstanding; a 10-year-old Madeira at €25–40. The acid-sweetness tension is delivered with real precision and length. Premium on-trade is the natural channel, where near-indestructible shelf life after opening is a genuine by-the-glass advantage, alongside export to the USA, UK and Scandinavian monopolies where sommelier-led revival of the category is underway.

## a) Country and Region of Origin (4 + 4×5 marks = 24 marks)

All four wines are from **France** — a pétillant rosé, a late-harvest Alsatian white, a fortified sweet red and a traditional-method Blanc de Noirs.

**Wine 1 — Languedoc (Hérault / IGP).** Salmon-pink, low-pressure mousse, stone fruit, dried herbs and an earthy-animal note point to a warm southern origin. The absence of autolytic character rules out Champagne; the rustic herbal earthiness and multi-variety red fruit indicate the Languedoc, most plausibly Hérault under IGP or Vin de France.

**Wine 2 — Alsace.** Rose petal, lychee and exotic spice with unctuous texture, notable sweetness and electric acidity: Gewurztraminer, Alsace. Sweetness and glycerol body without botrytis-driven marmalade suggests Vendanges Tardives rather than SGN.

**Wine 3 — Roussillon (Banyuls).** Ruby-garnet, red fruit and chocolate, spirit warmth clearly above 15%, and sweetness reading as halted fermentation rather than botrytis. Grenache-dominant mutage points to Banyuls; the fresh red-fruit profile separates it from Port and from the oxidative Tawny styles of Maury.

**Wine 4 — Burgundy (Crémant de Bourgogne).** Lemon-green, fine persistent mousse, chalky minerality, red apple and white cherry with a hint of brioche — traditional method from a cool northern origin. The red-fruit finish indicates Pinot Noir; Champagne is ruled out because autolytic complexity and chalk minerality would be more pronounced.

---

## b) Style and Method of Production (4×20 marks = 80 marks)

**Wine 1**

A pétillant naturel, not a traditional-method wine: the modest mousse and total absence of brioche or biscuit indicate CO₂ captured during primary fermentation (ancestral method) rather than an induced second fermentation with extended lees contact. Layered stone fruit, dried herb and animal-hide complexity suggest a multi-variety blend of Grenache, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon — a diversity no single southern grape achieves alone. Stainless-steel fermentation preserves primary fruit; no oak. Low apparent alcohol and a refreshing finish suggest fermentation was arrested early, leaving residual CO₂ and a trace of sweetness for balance. Drink-young and pleasure-driven — informal and unusual within serious French appellation wine.

**Wine 2**

A rich unfortified sweet white consistent with Vendanges Tardives Gewurztraminer. Opulent rose-petal, lychee and spice aromatics with glycerol viscosity point to very high must weight from overripe but largely healthy fruit; the absence of honey, saffron and marmalade rules out botrytis-dominant SGN. Penetrating acidity beneath the sweetness indicates whole-bunch pressing, and the pristine aromatics suggest temperature-controlled stainless-steel fermentation halted before dryness. No oak — Alsace VT is almost never barrel-aged. The tension between residual sugar and high natural acidity is what marks out a serious example.

**Wine 3**

Spirit warmth, deep colour, ripe tannin and sweet red-fruit concentration indicate Banyuls rouge in the Rimage (vintage) style, made by mutage sur grains: spirit added mid-fermentation while still on skins, extracting colour and tannin while halting fermentation and retaining sugar. Bright cherry and chocolate with little oxidative development show a young wine aged reductively in bottle, distinguishing it from Tawny-style Banyuls Grand Cru. Grenache dominates, consistent with the transparent ruby and soft tannin; spirit integration is good but incomplete, confirming youth.

**Wine 4**

Fine persistent mousse, subtle brioche and chalky texture confirm traditional method with meaningful lees contact. The base is almost certainly Pinot Noir — the red-apple and white-cherry mid-palate and delicate red-fruit finish are inconsistent with Chardonnay alone. Whole-bunch pressing achieves the pale lemon-green colour from a red base. Emerging brioche alongside fresh fruit suggests 18–24 months sur latte rather than the nine-month Crémant minimum. An Extra Brut dosage (under 3 g/L) leaves the wine very dry, emphasising chalky structure and fruit definition — a deliberately precision-focused style.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (4×5 marks = 20 marks)

**Wine 1.** Good to very good for the style. At €15–20 it sits in the premium natural-wine segment: independent shops, biodynamic wine bars and by-the-glass lists in France, the UK and Scandinavia. The unfamiliar category demands consumer education.

**Wine 2.** Outstanding — fruit purity, structural tension and aromatic intensity well above appellation minimums. At €60–100+ per half-bottle: specialist merchants, fine dining, private cellars, with Germany, Switzerland, the USA and Japan the key exports. Limited volume and low category awareness are the constraints.

**Wine 3.** Very good at Banyuls AOC Rimage level, true to the schist terroir. At €20–30 a compelling chocolate-pairing wine, with growing interest in the UK, Belgium and North America. The challenge is category obscurity: few consumers can place Banyuls without shelf context.

**Wine 4.** Very good, upper-tier Crémant de Bourgogne. At €20–30 it offers strong value against NV Champagne at double the price — premium supermarkets, independents, smart by-the-glass lists in France and the UK. The task is persuading drinkers to trade up from entry Crémant rather than down from branded NV Champagne.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Country and Region of Origin (3 × 8 marks)

All three show raisined concentration and spirit warmth pointing to Spain's fortified tradition. Madeira or Setúbal would share the oxidative frame, but the liquorice/coffee register of Wine 1 and the saline lift of Wine 2 are Iberian rather than Portuguese.

**Wine 1** — Opaque mahogany, extreme viscosity, dates, dried figs, roasted coffee and orange peel over molasses sweetness: a PX-style fortified. Rutherglen Muscat matches the sweetness but not the bitter coffee finish or citrus acid spine. The sheer sugar concentration favours **Montilla-Moriles**, where sun-drying is the norm and PX reaches greater extremes, over Jerez.

**Wine 2** — Burnt amber, toasted hazelnut, toffee, sea air, with a fresh, long palate. Amontillado would be paler and lighter-bodied; Oloroso would carry the weight but not this residual saline flor lift. That bridging character marks it as **Palo Cortado from Jerez**, at VORS-level depth.

**Wine 3** — Deep ruby without browning, dried cherry, stewed plum, cinnamon and garrigue earth, with markedly less spirit warmth than the others: a naturally sweet Garnacha rather than a full fortified. Priorat would show greater density and licorella minerality; the mid-weight, accessible fruit places it in **Montsant**.

---

## b) Method of Production (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Pedro Ximénez sun-dried on mats (*asoleo*) to concentrate sugars before pressing; fermentation barely begun before neutral spirit arrested it, leaving near-total residual sugar. Decades of oxidative ageing in seasoned American oak butts built the coffee, chocolate and balsamic layers and absorbed the spirit; the variety's acidity keeps it from cloying.

**Wine 2** — Unlike Wine 1, this began biologically, under flor as a Fino, before the veil died or was killed by refortification to around 18–20%, redirecting it onto an oxidative path — the classifying decision that defines the style. Long solera ageing in butts then concentrated the wine and built the hazelnut and toffee depth.

**Wine 3** — Fortification here is partial and lighter-handed than in either Sherry: enough spirit to arrest fermentation with sugar remaining, but at a lower addition rate, hence the softer warmth. The retained ruby colour indicates short, largely reductive ageing, with a period in oak supplying the cinnamon and vanilla.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding, at VORS/Gran Reserva level for the category; extreme sweetness balanced by citrus bite is rare. Around £60–100 per 50cl through specialist merchants, competing with aged Tokaji Aszú and vintage Sauternes. Export to the US, UK and Northern Europe; premium restaurant dessert lists by the glass are a key channel, since small measures suffice.

**Wine 2** — Very high quality, VORS classification, a benchmark for the style. A narrower audience than Wine 1 — sommeliers, trade and committed sherry drinkers rather than dessert-wine buyers — at roughly £50–80 per 75cl from specialist importers, set against aged Amontillado VORS and premium Oloroso. Strong in the UK, Scandinavia and Spanish gastronomy; category awareness, not quality, caps growth.

**Wine 3** — Good to very good, Reserva equivalent, with genuine regional character. Its competitive set sits outside Spain — Banyuls and Maury — as much as within it. At £20–35 it reaches adventurous on-trade lists via specialist importers, with best potential in Scandinavia, the UK and the US.

Under the skin, the flight shows three uses of the same tool: spirit as a sweetness-preserving device (Wine 1), as an oxidative gatekeeper killing flor (Wine 2), and as a light brake on a table-wine ferment (Wine 3).

---

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Identify the region of origin and grape variety or varieties (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Fine persistent mousse with pronounced brioche and toasted almond confirms traditional method. Alongside the autolysis sit quince-honey and apple-skin notes atypical of pure Chardonnay, suggesting a blend: quince and florality read as Chenin, the rustic apple-skin as Mauzac. Champagne and Crémant de Bourgogne were weighed and rejected — neither permits Mauzac, and the broader, less chalk-austere mid-palate with moderate warmth argues against Champagne. This is **Crémant de Limoux**, Languedoc, from **Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc and Mauzac**.

**Wine 2** — Soft, quick-fading mousse and purely primary green apple, pear and banana, with no brioche or almond, rule out any traditional-method origin: this is tank method. Prosecco was considered but the firmer acid line and absence of Glera's creamy pear-drop signature eliminate it; the moderate sweetness against medium-plus acidity fits a neutral German base. This is **Rheinhessen Sekt**, from a neutral variety such as Müller-Thurgau.

---

## b) Compare methods of production (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1**: secondary fermentation in bottle with extended lees ageing — the fine bead and depth of autolysis imply at least twelve months *sur lie*. Dosage is minimal, near Brut Nature, so the acid-fruit balance and Mauzac's apple-skin grip carry the finish unaided rather than being softened by sugar.

**Wine 2**: secondary fermentation in sealed autoclave, bottled young under pressure. The frothier, less persistent bead and total absence of autolytic character are the direct consequence — the decision preserves primary aromatics instead of building complexity. A modest dosage in the Trocken range buys approachability that lees contact would otherwise have supplied.

---

## c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** is very good — upper-tier Crémant, above generic Cava if short of 1er Cru Champagne. At roughly 2–3 years old it is drinking now; expect a further 2–3 years before the mousse coarsens and the autolytic freshness gives way to oxidative honey. Sells at £18–22 through independents and on-trade lists as a Champagne alternative, its zero-dosage stance targeting low-intervention drinkers in the UK, Benelux and Scandinavia.

**Wine 2** is acceptable quality, non-vintage, £9–12. Wholly primary and youthful, it gains nothing from keeping. This is off-trade volume, competing with entry-level Prosecco and Cava for the celebration occasion. The underlying difficulty: at this price the purchase is driven by category brand equity, and Prosecco owns it — Sekt must discount to hold shelf space.

---

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## Wine 1

### a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Pale lemon, high viscosity, pronounced candied citrus, rose and saffron: a botrytis wine. Purity of fruit with high acidity cutting concentrated sugar, plus a rounded waxy texture, indicates Sémillon-led Bordeaux. Sauvignon Blanc as lead is ruled out by the absence of any grassy or herbaceous edge; Riesling by the lack of petrol and slate lift. The citrus-driven, medium-plus-bodied profile rather than heavy unctuousness points to Barsac rather than Sauternes proper.

### b) Sweetness Mechanism (7 marks)

Noble rot. The confit quality of the citrus, saffron lift and honeyed yet penetrating freshness separate botrytis concentration from over-ripeness or drying. Rot dehydrates berries on the vine, concentrating sugar, glycerol and acid together — hence the freshness and length at this sweetness, and the high viscosity from elevated glycerol.

### c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Outstanding, equivalent to a classed-growth Barsac, €40–60. Refined rather than opulent: crystalline citrus precision, exemplary sweetness/acid balance, long finish.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Fine wine specialists and high-end on-trade in France, the UK and Hong Kong/Japan, where classified Bordeaux sweet wine still sells. Competes with lesser Sauternes and Loupiac. Target: the classicist fine-wine buyer; by-the-glass with foie gras is a strong premium restaurant channel.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Deep gold, full body, obvious spirit warmth — a fortified wine. The intensely grapey nose of orange blossom, peach and fresh almond is Muscat, and the freshness of that fruit with medium-plus acidity rules out oxidative Muscat du Cap Corse or raisined Rutherglen. Aromatic intensity favours Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains over Muscat d'Alexandrie; the warm Mediterranean exuberance places it in Roussillon — Muscat de Rivesaltes.

### b) Sweetness Mechanism (7 marks)

Mutage: neutral grape spirit added to fermenting must, arresting fermentation with sugar remaining. Evidence is spirit warmth alongside intact primary grapiness — fermentation stopped early. No botrytis funk, no dried-fruit character, so neither noble rot nor passerillage. A Vin Doux Naturel.

### c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Very good, upper end of the appellation, €12–18. Exuberant and aromatic, built for immediate drinking rather than complexity or ageing.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Off-trade — independents and premium supermarkets — plus casual on-trade as an aperitif or with fruit desserts. Strong domestically, with modest volume in Belgium, Germany and the UK. Target: value-driven drinker wanting aromatic sweetness; competes with Moscato d'Asti in occasion if not in price.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Deep gold, high viscosity, white truffle, quince, marmalade, pineapple and chestnut. Thick, glycerous texture with tropical concentration and retained freshness indicates Petit Manseng from Jurançon. Gros Manseng is ruled out: it would not carry this depth or chestnut-honey complexity at this sugar level. The south-west French, Pyrenean-foothill profile — baroque richness with mountain acidity — fixes the origin.

### b) Sweetness Mechanism (7 marks)

Passerillage, not botrytis. Petit Manseng's thick skins resist rot; instead the foehn winds dehydrate berries on the vine into late autumn. The marmalade, quince and chestnut register as dried, concentrated fruit rather than Wine 1's honey-saffron botrytis signature, and there is no crystalline citrus purity. Density and length without spirit warmth confirm late harvest rather than fortification.

### c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Outstanding, top tier of Jurançon Moelleux, €25–40. The under-the-skin point: Petit Manseng holds high acidity even at extreme ripeness, preserved by altitude and late-season cool, and that alone stops this baroque density reading as cloying.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Independent fine wine specialists and premium on-trade; UK, Belgium and Japan follow artisan South-West producers. Target: the enthusiast who already knows Sauternes and wants comparable complexity for less. Matches classified Sauternes on quality while undercutting it on price — a merchant's argument.

---

## Wine 4

### a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Chenin Blanc, Vouvray Moelleux. Pale-to-medium gold, medium body, noticeably less warmth than Wines 2 and 3, suggesting modest alcohol from arrested fermentation. Quince, beeswax, lanolin and ripe apple under piercing, near-malic acidity separate it from Wine 2's Muscat aromatics and Wine 3's tropical density. Within Loire Chenin, the taut sweetness/acid tension rather than raisined weight points to Vouvray over Coteaux du Layon.

### b) Sweetness Mechanism (7 marks)

Selective late harvest by tries successives, with fermentation naturally arresting as sugar overcomes the yeast. Beeswax and quince with honey overtones sit under very high linear acidity, so the sugar never reads as heavy. Leaner and more mineral than Wine 1, and without Wine 3's dried-fruit density — late harvest with some botrytis, not passerillage.

### c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Very good, appellation level, €20–35. Precise and linear; acidity lifts the sweetness and drives length, but it lacks the concentration of the Jurançon or Barsac. A food wine rather than a show-stopper.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Independents and mid-to-premium on-trade in France, the UK and the Netherlands. Target: the drinker who values acid-driven sweetness and recognises the appellation — not mass market. Competes with Coteaux du Layon and demi-sec Vouvray below it on price; by-the-glass with a cheese course is the natural placement.

Mas Amiel Vintage Maury 2020. Roussillon, France. (16.5%)

modelAnswer:
**a) Country and regional origin (15 marks)**

Both wines are fortified, yet their visual contrast — one clear gold with pronounced viscosity, the other deep ruby-purple and opaque — signals different grape families within the same country: **France**.

The gold wine's candied apricot, orange blossom and rose water, combined with sweetness, warmth and high viscosity, point to a Muscat-based Vin Doux Naturel. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise shares the floral-apricot signature, but the elevated perceived alcohol and greater aromatic density exceed its lighter style. That concentration points more specifically to **Muscat du Cap Corse**, Corsica's AOP VDN, where very low yields push Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains to exceptional intensity.

The ruby-purple wine shows dense blackcurrant and blackberry fruit, compact structure and warmth — unambiguously a red Grenache Noir VDN. Banyuls shares this profile, but the fresher, primary rather than oxidative character points to **Vintage Maury** from Roussillon, where reductive ageing post-fortification preserves primary fruit.

**b) Methods of production (35 marks)**

*Wine 1 (Muscat du Cap Corse):* Fully ripe Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is gently whole-bunch pressed — the clean, non-phenolic palate indicates minimal skin contact. Fermentation begins in temperature-controlled stainless steel, then is arrested by mutage with neutral grape spirit, retaining natural grape sugars. Early mutage accounts for the pronounced residual sweetness. Subsequent reductive ageing preserves fresh floral and citrus character, confirmed by the clean gold colour and absence of any nutty or caramelised development.

*Wine 2 (Vintage Maury):* Grenache Noir is harvested at high ripeness — dense colour and concentrated black fruit confirm extraction from very ripe skins. Short maceration extracts colour and tannin before mutage arrests fermentation, preserving residual sugar and fruit intensity. Post-fortification maturation is reductive — sealed inert vessel — protecting vivid primary fruit and separating this wine from the oxidative Maury Ambré style. This mirrors Vintage Port's philosophy and distinguishes Vintage Maury from the Grenat or Ambré categories. Bottled young, it retains the compact, dense character evident in the glass.

**c) Style, quality, and commercial position (2 × 7.5 marks)**

*Wine 1:* Rich, opulently sweet, with very good aromatic precision — outstanding quality for a Corsican VDN, retailing around €20–28. Its rarity and artisanal provenance suit specialist independents and high-end French épiceries fines, with export appeal among Francophile specialists in the UK, Benelux and Japan.

*Wine 2:* Youthful, primary and full-bodied, of very good quality — equivalent in ambition and price to a declared LBV Port, retailing around €18–25. The non-oxidative style differentiates it from commodity VDN, targeting independent specialists and restaurant lists seeking an alternative to Vintage Port, with strong domestic French demand and growing export interest in premium Roussillon.

modelAnswer:
## a) Region and Grape Variety (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Alvarinho, Vinho Verde (Monção e Melgaço sub-region), Portugal. Lemon-green colour, pronounced aromatic intensity showing white peach, grapefruit, and jasmine, with high acidity, medium-minus body, and a saline mineral finish. Grüner Veltliner was considered but would show white pepper; Riesling at comparable alcohol would show more citrus tartness and petrol lift. The tropical-and-stone-fruit profile with a saline thread points decisively to Alvarinho. Monção e Melgaço follows from the aromatic concentration and depth, which consistently exceed the broader Vinho Verde expression.

**Wine 2** — Encruzado, Dão, Portugal. Lemon colour, high acidity, medium-plus body, and a long structured finish with a subtle resinous note point to a cool elevated plateau. Verdelho was considered but lacks this breadth and tannin-adjacent texture; Arinto produces high acidity but a leaner, more citrus-driven profile. The weight and resinous quality — characteristic of Encruzado — narrows the call confidently to Dão.

**Wine 3** — Verdelho, 10 Years Old, Madeira, Portugal. Deep amber, high viscosity, clear spirit warmth, and powerful Seville orange, grapefruit pith, walnut, and honey with oxidative depth confirm a fortified, oxidatively aged wine. The medium-dry sweetness and searing acidity identify Madeira specifically; Verdelho sits between bone-dry Sercial and sweeter Bual, retaining high acidity with more weight than Sercial. The 10-year age statement is consistent with the amber development and layered complexity.

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Fresh, aromatic, unwooded dry white. The pure fruit-forward profile with no phenolic grip indicates whole-bunch pressing at cool temperatures. No oak and no MLF — a deliberate choice to preserve the naturally high acidity. Short lees contact contributes the saline-textural quality without overshadowing the variety's primary character.

**Wine 2** — Fuller, structured dry white with evident winemaking ambition. Complexity and long finish point to extended lees ageing in neutral vessel — likely older barrel and stainless combined — providing texture without imposing toast or vanilla. MLF appears suppressed or partial, preserving structural acidity as a defining feature rather than softening it.

**Wine 3** — Deliberately oxidative production. Canteiro ageing — almost certain at this quality level — drives the volatile lift and caramelised complexity. Fortification to approximately 19% arrests fermentation at the desired sweetness. Ten years in partially filled casks builds walnut, orange-peel, and honey character; the island's natural acidity remains structurally intact throughout.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position in Export Markets (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, equivalent to a mid-tier single-variety regional benchmark; around €15–20, comparable to a mid-tier Pouilly-Fumé. The aromatic definition and saline precision distinguish it from generic Vinho Verde. Export appeal is strong in the UK, Scandinavia, and the US East Coast among consumers seeking alternatives to Sancerre. Best placed in independent merchants and premium on-trade by-the-glass lists. The central challenge is consumer unfamiliarity with the Alvarinho name outside Portugal and Spain.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding quality at the top of Dão's white hierarchy; around €20–30. Length and structural complexity rival Village-to-1er Cru white Burgundy. Export markets are nascent — UK specialist merchants and Scandinavian monopolies offer the best opportunity — but Encruzado carries almost no recognition outside Portugal. The commercial opportunity lies in that gap: sommeliers seeking Burgundy-like whites at meaningfully lower prices.

**Wine 3** — Very good quality at the 10-year Reserva tier; around €30–40. Export markets are mature in the UK, US, and Benelux among Madeira specialists, and growing in fine dining where sommelier education has raised the profile of aged Madeira as an aperitif and dessert alternative. The challenge is niche positioning; the opportunity is unique longevity and food versatility that no other fortified wine can match.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Region of origin and grape variety (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Barsac, Bordeaux. Sémillon-dominant with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle.

Deep old gold with viscous legs; dense honey, candied apricot and saffron confirm botrytis, while a spicy-floral lift beyond Sémillon or Sauvignon suggests a Muscadelle fraction. The incisive, mineralised citrus cut through very high sugar points to limestone Barsac rather than the broader, warmer Sauternes finish. Alsace Vendange Tardive was ruled out by the absence of petrol/exotic spice; Tokaji by the missing orange-peel and ginger of Furmint.

**Wine 2** — Vouvray, Loire. Chenin Blanc.

Paler gold, tighter frame. Quince, honeysuckle and beeswax over a waxy-lanolin texture, with electric acidity markedly higher than Wine 1 at comparable sweetness — this alone eliminates a Sémillon blend. Its austerity and vertical structure separate it from the broader, more overtly fruity Coteaux du Layon.

## b) Methods of production — sweetness achieved and managed (18 marks)

Both rely on selective harvest of botrytised fruit, but diverge in how sweetness is arrived at and held.

Wine 1: Ciron river fog drives reliable *Botrytis cinerea*; multiple *tries* pick only fully botrytised berries. Fermentation in barrique — the vanilla and toast integration suggests a high proportion of new oak — stops naturally as yeast fail at extreme sugar concentration, with sulphur and cold stabilisation fixing the balance. Oak supplies both complexity and micro-oxidative texture to carry the sugar load.

Wine 2: an early *trie* selects delicately botrytised bunches before richness overwhelms; vessels are older demi-muids or large format, evidenced by the lack of vanilla and the prominence of Chenin's own phenolic grip. Fermentation is arrested by chilling and sulphur at a chosen point, because the acidity demands a precise balance.

The distinction: Wine 1's richness is cushioned by new oak; Wine 2's sweetness is disciplined by acidity alone, giving a tighter, more tensioned wine.

## c) Style, quality, and commercial position (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Opulent and full-bodied, defined by tension between honeyed fruit and limestone-driven freshness. Outstanding; Premier Cru Classé Barsac, £80–£150. Sold through fine wine merchants, auction and top on-trade in the UK, USA and Asia, to collectors who understand Barsac's incisiveness against Sauternes' breadth. The challenge is shrinking demand for sweet wine; the opportunity is that terroir distinction against equally priced Sauternes.

**Wine 2** — Restrained, precise moelleux, vertical rather than broad. Very good to outstanding; single-vineyard Vouvray Moelleux, £40–£70. Fine wine independents and Loire specialists in the UK, Belgium and USA, targeting younger terroir-conscious buyers. Less immediately giving than Wine 1 but will reward 15–20 years, gaining lanolin and toasted hazelnut.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Region and Principal Grape Variety (4 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Franciacorta, Lombardy; Chardonnay (with Pinot Nero/Bianco). Fine persistent mousse plus clear autolysis — subtle brioche, satin texture — confirms traditional method. Champagne was the main alternative: comparable autolytic complexity, but the broader texture, rounder white-peach and honeydew fruit and absence of chalky acid tension argue against it, as does the perceived alcohol around 12.5% with moderate rather than lean body. English sparkling would show a greener, more angular acid line. Chardonnay-led blend with peach ripeness and a smoky finish points to Franciacorta DOCG.

**Wine 2** — Conegliano Valdobbiadene, Veneto; Glera. Read against Wine 1, the mousse is frothier and less persistent and there is no autolytic character at all — no biscuit, no lees-derived creaminess — indicating tank method. Aromatics are floral and delicate (acacia, apple blossom, green apple, white peach) with an almond finish and mineral lift; that concentration and precision lifts it above generic Treviso Prosecco DOC into the Superiore DOCG zone.

**Wine 3** — Sorbara, Emilia-Romagna; Lambrusco. The visual break is decisive: transparent ruby-pink rather than white. Violet-tinged cherry and red berry with a faint tannic grip absent in Wines 1 and 2, low perceived alcohol, moderate acidity and no oak or autolysis indicate a tank-method sparkling red. Among Lambrusco varieties only Sorbara gives this pale colour with high floral aromatics; Grasparossa would be deeper, darker-fruited and firmer in tannin.

**Wine 4** — Canelli, Asti, Piedmont; Moscato Bianco. Golden-lemon, viscous, with a gentle creamy mousse. Intensely grapey primary aromatics — candied peach, apricot, orange blossom, lemon peel — are Moscato's signature. Very low perceived alcohol (barely any warmth), pronounced sweetness cut by fresh acid. Asti Spumante was weighed and rejected: pressure here is clearly lower and the palate lighter, placing it as frizzante Moscato d'Asti DOCG.

## b) Method of Production (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1:** Traditional method. Clean, unphenolic fruit suggests whole-bunch pressing; stainless-steel primary fermentation, no oak (no vanilla or toast). The satin texture and integrated bead indicate extended lees ageing at or beyond the 18-month DOCG minimum, then riddling, disgorgement and brut dosage.

**Wine 2:** Tank (Charmat) method — secondary fermentation in sealed autoclave at low temperature, minimal lees contact, early bottling under pressure to protect Glera's fragile floral esters. The ephemeral mousse and total absence of autolysis are the evidence.

**Wine 3:** Brief cold maceration on Lambrusco's thin skins to draw colour and aroma without tannin, then secondary fermentation in tank under pressure and early bottling, retaining vivid red fruit and only a trace of grip.

**Wine 4:** Arrested single fermentation (Asti method). Chilled must is fermented in pressurised tank and stopped by chilling and sterile filtration, leaving roughly 120–130 g/L residual sugar at only about 5% alcohol. The soft, creamy bead reflects the lower bottle pressure of the frizzante style.

## c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1:** Very good quality; Franciacorta Brut DOCG, around €18–25 retail. Aperitif-positioned but complex enough for fine dining, competing directly with non-vintage Champagne and premium Crémant. Export focus: Germany, Switzerland, USA, Japan. The commercial obstacle is name recognition — at this price the consumer defaults to Champagne, so the wine sells on sommelier advocacy rather than shelf pull.

**Wine 2:** Very good for its category; Prosecco Superiore DOCG, around €12–18. A by-the-glass aperitif for premium casual dining and specialist off-trade. Broad demand in the UK, USA, Germany and Scandinavia. The task is differentiating the DOCG from the flood of Prosecco DOC three to four euros below it — hillside provenance and this level of aromatic definition are the only credible arguments.

**Wine 3:** Good quality; Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC, around €10–14. Dry-leaning, structured and gastronomic — a natural on-trade pour with charcuterie and rich pasta. Growing traction in the USA and Northern Europe among sommeliers seeking authentic, lower-alcohol sparkling reds; the residual barrier is memory of the sweet industrial exports of the 1970s–80s.

**Wine 4:** Excellent for the appellation; Moscato d'Asti DOCG, around €14–20, the delicacy and length placing it above entry-level. Sold for dessert service and increasingly as a low-alcohol aperitif in the USA, Japan and Northern Europe. Its 5% alcohol is a genuine commercial asset in the no/low conversation — but the sweetness that comes with arrested fermentation is inseparable from that low alcohol, which caps its food versatility.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 4

## Wine 1

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Deep gold, viscous, with pronounced candied citrus, beeswax, apricot and honey over preserved lemon and crystallised grapefruit: a botrytis-affected wine of concentration. Firm integrated acidity balances high sweetness, with warmth suggesting around 14%. Tokaji Aszú was weighed — the orange-peel and ginger fit — but the savoury vanillin oak and absence of volcanic mineral grip rule it out; German TBA would show markedly lower alcohol. This is Sémillon-dominated Sauternes, Bordeaux, with Sauvignon Blanc and probably a little Muscadelle, at Premier Cru Classé level.

### b) Sweetness mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Sweetness comes from *Botrytis cinerea*, concentrating sugar, acid and glycerol while contributing honey, beeswax and saffron notes. Multiple selective passes (*tries successives*) pick only fully botrytised berries. Fermentation in barrel — indicated by integrated vanillin — proceeded slowly against extreme sugar, arresting naturally as yeasts were inhibited. Silky viscosity confirms botrytis-derived glycerol; the sweet spice and long finish indicate roughly 18 months in French barriques with a proportion of new oak, restrained enough not to mask the fruit.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Outstanding: rich and complex, with the sweetness-acidity balance that defines Sauternes at its best, and genuinely age-worthy. Premier Cru Classé, around £60–80 per half-bottle.

### d) Commercial position (2 marks)

Fine wine specialists, auction and top-end on-trade. Principal exports the US, China and Hong Kong, and Scandinavian monopolies.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Pure lime blossom, white peach, slate and emerging petrol, with strikingly low apparent alcohol and racy acidity: Riesling. That combination of low alcohol, high acidity and residual sugar narrows to Germany. Against the Rheingau, which would give a broader, riper frame, the flinty slate-driven minerality and precision of fruit confirm the Mosel, most likely a steep south-facing *Einzellage*.

### b) Sweetness mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Sweetness derives from selective late harvesting of shrivelled, partly botrytised berries at Auslese must weight (roughly 83–100° Oechsle). Unlike Wine 1, fermentation was deliberately arrested — chilling and sulphur — rather than stopping of its own accord, leaving substantial residual sugar at low alcohol. Cool stainless-steel fermentation and reductive handling are shown by the absence of oak or dairy character; no malolactic, consistent with the high malic acidity. Early bottling preserves freshness.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Outstanding: delicate yet concentrated, with exceptional tension and length. Auslese Prädikat from a leading estate, around £40–60 per half-bottle.

### d) Commercial position (2 marks)

Fine wine specialists, high-end on-trade and auction; strongest domestically and with committed Riesling collectors in the UK, US and Scandinavia.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Pronounced mango, tangerine, yellow plum and candied citrus with a syrupy texture and very low apparent alcohol suggests freeze-concentration rather than noble rot. Riesling Eiswein was considered on the alcohol, but the mango and melon are inconsistent with Riesling's lime and petrol, and the acidity lacks its piercing malic drive. Tropical fruit, very high sugar, medium-minus finish and a faintly metallic close point to Vidal — Icewine from the Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada.

### b) Sweetness mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Grapes are left to freeze on the vine, harvested at −8°C or colder and pressed while frozen so ice crystals are retained in the press and only concentrated juice runs off. Fermentation is slow, halted by cold and yeast inhibition, leaving roughly 200–250 g/L residual sugar at 7–8% alcohol. Crucially, the fruit character is pure frozen-fruit rather than the honey and beeswax of Wine 1, confirming no botrytis. Clean, reductive stainless-steel handling; no oak.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Very good: richly sweet and tropical, though the medium-minus finish and metallic edge fall short of the finest Riesling Icewines. Around CAD $60–80 per 375ml.

### d) Commercial position (2 marks)

Gift and luxury retail domestically; key exports China, Japan and Taiwan, where Icewine carries prestige, plus premium duty-free.

---

## a) Grape variety or varieties (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Palomino Fino. Green apple, green olive, almond and intense steely salinity point to a biologically aged Sherry; the flor-derived saline/almond signature alongside emerging oxidative caramel is decisive for Palomino under extended flor. Pedro Ximénez shares the Jerez origin but shows mahogany colour and raisin-fig sweetness — the bone-dry, aggressively saline palate rules it out. Muscat is eliminated: no floral-grapey aromatics, and saline bitterness on the finish is inconsistent. Manzanilla Pasada, Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

**Wine 2** — Moscatel. Dark mahogany with pronounced elderflower, orange marmalade, prune and citrus spice. Palomino cannot give this floral intensity or sweetness. PX was weighed — both sweet, dark Jerez fortifieds — but PX is treacly fig without orange-blossom perfume, and relies on weight rather than acid tension; the great natural acidity balancing the sugar here confirms Moscatel.

## b) Style and method of production (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** shows two overlapping ageing phases. Bruised-apple notes indicate long time under living flor, which shields the wine from direct oxidation and drives acetaldehyde salinity. The caramel depth reveals the flor has thinned, allowing controlled oxidation — the mark of Pasada rather than fresh Manzanilla. Fortification is moderate, enough to sustain the solera without killing the flor. American oak butts in Sanlúcar's cool coastal air give a more delicate, saline flor than the warmer Jerez town.

**Wine 2** takes the opposite route: fermentation arrested with grape spirit, retaining high residual sugar alongside Moscatel's acidity. The añada designation confirms a single vintage, unblended. Roughly 16 years of slow oxidative ageing in old neutral casks has turned grapey primary fruit into dried fruit, spice and caramel — with no biological stage at all.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** is outstanding, at the apex of the Manzanilla category, around £50–70 per 50cl from specialists against £8–15 for commercial Manzanilla. # Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Country and Region of Origin (4 × 8 marks)

All four are fortified and sweet with pronounced oxidative or spirit character: **Portugal**.

**Wine 1** — Pale tawny-amber, medium weight, volatile lift with walnut and dried citrus. The electric, searing acidity cutting the sweetness is unlike any Port or mainland fortified style and points to **Madeira DOC**; medium-sweet rather than bone-dry (Sercial) or unctuous (Malmsey) suggests **Verdelho, 10-year**.

**Wine 2** — Deep opaque ruby, blackberry and chocolate, sweet palate, grippy but ripe tannin. Bright primary fruit and youth rule out tawny-style ageing; concentration falls short of a declared Vintage. **Ruby Reserve, Douro DOC**.

**Wine 3** — Tawny-amber, viscous, dried fig, orange peel, walnut, rancio; no fresh fruit remains. Long oxidative ageing in small wood. The focused vintage intensity, rather than the seamless homogeneity of a blended age statement, indicates a **Colheita, Douro DOC**, reading 12–14 years in cask.

**Wine 4** — Deep amber-gold, dried apricot, marmalade, roasted nut, and a persistent floral, grapey Muscat character absent from the others. Muscat typicity rules out Madeira's white varieties and the Douro's Touriga family. **Moscatel de Setúbal, Setúbal Peninsula**.

---

## b) Style and Method of Production (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 (Madeira)** — Fermented to partial dryness, then fortified with grape spirit to retain sugar. The defining feature is canteiro ageing: cask maturation under the warm lodge eaves for a decade, giving gentle oxidation at elevated temperature. This produces the volatile lift, caramelised toffee and rancio, while the island's naturally high acidity concentrates rather than fades — a wine simultaneously sweet, oxidative and searingly fresh.

**Wine 2 (Ruby Reserve)** — Rapid extraction in lagar or autovinifier, fermentation arrested with aguardente at around 77% abv after two to three days once target sugar is reached. Maturation is then in large wooden vats or tank for only 2–4 years, deliberately limiting oxygen exposure so the colour stays ruby and the fruit primary. Unlike Wine 3, no small-cask ageing has occurred at all.

**Wine 3 (Colheita Tawny)** — Fortified identically to Wine 2; the divergence is entirely in maturation. Ageing in 550-litre pipes gives high surface-to-volume oxidation over a single vintage, with slow evaporative concentration. Colour moves ruby to amber, tannin resolves, and rancio, nut and caramel build. The glycerol weight and integration exceed what a blended age-statement Tawny at similar price achieves.

**Wine 4 (Moscatel de Setúbal)** — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains fermented only briefly before fortification locks in high residual sugar and aromatics. Distinctively, additional Muscat skins are macerated in the young fortified wine for several weeks, extracting further terpenes — this explains why orange blossom survives alongside oxidative development. Subsequent cask ageing supplies the amber colour and roasted-nut layer without burying the varietal lift.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 (Madeira)** — Very good; a 10-year varietal age statement, €30–45, clearly above a 5-year blend in acid-sweet tension and complexity. Independent specialists and premium on-trade in the UK, Germany, Japan and US, where the following is loyal but narrow. Consumer unfamiliarity is the barrier; the by-the-glass argument is its months-long stability once opened.

**Wine 2 (Ruby Reserve)** — Good to very good, €12–18. Clean spirit and sound fruit, but built for immediate drinking, not cellaring. Supermarket off-trade and on-trade by the glass in the UK, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, competing directly with branded Reserve peers under real commodity price pressure. Its role is recruitment: the entry point into the category for younger drinkers.

**Wine 3 (Colheita Tawny)** — Outstanding. Colheita outranks a blended 20-year in prestige among informed buyers; €40–65. Vintage specificity and rancio depth make this the flight's most complete wine. Independent specialists, fine dining and sommelier lists in the UK, US, Japan and Switzerland. The commercial obstacle is category literacy — buyers understand "20-year-old" instantly, but a bottling year on a Tawny still needs explaining at the point of sale.

**Wine 4 (Moscatel de Setúbal)** — Very good, Superior tier, €25–40. The genuine point of difference is that aromatic Muscat and long oxidative wood ageing coexist here; Beaumes-de-Venise offers the aromatics without the wood, Rutherglen the wood without the floral lift. Specialist off-trade and premium on-trade, best prospects in Northern Europe and Scandinavia. The DOC's near-invisibility in export markets, not the wine, limits it.

Under the skin, the flight is a study in how one variable — oxygen — divides Portuguese fortification. Wines 2 and 3 are the same must, fortified the same way, separated only by vessel size and time; Wines 1 and 4 show that oxidative handling preserves rather than destroys the raw materials' defining traits, acidity in one case and terpenes in the other.

**Wine 1 — b) style and winemaking (13 marks).** An off-dry, savoury aperitif style. **Wine 3 — Loire Valley, Muscadet (Melon de Bourgogne).** The lightest body of the flight, low viscosity, high acid, crushed oyster shell and iodine. That saline, gunflint-free austerity with markedly neutral fruit is Melon; Chenin would give more quince and phenolic grip.

**Wine 4 — South West France, Jurançon (Gros/Petit Manseng).** Grapefruit pith, pineapple, beeswax and a waxy texture with a herbal bitterness on the mid-palate — an aromatic signature not found in the Loire or Champagne, and the exotic fruit at high acid indicates Pyrenean foothill altitude rather than heat.

#### Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1 — b) Style and winemaking (12 marks).** A rounded, autolytic, house-style Brut built for consistency. Whole-bunch pressing is evident in the clean, phenolic-free palate; the absence of vanilla or buttery lactic breadth suggests stainless-steel fermentation with malolactic largely blocked, preserving the citrus spine beneath the toast. The gold hue and marzipan against only medium(+) acidity is the tension worth resolving: it reads not as age in bottle alone but as a high proportion of older reserve wines, then three or more years on lees — the house buying roundness through blending rather than through dosage, which tastes low, around 8 g/L, leaving a dry, clean finish.

**c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks).** Very good quality, at the upper end of the non-vintage Brut tier and outperforming supermarket own-label Champagne. Retailing around £45–50 / US$55, its route is the independent specialist and the better on-trade wine list rather than the deep-discount grocery aisle, competing with the classic Grande Marque NVs in export markets such as the UK, US and Japan.

**Wine 2 — b) Style (12 marks).** A leaner, mineral-driven Blanc de Blancs. Early picking is implied by the high, taut acidity; the chalky texture and toasted-almond notes indicate 18–24 months on lees, longer than Crémant regulation demands. No malolactic — the acid line is unbuffered — and no oak. Brut dosage, but modest.

**c) Quality and commercial (7 marks).** Very good for its appellation, clearly above generic Crémant, retailing around €18–22 — an Independent Specialist wine sold as a serious Champagne alternative to consumers who prize dry, saline styles.

**Wine 3 — b) Style (12 marks).** A minimalist, terroir-driven Brut Nature. Zero dosage explains the bracing, drying finish; the faint autolysis with light body suggests 24 months on lees but a very lean base wine, unchaptalised, no malolactic, likely low-sulphur and possibly ambient-yeast fermented.

**c) Quality and commercial (7 marks).** Good quality, distinctive rather than profound; €16–18, sold through natural-wine retailers and oyster-bar by-the-glass lists in Paris, New York and Copenhagen.

**Wine 4 — b) Style (12 marks).** A precise, aromatic, oak-free Brut Zéro. Manseng's thick skins are handled with gentle pressing, though a trace of herbal phenolic bitterness remains; cool fermentation preserved the exotic fruit, malolactic avoided, around 18 months on lees, no dosage.

**c) Quality and commercial (7 marks).** Good to very good, a benchmark for an unclassified regional sparkling category; €20, a curiosity wine for sommelier-led lists in France and Benelux, its challenge being an appellation with no sparkling reputation to trade on.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Practice Question (Madeira Pair)

## a) Region and Grape Variety (2 × 8 marks)

Both wines are Madeira, Portugal. The shared signature is decisive: pronounced volatile lift and curry-like notes over piercing acidity, with caramelised rancio from long oxidative ageing. Sherry was weighed — the oxidative profile and spirit warmth overlap — but the high-toned acidity, volatile/curry character and amber-gold viscosity belong to estufagem/canteiro oxidation on an island of naturally very high acidity. Port was ruled out at once: no sweet red fruit, no tannin.

**Wine 1**: Tinta Negra, the island's dominant blending variety. Rounder mocha-almond fruit, without Sercial's lime-petrol cut or Malmsey's beeswax richness.

**Wine 2**: also Tinta Negra, but in a single-vintage Colheita register — amber-gold, more refined, medium-sweet.

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** is a rich, sweet five-year-old blend. The rounded, viscous texture and cooked-sugar edge point to estufagem: heated tanks accelerating development, with fortification arresting fermentation at high residual sugar. Oxidative contact in large old vats, followed by only brief canteiro time, explains mocha and almond without deep rancio; the spirit is only loosely knitted in.

**Wine 2** reverses that logic. Apparent age well beyond the vintage, silky texture and layered almond-mocha indicate canteiro — casks stored in warm attic lodges, ageing slowly by natural heat over many years. Fortification retained comparable sugar, yet the long finish shows spirit fully absorbed, which estufagem rarely achieves at equivalent age. Colheita status requires a single declared harvest and a minimum five years in cask, usually far longer.

---

## c) Quality, Maturity, and Commercial Position (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** is good quality at the 5-Year-Old tier, around £15–20. Heat-driven development means it is at its plateau now and will gain nothing from cellaring. Its route to market is specialist off-trade and on-trade by-the-glass as a dessert or aperitif pour in the UK, US and Scandinavia; category unfamiliarity caps mainstream listings.

**Wine 2** is very good to outstanding at Colheita level, £35–50. Drinking at peak but still fresh within its oxidative frame, it will hold a decade or more, concentrating toffee and dried-fruit notes rather than fading — the point worth grasping is that in Madeira maturity is not a window but a slope, and bottle age is effectively arrested. Fine wine merchants and premium on-trade are the channels, with Japan and the US the strongest export targets for aged Madeira; the constraint remains niche positioning.
