## a) Country and Region of Origin (9 marks)

All three wines are **French**. A botrytised sweet wine, an oxidative fortified and a late-harvest aromatic white sit together in no other country: Germany and Hungary overlap on one or two styles but produce no Grenache-based oxidative fortified.

**Wine 1: Barsac, Bordeaux.** Honey, apricot and saffron with acidity vibrant enough to carry the sugar establish the southwestern botrytis tradition. Alsace VT shows lower acidity relative to sweetness; Loire Chenin is quince-driven. The saline, chalky finish, rather than broader Sauternes opulence, points to Barsac.

**Wine 2: Rivesaltes, Roussillon.** Amber colour, pronounced rancio, roasted hazelnut and candied orange peel indicate oxidative ageing; spirit warmth confirms fortification. Madeira is ruled out — its electric acidity and volatile lift are absent. Maury is predominantly Grenache Noir and darker, red-fruited; the amber hue and white-fruit oxidative profile indicate Rivesaltes Ambré from Grenache Blanc/Gris and Macabeu.

**Wine 3: Alsace Vendanges Tardives.** Lychee, rose petal and cardamom leave no alternative to Gewürztraminer. Concentration and sweetness rule out a dry style; the absence of deep botrytis complexity and extreme viscosity rules out Sélection de Grains Nobles.

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (3 × 13 marks)

**Wine 1** is a lusciously sweet botrytised white of outstanding concentration. Selective harvesting (*tries successives*) is indicated by the purity and evenness of the noble rot character. Fermentation in barrique, suggested by vanilla-tinged richness, was arrested naturally by high sugar. Extended ageing of 18–24 months explains the seamless oak integration and golden hue. MLF was blocked: it would have broadened the acidity that balances the sugar.

**Wine 2** diverges from Wine 1 at the point of fermentation: it was arrested early by grape spirit, fixing residual sugar at higher alcohol. Ageing then followed a deliberately oxidative path in partially filled older casks, likely over a decade, producing rancio, walnut and toffee and the amber colour. No flor, and no biological protection at any stage.

**Wine 3** achieves its sweetness by neither botrytis nor fortification but by ripeness alone — harvesting at the minimum 15° potential alcohol required for VT, giving the deep gold and viscosity. Fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel preserved aromatic purity; no oak is detectable. Fermentation stopped naturally through alcohol. MLF avoided: the modest acidity is the only structure preventing cloying.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** is outstanding, at Grand Cru Classé level within the Sauternes-Barsac classification. Precision of botrytis and acid-sugar balance place it at the top of the appellation. At £80–120 per half-bottle it sells through specialist merchants and top-end restaurant lists in the UK, USA and Hong Kong. The challenge is the declining global market for botrytised sweets even at this quality.

**Wine 2** is very good, well above entry-tier Ambré, its decade-plus of cask age placing it in a small premium tier at roughly €20–30 per 50cl. Sommelier-led interest in oxidative styles in France, the UK and USA is the opening; the obscurity of the appellation to consumers is the obstacle.

**Wine 3** is very good to outstanding, above standard VT bottlings in aromatic intensity and harmony. At approximately €30–45 per 50cl it targets specialist merchants and premium lists in France, Germany, the UK and North America. The principal challenge is the perception of Gewürztraminer as a simple aromatic variety rather than an age-worthy sweet wine.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 2

---

## a) Country and Region of Origin (3 + 3 × 6 marks)

All three wines are from **France** — only France pairs a hot Mediterranean south with a cool, mist-prone Atlantic zone capable of noble rot.

**Wine 1 — Maury Sec, Roussillon.** Deep ruby, damson and violet, warm palate with tight, angular tannins: Grenache Noir in a hot climate. Bone dry, so not the fortified VDN; the firmer tannic frame and denser fruit rule out southern Rhône in favour of Roussillon schist.

**Wine 2 — Châteauneuf-du-Pape.** Garnet with development, dried flowers, white pepper, kirsch; silky tannins and large-vessel oak. A Grenache-led blend. Gigondas or Vacqueyras were the alternatives, but neither typically reaches this breadth and lift.

**Wine 3 — Barsac, Bordeaux.** Deep gold, viscous, apricot–malt–bitter almond botrytis. Cadillac and Monbazillac lack this concentration; the slightly lighter frame and sharper acid line, against the richest Sauternes, point to Barsac.

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (3 × 19 marks)

**Wine 1.** A deliberate choice to ferment fully dry, presenting Grenache as a serious table red rather than a VDN. Preserved violet and cassis lift indicates cool, temperature-controlled fermentation in inert vessel. The tannins are firm but not coarse, suggesting gentle extraction — punch-downs or short maceration — avoiding the over-extraction Grenache suffers in heat. No new oak signature: ageing in old large wood or concrete, so fruit and stone-fruit bitterness carry the finish. Warm alcohol and firm acid make this gastronomic rather than hedonistic.

**Wine 2.** A blended assemblage, Grenache-dominant with Syrah supplying pepper and Mourvèdre the darker fruit and grip. No stemmy greenness: full destemming. Oak is present but recessive — foudre or demi-muid, not new barriques, which would have buried the dried-flower and iris register that distinguishes this wine from Wine 1's primary fruit. Freshness on a warm-vintage frame suggests earlier-picked parcels or a cooler sub-zone, and the velvety texture points to extended, unhurried élevage allowing tannin polymerisation.

**Wine 3.** Noble rot on thin-skinned Sémillon in the Ciron mists. Botrytis is even, with no green or unripe notes, so multiple selective hand-harvest passes rather than a single sweep. Barrel fermentation, arrested by rising alcohol overwhelming the yeasts rather than by chilling and heavy sulphuring, explains how the spicy-malty barrel note is woven into the sugar instead of sitting on top. Crucially, the acid holds the 130g/L or so of residual sugar taut — the difference between Premier Cru Barsac and flabby generic Sauternes.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1.** Very good; cru-level Roussillon. €18–22, specialist off-trade and premium on-trade, competing with Gigondas and Minervois La Livinière for the buyer seeking structured southern French reds. Drinking now, will hold 5–7 years. Exports to UK, Benelux and US, where Roussillon sells as the affordable alternative to the Rhône.

**Wine 2.** Outstanding, at the apex of its appellation. €70–100, premium restaurant lists and private cellars. Will improve a decade and hold twenty, the kirsch fruit drying towards leather and truffle. Its competitive set is top Gigondas and Bandol; the appellation name secures shelf position in the US and Asia that neither rival enjoys.

**Wine 3.** Outstanding, classed-growth Barsac, €80–140. The commercial problem is category, not quality: sweet wine is retreating from on-trade lists outside fine dining. Opportunity lies in Asia, where sweet wine with food is culturally normal, and in somm-led US restaurants selling it by the glass. Will develop marmalade and hazelnut over 20–30 years — a wine whose cellar life outruns the market's patience for it.

## Wine 1

**a) Origin.** A fortified sweet red. The spirit warmth reads moderate for the category, around 16%, well short of Port's 19–20% lift, and the tannin is fine and grippy rather than muscular. Kirsch, cocoa and garrigue over that frame point to Grenache Noir in Roussillon vin doux naturel. Banyuls was weighed, but the pure reductive black fruit with no rancio or saline oxidation narrows this to a vintage-bottled Maury.

**b) Style / winemaking.** *Mutage* on the skins — fermentation arrested with neutral spirit at roughly 90 g/L sugar — with maceration long enough to extract colour and structure. Reductive élevage in tank and early bottling preserve primary fruit: a deliberately modern "vintage" style, not an oxidative one.

**c) Quality / commerce.** Very good, at the top of the Maury vintage tier, around €22/50cl. Independent specialists and sommelier by-the-glass with dark chocolate; the challenge is a contracting fortified-dessert category.

## Wine 2

**a) Origin.** Deep amber-gold, viscous tears, no spirit heat at all, alcohol modest near 13% against searing acidity — a dried-grape sweet wine from north-east Italy. Vin Santo would show more oxidative walnut; Recioto di Soave more almond and quince. The apricot, candied citrus and malic bite point to Vespaiola in Breganze, Veneto.

**b) Style / winemaking.** Whole bunches hung to raisin through winter, with some noble rot in the mix; a long cool ferment stalling naturally in barrique, giving integrated toast rather than overt vanilla; bottled around 130 g/L residual sugar, unacidified.

**c) Quality / commerce.** Outstanding — the benchmark of its DOC, ~€38/50cl. That only 13% alcohol accompanies such sugar shows the ferment was allowed to stall of its own accord, and the acid line that carries it is a cool Prealpine site preserving malic acid, not cellar correction. Restaurant lists in Italy, the US and Japan.

## Wine 3

**a) Origin.** Golden, tannin-free, fortified around 15%, with pronounced orange blossom, rose and fresh grape — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. A southern French VDN is the reflex call, but wine 1 already accounts for France; the deeper colour, sun-baked apricot and softer acid line send me east, to Samos.

**b) Style / winemaking.** Spirit added to partly fermented must, leaving very high sugar; a proportion of sun-dried fruit adding depth; no oak, brief reductive tank ageing, bottled young for aromatic purity.

**c) Quality / commerce.** Very good — the appellation's Grand Cru tier, ~€14/75cl, conspicuous value. Greek domestic trade, duty-free and northern European retail; it undercuts Beaumes-de-Venise by half.

## Wine 4

**a) Origin.** Mahogany with an olive rim, viscous, obvious spirit near 17.5%, hugely sweet, rancio toffee and malt — yet unmistakable muscat grapiness. That combination is Rutherglen, Victoria. PX gives figs and molasses without floral lift; old Tawny lacks the grape aromatic entirely.

**b) Style / winemaking.** Shrivelled Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge picked very late, fortified early to retain 200 g/L-plus; blended across vintages, matured in old casks in hot sheds where evaporation concentrates the wine. Average age suggests Classic.

**c) Quality / commerce.** Very good within a great category — Classic, a tier below Grand and Rare — ~AU$30/50cl. Australian off-trade, specialist UK on-trade; small, loyal, ageing audience.

## Wine 1

**a)** Grüner Veltliner Eiswein, Kamptal, Austria. Pale lemon but with thick, slow-moving tears; barely any warmth on the finish (~9.5%) against very high sugar held by a searing tartaric line. The fruit is pure — greengage, lime, quince — with no botrytis honey or saffron and no raisin or fig, which points to freeze concentration rather than noble rot or drying. White pepper, lentil and wet stone indicate Grüner Veltliner; Riesling would give lime-slate and petrol, Vidal something more overtly tropical. Grüner plus Eiswein narrows to Niederösterreich, and the fine loess-chalk finish to Kamptal.

**b)** Naturally frozen grapes pressed while still solid so only the concentrated must runs; slow, cool stainless ferment arrested by chilling and sterile filtration; no oak and no malolactic — the acid line is untouched.

**c)** Outstanding, the summit of a Kamptal estate range; around €50 per 375ml through Independent Specialists and fine dining in Germany, Austria and the USA. Scarcity sells it; vintage risk caps volume.

## Wine 2

**a)** Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives, Alsace. Medium gold, oily; distinctly warm (~13%) yet clearly sweet, with low-to-medium acidity and a phenolic bitterness closing the palate. Lychee, rose petal and ginger are unmistakable — Muscat would be grapier and leaner, Pinot Gris smokier with quince. Ripeness achieved through passerillage with only a trace of rot, at this alcohol and with real sugar retained, points to Alsace VT.

**b)** Successive *tries* hand-picked, whole-bunch pressed, long indigenous ferment in old large casks stalling naturally; no malolactic, no new oak — texture comes from glycerol and skin phenolics. That it carries sugar well beyond the VT minimum must weight while alcohol stops at 13% shows a domaine picking far past the legal threshold rather than fermenting toward dryness.

**c)** Outstanding, benchmark VT; ~€65 per bottle, Independent Specialists and Michelin lists in France, Japan and the USA.

## Wine 3

**a)** Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria) passito, Etna, Sicily. Deep amber-gold, very viscous; clearly warm (~15%) with high sugar, only moderate acidity and a faint nutty oxidative edge — grapes dried after picking, not botrytised. Orange marmalade, dried apricot and grapey blossom indicate Muscat of Alexandria; Malvasia is less grapey, Vin Santo's Trebbiano far nuttier. Pantelleria's raisining is fuller and softer, so the saline, volcanic tension suggests Etna.

**b)** Ripe fruit dried on mats for some weeks; gentle pressing, ferment in old wood halting naturally near 15%, then brief cask ageing giving the oxidative lift.

**c)** Very good to outstanding among Sicilian sweet wines; ~€40/500ml, pulled through export by the estate's dry Etna reds.

## Wine 4

**a)** Semillon, late harvest, Napa Valley. Medium gold; low warmth (~10.5%) with medium-plus sugar and only medium acidity — a ferment arrested, not exhausted. Lanolin, beeswax, honeyed citrus and hay indicate Semillon; Chenin would bring higher malic bite and quince, Riesling lime and petrol. **b)** Picked late with partial shrivel, pressed and fermented cool in stainless, stopped by chilling, sulphur and filtration to hold sugar; unoaked, no malolactic.

**c)** Very good, estate level; ~$40/375ml, cellar-door and mailing-list sale beside the estate's dry whites rather than an export line.

Crémant d'Alsace (Pinot Blanc/Auxerrois) was the main alternative but would be rounder and less smoky-savoury, without this tension. Alcohol is modest, the wine bone-dry and pure. Austria — Kamptal.

**Wine 3.** Traditional method again, though autolysis is more restrained: green apple, lemon curd, light brioche, toasted hazelnut over fine chalky texture. The purity and single-year focus suggest a vintage cuvée. Chardonnay-led with Pinot Noir. Structurally the discriminator: high, mouthwatering acid, medium-minus body and low perceived alcohol (~12%), yet fruit is ripe rather than green — cool New World rather than Europe. Tasmania was considered but would show a more citrus-saline edge; California is too broad and riper. Willamette Valley, Oregon.

## b) Style and winemaking (3 × 8)

**Wine 1.** A house-style NV built for consistency: gentle whole-bunch pressing, stainless-steel primary, no oak, likely partial malolactic given the round, creamy attack. The distinction: those cooked-fruit, honeycomb notes sitting over still-vibrant acid indicate a substantial reserve-wine fraction plus roughly four years on lees — far beyond the 15-month minimum — so richness is bought with library reserves rather than dosage, which tastes modest at 8–9 g/L.

**Wine 2.** Here the fine oak note and nutty depth suggest base wines part-fermented or aged in large neutral casks, malolactic largely suppressed to preserve the taut line, then long lees ageing and low dosage — brut but tasting almost zero.

**Wine 3.** More reductive handling: cool stainless primary, MLF blocked (no buttery breadth), a shorter 2–3 years sur lie giving cream and vanilla-like lees notes without heavy toast, and a low, clean dosage.

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 7)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding quality, benchmark Grande Marque NV; £45–55, off-trade premium multiples and international on-trade lists, competing directly with the other big houses.

**Wine 2.** Very good quality, Grosse Reserve level Sekt g.U.; €28–35, sold through Austrian and German specialists and Vienna's fine-dining lists — a Champagne alternative whose challenge is category recognition abroad.

**Wine 3.** Very good quality for its appellation, above regional entry level; $28–35 domestically, cellar-door and US specialist retail, competing with Cap Classique and Crémant rather than Champagne.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, four sweet wines from four countries

## Wine 1

**a) Riesling, Mosel — Ruwer side valley, Auslese.** Lemon-gold, medium viscosity only, and a weightless medium-minus body carrying obvious sweetness: the perceived alcohol is very low, barely warming, around 8%, which is the single most diagnostic reading in the glass. Only a handful of styles hold sweetness at that alcohol without fortification or freezing, and the racy, tartaric, apple-skin acid line with white peach, garden herb and summer berry fruit is Riesling. Chenin from the Layon was considered — it can be sweet and high-acid — but Chenin brings quince, wax and more phenolic breadth, and would not be this ethereal. The filigree, almost transparent build and the herbal rather than tropical fruit point to the Ruwer/Saar side valleys rather than the warmer Middle Mosel.

**b)** Sweetness here is unfermented must sugar, not concentration by drying: the fruit is fresh and primary, with no raisin or oxidative edge. Late-picked, botrytis-influenced but selectively so — some individually selected berries, hand-harvested in tries. Fermentation with ambient yeast in stainless or old Fuder, arrested naturally as the yeast stalled at low alcohol, then chilled and sulphured to hold roughly 60–80 g/L. No malolactic — the acid is too incisive — and no oak flavour whatsoever.

**c)** A classic *fruchtsüss* Prädikat style, off-dry-to-sweet but built as an aperitif/food wine rather than a dessert wine. Outstanding quality at Auslese level from a top single-vineyard estate; retailing around €45–55, half-bottle equivalents higher. Sells through independent specialists and Riesling-literate sommeliers in Germany, the US East Coast, Scandinavia and Japan. Drink now to 5 years, will improve 10–15 and hold 30+.

## Wine 2

**a) Garganega, Recioto di Soave, Veneto, Italy.** Gold with high viscosity, full body, pronounced acacia honey, candied apricot, pineapple, white flower and clear raisin, yet a savoury, almost dry-tasting finish and only medium warmth on the palate. That combination — dried-fruit sweetness at moderate alcohol with a bitter-almond savoury close — reads Italian *passito*. Vin Santo was weighed but shows nutty oxidative rancio and Trebbiano/Malvasia's flatter acid; here the acid is high and the florals lifted, which is Garganega's signature.

**b)** Dried-grape sweetness: healthy bunches picked ripe, then air-dried on racks over winter (*appassimento*), losing perhaps 40% of weight and concentrating sugar and acid together. The raisin/pineapple duality plus the honeyed lift suggests some noble rot developed during drying. Slow, cool ferment arrested by alcohol exhausting the yeast, leaving ~100 g/L. Ageing in large neutral wood — no vanilla, no toast.

**Under the skin:** the finish is *dry-feeling* despite the sugar. That tells me the drying was pushed for concentration of extract and acid, not merely sugar — a producer deliberately exceeding what the appellation minimum requires, which is why it reads as a serious wine rather than a sweetmeat.

**c)** DOCG Recioto di Soave, top of its appellation; excellent quality, around €35–45 per 50cl. Narrow but real market: Italian fine-dining lists and specialist retail in the UK, Germany and the US. Challenge is category obscurity against Sauternes.

## Wine 3

**a) Vidal, Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Canada.** Gold, thick, luscious — the sweetest wine of the flight — yet the alcohol reads low, around 10%, with high acid. Extreme sugar at low alcohol means cryoextraction, not drying and not fortification. The exuberant grilled pineapple, mango, passionfruit and ginger against candied apricot is not Riesling's lime/petrol; the fleshy tropicality points to Vidal.

**b)** Grapes left netted on the vine to freeze naturally to roughly −8°C, harvested and pressed frozen so ice is separated and only concentrated juice runs — around 35°Bx must. Long, cold, difficult ferment with a robust yeast, stopped by osmotic stress and chilling near 10% alcohol, leaving 200+ g/L. Inert vessel; no oak, no malo.

**c)** Full-blown dessert style. Very good to excellent VQA Icewine, ~CAD 60–80 per 375ml. Duty-free, travel retail and gifting in East Asia dominate; premium restaurant by-the-glass elsewhere. Drink now to 10 years.

## Wine 4

**a) Moscatel de Setúbal, Portugal.** Topaz, high viscosity, full body and an unmistakable spirity warmth well above table strength — around 17–18% — with medium-plus rather than high acid. That heat plus sweetness means fortification. Orange blossom, orange peel and raisin over grapey musk confirm Muscat of Alexandria; a Rutherglen Muscat was considered but would be browner, more treacly and more rancid-oxidative.

**b)** Sweetness retained by *mutage*: grape spirit added mid-ferment to kill the yeast at ~110 g/L. Skins macerated in the fortified wine for aromatic extraction, then oxidative cask ageing giving the topaz hue while retaining freshness.

**c)** Very good quality, DOC Setúbal, around €18–25 — strong value. Off-trade and specialist retail, Portugal, Brazil, Northern Europe; competes below Port.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, three fortified/sweet wines

## a) Origin and variety (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Durif, Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia.** Opaque black-purple with staining legs, sweet (around 90–100 g/L), chewy tannin and obvious spirit heat well above 19%: a red fortified mutéed after substantial skin extraction. Vintage Port was the first alternative, but I would expect violet-floral Touriga lift, drier extract and firmer schistous grip; here the plush plum-and-dark-chocolate breadth, an unmistakable eucalypt edge and no rancio whatsoever point to warm inland Australia. Shiraz was plausible; the sheer inkiness and bruising, thick-skinned tannin scale argue for Durif — Rutherglen's signature vintage-fortified grape.

**Wine 2 — Furmint, Tokaj, Hungary; Aszú, 5 Puttonyos.** Deep amber-gold, viscous, with saffron, dried orange peel, quince, beeswax and ginger — textbook noble rot. Modest warmth (~11–12%) against searing acidity and very high sugar rules out any fortified style: alcohol this low with sugar this high demonstrates a naturally arrested botrytis ferment. Sauternes considered and rejected — Sémillon would give more alcohol (~13.5%), creamier new-barrique vanilla and citrus-honey rather than this smoky, dried-marmalade and earthy tone. The wine tastes richer than the 120 g/L floor for 5 Puttonyos: a serious estate here habitually overshoots the legal minimum, yet the pinpoint acid keeps it leaner than 6 Puttonyos weight.

**Wine 3 — Grenache Noir, Banyuls, Roussillon, France; Rimage.** Deep ruby with purple flash, spirit warmth clearly gentler than Wine 1 (~16%), sweet around 90 g/L, kirsch, raspberry liqueur, cocoa and garrigue over fine dusty tannin, with no oxidative walnut. Maury was weighed; the saline, iron-schist minerality and maritime lift favour Banyuls. Ruby Port eliminated: lower alcohol, no aguardente bite.

## b) Style and winemaking (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1:** picked very ripe (~15 Baumé), fermented on skins for colour and tannin, then fortified with neutral spirit while several degrees of sugar remained; basket-pressed, briefly rested in large old oak and bottled young — a vintage-dated, fruit-driven fortified, not a solera or tawny style.

**Wine 2:** repeated tries of hand-picked aszú berries macerated in must for a day or two, pressed, then a long cool barrel ferment stalling near 11–12% as alcohol and sugar overwhelmed the yeast, finished by racking, chilling and sulfur; roughly two years in small Gönci casks gives the light oxidative nuttiness.

**Wine 3:** *mutage sur grains* — spirit run onto fermenting skins after a short maceration, arresting fermentation with sugar intact; then deliberately reductive, tank-and-bottle handling within the year to preserve primary fruit, the opposite of the traditional rancio route.

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1:** outstanding for the category, top of the Rutherglen vintage-fortified ladder; around AU$40/500ml; cellar door and independent specialists, niche sommelier listings in the UK/US. Challenge: a shrinking domestic fortified audience. Drink now to 20 years.

**Wine 2:** very good to outstanding, one rung below 6 Puttonyos; €35/500ml; fine-dining by-the-glass and specialists in Japan, the US and Poland, competing with premium Sauternes and German BA.

**Wine 3:** good quality Banyuls, benchmark for the Rimage tier rather than aged Grand Cru; around €20, French on-trade and specialist retail — an accessible entry point against Ruby Port. Drink now to 8 years.

**Wine 1** — Rich non-vintage traditional method: bottle-fermented, with at least 18 months and likely considerably longer on lees given how far the autolytic character has integrated. **Wine 2** — Bottle-fermented with roughly 18–24 months on lees — brioche and hazelnut are present but not pronounced. Unlike Wine 1, there is no reserve-wine layering: this reads as single-vintage, cold-fermented in steel or neutral vessels to hold primary citrus, with only a whisper of older oak. Low to moderate dosage, brut.

**Wine 3** — Traditional method well beyond the nine-month Cava minimum; the cream and toast suggest around 15 months. Temperature-controlled steel fermentation preserves the tropical fruit, and fruit was clearly picked at full ripeness. Dosage at the upper brut end reads sweeter than it is because the acidity is broader than in the other three.

**Wine 4** — The shortest lees ageing of the flight, perhaps 12–15 months, judged by the less integrated autolysis. Steel fermentation and early bottling protect the guava and apple. **Wine 1** — Outstanding; top of the Grande Marque non-vintage tier, £55–75 in UK specialist independents and premium on-trade. Reserve-wine integration and length place it clearly above basic NV. **Wine 4** — Good; entry to mid-tier Australian traditional method, A$25–35. Its tropical aromatics genuinely differentiate it from European rivals — but at this price it meets Prosecco, Cava and New Zealand traditional method head-on, and volume, not style, will decide the outcome.

Also a pale rosé, but where Wine 2 is purely fruity this shows pomegranate, dried rose petal, sour cherry, garrigue and a saline edge — indigenous Mediterranean, not international. Savagnin, Château-Chalon, Jura, France. The deep gold, high viscosity and intense curry, baked apple and smoke point unmistakably to oxidative ageing under *voile*. Viognier was briefly considered given the viscosity, but shows no oxidative character and far more overt apricot-blossom perfume rather than the savoury, walnut-inflected depth here. Jura Chardonnay can approach this profile but lacks Savagnin's curry intensity. The sustained yellow-gold and glycerol-heavy tears confirm extended *sous voile* ageing; warmth consistent with ~14–14.5% and complete dryness confirm full fermentation. Within the Jura, the extraordinary depth, integration and length point to Château-Chalon — the single appellation reserved exclusively for Vin Jaune — rather than generic Vin Jaune AOC.

## Wine 1 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Late-picked Savagnin fermented to dryness in neutral vessels, then aged in partially-filled, unsealed barrique for a minimum of six years and three months under *voile* of film yeast. The deliberate absence of topping-up drives controlled oxidation and acetaldehyde development, evident in the vivid curry and almond notes. No malolactic conversion, consistent with the acidity underpinning the oxidative richness. Bottled unfined in the 62cl *clavelin*.

## Wine 1 — c) Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality — Château-Chalon is Jura's most prestigious designation, retailing at £60–90 per *clavelin* through specialist merchants and premium on-trade. Ageing potential of 20–30 years. Export markets — UK, USA, Japan, Benelux — are growing, though consumer unfamiliarity with oxidative dry whites remains the principal commercial challenge.

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Furmint, Tokaj, Hungary. Lemon-gold colour; pronounced flinty minerality, cloves, white pepper, ripe fig and lemon zest on the nose; laser acidity and a dry palate with tropical mango and green tea. Riesling was the principal alternative — both show electric acid-mineral tension — but Riesling leads with lime citrus and early petrol development and lacks the cloves-and-white-pepper register here. Grüner Veltliner was also considered given the white pepper, but shows a leaner mid-palate without this tropical fruit weight. The combination of fig, mango, chalk-mineral intensity and warmth consistent with ~13% places this decisively in Tokaj, where volcanic Zemplén soils deliver precisely this profile.

## Wine 2 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Whole-cluster pressing indicated by the clean, phenolic-free palate. Fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel preserves the variety's aromatic precision — no new oak is evident, which would have softened the angular minerality. Full fermentation to dryness; the absence of lees-derived creaminess suggests early bottling to maximise freshness.

## Wine 2 — c) Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good quality, equivalent to a single-vineyard estate dry Furmint; around £20–30. Fresh, dry and highly aromatic — a rival to top Alsace Riesling and Austrian Grüner Veltliner on restaurant lists. The challenge is that Tokaj remains associated with sweet Aszú; the opportunity for those who establish the dry category early is considerable in the UK, Germany and USA.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Palomino Fino, Jerez, Spain — an unfortified *vino de pasto* style. Ripe pineapple, lemon peel, dried banana, almond and savoury notes, with a chalky, salty finish, immediately suggest flor-yeast influence in a warm southern setting. Crucially, no spirit heat is detectable — alcohol reads at roughly 12–12.5% — which rules out any fortified Sherry category. Viura from Rioja was considered but shows none of this flor-derived or saline-maritime character. The low alcohol, almond-bakery notes, herbal tanginess and saline finish on *albariza* soils place this firmly as an unfortified Palomino aged under flor.

## Wine 3 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Early-picked grapes, gently pressed, fermented in stainless steel to dryness — no new oak evident. The defining decision is deliberate exposure to *flor* yeast during ageing in older barrels without fortification, generating the almond, dried banana and saline complexity at natural alcohol. Aged six to twelve months under partial flor, then early-bottled to preserve fragrance. Bright citrus acidity indicates no malolactic conversion.

## Wine 3 — c) Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good to very good; around £18–28 at specialist retail. Dry, saline and genuinely distinctive, sitting at the intersection of natural wine and emerging unfortified Spanish whites. The challenge is educating buyers that this is not a Sherry; the opportunity is a real category gap with no established competitor at this style and quality level.

Torrontés, Salta, Argentina. The lemon-green colour and extravagant nose — roses, orange blossom, grapefruit, nutmeg — is immediately striking. Gewürztraminer was also weighed: it shares floral intensity and spice but shows more lychee, heavier body and typically higher alcohol. This wine's grapefruit freshness and taut acid line holding the aromatics together are the decisive signatures of Torrontés Riojano from high-altitude Salta, where elevations above 1,700 metres preserve aromatic intensity while cool nights retain the acidity that stops the variety reading flat.

## Wine 4 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Very early picking at low sugar accumulation to retain acidity. Whole-bunch pressing and cold settling indicated by the clean, non-phenolic finish — prolonged skin contact would bring bitterness. Fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel preserves the volatile aromatics; no oak evident. Early inert bottling captures the primary perfume. No malolactic conversion, consistent with the bright grapefruit acidity.

Very good for the category; around £14–20. Exuberantly aromatic, dry and medium-bodied — a natural by-the-glass aperitif. Key channels are premium supermarkets and independent specialists in the UK and USA, competing with Albariño and Pinot Gris at similar prices. The main consumer resistance is perceived sweetness despite full dryness; Argentina's rising export profile creates real upside.

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (8 marks)

Tawny-amber colour and high viscosity confirm fortified and oxidatively aged, but where this differs from Wine 3 is the aromatic register: Christmas pudding, malt chocolate, baked fig, vanilla bean, and an exotic sassafras note — more spiced, more perfumed than PX's dried-fruit severity. The extraordinary caramel-and-spice depth combined with unmistakable grapey Muscat perfume points away from Sherry or Madeira toward a Muscat-based fortified from a very warm climate. Rutherglen Muscat — made from the dark-skinned rouge clone of Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains — is the only style combining this caramel intensity with persistent Muscat terpene character. Origin: Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia; variety: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (rouge clone).

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Grapes harvested at very high sugar levels from partially raisined fruit, then fortified to arrest fermentation and preserve both sugar and Muscat's characteristic grapiness. Extended oxidative ageing in a solera-like tiered system develops layered rancio and caramel. Crucially, unlike Wine 3, the exotic sassafras and spice notes reflect Muscat terpene character surviving and evolving through long ageing — the key quality marker distinguishing great Rutherglen Muscat from lesser examples.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Outstanding quality; a benchmark at the Classic or Grand Rutherglen Muscat tier, retailing around AUD $60–80 (approximately £35–45) per 375ml through specialist merchants and fine dining. Export strongest into the UK, Japan, and Hong Kong. By-the-glass dessert placement is the strongest channel; the wine competes directly with aged Tawny Port and premium PX for the same shelf position.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## Wine 1

**a) Origin and variety**

Pale lemon-green, with pronounced lime, green apple and white peach, off-dry sweetness cut by racy acidity, and very low perceived alcohol (~8–9%, no warmth at all). Gewürztraminer is ruled out by the absence of rose petal and lychee and by the acid level, which is far too high for that variety. Chenin Blanc can show comparable tension but would read at 12%+ and lacks the lime-and-slate signature. The combination of electric acidity, featherweight alcohol and pure citrus fruit is unique to the Mosel. **Mosel Riesling Spätlese**, from a steep south-facing slate site.

**b) Style and winemaking**

Fermentation was arrested with sugar remaining — chilling and filtration, not chaptalisation or fortification, hence the low alcohol alongside high residual sugar. No oak: pristine primary fruit indicates stainless steel and cold settling. The persistent apple-peach finish suggests some lees contact for texture without blurring aromatic clarity.

**c) Quality and commercial position**

Very good; vineyard definition lifts it above generic QbA, but it lacks the botrytis and extract of Auslese. £20–25 in specialist merchants and premium independents; progressive by-the-glass on-trade. Key exports UK, USA, Japan. Will drink well now but gains kerosene and honey over 10–15 years.

---

## Wine 2

**a) Origin and variety**

Deep gold, viscous, with baked peach, dried apricot, lychee, jasmine and candied orange. The palate reads warm (~15%) with spirit heat at the back of the throat: fortified, which eliminates late-harvest and Icewine routes. Within Muscat fortifieds, the fresh grapey floral lift separates it from the raisined, rancio character of Rutherglen Muscat, and its weight and alcohol exclude Moscato passito. **Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, Southern Rhône**, from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.

**b) Style and winemaking**

A Vin Doux Naturel: mutage with neutral grape spirit early in fermentation, retaining roughly 100 g/L residual sugar and locking in primary aromatics — the reason the fruit reads fresh rather than cooked. A slight walnut edge suggests brief time in old oak or concrete, but the pale gold colour and vivid fruit rule out extended oxidative ageing.

**c) Quality and commercial position**

Good to very good, upper tier of the appellation. £15–20 per 50cl through independents and fine-dining dessert lists. Competes with Rivesaltes Ambré and Moscatel de Setúbal; its aromatic precision is the differentiator. Drink young — freshness is the selling point and will fade within five years.

---

## Wine 3

**a) Origin and variety**

Gold, viscous, with dried apricot, honey, orange marmalade and a nutmeg-tobacco spice: botrytis, at moderate alcohol (~11%) with firm acidity. Sauternes was the main alternative, but the marmalade-and-tobacco spectrum, the sharper acid spine and the leaner texture separate this from a Semillon/Sauvignon blend, which would be broader and creamier. That acid-driven structure under high sugar is the Furmint fingerprint. **Tokaji Aszú, Hungary**, at five-puttonyos concentration on the evidence of the sweetness level and the length.

**b) Style and winemaking**

Hand-selected aszú berries macerated in base wine or must for 12–48 hours before pressing, giving the extract. Vanilla and gentle spice indicate Hungarian oak maturation, minimum two years; the tobacco and nutmeg confirm a controlled oxidative element. Crucially, acidity has been preserved rather than tamed — the quality marker that distinguishes fine Tokaji from merely sweet Tokaji.

**c) Quality and commercial position**

Outstanding. £35–50 per 50cl in specialist merchants, auction and premium hotel lists; exports to UK, Germany, USA, Japan. Ten years old or so in style terms and will develop toward caramel, walnut and dried orange over 20+ years, which supports genuine collector positioning.

---

## Wine 4

**a) Origin and variety**

Clear ruby, medium(+) red fruit, blackberry, balsamic and black liquorice with spice; soft silky palate, medium(-) tannin, perceptible residual sugar, and — decisively — no spirit heat. That absence rules out Port and Douro fortifieds, which was the obvious alternative given the fruit and mineral edge; the tannin is also too fine and the alcohol too modest. **Late-harvest (Cosecha Tardía) Tempranillo, Ribera del Duero, Spain.**

**b) Style and winemaking**

Very ripe late-picked fruit concentrating sugar while retaining acid, with fermentation chilled to a halt before dryness — hence sweetness at restrained alcohol, the reverse of the region's normal full-bodied dry reds. Balsamic and spice complexity without vanilla or char points to large-format or older French oak, protecting freshness. This is the one wine in the flight where sweetness is achieved with tannin in the frame.

**c) Quality and commercial position**

Very good, Reserva-equivalent in weight though outside the standard classification ladder. £25–35, specialist and on-trade only. A deliberate curiosity — an elegant rather than heavy sweet red — competing on novelty with Brachetto d'Acqui and Loire late-harvest Cabernet Franc. Drink within five years; the fruit is the point and tannin will not carry it further.

---

## Wine 5

**a) Origin and variety**

Gold, high viscosity, searing acidity, pronounced pineapple, mango, lemon and orange peel over apricot and peach skin, very high sugar, low alcohol (~9%). The fruit is pure and cryo-concentrated with no rot character, which excludes botrytis wines; there is no spirit and no oxidation, excluding VDN and passito. Tropical pineapple-mango rather than lime-petrol points to Vidal over Riesling Eiswein. **Vidal Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario.**

**b) Style and winemaking**

Fruit left to freeze on the vine to at least −8°C and pressed frozen, so only concentrated juice is extracted. Fermentation is slow and cool, stalling near 9% with sugar well above 180 g/L. Stainless steel and cold stabilisation throughout; no oak, because the commercial proposition rests entirely on vivid primary fruit and acid contrast.

**c) Quality and commercial position**

Outstanding, top tier of Niagara. CAD $50–80 per 375ml, among Canada's highest prices per litre. Specialist merchants, travel retail and gift-driven retail in Canada, USA, UK, Japan and China. Presentation and gifting are the real differentiators here. Best drunk within eight years, before the tropical top notes flatten toward marmalade.

---

## Wine 6

**a) Origin and variety**

Deep amber, viscous, with roasted cashew, dried fig, candied orange, apricot jam, maple and a nail-varnish lift. No spirit heat (~14% perceived) excludes fortified categories; the amber colour and nut-and-caramel oxidation exclude both botrytis and Icewine. This is dried-grape wine with long oxidative barrel age. The apricot-honey fruit under the oxidation reads as Trebbiano Toscano and Malvasia rather than Jura Vin de Paille, which would be fresher and less rancio. **Vin Santo del Chianti Classico, Tuscany**, top tier.

**b) Style and winemaking**

Appassimento on racks for three to six months, then fermentation and ageing in small sealed caratelli for well beyond the three-year minimum. The volatile lift and nutty depth come from film-yeast activity and prolonged oxidative ageing in partially filled barrels under fluctuating cellar temperatures. The clean tart finish shows the base fruit carried enough acid — what separates fine Vin Santo from cloying examples.

**c) Quality and commercial position**

Outstanding, Riserva level. £40–60 per 375ml through fine wine specialists and top Italian restaurant lists in Italy, UK and USA. Fully mature and stable for decades; the commercial challenge is category unfamiliarity, so the route forward is food-pairing positioning with biscotti or aged Pecorino, and provenance storytelling on fine wine platforms to justify the price against better-known dessert wines in this flight.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 4

## Wine 1 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Sauternes, Bordeaux, France. Sémillon-dominant with Sauvignon Blanc. Deep gold, viscous legs, and a nose of marmalade, beeswax and dried apricot over a waxy lanolin note — the signature of Sémillon under noble rot. The acidity is moderate but structured rather than racy, and the palate is warm and broad at around 14%, which rules out a German Auslese or BA, where sweetness arrives at half that alcohol and far lower weight. Vouvray moelleux and Coteaux du Layon were weighed but lack the tropical botrytis signature and show quince instead. The layering of dried fruit over fresh citrus, closing on frangipane, argues Premier Cru Classé rather than generic AC.

## Wine 1 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Sweetness comes from botrytis cinerea, which dehydrates the berries to concentrate sugar while generating the beeswax, honey and saffron compounds on the nose. The evenness of that botrytis character and the total absence of green notes imply multiple selective passes (*tries successives*). Vanilla and toast sit beneath the fruit rather than on it, indicating barrique fermentation with perhaps 40–50% new oak, and the glossy, creamy mid-palate points to 18–24 months on lees. Freshness intact: careful SO₂ handling, no oxidative drift.

## Wine 1 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding. Premier Cru Classé Sauternes, £60–120 per half-bottle through specialist merchants and fine dining, with strong pull in the US, UK, Hong Kong and Japan. The commercial tension is structural: production costs per bottle are among the highest in France while sweet wine is losing younger drinkers, so the category survives on-trade, where cheese and foie gras pairings remain unrivalled.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Nahe, Germany. Riesling. Pale gold with a green tinge; slate, lime zest, white peach and a thread of petrol. The structure decides it: electric acidity slicing through the sugar, with a light body and only faint warmth suggesting roughly 8% — Auslese territory. Mosel was the serious alternative on the slate/lime axis, but the broader peach-apricot mid-palate and fuller extract fit Nahe's marly-clay sites, which sit between Mosel delicacy and Rhine breadth. Alsace Vendange Tardive is excluded by the low alcohol and lack of opulence.

## Wine 2 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Selective picking at Auslese ripeness, with fermentation arrested by chilling and sterile filtration, leaving perhaps 80–120 g/L. Whole-bunch pressing is implied by the clean fruit and absence of phenolic grip. No vanilla or toast whatsoever: stainless steel or old neutral casks. Acidity is linear and malic rather than lactic, so MLF was blocked — a reductive, aromatics-first approach, the opposite of Wine 1's oxidatively handled barrel regime.

## Wine 2 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good. Auslese, £25–40 per half-bottle, specialist merchants; UK, US and Scandinavia. Foil to blue cheese or stone-fruit desserts. Label complexity remains the barrier, but a sweet wine at 8% is precisely what the low-alcohol trend is asking for — the category's clearest premiumisation route.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

California, USA. Orange Muscat. Deep amber-gold and staining, with orange blossom, mandarin zest, apricot jam, dried rose and grapey exuberance — Muscat family beyond doubt. Perceived alcohol is full and warm, near 15%, with moderate acidity: a fortified style, not Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise's lighter frame or a German Muscat. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains was considered but does not deliver orange-peel marmalade at this intensity. Rutherglen would bring rancio, walnut and far deeper colour; this is brighter and more floral, and the jammy apricot ripeness reads Californian.

## Wine 3 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Fermentation arrested by grape spirit (*mutage*), preserving sugar and lifting alcohol to ~15%. The vivid primary grapiness indicates early fortification. No oak, and clarity suggests cold stabilisation. The decisive choice is varietal: Orange Muscat's linalool and orange terpenes do the stylistic work, so the winemaking is deliberately minimal — the inverse of Wine 1, where oak and lees build the wine.

## Wine 3 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good. Entry-to-mid fortified dessert wine, $20–30 per half-bottle: US premium supermarkets and large off-trade chains, by-the-glass in mid-market restaurants, plus travel retail. Competitive set is southern French VDN. Aromatics sell it instantly; the variety's name recognition is near zero, so it depends on shelf position rather than pull.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Marlborough, New Zealand. Riesling. Bright gold; lime zest, lemon curd, peach compote, honeysuckle. High, bright acidity from Marlborough's diurnal swing lifts the sugar; light body and gentle warmth suggest around 9%, fermentation arrested early. Against Wine 2, the tell is what is absent — no crystalline mineral precision, no botrytis markers — so late-harvest concentration, not noble rot. Vouvray demi-sec was weighed on the honeyed stone fruit but the lime-dominant citrus and acid shape rule it out.

## Wine 4 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Late harvest with sugar accumulation by hang time, fermentation stopped by chilling and sterile filtration. No beeswax or saffron confirms passerillage rather than botrytis. Stainless steel throughout — the fruit is wholly primary. Gentle pressing and cool ferment preserve the lime and floral volatiles. Crucially the winemaker arrested early to hold acidity rather than chase maximum sugar, giving a commercial late-harvest rather than a BA equivalent.

## Wine 4 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good. Late-harvest entry level, NZ$20–30 (£10–14), New Zealand supermarkets and off-trade chains, exported to the UK and Australia, with genuine by-the-glass dessert potential. Sitting in Sauvignon Blanc's shadow is the problem: the wine is well made and drinkable, but New Zealand Riesling has no premium equity, so price is capped by category rather than by quality.

**b)** A deliberately reductive, fruit-first style. The absence of any phenolic bitterness suggests gentle whole-bunch pressing with free-run juice only; the clean, unfermented-must purity indicates a cool stainless-steel fermentation with a neutral cultured yeast. The zesty malic bite and complete lack of dairy or buttery texture indicate malolactic fermentation was blocked — as much a decision as its use. The very slight creaminess and almond note point to a few months on fine lees with occasional bâtonnage, but no oak whatsoever. Bottled early to protect aromatics.

**c)** Very good quality at village level for the appellation — concentrated rather than merely intense, with a medium(+) finish, though without the depth of a single-old-vine parcel. An entry-to-mid tier estate wine retailing around €13–16 / £15. Independent specialists and by-the-glass in modern bistros; competes with premium Rías Baixas Albariño and Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine sur lie for drinkers who want dry, unoaked whites with saline personality.

## Wine 2

**a)** Blaufränkisch, Mittelburgenland, Austria. Medium ruby, with sour cherry, morello, blackcurrant leaf and a distinct black-peppery spice over dried herbs. The decisive evidence is structural: high, mouthwatering acidity sitting alongside genuinely ripe fruit, with fine-grained, taut tannin and only moderate warmth around 13%. Cabernet Franc was the leading alternative given the leafy top note, but the acid line is more tartaric and the tannin chalkier, without Franc's graphite. Zweigelt was rejected as too soft and confected. That high acid *held against* ripe fruit is the marker of a warm continental site cooled by altitude and shaded slope rather than a hot one — Mittelburgenland's inland, iron-rich slopes.

**b)** Traditional-leaning: partial whole-bunch inclusion for the stem-spice lift, ambient fermentation, gentle extraction — the tannins support rather than dominate. Matured in large old casks; there is toast but no vanilla or new-oak sweetness. Unfiltered impression, drink-now-to-cellar positioning.

**c)** Outstanding for the variety, comparable to a good Erste Lage; around €25–30. Independent merchants and sommelier lists in Germany, Scandinavia and New York; competes with Loire Cabernet Franc and cru Beaujolais.

## Wine 3

**a)** Pinotage, Stellenbosch, South Africa. Ripe black cherry, mulberry and cassis with mocha, espresso and dark chocolate, plus a telltale trace of banana/acetate ester — a Pinotage fingerprint. Warm, generous, medium(+) body suggesting roughly 14.5%, with softer acidity and rounded, mouthcoating tannin. Syrah was considered but there is no cracked pepper or violet; Merlot cannot deliver this coffee-and-ester profile.

**b)** Warm-region harvest at high ripeness, warm ferment with vigorous pumping over for colour, then extended maceration; the mocha layer indicates ageing in new French oak barriques, medium-toast, around 40% new for 14–18 months. Acetate has been controlled, not eliminated, by managed ferment temperature.

**c)** Very good quality, Reserve tier, around £18–22. Premium supermarket and independent trade in the UK, plus domestic on-trade; the challenge remains Pinotage's variable reputation abroad.

## Wine 4

**a)** Muscat of Alexandria — Moscatel de Setúbal, Portugal, with a ten-year age indication. Deep amber-tawny; orange peel, raisin, honey, toasted nut and rancio, yet still overtly grapey. Sweet, roughly 130–150 g/L, with obvious spirit warmth near 17.5% and high acidity keeping it buoyant. Rutherglen Muscat was weighed but is thicker, darker and far sweeter; Muscat de Rivesaltes is fresher and less oxidative.

**b)** Fermentation arrested by grape spirit at low sugar depletion, then — crucially — extended skin maceration *after* fortification, which is why a decade in old wood has developed rancio without stripping the terpenes: that retained grapey lift over oxidative nuttiness is the signature of Setúbal's post-fortification maceration, not cask time alone. Cask-blended to a consistent house style.

**c)** Very good quality within the aged-Muscat category; around €20 for 50cl. Specialist off-trade and dessert-wine lists; a value alternative to 10-year Tawny.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, four-country single-variety flight

## a) Variety and origin (4 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Rolle (Vermentino), coastal Côtes de Provence, France.** The lemon-green colour with barely a blush, and the total absence of red fruit on nose or palate, tell me straight away this is a white-berried variety pressed direct, not a pink wine. Structurally: dry, moderate rather than high acidity, medium body with a distinctly warm, glycerol-rich mid-palate suggesting around 13%, and a long, saline, chalky finish. That combination of warmth and salinity is Mediterranean. Sémillon was the first alternative — but it would give a waxier, broader mouthfeel and less cut; Picpoul de Pinet the second, which would be leaner and much shorter. The fine chalky drive and genuine length on a wine of only medium(+) aromatic intensity is the telling point: this is not aromatic showmanship but site and lees work, which reads as a low-yielding limestone coastal parcel rather than a blended appellation wine. Provence, near the sea.

**Wine 2 — Pinot Noir, Willamette Valley, Oregon.** Medium pink, so real skin contact. Ripe cherry, blood orange, hibiscus and crushed herbs, with medium(+) fresh acidity, low but perceptible tannin, medium(-) body and gentle warmth around 13.5%. The red-cherry/blood-orange axis with floral lift is Pinot Noir; Grenache-Cinsault from Provence was considered but would be paler, more herbal-saline and lower in acid, while a Sancerre rosé would be leaner and lighter in alcohol than this. The ripeness held by that acid line points to a cool-but-sunny New World site, and the herbal edge argues Oregon over California.

**Wine 3 — Pinot Gris, Marlborough, New Zealand.** Pale salmon, low viscosity, light-bodied, dry, crisp medium(+) acidity and modest warmth (~12.5%), with pure strawberry, watermelon rind, rose petal and citrus zest, finishing medium(-). Pinot Noir would be the reflex call, but wine 2 has already claimed it and the paler hue, lighter frame and citrus-zest/white-peach edge rather than cherry depth fit a pink-skinned white grape given short contact. The zippy, primary, screwcap-fresh profile is Marlborough rather than Central Otago, which would show more density.

**Wine 4 — Garnacha, Campo de Borja / Ebro Valley, Spain.** Pale pink, medium acidity only, medium(-) body but the most noticeable warmth in the flight, near 14%. Simple red fruit and a floral top note, medium(-) finish. Grenache-based Provence was weighed and rejected: it would carry more saline length and higher acid at lower alcohol. Tavel was rejected too — far deeper coloured and more structured. Warm, soft, generously alcoholic and inexpensive in profile: Spain's Ebro, Campo de Borja or Navarra.

## b) Style and winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — a serious, near-white gastronomic style. The purity and absence of any phenolic bitterness indicate whole-bunch direct pressing with juice run at low pressure; the retained tartaric freshness and lack of any lactic breadth indicate malolactic was blocked. The creamy underlay without oak vanilla points to eight or so months on fine lees in stainless or large neutral vessel with some stirring.

**Wine 2** — a deliberately gastronomic, textured rosé. The colour depth and cherry weight indicate a short cold maceration of a day or so (or a saignée fraction), cool stainless ferment with aromatic yeast, no oak and no malolactic, bottled the following spring with a trace of sugar to soften the acid.

**Wine 3** — a commercial aromatic style built for freshness. Very light extraction, protective juice handling, cool ferment, no lees or oak work, early bottling under screwcap to preserve the primary fruit.

**Wine 4** — volume winemaking, most likely a bleed off a red fermentation, cool-fermented in tank, no oak, no malolactic, bottled within months. Warm-climate ripeness rather than technique is doing the work here.

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — outstanding for its appellation, at the Cru Classé de Provence level; balance, salinity and length justify around €35–45. Independent specialists and fine-dining lists in France, Benelux and the USA; competes with white Bandol and premium Vermentino.

**Wine 2** — very good, premium single-estate tier, ~US$28–32. West-coast on-trade by the glass and wine clubs; its point of difference against premium Provence is fruit depth, though the price makes export hard.

**Wine 3** — good quality, sound commercial rosé at NZ$22 / £13–15. Premium supermarket and multiple-retailer shelves in the UK, USA and Australia; drink within a year.

**Wine 4** — acceptable to good, DO level, €7–9. Off-trade and own-label in Germany, the Netherlands and the UK; the challenge is that the softer acidity gives it less freshness than its Provençal competitors at the same shelf price.

# Mock Answer — Practice P3 Sweet Trio (75 marks)

## Wine 1 — a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Deep gold tending to amber, with high viscosity. Candied apricot, orange marmalade and beeswax over a full, velvety palate of mandarin zest and dried pineapple: botrytis-affected fruit. The structural anchors are high residual sugar against only medium-plus acidity, full body and a warmth suggesting around 14%. Late-harvest Riesling is eliminated by the absence of petrol and by sweetness that is broad rather than racy; the acid simply is not there. The citrus-and-preserved-fruit complexity, oak and sheer alcoholic weight fit a Sémillon-dominant blend with Sauvignon Blanc from Sauternes, Bordeaux, at classified-growth concentration.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Yields heavily suppressed by successive selective passes through botrytised fruit. Toasted brioche and caramel indicate fermentation and maturation in French barriques with a proportion of new wood, around 18 months, giving the slight bitter grip on the finish. High alcohol alongside high sugar shows a long, naturally halted fermentation, secured by chilling, filtration and SO₂ rather than early arrest.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Outstanding; Premier Cru Classé level, £80–120. The balance of sugar against fresh citrus acidity, and the length, place it above unclassified Sauternes. Specialist merchants and fine-dining on-trade in the UK, US and Asia; it has no mainstream off-trade route.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Gold, viscous, but a different register from Wine 1: marzipan, fresh fig and bread-dough botrytis, with perceived alcohol only 10–11% and sweetness that stays juicy rather than unctuous — evidence of fermentation stopped early at low alcohol. German Riesling BA was weighed, but the fig-and-nut profile lacks Riesling's lime and petrol, and the acid is softer. That honeyed, faintly oxidative fig character points to Welschriesling from Burgenland, Austria, in Ruster Ausbruch style.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Whole-cluster pressing of heavily botrytised bunches, fermented in neutral wood or steel; the absence of vanilla or toast confirms no new oak, the delicate marzipan aromatics preserved rather than overlaid. Fermentation arrested early, retaining high sugar at modest alcohol — the key stylistic divergence from Wine 1.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Very good; Ruster Ausbruch level, €30–50. Complexity and length justify premium positioning with specialist merchants and wine-focused on-trade in Austria, Germany and the UK. The category's obstacle is negligible recognition of the appellation outside Austria.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Region and Variety (8 marks)

Honeyed apricot, a petrol hint, beeswax, ginger and candied citrus peel, with a waxy lanolin mid-palate and racy citrus acidity: Riesling, and the acidity separates it sharply from both other wines. Gewürztraminer was considered on the spice and orange blossom, but its low acidity and oily broadness are absent. Perceived alcohol around 11% with genuine botrytis concentration indicates a cool-climate noble-rot style; the ripe, generous fruit weight beneath the acidity suggests New Zealand, Hawke's Bay, rather than Mosel.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (9 marks)

Selective harvesting of noble-rot bunches gives the marmalade and apricot jam. Fermentation arrested to retain substantial sugar at low alcohol, in stainless steel under cool temperature control to protect the aromatics — no oak signature at all, unlike Wine 1. The lanolin texture is Riesling's own phenolic structure, not winemaking.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (8 marks)

Very good; a top New Zealand producer's noble-rot bottling, around NZ$40–60 (£20–30), competitive on quality with German Auslese but sold at a discount to it. Specialist merchants and premium on-trade domestically, with export to the UK and US on the back of New Zealand's white wine reputation. Volumes are tiny and the country has no established sweet-wine identity to trade on.

---

Under the skin: all three are botrytis wines, but they divide on where fermentation was stopped. Wine 1 ran long to high alcohol and was oak-raised; Wines 2 and 3 were arrested early, keeping sugar at 10–11% and preserving primary aromatics in neutral vessels. That single decision, not fruit ripeness, explains the differences in weight, texture and price positioning across the flight.

## Wine 1 — France

### a) Country and variety (10 marks)

Chardonnay, France — Champagne. Pale lemon-green with a persistent, fine mousse. The nose shows chalky minerality, wet flint, lemon zest and acacia blossom, backed by toasted almond and singed-bread autolytic character. High acidity and a bone-dry, chalky finish narrow the origin decisively. Pinot Noir and Meunier were considered, but the absence of red-fruit character or vinous body, combined with crisp green-apple drive and a wholly white floral profile, confirms a pure Chardonnay base. Linear tension and flint minerality point specifically to the Côte des Blancs or Montagne de Reims Blanc de Blancs heartland.

### b) Method of production (8 marks)

Traditional method confirmed by fine, persistent mousse and autolytic complexity — toasted almond, biscuit — indicating extended lees contact in bottle, likely 36 months or more. Light MLF softens the racy acidity without broadening it. No overt oak is detectable, consistent with stainless-steel fermentation. Very low dosage — Brut or Extra Brut — leaves the chalky mineral precision unmasked.

### c) Style, quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Dry, precise, high-acid Blanc de Blancs of very good quality, equivalent to 1er Cru level, retailing around £30–40. Autolytic depth and mineral vivacity suggest 3–5 further years of development. Natural home is specialist independent merchants and fine dining across the UK, Europe, US and Japan, competing with other 1er Cru Côte des Blancs bottlings.

---

## Wine 2 — Spain

### a) Country and variety (10 marks)

Xarel-lo, Macabeo and Parellada — Cava Gran Reserva, Penedès, Spain. Deeper golden colour and a broader, warmer-climate fruit profile distinguish this from Wine 1: mature stone fruit, dried citrus peel and smoky, stony mineral character without Champagne's chalk tension. English sparkling and Crémant de Bourgogne were considered — both show autolytic character and high acidity — but neither delivers the warm, near-oxidative complexity and weight found here. Bone-dry, near-zero dosage and a marked savoury almond note are highly consistent with a long-aged Cava Brut Nature Gran Reserva.

### b) Method of production (8 marks)

Traditional method confirmed by fine, persistent mousse and clear autolytic development — almond, toasted notes. Extended bottle ageing well over 36 months has contributed textural complexity. Brut Nature — zero dosage — leaves the wine completely unmasked, explaining the firm, bone-dry finish. A mild oxidative edge to the mature fruit suggests micro-oxygenation through prolonged ageing, though no overt oak flavour is detectable.

### c) Style, quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality at Gran Reserva level, approaching the Corpinnat benchmark, retailing around €20–30. The savoury, bone-dry complexity targets enthusiasts who find standard Cava too simple, positioning it in specialist retail and fine dining. Export potential is strong in the UK, Germany and the US, though communicating the quality step-up from generic Cava remains the key commercial challenge.

---

## Wine 3 — Italy

### a) Country and variety (10 marks)

Lambrusco di Sorbara, Emilia-Romagna, Italy. Deep ruby-red with vibrant crimson-pink hues and a softer, frothier mousse than Wines 1 and 2 immediately signal a tank-method sparkling red. Fresh red cherry, pomegranate, violet and sour-edged acidity with light tannin are the hallmark of Sorbara specifically. Brachetto d'Acqui was briefly considered — it also shows red colour and bubbles — but Brachetto is fragrant, low-alcohol and sweetly confected, whereas this wine is dry to off-dry, savoury and has a tangy tartaric bite inconsistent with that variety.

### b) Method of production (8 marks)

The soft, frothy mousse confirms Charmat (tank) method. Fermentation in pressurised autoclave preserves the primary red-cherry and violet freshness that defines this style; extended lees contact in bottle would suppress those aromatics entirely. Light tannin suggests brief, controlled skin contact.

### c) Style, quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good quality at DOC level, retailing around €12–18. The dry, savoury style targets food-oriented markets — Italian domestic trade alongside charcuterie and parmesan — and export to the UK, US and Germany, where lighter sparkling wines with tannic grip are trending. Overcoming the perception of Lambrusco as cheap, sweet fizz requires trade education focused on the Sorbara sub-appellation.

---

## Wine 4 — Germany

### a) Country and variety (10 marks)

Riesling, Germany — Pfalz Sekt. Pale lemon with green tints and a fine, persistent mousse. The nose delivers ripe apple, pear, lemon and jasmine alongside a bread-dough autolytic note and a distinctive stony, enamel-mineral quality that immediately identifies Riesling rather than Chardonnay. The off-dry palate, with residual sweetness balanced by high acidity, separates this from Wines 1 and 5. Austrian Sekt from Grüner Veltliner was briefly considered but lacks the peach and pear fruit depth; Champagne was ruled out by the more overt fruit sweetness and the absence of chalky minerality. The additional richness and body point to the Pfalz over the Mosel.

### b) Method of production (8 marks)

Traditional method confirmed by fine, sustained mousse and autolytic complexity — brioche, baked biscuit — suggesting 30-plus months on lees. A slightly rounder mid-palate than pure stainless-steel handling would yield suggests partial fermentation in large-format oak. The off-dry dosage is calibrated to balance Riesling's naturally high acidity — a deliberate contrast to the zero-dosage approach of Wine 2.

### c) Style, quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good quality at Sekt b.A. level from a classified Pfalz estate, retailing around €25–35. The off-dry, autolytically complex profile offers a genuine point of difference to dry Champagne-style wines. The core market is the German domestic trade, where estate Sekt premiumisation is an active trend, with secondary export to Scandinavian monopolies and the US.

---

## Wine 5 — England

### a) Country and variety (10 marks)

Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier — English sparkling wine, Kent. Fine, persistent mousse; pale gold. The nose shows green apple, lemon zest, white peach, light brioche and a pronounced saline, fleur-de-sel minerality. Very high acidity — marginally higher than Wine 1 — with a bone-dry, lean finish. The direct comparison with Wine 1 is the critical discriminator: both share a Champagne-method skeleton and Chardonnay-driven character, but this wine shows less autolytic development, more restrained fruit ripeness and a distinctive saline, Atlantic mineral quality absent in the French example. A young Blanc de Blancs Champagne was the most credible alternative, ruled out by the slightly greener fruit and that particular saline mineral expression.

### b) Method of production (8 marks)

Traditional method confirmed by fine, persistent mousse and biscuit autolytic notes. Chardonnay dominance with Pinot Noir adding structure is consistent with a Kent single-estate approach and 24–36 months on lees. Stainless-steel fermentation preserves primary citrus and orchard fruit clarity. Brut dosage adds roundness while retaining the high natural acidity characteristic of the English climate.

### c) Style, quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality for English sparkling wine, retailing around £35–50, directly challenging lower-tier Champagne. The saline mineral precision and pure fruit clarity give this wine a distinctive identity beyond simple Champagne imitation. Positioned through specialist merchants and premium restaurants domestically, with growing export to the US, Japan and Scandinavia. Small production volumes remain the principal constraint on global distribution.

---

## Wine 6 — Australia

### a) Country and variety (10 marks)

Shiraz — sparkling red, Victoria, Australia. Deep ruby-red with vivid crimson hues; full-bodied and medium-sweet, with generous warmth on the palate. The nose delivers Christmas spice, crushed mulberries, blackberry compote, mocha and violet — immediately recognisable as Sparkling Shiraz. Sparkling Cabernet from South Africa was briefly considered but lacks the specific combination of dark berry compote, mocha and the characteristic Shiraz pepper note. The warmth and concentration are consistent with Great Western or Grampians, Victoria, rather than Barossa, which would show even greater weight and more extracted tannin.

### b) Method of production (8 marks)

Fine mousse on a wine of this depth and sweetness indicates traditional method, with a generous dosage incorporating sweet Liqueur Muscat material — a defining feature of the Great Western tradition that imparts characteristic caramelised, fruit-cake richness. Deep colour and concentration suggest extended cold-soak maceration before pressing. Integration of spirit warmth and fruit suggests some bottle age prior to release.

### c) Style, quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Medium-sweet, full-bodied sparkling red of very good quality within its category, retailing around A$40–60. This style has no direct international competitor, which is simultaneously its greatest commercial strength and its biggest challenge: consumers unfamiliar with the combination of tannin, sweetness and bubbles can find it disconcerting. The primary market is Australian domestic, where it is a celebrated festive wine, with export to enthusiasts in the UK and US through fine-dining and premium bottle-shop channels.

Riesling was considered but eliminated — it would show lime, petrol, and a leaner, more taut structure at lower alcohol. The weight and intensity sit above Monbazillac or Barsac.

**Conclusion: Sémillon-dominant blend, Sauternes, Bordeaux, France.**

### b) Sweetness mechanism (9 marks)

Sweetness is achieved through *Botrytis cinerea*, which dehydrates the grape on the vine, concentrating sugars, glycerol, and botrytis-specific compounds. The sensory evidence is decisive: deep gold colour, beeswax and saffron overtones, marmalade and dried-apricot concentration, and a luscious but never cloying texture. The vibrant acidity — amplified alongside sugar as water is lost — confirms botrytis rather than simple late harvest, which would deliver sweetness without this acid precision.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Outstanding quality, consistent with Premier Cru Classé level; retails around £80–120 per 375ml through independent specialists, fine-dining on-trade, and auction allocation lists. The UK, USA, and Japan are the key export markets, where collectors remain loyal despite mid-market decline in sweet wine demand.

---

## Wine 2 — Germany

### a) Grape variety and region (8 marks)

Pale gold, barely warming the throat (~8% apparent alcohol), with electric acidity, fresh lime, slate-driven minerality, and an emerging petrol note — this is Riesling. Chenin Blanc was considered but eliminated: it would be fuller-bodied with quince rather than lime aromatics. Muscat was ruled out by the absence of grapey florality. The very low alcohol, flinty minerality, and precise acid/sugar interplay are the Mosel's calling card; the honey and dried-apricot depth alongside the fresh lime suggest botrytis influence rather than simple Spätlese ripeness.

**Conclusion: Riesling, Mosel, Germany. Auslese.**

### b) Sweetness mechanism (9 marks)

Selectively harvested botrytis-affected and over-ripe grapes are fermented and the process arrested — by chilling or sterile filtration — preserving high residual sugar at low alcohol. The evidence for botrytis over simple late harvest: honey and beeswax alongside fresh lime, luscious sweetness offset by high acidity rather than a flat ripe-sweet character. The very low alcohol confirms fermentation halted well short of completion.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good to outstanding; equivalent to Auslese Grosse Lage, retailing around €40–80 per 375ml. The purity of fruit and impeccable acid/sugar tension mark this well above basic Auslese production. Primary markets are Germany domestically, UK and US fine-wine specialists, and East Asian markets where Mosel Riesling commands strong premiums.

---

## Wine 3 — Spain

### a) Grape variety and region (8 marks)

Dark mahogany with an iodine rim and very high viscosity. The pronounced nose delivers elderflower, orange peel, dried fig, raisin, walnut, rancio, and mocha alongside a warm spirit presence. Fortified Muscat from southern France (Beaumes-de-Venise) was considered but eliminated: it would not develop rancio or walnut, and the spirit integration here is far more complete. The mahogany depth, rancio complexity, and orange-led dried fruit confirm extended oxidative ageing in the Jerez tradition.

**Conclusion: Moscatel (Muscat of Alexandria), Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, Spain.**

### b) Sweetness mechanism (9 marks)

Sweetness derives from *apasamiento* — sun-drying of Moscatel grapes to concentrate sugars — followed by fortification to arrest fermentation. The raisin, dried fig, and prune character points to dried-grape concentration, not botrytis (which would show honey, beeswax, and saffron). The walnut, rancio, and dark caramel complexity reflects subsequent oxidative ageing in partially filled casks; the fully integrated spirit warmth confirms fortification rather than late harvest.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Outstanding for the style; equivalent to a premium NV solera bottling, retailing around £15–25 per half bottle through specialist merchants and Spanish restaurant on-trade. Export focus on the UK, where Sherry premiumisation is advancing, plus the US and Scandinavia via state monopolies.

---

## Wine 4 — Canada

### a) Grape variety and region (8 marks)

Gold, viscous, with slow tears. The nose is pronounced: peach conserve, apricot jam, candied pineapple, crème brûlée, and orange blossom with subtle toasted oak. Palate shows luscious sweetness, high vibrant acidity, and very low apparent warmth (~7%) — the structural signature that separates this from a botrytised Sauternes. Vidal was the main alternative; it would show more tropical mango and slightly more phenolic grip. The peach-and-pineapple profile with rounded texture and integrated oak points instead to Chardonnay grown in a cold continental climate.

**Conclusion: Chardonnay Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada.**

### b) Sweetness mechanism (9 marks)

Grapes are left on the vine until harvested frozen (−8°C or below); pressing while frozen retains water as ice crystals so only concentrated sugar-rich juice runs free. In the glass: intense peach-preserve concentration and very high residual sugar lifted by vibrant acidity — the sensory hallmark of freeze-concentration. Botrytis is ruled out by the absence of saffron or fungal notes; passito by the absence of raisin or fig. Low alcohol confirms the must was too sweet to ferment to dryness.

### c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Outstanding; equivalent to a VQA single-vineyard Icewine, retailing around CAD 80–120 per 200ml. The acid/sugar tension and subtle oak integration mark a top-tier Niagara producer. Canada and Japan are the primary markets — Canadian Icewine has an exceptionally loyal following in Japan and South Korea as a luxury gift product — with UK specialist on-trade offering growth potential.
