modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — a) Region and grape variety (8 marks)

Deep gold, viscous, with pronounced honeyed apricot, beeswax, marmalade and saffron: a botrytis-affected sweet wine. Apparent alcohol 13–14%, rich glycerol texture and candied citrus/lanolin complexity narrow this to Sauternes, predominantly Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc lifting the citrus and a little Muscadelle. Barsac was weighed but the weight and body are more typical of Sauternes proper; the concentration and structured finish suggest Premier Cru Classé level.

## Wine 1 — b) Mechanism and winemaking (9 marks)

Sweetness comes from noble rot, concentrating sugars, acids and glycerol and introducing the saffron and marmalade notes. Purity and concentration indicate multiple selective picking passes (*tries successives*). Fermentation in barrique — integrated vanilla and spice — was arrested naturally by high sugar; eighteen to twenty-four months in wood accounts for the seamless oak and emerging tertiary character.

## Wine 1 — c) Style, quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Opulent, richly sweet, with excellent balancing acidity. Outstanding quality consistent with Premier Cru Classé Sauternes, around £60–90 per half bottle. Fine dining on-trade and premium independents; export appeal in the UK, US, Japan and Hong Kong.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Region and grape variety (8 marks)

Pale straw-lemon, low apparent alcohol (7–8%), piercing lime and green apple acidity, developing petrol and slate: Riesling. The malic-tinged acidity and absence of warmth eliminate Muscat, Chenin Blanc and Gewurztraminer. The slate-mineral character and knife-edge sweet/acid tension, rather than the broader fruit of the Nahe or Rheingau, anchor this in the Mosel. Sweetness weight suggests Spätlese — beyond Kabinett's delicacy, short of Auslese's honeyed richness.

## Wine 2 — b) Mechanism and winemaking (9 marks)

Selective late harvest of partially botrytis-affected fruit concentrated the sugars naturally. Fermentation in stainless steel — pristine fruit, no oak — was arrested by chilling and sulfur, leaving roughly 60–90 g/L residual sugar. Malolactic conversion was deliberately avoided; the racy malic acidity that carries the style is intact.

## Wine 2 — c) Style, quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Delicate and off-dry, the antithesis of Wine 1's opulence, with laser acid definition. Very good quality at Spätlese Einzellage level, £18–25. Strong in Germany, UK specialist merchants and Asian-cuisine restaurants; the low alcohol is a by-the-glass opportunity but the Prädikat system remains a barrier to unfamiliar consumers.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Region and grape variety (8 marks)

Deep amber-brown, viscous, with roasted cashew, dried fig, candied orange peel and oxidative nuttiness over a tart finish. The oxidative character eliminates botrytis wines and Icewine; medium-high alcohol without spirit heat rules out fortification, so PX Sherry is out. Tokaji is excluded by the absence of botrytis apricot. This is a passito wine: dried citrus peel, nuts and a celery-like undertone point to Trebbiano Toscano and/or Malvasia, consistent with Vin Santo del Chianti Classico.

## Wine 3 — b) Mechanism and winemaking (9 marks)

Sweetness derives from *appassimento* — months of drying on racks — concentrating sugar by evaporation, hence raisin and fig rather than saffron and honey. Slow fermentation in sealed *caratelli* under oxidative conditions creates the rancio, nutty profile; six to ten years in cask explains the deep amber and tertiary complexity. Fermentation stopped naturally as alcohol rose against high sugar.

## Wine 3 — c) Style, quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Richly oxidative and complex, firmly in the dried-grape tradition. Outstanding quality for Vin Santo del Chianti Classico, £40–60 per 375ml. Consumer unfamiliarity is the key challenge; best sold through Italian specialist importers, fine dining and wine clubs in the US, UK and Scandinavia.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Region and grape variety (8 marks)

Gold, viscous, with dried apricot, peach conserve, beeswax and an emerging petrol note: ripe Riesling. Apparent warmth is closer to Wine 2 than Wine 1, indicating late harvest rather than a fully botrytised style. Stone-fruit richness, ginger and glycerol texture suggest a warmer, drier ripening context than the Mosel's stony precision, so a New World cool climate — botrytis-inflected richness with high sugar/acid tension fits Central Otago and its high-altitude diurnal shift. Clare Valley was considered but its late-harvest style is typically drier and lacks this glycerol richness.

## Wine 4 — b) Mechanism and winemaking (9 marks)

Late harvest with partial botrytis — honeycomb alongside citrus purity — with fermentation arrested by chilling and sulfur. Textural weight without overt oak suggests older or neutral vessels and some lees contact. Malolactic conversion was avoided; the malic freshness is structurally central and separates this from Wine 3's rounder oxidative texture.

## Wine 4 — c) Style, quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Concentrated yet fresh, sitting between Wine 2's delicacy and Wine 1's weight. Very good quality at premium late-harvest tier, NZ$45–65 per 375ml. Premium independents and fine dining in New Zealand and Australia, with growing export to the UK, US and Asia; low awareness of Central Otago as a sweet wine source is the main obstacle.

---

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — a) Grape variety and region (8 marks)

Tawny colour, high viscosity, and aromas of preserved orange peel, dried fruits, caramel, and spiced cake point to an oxidatively aged fortified wine. Spirit warmth feels around 16%, below typical Port levels; the amber-tawny hue rather than deeper mahogany suggests mixed white and dark-skinned varieties. Sweet orange-peel and aromatic spiced notes combined with this mixed varietal character point to a Grenache-dominated Rivesaltes Ambré from Roussillon, France — a VDN using Grenache Blanc, Grenache Noir, and Macabeu. Tawny Port was eliminated on the amber rather than deep-red oxidative core, and the aromatic sweetness reads as Midi candied fruit rather than the rancio richness of aged Tawny.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and production (9 marks)

Sweet, oxidatively aged VDN with generous dried-fruit concentration and persistent warmth. Mutage with neutral grape spirit arrests fermentation, preserving natural grape sugars well above 50 g/L. Extended ageing in old oak demi-muids or heat-exposed bonbonnes develops the amber colour and orange-peel caramel notes characteristic of the Ambré designation, with a deliberate rancio edge through multi-year oxidative exposure.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good quality, above basic VDN level; equivalent to a well-aged single-vintage expression retailing around €20–30. The primary opportunity is UK and Northern European specialist off-trade seeking alternatives to Tawny Port. The challenge is low consumer awareness — many shoppers cannot distinguish Ambré from Tuilé. Ready to drink now; will hold a further decade without meaningful improvement.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Grape variety and region (8 marks)

Deep tawny with high viscosity; overwhelming concentration of raisin, fig, toffee, dark chocolate, and roasted coffee, with a delicate Muscat blossom note threading through. That floral signature is diagnostic: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains retains grape-derived terpenes even through heavy oxidative fortification. Rutherglen Muscat was the immediate reference, but spirit warmth feels slightly lighter and viscosity marginally lower than a Classic or Grand tier; the floral note is more precise and less syrupy. This combination — oxidatively fortified Muscat with excellent concentration, terpene lift, and spirit warmth at approximately 17% — is consistent with a boutique Liqueur Muscat, most plausibly from New Zealand, where Waiheke Island produces small quantities in this style.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and production (9 marks)

Non-vintage oxidatively aged fortified sweet wine. Fermentation is arrested with grape spirit, preserving around 150–200 g/L residual sugar. Ageing in small seasoned casks with a solera-like blending system concentrates the wine and develops toffee, caramel, and roasted coffee character while the terpene backbone of Muscat survives intact.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Outstanding quality, comparable to a Classic Rutherglen Muscat in ambition. Retailing at approximately NZ$60–80 per half-bottle, the natural audience is premium specialist retailers and fine-dining on-trade in Australasia, with niche UK and US importers. Very small production limits export reach; the principal challenge is that Liqueur Muscat carries almost no consumer recognition outside Australia and New Zealand. Drink now; will hold 10+ years without further development.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Grape variety and region (8 marks)

Virtually opaque mahogany-black with syrup-like viscosity. Intensely sweet nose: dates, dried figs, raisined plums, roasted coffee, dark chocolate, and orange rind, with a balsamic lift. Sweetness exceeds 300 g/L to judge from viscosity and persistence, yet a citrus-acid spine and bitter coffee finish prevent cloying. This is the defining signature of Pedro Ximénez — no other variety produces near-black opacity from sun-drying, this sugar level, and the dark-chocolate bitterness that balances the sweetness. Both Jerez and Montilla-Moriles produce PX; the relatively lower spirit warmth and silky elegance point to Montilla-Moriles, Córdoba, Spain, where extreme grape sugars allow fortification at a lower addition rate.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and production (9 marks)

Grapes are sun-dried (*soleo*) on esparto mats for 10–15 days before pressing. The must is fortified almost immediately, preserving extreme residual sugar. Subsequent ageing in American oak butts under fully oxidative conditions — no flor — develops balsamic and roasted coffee notes; seamless texture and fully integrated spirit confirm decades of oxidative maturation at Gran Reserva level.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Exceptional quality — an iconic-level PX Gran Reserva, equivalent in ambition to a VORS-tier Jerez expression. The balance between extreme sweetness and citrus-acid freshness is the hallmark of the highest-order ageing programme. Retail value approximately £60–80 per half-bottle; route to market is fine-wine specialists and Michelin-starred restaurant lists in the UK, US, and Scandinavia. The challenge is PX's niche image as a sweetening agent rather than a standalone wine of genuine complexity. Drink now with pleasure; will hold 15–20 more years.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 2

## Wine 1 — a) Grape variety and region of origin (8 marks)

Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, Southern Rhône. Pronounced orange blossom and fresh grape over a viscous golden appearance points to a Muscat vin doux naturel. The diagnostic is aromatic purity: no dried fruit or rancio, which rules out Muscat de Rivesaltes and Rutherglen. The refinement of the floral register argues Petits Grains over Muscat of Alexandria, which is coarser and more musky. The lifted lavender/herbal lift alongside candied citrus is the Beaumes-de-Venise typicity cue.

## Wine 1 — b) Method of production (9 marks)

*Mutage* on the must: grape spirit arrests fermentation, leaving roughly 110–120 g/L sugar. The intact grapey esters indicate early fortification, before they are metabolised; the clean spirit entry indicates well-rectified spirit at close to the 5% minimum addition. No vanilla or toast — stainless steel throughout, protecting primary character, with cool fermentation preserving the herbal top note.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good; sweetness, acidity and spirit are well-integrated. Around £18–22 per half-bottle through UK independents and fine-dining lists, where it earns its place as a by-the-glass dessert pour. Export strength in Northern Europe and Japan, but the category remains niche.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Grape variety and region of origin (8 marks)

Touriga Nacional-led blend, 10 Year Old Tawny Port, Douro. The amber-orange colour with greenish rim excludes Ruby and LBV. Prune, walnut, coffee and caramelised orange place it in the oxidative family; the residual red-fruit sweetness and perceived spirit warmth well above 18% separate it from Amontillado, and the absence of volatile, curry-like lift from Madeira. Development is moderate — beyond a young Tawny, short of the mahogany depth and intense rancio of a 20 Year Old. Peppery spice, fine acidity and a retained dark-plum backbone indicate Touriga Nacional/Franca rather than a Grenache-based Roussillon VDN, which would not hold that structure.

## Wine 2 — b) Method of production (9 marks)

Brief, high-extraction fermentation in *lagares* or autovinificators, arrested by neutral spirit — the same *mutage* logic as Wine 1, but on a tannic red base. Ageing follows in seasoned pipes and *toneis* with deliberate ullage: oxygen polymerises tannin to that silky texture, drives colour to tawny and builds the nutty, caramelised layer. Multi-vintage blending delivers the house style consistency the age indication requires.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good, at the upper end of its tier; the rancio complexity reflects careful cask selection. Roughly £30–40 (50cl) in the UK, sold through premium specialist off-trade and upscale on-trade, against other single-quinta 10 Year Olds. Traction in the UK, Benelux, Scandinavia and the US fine-wine trade.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Grape variety and region of origin (8 marks)

Shiraz, sparkling red, South Australia — likely a Barossa/Grampians blend. Opaque ruby-purple with staining legs excludes every other sparkling category. Dark plum, violet and warm pepper over a full body confirm Shiraz; sparkling Pinot Noir lacks the colour, Malbec the peppery spice. Fine persistent mousse with a biscuit undertone plus generous warmth identifies the Australian cross-regional style.

## Wine 3 — b) Method of production (9 marks)

Traditional method: the fine bead and autolytic note rule out tank, which gives a coarser mousse and no aged character. Extended skin contact on the base wine supplies colour and tannin, then several years on lees in bottle. Dosage appears low — sweetness derives from fruit ripeness, not liqueur. Warm ripe Barossa fruit gives the flesh; the cooler Grampians component supplies the aromatic lift and acid line that stop it turning jammy.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and commercial position (8 marks)

Very good — top of its category, show-reserve tier, around AUD 60–80 / £35–45 exported. The domestic market drives it, where sparkling Shiraz has a fixed festive occasion; abroad it sells as a curio through specialist merchants in the UK, US and Scandinavia. Its commercial problem is that no consumer frame exists for a premium red sparkling wine outside Australia — that same uniqueness is its only real defence, since it competes against nothing.

## Wine 2 — b) Method of Production (9 marks)

Tank method: secondary fermentation in sealed autoclave retains primary aromatics and prevents autolysis. Cool fermentation (~15–18°C) preserves the pear and floral profile. Brief lees contact in tank, then isobaric filtration and bottling. Dosage to Brut, roughly 7–12 g/L.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, Question 1 (three sparkling wines, three countries)

## a) Compare and contrast the methods of production (3 × 8 marks)

All three show a fine, persistent bead and evident autolytic character, so all three underwent a second fermentation in bottle. The contrast therefore lies in the regime, not the route.

**Wine 1** — pure apple and quince with no phenolic bitterness points to direct pressing of whole bunches and use of the first press fractions only. The searing, malic-dominated acid at modest warmth (~12%) indicates a cool stainless-steel ferment with malolactic blocked to preserve that acid line. Autolysis is faint — bread dough at most — so lees contact was short, in the order of 9–12 months on tirage. A dosage around 8–10 g/L is needed to carry the acidity.

**Wine 2** — pastry, hazelnut and a silky, almost creamy bead point to far longer tirage contact, four to five years, i.e. a Riserva-length regime. No vanilla or toast, so an unoaked stainless ferment; the taut acid line suggests malolactic was at most partial. Homogeneous fruit and no oxidative reserve-wine note indicate a single-vintage base.

**Wine 3** — baked apple, lemon curd and a broader, rounder mid-palate indicate a barrel-fermented fraction and fuller malolactic, with roughly two years on lees before disgorgement and dosage near 8 g/L.

## b) Region of origin and grape variety (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Chenin Blanc, Vouvray Mousseux, Loire.** Quince, beeswax, wet wool and a chalky, pithy finish over searing acid at low perceived alcohol. Crémant de Loire was the leading alternative, but this shows more quince depth and tuffeau grip than a multi-regional blend. Cava is ruled out (no earthy, bitter-almond Xarel-lo), Champagne too (the fruit is apple-wax, not citrus-chalk).

**Wine 2 — Chardonnay, Trento DOC Riserva.** A Blanc de Blancs: green apple, white blossom, hazelnut, saline close. The tension of fully ripe fruit held by a firm high acid line at modest weight reads as altitude rather than latitude — alpine Trentino, not Franciacorta, which would be broader and softer. Champagne eliminated: no chalk-gunflint spine, and the almond-saline edge is Italian.

**Wine 3 — Chardonnay, North Coast, California.** Riper yellow apple and lemon curd, generous warmth, medium-plus body, acidity high but rounded rather than malic — cool coastal California, a Carneros/Anderson Valley sourcing. English sparkling and Tasmania were considered; both would give greener fruit and a leaner, sharper line.

## c) Style, quality and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — dry, brisk aperitif style, drink now. Good quality at AOC Vouvray Mousseux level; €12–16 through cellar door and independents, competing with Crémant de Loire and undercutting NV Champagne for drinkers wanting bone-dry, mineral fizz.

**Wine 2** — restrained, long-aged, gastronomic. Outstanding, at the top of Trento DOC Riserva; around €55 on Italian and export fine-dining lists (US, Japan), a genuine alternative to vintage Champagne.

**Wine 3** — polished, creamy, but seriously built. Very good, estate-flagship tier; about $45 in US premium off-trade and Canadian monopolies, positioned squarely against Champagne NV on price and domestic loyalty.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, fortified flight (Wines 1–3)

## Wine 1

**a) Origin — France, Charentes (Pineau des Charentes).** Medium amber, moderate viscosity, and a nose of quince, dried apricot and grapey confit over a light walnut edge. Sweetness is medium-rich only (~120–140 g/L), acidity moderate, and the spirit reads as gentle, clean warmth around 17% — a refined brandy character rather than neutral alcohol. Crucially there are no fermentative esters and no vinous depth: the sugar tastes like unfermented must, which points to a mistelle. Muscat de Rivesaltes was the main alternative but the fruit is orchard and quince, not terpene and orange-blossom; a young Tawny is ruled out by colour and the absence of red fruit. The amber tone and faint rancio indicate roughly a decade in cask.

**b) Style and winemaking.** A sweet, lightly oxidative aperitif style. Fresh must was fortified before fermentation began with young Cognac eau-de-vie, arresting sugar at source; long ageing in old, large oak with modest ullage delivered the amber colour and nutty overlay. No new wood, no lees influence.

**c) Quality and commercial position.** Good quality at the Vieux / ten-year tier — clearly above one-year entry Pineau, short of Extra Vieux complexity. Around €25–30, sold through French domestic on-trade and independent specialists as an aperitif or foie-gras wine; competes with young Tawny and VDN. Challenge: negligible brand recognition in export markets.

## Wine 2

**a) Origin — Australia, Rutherglen, north-east Victoria.** Deep mahogany with an olive rim and staining tears; pronounced raisin, malt, toffee, cold tea and coffee, yet an unmistakable grapey Muscat lift beneath the rancio. Spirit is generous, ~18%, sugar very high (~300 g/L). An old Tawny would show more nut and less overt Muscat; Moscatel de Setúbal is lighter and less baked. That kiln-hot maturation signature points to inland Victoria.

**b) Style and winemaking.** Brown Muscat picked semi-raisined, brief skin contact, fortified early at high sugar, then multi-vintage blending in very old casks stored in hot sheds — deliberate heat-accelerated oxidation, not cellar-cool ageing.

**c) Quality and commercial position.** Very good, Grand tier (average age ~11–19 years). At this sugar it ought to cloy; that it does not is the argument for Grand over Classic — extended cask evaporation has concentrated acidity in step with sugar, giving lift a younger blend lacks. Around £40/500ml; specialist merchants and dessert-wine lists in the UK, US and Canada.

## Wine 3

**a) Origin — Spain, Jerez.** Opaque black-brown, syrupy, staining; molasses, fig, prune, liquorice and espresso; sugar extreme (400+ g/L), acidity low, spirit near-invisible at ~17%. This is sun-dried fruit, not botrytis. Montilla-Moriles was seriously considered, but the cask-derived rancio and saline lift favour Jerez. Malmsey Madeira is excluded — no searing acid, no volatile edge.

**b) Style and winemaking.** Pedro Ximénez raisined on mats (*asoleo*), pressed to a hugely sugary must, fermentation arrested almost immediately by fortification, then criaderas y solera blending in old butts.

**c) Quality and commercial position.** Very good; solera age tastes around 8–12 years — richer than entry PX, below VOS/VORS. Around £20/500ml, premium supermarket and specialist off-trade.

# Mock answer — 2019 Paper 3 Question 4

## Wine 1

**a) Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Jerez, Spain — Manzanilla (Pasada leaning).** Pale gold with low viscosity, a bone-dry palate, and a warming but not aggressive spirit note (~15%) put this in the biologically aged Sherry family immediately. The pronounced sourdough, roasted almond and green-olive brine are flor-derived, not oak-derived. Fino from Jerez de la Frontera was the main alternative, but the insistent sea-spray salinity, chamomile and iodine on the back palate point to the maritime bodegas of Sanlúcar, where a thicker year-round veil gives exactly this delicacy. Amontillado is ruled out: the colour is gold, not amber, and flor character still dominates the light nutty oxidative depth rather than the reverse.

**b)** Palomino picked at modest ripeness, free-run and first press fractions only, fermented out fully dry, then fortified with grape spirit to around 15% — precisely the level that permits *flor* rather than killing it. Oxidation was managed **biologically**: butts filled to roughly five-sixths, left unbunged so the veil can respire, and refreshed through criaderas y solera so young wine continually feeds the yeast. The trace of acetaldehyde and the light hazelnut suggest the veil has thinned in the oldest scales, admitting a little air. Minimal SO₂, cold stabilisation, tight filtration and inert-gas bottling to protect the fragile aromatics.

**c)** Bone-dry, low-alcohol-by-fortified-standards aperitif style. Very good quality for the biological category, well above a generic supermarket Fino, retailing around £12–15. Off-trade specialists and tapas-driven on-trade by the glass; UK, Netherlands and Spain domestically. Its commercial challenge is fragility — it needs half bottles, fast stock rotation and staff who chill it.

## Wine 2

**a) Côtes du Jura, France — Savagnin, topped-up (ouillé).** No spirit heat at all, so unfortified; the weight and warmth read around 13%. High, tense acidity, medium body and pale gold with only a *whisper* of oxidative hazelnut. That whisper is the clue: Vin Jaune was considered and rejected, because sous-voile ageing would deliver penetrating curry, walnut and aldehyde, not Meyer lemon and white flowers. Jura Chardonnay was the other candidate, but the fresh-almond bitterness, lime blossom and saline grip on a taut frame are Savagnin's signature.

**b)** Hand-harvested, gently whole-bunch pressed given the absence of phenolic bitterness; cool fermentation with indigenous yeast in older barrels, malolactic largely avoided to preserve that piercing malic line. Here oxidation was **deliberately suppressed**: ageing 12–18 months in old, neutral demi-muids kept scrupulously topped up — the *ouillé* choice — with light lees contact for the brioche note. Low-oxygen racking and modest SO₂ at bottling.

**c)** A precise, mineral, unoxidised style made to show terroir rather than tradition. Very good quality, equivalent to a strong Village Meursault; around £28–35. Independent specialists and sommelier lists; strong in Nordics, New York and Tokyo, where it competes with premium Chablis 1er Cru.

## Wine 3

**a) Madeira, Portugal — Sercial, 10 Year Old.** Pale tawny, dry, medium-plus body and clear spirit warmth (~19%), with searing acidity, walnut, burnt orange peel, resin, ginger and old wood. That combination of high volatile lift and *tartaric* rather than flor-derived acidity separates it from Palo Cortado, which was the plausible alternative. Dryness plus the pale tawny hue and lemon-citrus persistence indicate Sercial rather than Verdelho or Bual.

**b)** Fermented right out to near-zero sugar *before* fortification to around 19% — the reason it finishes so dry. Oxidation was then **applied as a tool**: long *canteiro* ageing in the warm lofts in partially ullaged casks, slow controlled heat and air producing the resinous, nutty rancio, then blending to an average of at least ten years. Going under the skin: for the wine to retain medium-plus body at this acid level after a decade of evaporative concentration, the base must have come from the coolest, highest plantings — lesser Sercial fermented dry then heat-aged would read attenuated and hollow.

**c)** Uncompromising, austere aperitif style. Outstanding for the 10 Year Old tier, around £38–45; specialist retail and fine-dining by the glass — its virtual indestructibility once opened is its strongest commercial argument.

## Wine 4

**a) Barossa Valley, South Australia — Shiraz-based vintage-dated tawny.** Deep tawny, high viscosity, spirit warmth around 19–20%, with sultana, toffee, salted caramel, mahogany, varnish and clove. A Douro Colheita was my first instinct, but Portugal is already taken by Wine 3, and the overtly roasted, rum-and-crème-brûlée profile is warmer and less elegantly rancio than Douro. Rutherglen Muscat is excluded — no grapey, rose-petal Muscat lift.

**b)** Fermented essentially to dryness on skins before fortification with high-strength grape spirit, so the sweet impression is textural — glycerol and dried fruit — not sugar. Oxidation was then **maximised**: decades in small, ullaged old oak in hot Barossa sheds, evaporative concentration and warm-cycle oxidation driving the varnish, mahogany and fruitcake.

**c)** A concentrated, drink-now-and-forever collectible. Outstanding for Australian fortified, around AUD$90; cellar door, gifting and specialist retail, competing with 20 Year Old Tawny and old Madeira.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, Question 1 (five sweet wines, five countries)

## a) Region of origin and grape variety (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Vouvray, Loire Valley, France; Chenin Blanc.** Mechanism first: gold colour, thick slow tears, honey and quince alongside saffron and lanolin indicate noble rot, but the moderate warmth and medium body (~12%) show a wine that was not fortified and not dried. Chenin is the call — quince paste, beeswax, ginger and that lemon-curd core sit over searing, mouthwatering tartaric acidity that keeps a sweet wine linear rather than fat. Sauternes was weighed and rejected: no Sémillon lanolin-plus-oak vanilla, no barrel toast at all, and the finish is saline and chalky rather than creamy. Riesling is ruled out by the absence of lime and petrol. The tuffeau salinity and faint fresh-walnut oxidative edge narrow to Vouvray, moelleux level, from a traditional cellar.

**Wine 2 — Pantelleria, Sicily, Italy; Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria).** Amber-flushed gold, viscous, with candied orange peel, apricot, mango and papaya over Mediterranean scrub and dried herbs. The grapey, orange-blossom lift is unmistakably Muscat. Generous warmth, ~14.5%, is the discriminator: this is too alcoholic for botrytis or freezing and shows no spirit heat, so the sugar came from raisining on the vine and on drying racks. Rutherglen Muscat was considered and eliminated — no rancio, no fortification. The saline, sun-baked herbal signature and complete absence of oak point to island Sicily, Passito di Pantelleria.

**Wine 3 — Wachau, Austria; Riesling, Trockenbeerenauslese.** Deep gold and luscious, yet the wine feels almost weightless — low alcohol, around 7%, with racy acidity slicing the sugar. That alcohol/sugar ratio only comes from massively shrivelled botrytised berries whose must the yeast could not finish. Petrol, white pepper, dried apricot, marmalade and saffron confirm Riesling with noble rot. German TBA was the main alternative; the broader, drier-spiced palate and firmer, more tartaric structure with a nutty oxidative tail read Austrian rather than Mosel.

**Wine 4 — Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada; Vidal, Icewine.** Gold, syrupy, with peach, mango, tangerine, melon and candied citrus — pure, primary, tropical fruit with no botrytis funk, honeyed rot or dried-fruit character. That purity plus low-to-moderate warmth (~9%) and very high sugar signals cryoextraction: frozen berries pressed whole. Eiswein from Germany was the alternative, but the fleshy tropical fruit and slightly broad, non-petrol profile point to Vidal rather than Riesling, hence Canada, and Niagara specifically.

**Wine 5 — Rueda, Spain; Verdejo (with a Sauvignon component).** Straw-yellow, the palest in the flight, indicating a young wine with no rot and no drying. Boxwood, lime, pineapple, fennel-like herbs and a balsamic twist over pear conserve and candied peel; sweet but moderate, ~11%, with high, zesty acidity. Late-harvest, unbotrytised. Loire Coteaux du Layon was excluded on aromatics — this is greener and more pungent. The boxwood-plus-bitter-fennel pairing is Verdejo's signature, placing it in Rueda.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (5 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** A serious moelleux built for the cellar. Successive tries through the vineyard gathered rot-affected and passerillé fruit; whole-bunch pressing gave clean juice, and the phenolic grip suggests slow pressing of shrivelled berries. Fermentation with indigenous yeasts in old demi-muids stalled naturally, leaving high sugar with no new-oak signature; the faint walnut note indicates long ageing under a slightly oxidative regime, no malolactic, minimal sulphur.

**Wine 2.** Two harvests: early-picked fruit fermented to dryness, then sun-dried raisins steeped in that base to extract sugar, colour and aromatics — the amber hue and infused candied-peel intensity betray this maceration. Stainless steel throughout, cool ferment to hold the terpenes, no wood.

**Wine 3.** Berry-by-berry selection of shrivelled botrytised fruit at extreme must weights. A very long, cold, struggling ferment in neutral vessels, arrested by the yeast's own alcohol tolerance meeting osmotic pressure, then chilled, sulphured and filtered to hold the sugar. No oak flavour, but extended cask ageing explains the nutty tail.

**Wine 4.** Netted fruit left to freeze on the vine and harvested at around −10°C, pressed frozen so ice crystals stay behind. Cool, protracted ferment with sugar-tolerant yeast stopped by chilling; the whisper of sweet, smoky spice suggests a small proportion of barrel or oak contact for texture. Sterile filtration at bottling.

**Wine 5.** Late-hanging fruit picked at high sugar, gently pressed, fermented cool in tank to preserve thiol-driven boxwood, then arrested by chilling and filtration to leave sugar in balance with the acid. No wood, no lees weight — freshness is the entire intent.

## c) Quality, maturity, commercial position (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding, at the top of the Vouvray moelleux hierarchy — the equal of a good Sauternes classé at £50–70. Around 6–8 years old; drinking beautifully but will improve a decade and hold 25+, gaining honeyed, mushroomy tertiary depth. Independent specialists and Loire-literate sommeliers; UK, Belgium, Japan.

**Wine 2.** Very good to outstanding for its DOC; around £30 per 50cl. Youthful, three to five years old, at its aromatic peak now, holding eight years while fruit turns to fig. Sold in Italian fine-dining, premium off-trade, US and Germany; the 50cl format and dessert-only occasion are the commercial brake.

**Wine 3.** Outstanding, an authentic TBA — the rarest Prädikat — at £90+ per 37.5cl. Ten years old, fully mature but nowhere near decline; will hold 20–30 years. Auction and collector channels rather than restaurant lists.

**Wine 4.** Good quality VQA Icewine, correct but with a medium-minus, faintly metallic finish that separates it from the top tier; £40 per 37.5cl. Drink now to five years. Duty-free, gifting and Asian export markets — reliant on occasion, not connoisseurship.

**Wine 5.** Very good value late-harvest at £12–15 per half-bottle; a supermarket and by-the-glass proposition for younger sweet-wine drinkers. Drink now to three years, while the thiols last.

Savagnin, Château-Chalon, Jura. The deep gold colour, marked viscosity and pronounced walnut, curry powder and rancio point to prolonged oxidative ageing. No fortification and no solera, unlike Jerez; at least six years under veil before bottling in the 62cl clavelin.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, two wines from the same region

## a) Region and variety (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 2 — Savagnin, Château-Chalon, Jura.** This is the wine that opens the flight. Gold, high viscosity, pronounced toasted walnut, curry-leaf, mushroom, dried resin and searing salinity over a long, dry, high-acid finish. Warmth is generous, around 14.5%, but there is no spirit burn or eau-de-vie lift, so a fortified style is out: Amontillado would show that spirit edge and a leaner frame, and oxidative Rioja blanco would carry vanilla and coconut oak that is absent here. Film-yeast (voile) ageing of an unfortified white in a cool continental climate points to Savagnin in the Jura. The sheer concentration, penetrating sotolon and persistence take it to the top of that hierarchy — Château-Chalon rather than a generic vin jaune. The under-the-skin point: the alcohol has climbed while the acidity has *not* softened, which reads as evaporative concentration under the veil on cold marl slopes, not as harvest ripeness.

**Wine 1 — Savagnin, Côtes du Jura.** Same gold hue, same star-fruit and silex signature, the same taut saline line and very fine phenolics, but only a whisper of oxidation and clear bread-dough/wheat lees character. Alcohol reads moderate, around 13%. Chardonnay, the region's other grape, was weighed and rejected — it would give a broader, creamier, more orchard-and-butter frame, not this incisive star-fruit tension. Savagnin, made *ouillé*.

## b) Method of production (2 × 8 marks)

Wine 1: gentle whole-bunch pressing (the phenolics are notably fine), fermentation and roughly a year in older foudre or barrel kept **topped up**, malolactic largely restrained to hold the acid line, regular lees contact giving the wheat and fresh-bread notes, early bottling to protect primary fruit.

Wine 2: identical fruit sourcing, then the decisive divergence — barrels deliberately **not topped up**, allowing a voile to form. No racking, no topping, minimum six years and three months in old 228-litre casks; sotolon and acetaldehyde accumulate, evaporation concentrates extract and alcohol, and the wine is bottled in the 62cl clavelin.

## c) Quality, maturity, commercial (2 × 7 marks)

Wine 1: very good quality, top domaine-level Côtes du Jura, around €25–30. Drinking well now at three years, will improve two to three more and hold five. Independent specialists and sommelier-driven lists in Paris, London, New York and Tokyo; competes with village white Burgundy for buyers wanting salinity over richness.

Wine 2: outstanding, the appellation benchmark, €90–120 for a half-size bottle. Six years old, only beginning; it will improve fifteen years and hold thirty-plus. A tiny allocation wine for collectors and gastronomy — the challenge is that its oxidative register and clavelin format limit it to the converted.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, sparkling flight

## Wine 1

**a) Champagne, Vallée de la Marne; traditional method, zero dosage.** The fine, persistent bead and the toasted hazelnut/fresh brioche autolysis point immediately to a second fermentation in bottle with long lees contact — three years or more. Origin: high, racy tartaric acidity with a chalky, saline grip and only medium body indicates a cool, marginal, limestone origin at around 12%; English sparkling was the main alternative but that would give greener, sharper malic acid, less mid-palate flesh and almost always a few grams of dosage. Franciacorta is ruled out by the acid line, which is far too taut. The riper pear and white peach alongside the chalk narrow it within Champagne away from the Côte des Blancs towards the Marne.

**b)** Bone dry, austere, vinous rather than fruity, and built for the table. The key decisions read as: gentle whole-bunch pressing (no phenolic edge), a proportion of base wine fermented and held in old oak — the ginger spice and nutty breadth suggest a perpetual reserve rather than a young stainless blend — and the withholding of dosage entirely. **The insight here is that zero dosage is only survivable where the mid-palate is already filled**, and it is the oxidatively-handled reserve component, not sugar, that is doing that work; a lesser house would taste hollow and angular at the same dosage.

**c)** Outstanding quality, well above NV Brut house level and comparable to a grower's flagship or a vintage cuvée; around £55–70 / $75 retail. Independent specialists and sommelier-driven lists, strong in the UK, Japan and the US; the audience is the low-dosage collector, not the celebration buyer.

## Wine 2

**a) Alto Adige, Italy; traditional method blanc de blancs, extended lees ageing.** Same autolytic signature but a very different fruit: chervil, tarragon, aniseed and pomelo alongside mango. Lemon-green colour and high acid at moderate alcohol.

**b)** The tension is diagnostic — genuinely tropical ripeness (mango, passion fruit) held by a taut, linear acid line. That combination is a mountain signature: warm days ripening the fruit, cold nights preserving the acid. Heat alone would have flattened the acidity. Add the savoury, umami lees character and toasted tobacco, and this reads as a long-aged Chardonnay-based blanc de blancs from a co-operative with reductive stainless base wines, no malolactic (the acid is unbroadened), and a low Brut dosage. Trentodoc was weighed and is very close; the herbal-alpine aromatic set tips it slightly further north.

**c)** Very good to outstanding; the top end of an Alto Adige DOC sparkling range, ~€30–40. Sells largely on domestic Italian fine-dining lists and to German-speaking export markets; it is a hard sell blind against Champagne at similar money.

## Wine 3

**a) Vinho Verde, Monção e Melgaço, Portugal; traditional method, vintage-dated brut nature.** Deeper yellow, pronounced mineral intensity, medium(+) body and a persistent, saline-stony finish with no perceptible sugar.

**b)** The colour depth with pronounced aromatics and no reductive protection suggests deliberately minimal sulphur — there is a faint oxidative broadening and a slightly wild edge that a conventionally-protected base wine would not show. Aromatic-varietal sparkling (Alvarinho) rather than the classic Chardonnay/Pinot template: fuller-bodied, more textural, less autolytic. Cava was considered — the earthy Xarel-lo mark is absent — as was Crémant de Loire, ruled out by the lack of Chenin's quince and wax.

**c)** Very good quality, a serious estate espumante at €25–30, punching above its appellation's reputation. Natural-leaning independents and by-the-glass in adventurous restaurants; the challenge is that Vinho Verde reads "cheap and fizzy" to consumers, so this needs hand-selling.

## Wine 4

**a) Napa Valley (Carneros), California; traditional method blanc de blancs.** Toasted biscuit and cream confirm bottle fermentation on lees, but only medium(+) acidity, softer citrus and pear, and a medium finish signal a distinctly warmer growing season than Wine 1.

**b)** Lighter-bodied and gently creamy — partial malolactic and lees stirring have rounded the acid, and the dosage sits at a comfortable Brut level to flatter the fruit. Riper picking than Champagne, shorter lees ageing (perhaps 18–24 months), stainless throughout.

**c)** Good quality, a premium commercial house style at $28–35, the American answer to mainstream NV Brut. Broad off-trade and premium supermarket distribution, hotel and by-the-glass programmes; a volume brand rather than a collector's wine.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, four wines from four countries

## a) Origin, and how production shaped style (4 x 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — France, Languedoc.** Method first: a coarse, frothy bead that collapses within seconds indicates low pressure, around 2–2.5 bar — semi-sparkling, not traditional method. There is no autolytic character at all, only primary redcurrant and wild strawberry with a garrigue lift, so this is a single cool tank fermentation with the CO2 retained under pressure, then chilled, filtered and bottled early. Pale salmon with no bronze suggests direct pressing rather than saignée. Warmth is modest, weight light (~12%), yet the acid line is firm — early picking in a warm Mediterranean climate. Prosecco Rosé was weighed and rejected: no pear/acacia Glera signature and less sugar.

**Wine 2 — Italy, Franciacorta DOCG (Satèn).** The mousse is fine and persistent but noticeably *soft* — creamy rather than driving. Pair that with pronounced brioche, hazelnut and a silky, low-phenolic texture and this is traditional method held deliberately below full pressure. This is the wine's key: a reduced tirage sugar, roughly 4.5 bar instead of 6, is a stylistic decision that removes mousse aggression so the 24–30 months of lees texture carries the palate — only a white-grape cuvée with no Pinot Nero would be built this way. Champagne was considered but the acid is rounder and the fruit riper; Crémant de Bourgogne lacks this lees depth.

**Wine 3 — USA, Carneros, California.** Deeper salmon-copper with real red-fruit weight, but underpinned by high, taut acidity and pronounced brioche/almond autolysis — traditional method, extended lees, from Pinot Noir-dominant fruit. A short skin maceration or blending-in of still red gives the colour. Ripe strawberry generosity at only medium alcohol (~12%) points to a cool, fog-moderated pocket inside a warm state rather than to Champagne, whose rosé would be leaner and chalkier.

**Wine 4 — Australia, Barossa Valley (wood-aged Tawny).** Style first: deep mahogany with an olive rim, viscous legs, and searing spirit warmth (~19–20%) — fortification mid-ferment, then long oxidative maturation in small old oak in a hot store. Rancio, molasses, dried fig, mocha and volatile lift confirm cask ageing, not solera-free bottle age. Tawny Port was the alternative, but the raisined, coffee-toned fruit and lower ferrous edge point to Australian Shiraz/Grenache material; Rutherglen Muscat is excluded — no grapey floral character.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, five sweet wines from five countries

## a) Variety and origin (5 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Petit Manseng, Jurançon (moelleux), South-West France.** Deep gold and thickly viscous, yet the nose is oddly withheld: wet stone, honey, spice, no marmalade or botrytis funk. The palate is genuinely sweet but carried by searing, tartaric acidity, with a saline, spicy grip and only medium body and moderate warmth (~13%). Chenin from Coteaux du Layon was the first alternative, but that shows quince and beeswax with softer, more malic acid. A German Beerenauslese was rejected too: lime/petrol aromatics and far lower perceived alcohol. Sweetness achieved without noble-rot aromatics, plus that mineral-saline signature and Pyrenean acid line, points to Petit Manseng dried on the vine — Jurançon.

**Wine 2 — Garganega, Recioto di Soave Classico, Veneto, Italy.** Deep golden with amber edges, viscous; peach, apricot and lychee over a warm, smooth, full-bodied palate that finishes with a distinct almond bitterness and saline twist. Acidity only medium-plus, alcohol modest for the sugar. Moscato was considered — but there is no grapey terpene lift; Vin Santo was too, and ruled out by the absence of nutty oxidative rancio. Ripe-fruit sweetness plus that bitter-almond finish and Italian salinity is Garganega, dried, from the Soave Classico hills.

**Wine 3 — Sémillon, botrytised, New Zealand (Waiheke/Hawke's Bay).** Gold, viscous, pronounced nose of honeyed apricot, dried mango, marmalade, beeswax and candied ginger — textbook noble rot — with light toast and lanolin. High acid, full body, and strikingly low alcohol warmth (~10%), so sugar is high. Sauternes was the obvious call but the fruit is too tropical-exuberant, oak too discreet, and the alcohol too low; Tokaji Aszú would bring orange-peel and firmer structure. Lanolin plus botrytis and this fruit spectrum reads Sémillon from a maritime New World climate — New Zealand.

**Wine 4 — Verdelho, late harvest, Alentejo, Portugal.** Gold, only medium viscosity; apricot, pear, citrus and a stony edge at medium-plus intensity. Medium-sweet rather than sweet, medium-plus acid, light body, low alcohol warmth. The lightest wine of the flight, so neither botrytis nor appassimento. Airén/Moscatel-based Spanish styles lack this citrus-mineral cut; Alsace Vendange Tardive would be broader and higher in alcohol. Firm citrus-stone character with modest weight points to Verdelho picked late in southern Portugal — Alentejo.

**Wine 5 — Torrontés, late harvest, Calchaquí Valley (Cafayate), Argentina.** Pronounced rose petal, jasmine, orange blossom, lychee and candied citrus — an intensely terpene-driven aromatic. Medium-sweet, medium-plus acid, low alcohol warmth, no oak. Gewurztraminer was the closest alternative, but this has none of that variety's oily, low-acid breadth; Muscat would be grapier and less floral-perfumed. Here is the flight's key insight: ripeness sufficient for late-harvest sugar, yet aromatics undegraded and acid retained at low alcohol — that combination is only achieved by very high-altitude, high-UV, wide-diurnal sites rather than by heat. Torrontés Riojano from Cafayate.

## b) Style and winemaking (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Passerillage: thick-skinned bunches left into late autumn, picked in successive tries; sugar concentrated by dehydration, not fungus, hence the mineral rather than honeyed profile. Barrel fermentation and ageing gives the spice frame; fermentation stopped by chilling, racking off lees and sulphuring at roughly 55 g/L, leaving alcohol moderate. No malolactic — the acid line is untouched.

**Wine 2** — Appassimento: healthy bunches dried on mats or in lofts over winter, losing ~40% weight, then pressed and slowly fermented at cool temperature. Yeast struggles in the high-sugar must, so alcohol stalls around 12–13% with roughly 100 g/L retained; large old wood, not new, since there is no vanilla — only oxidative amber tinge and that varietal bitterness left intact.

**Wine 3** — Deliberate noble rot: successive hand passes through infected berries, whole-bunch pressed slowly to extract glycerol and botrytis compounds. Cool ferment in a mix of tank and seasoned barrique, arrested early by chilling and SO₂ at very high sugar (~150 g/L) — hence the low alcohol against high acid. Oak deliberately restrained to keep the fruit forward.

**Wine 4** — Simple late harvest: fruit left a few extra weeks for modest raisining, pressed and fermented cool in stainless steel, stopped by chilling and filtration at around 45 g/L. No oak, no lees weight — the intent is freshness and drinkability, not concentration.

**Wine 5** — Late harvest with aromatic preservation as the whole objective: night picking, protective handling, cool fermentation in inert vessels with an aromatic yeast, arrested at roughly 60 g/L. No oak, no skin contact beyond brief settling, since phenolic extraction would blur the terpenes.

## c) Quality, maturity, commercial position (5 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; top-estate Jurançon moelleux, around €28 ex-cellar. Youthful at 3–4 years, will improve 8 years and hold 15+, gaining candied citrus and toast. Independent specialists and gastronomy lists in France and Northern Europe; competes with Vouvray moelleux.

**Wine 2** — Very good, at DOCG Recioto level rather than a mere Soave Superiore, and priced accordingly at €30 per 500ml. Drinking well now at 7 years; holds another 8. A restaurant dessert-list wine in Italy, USA and UK — its bitter-almond cut makes it a better cheese partner than most.

**Wine 3** — Very good indeed, the flight's most complete wine — comparable in intensity to a decent Barsac at half the price, around NZ$40 per half. Drink now to 8 years. Cellar-door and premium restaurant by-the-glass; the challenge is category demand, not quality.

**Wine 4** — Good, an estate-tier late-harvest at €12–14 per half. Drink now, holds 3 years, no upside. Portuguese on-trade, supermarket premium shelf, export as an approachable entry to sweet wine.

**Wine 5** — Good to very good for its category; a boutique volume at US$20. Drink now to 4 years while the florals last. Independents and adventurous by-the-glass lists in the USA and Brazil; sells on aromatic novelty, competing with off-dry Muscat.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, oxidative pair

## a) Grape variety (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 — Savagnin.** Deep gold, viscous, with a nose led by walnut, toasted hazelnut, curry and saffron: the sotolon signature of ageing beneath a film yeast. Decisively, the palate shows generous warmth but no spirit burn — I read it around 14–14.5% — so the wine is unfortified, which eliminates Palomino under flor. A mature oaked Viura was also weighed, but there is no vanilla or cedar and the preserved-lemon acidity is far too taut. Savagnin is the variety that permits this: its high natural sugars alone sustain a voile without fortification.

**Wine 2 — Palomino.** Amber, medium bodied, bone dry, with unmistakable spirit heat in the 17–18% band and high, drying acidity. Iodine, sea air and salted almond over a neutral base point to Palomino Fino; Pedro Ximénez is ruled out by the absence of sugar, Madeira grapes by the absence of volatile lift and estufagem's scorched bite. Residual flor markers under deeper rancio, toffee and cocoa indicate Amontillado.

## b) Production and the role of oxidation (18 marks)

Both wines mature under ullage in old, neutral casks, but the mechanisms diverge. Wine 1 was fermented dry to full natural alcohol and racked to 228-litre barrels that were deliberately never topped, allowing a voile to establish; the veil consumed oxygen and ethanol, generating acetaldehyde and sotolon over what the depth of colour and umami suggest is six-plus years of static, vintage-specific ageing with no blending and no new oak. The telling point is that it remains fresh and citric after that exposure — evidence of biological, veil-mediated oxidation rather than the flat browning of simple air contact.

Wine 2 was fortified after fermentation to roughly 15%, low enough for flor to grow, giving the biological, saline almond phase; a second fortification then killed the veil and the wine passed into genuinely oxidative ageing, hence the toffee, coffee and rancio layered over that saline core. Fractional blending through a solera explains the seamless integration and non-vintage consistency, while evaporation in the humid maritime cellars concentrated extract, giving the viscosity and amber hue.

## c) Style, quality, commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — an uncompromising dry savoury white, outstanding quality at the apex of the Jura's oxidative hierarchy, comparable to a top Château-Chalon; tiny volumes for independent specialists and sommelier lists at around $110 a 62cl clavelin. Challenge: the style divides consumers.

**Wine 2** — dry, refined, mid-weight; very good quality, well above entry solera level but short of VORS concentration, around $28. Sells by the glass in tapas-focused on-trade and specialist off-trade in Spain, the UK and the Netherlands; the category's ageing perception remains the obstacle.

Under the skin: sugar of this concentration held by such firm acidity, with no flab, reads as altitude and wide diurnal range rather than heat — sugar won by dehydration, not by sun.

**Wine 2 — Samos, Greece.** Fortified Muscat runs from Beaumes-de-Venise and Rivesaltes to the Aegean; since wine 1 is French, and the dried fig, warm cinnamon depth and faint rancio edge exceed the primary French VDN style, Samos.

## c) Production compared (10 marks)

Both retain natural grape sugar, but by opposite routes. Wine 1: successive tries, fruit left to shrivel into late autumn; cool ferment, some barrel, arrested by chilling, racking and sulphur once alcohol reached the low-13s, leaving perhaps 50–60 g/L. Sugar is held by sterile filtration plus that high acidity. Wine 2 shows skin maceration — hence the depth and slight oxidative note — with ferment stopped early by mutage, neutral spirit taking it to about 15% and locking in far more sugar; here alcohol itself is the preservative, and non-vintage blending smooths the house style.

## d) Style, quality, commercial (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — a restrained, saline moelleux finishing almost dry; very good quality, top of its appellation, around €25 for 75cl. Independent specialists and sommelier by-the-glass as an apéritif; competes with Vouvray demi-sec and Alsace Vendange Tardive. Challenge: an obscure name.

**Wine 2** — richly sweet, pronounced, unctuous; good quality PDO, excellent value at €12–15. Supermarket, monopoly and diaspora export channels, plus dessert lists. Challenge: shrinking sweet-fortified demand.

## a) Grape variety (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Muscat of Alexandria (Zibibbo), Pantelleria. Deep amber, viscous, with dates, candied orange peel and orange blossom: grapey Muscat character at extreme ripeness. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is ruled out by the jammy, date-like density rather than delicate florals; Moscato d'Asti-style Muscat by the sheer body and sugar. A saline, volcanic lift on the finish points to a Mediterranean island.

**Wine 2** — Grenache-dominant. Mahogany-amber, very slow tears, with dried fig, roasted walnut, rancio and caramelised peel — an oxidatively aged fortified. Portuguese Tawny was weighed, but the lifted Christmas-cake sweetness and silky, unctuous texture exceed Douro levels of residual sugar, indicating Australian Grenache, possibly with Shiraz or Mataro.

## b) Method of production — how sweetness achieved (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Passito. Hand-picked grapes sun-dried on mats for 3–4 weeks concentrate sugars before pressing. Fermentation halts naturally near 13–14% as high potential alcohol stresses the yeast, leaving roughly 190–200 g/L residual sugar. Ageing is reductive, preserving pure dried fruit. Botrytis is excluded: no honeyed, saffron note and acidity too moderate; enrichment is not permitted.

**Wine 2** — Sweetness comes from arrested fermentation, not raisining. Grape spirit is added to overripe fruit partway through fermentation, retaining perhaps 180–250 g/L sugar and lifting alcohol to a perceived ~20%, warm but fully integrated. Extended fractional-blending maturation in small old casks (300–500L) in a hot climate drives evaporation and oxidation — hence the rancio, walnut and amber colour, and a glycerol-rich texture that amplifies perceived sweetness. Twenty years-plus of average age.

## c) Style, quality and commercial position (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Luscious but savoury, the volcanic salinity lifting it above confected sweetness. Very good quality, top-tier DOC Passito, €35–55. Sold through specialist independents and premium Italian on-trade in Europe and the USA to the enthusiast seeking an alternative to Sauternes or Tokaji. Low awareness of the appellation is the barrier. At peak; will hold 5–8 years, deepening in toffee notes.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding, benchmark aged Australian Tawny, equivalent to a 20–30 year classification, AUD $80–120. Suits specialist off-trade, by-the-glass programmes and dark-spirit drinkers; the UK, USA and Asia are the export opportunities. The obstacle is category perception — Australian fortifieds are poorly understood abroad. Being a blend of aged components it is ready now and will hold a decade without changing.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Gros Manseng/Petit Manseng, Jurançon Moelleux, South-West France. Deep gold, viscous, with pineapple, candied peel, dried apricot, honey and ginger; the palate is warm but only moderately so, so this is unfortified concentration. Sauternes was weighed and rejected: no botrytis saffron or wax, and the exotic ginger-clove spice is wrong for Sémillon. Late-harvest Alsace Riesling would give lime and a linear, cutting acid line, not this broad, glycerol-rich, oily texture. Passerillage on Manseng gives exactly this combination of tropical opulence and high, driving acidity.

**Wine 2** — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Rutherglen, Victoria. Tawny, exceptionally viscous, with rose petal, musk, raisin, caramel and candied orange; spirit warmth throughout confirms fortification well above 15%. Tawny Port shares the colour and dried fruit, but the floral-musk lift is Muscat, not a Douro red blend. The layering of honey, sultana and old-wood caramel at this sugar level is Rutherglen's fractional-blending style.

**Wine 3** — Touriga Nacional/Touriga Franca/Tinta Roriz, 10 Year Old Tawny, Douro. Amber-tawny, medium viscosity, medium intensity — leathery and restrained where Wine 2 is perfumed. Cinnamon, tobacco, candied apple and nuts over a sweet cherry mid-palate. Aged Amontillado was considered but ruled out by that sweet fruit core and the red-grape structure beneath. Nutty and mellow, yet without the rancio of a 20 Year Old.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Sweetness comes from the vine, not the still: grapes shrivel through autumn under dry Föhn winds, concentrating sugar so that fermentation stalls naturally, leaving substantial residual sugar at only moderate alcohol. A light toasty spice suggests older barrique; malolactic has been blocked, preserving the acidity that keeps the wine buoyant rather than cloying.

**Wine 2** — Fermentation arrested early by grape spirit, locking in primary grapey-floral character at very high residual sugar. Decades in small old casks under Rutherglen's extreme summer heat drive evaporative concentration and oxidative caramel-vanilla development; fractional blending of solera material explains the NV designation and the seamless spirit integration.

**Wine 3** — Fortification of fermenting red must retains sugar and anthocyanins; roughly ten years in small pipes then oxidises colour from ruby to amber and converts fresh fruit to nut and baking spice. The moderate viscosity, against Wine 2's syrup, marks a deliberately lighter sugar and extract level appropriate to the 10 Year tier.

## c) Commercial position (3 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Around €25–40; independent merchants and specialists selling to consumers seeking a Sauternes alternative at half the price. Export to Belgium, Switzerland and the UK. The constraint is Jurançon's low name recognition.

**Wine 2** — Museum Reserve tier, roughly AUD $50–80 per half-bottle. Predominantly domestic, with selective premium on-trade export to the UK, USA and Japan; the collector and by-the-glass restaurant pour are the targets. Format resistance is the barrier.

**Wine 3** — £25–40 in the UK, strongest by-the-glass in restaurants and gastropubs as a dessert or aperitif pour. The 10 Year Old designation is a legible quality cue for trade buyers; key markets are the UK, France and Belgium. It competes against large-house Ports below it, but offers a better quality/price ratio than Vintage.

**Under the skin:** all three are sweet, yet each achieves it differently — by dehydration, by spirit into white must, by spirit into red must — and each is priced according to how much time, not how much sugar, it has absorbed.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## Wine 1 — a) Variety and Origin (7 marks)

Chardonnay, Auckland/Kumeu, New Zealand. White peach and grapefruit zest over toasted hazelnut and brioche give the variety. Village Meursault was the main alternative — the struck-flint reduction and lees creaminess are Côte de Beaune in register — but the fruit sits fuller and riper than Burgundy at this weight, and the finish carries a saline rather than chalky mineral edge, which places it in a maritime New World cool climate. Clay-influenced coastal Auckland fits the combination of generosity and citrus pith.

## Wine 1 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Whole-bunch pressed and barrel-fermented in French barriques, perhaps 30–40% new, cool enough to hold the citrus. Full malolactic in barrel gives the brioche and creamy mid-palate; the nougat persistence indicates 10–12 months on lees with bâtonnage or at least no early racking. Struck flint signals protective, low-oxygen handling and minimal racking; the saline length suggests light fining and filtration only.

## Wine 1 — c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Dry, full-bodied, high but integrated acidity. Outstanding — the marriage of stone-fruit intensity, autolytic complexity and saline precision puts it at premier cru Burgundy standard, well above regional norms.

## Wine 1 — d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

NZ$80–100 (£45–55), fine dining and specialist independents in the UK, US and Japan. Its competitive set is 1er cru Meursault, against which it offers clear value; the Burgundian register is the selling point to sommeliers.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (7 marks)

Assyrtiko, Santorini PDO, Greece. Lemon-lime purity, no herbaceousness, and a laser acid line over surprising palate breadth. Albariño would show lower alcohol and rounder fruit; Chablis Chardonnay would give chalk rather than this hard volcanic salinity, and less palate weight at this acidity. The combination of breadth plus electric tartaric acid is Assyrtiko's alone.

## Wine 2 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Whole-bunch pressed, reductively handled, fermented and held in stainless steel. No oak, and a linear rather than creamy texture indicating little or no lees work. The decisive choice is suppression of malolactic conversion: the acid is uncompromisingly tartaric. Bentonite-fined and released early to protect the primary fruit; the salinity is site, not cellar.

## Wine 2 — c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Bone dry, medium-plus body, searing acidity, long mineral close. Very good — estate/single-vineyard tier within the PDO, €25–35. Typicity is immaculate.

## Wine 2 — d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Around €30 via specialist importers into seafood restaurants and progressive wine bars in northern Europe and the US. Undercuts premier cru Chablis on price while matching it on tension; Santorini now sells itself to sommeliers without explanation.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Origin (7 marks)

Rkatsiteli, Kakheti, Georgia. Deep amber with slight haze is the flight's most diagnostic sight — extended skin contact. Dried apricot and ripe orchard fruit sit over high acidity, medium body and low, chalky tannin. Skin-contact Viognier would give more alcohol and lower acid; amber Pinot Gris from Friuli or Alsace would be broader and more phenolic. High acid with low tannin at this colour is Rkatsiteli's signature.

## Wine 3 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Three to six months' maceration in buried qvevri, whose steady cellar temperature explains extraction without harshness; the grape's low skin phenolics account for the modest tannin despite the colour. Spontaneous ferment on indigenous yeast, no fining or filtration — hence the haze — and minimal sulfur. The dried-fruit weight implies a late pick in Kakheti's warm continental summer.

## Wine 3 — c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Dry, medium-bodied, high acid, gentle grip. Good quality, artisan Kakheti level at €25–35. Strongly individual and unmistakably genuine rather than a stylistic imitation; it will divide drinkers.

## Wine 3 — d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Natural wine bars, sommeliers and specialist merchants in the UK, Scandinavia and urban US. €25–35 through small importers. Its competitive set is conceptual rather than geographic — Friulian amber wines — which it undercuts on price while carrying the authenticity of the qvevri tradition.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Origin (7 marks)

Palomino, fino, El Puerto de Santa María, Jerez. Pale straw-gold with pronounced saline, almond, bruised apple and yeast-bread: biological ageing under flor. Clean warmth around 15% with a bone-dry finish confirms fortification to the flor threshold rather than oxidative ageing. Manzanilla was the alternative; Sanlúcar gives a lighter, more sea-spray flor. The slightly broader, yeastier register here points to El Puerto.

## Wine 4 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Neutral must pressed pale, fermented to 11–12%, fortified to 15% with grape spirit — the precise point that sustains flor and kills it above. Aged in old American oak butts under an active veil, run through a solera and criadera system that blends out vintage variation. Flor consumption of glycerol and production of acetaldehyde explains the bruised apple and the bone-dry, saline finish. No MLF, no sweetening at bottling.

## Wine 4 — c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Bone dry, medium-bodied, alcohol cleanly carried, very long. Very good — NV fino at entry-to-mid estate level, €10–15 domestic, €15–20 export. Classic and correct.

## Wine 4 — d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

A by-the-glass on-trade wine for tapas bars and seafood restaurants in the UK, Netherlands and US, €15–20 retail. The barrier is the residual consumer belief that sherry is sweet; the opening is a younger gastro-bar audience already drawn to dry, saline, low-intervention styles.

---

## Wine 5 — a) Variety and Origin (7 marks)

Semillon, Hunter Valley, New South Wales. Crushed stone, sliced lemon, green mango and lemongrass over a taut, crunchy palate of remarkable depth relative to its light weight; alcohol warmth is low. Clare Valley Riesling overlaps on lime and stone but would show sharper acid and early petrol; Bordeaux or Margaret River Semillon carries more phenolic weight and is normally blended and often oaked. The lanolin nuance and depth-to-weight ratio settle it.

## Wine 5 — b) Winemaking (8 marks)

Whole-bunch pressed, cool-fermented in stainless steel, no oak whatsoever — no toast, vanilla or nutty character anywhere. Malolactic blocked, leaving the tartaric acid untouched; this is the structural decision that makes the ageing curve possible. Bottled early under screwcap, with careful sulfur management to hold the reductive early phase. The technique is deliberately minimal: complexity here is varietal and site-derived, not built in the cellar.

## Wine 5 — c) Style and Quality (5 marks)

Bone dry, light-to-medium bodied, high taut acidity, medium-plus length. Outstanding for the style, flagship single-vineyard level at AU$50–70. At about five years it is primary moving into transition; expect toast, honey and lanolin from around eight years and a 15–20 year window.

## Wine 5 — d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

The problem is that in youth it reads as underweight to consumers expecting tropical fruit, so it needs an aged-wine list or an educated merchant to sell it. UK, US and Scandinavian specialists with cellaring customers are the channel. At AU$50–70 it competes with Riesling GG on intellectual appeal at a materially lower price.

## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Port, Douro Valley, Portugal. Deep opaque ruby, high viscosity and pronounced black fruit immediately signal a fortified red. Intense aromas of blackberry, blackcurrant, liquorice, rock rose and eucalyptus, combined with spirit warmth and a black-tea finish, point to a blend anchored by Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca. Banyuls was weighed seriously: both share a dark-fruit, fortified red profile. However, Banyuls is Grenache-dominant and shows rancio, dried fig and garrigue rather than this wine's fresh black-fruit and floral intensity. The structured tannic grip and pronounced minty lift confirm the Douro. The unoxidised primary fruit and elevated spirit warmth suggest a bottled-young style — consistent with a Late Bottled Vintage rather than Vintage Port.

**Wine 2** — Grenache Noir, Banyuls, Roussillon, France. Garnet, slightly less opaque than Wine 1, with dried fig, prune, dark chocolate, roasted coffee and garrigue on the nose. A subtle rancio note with leather and walnut confirms oxidative development, pointing to Banyuls or Maury. Port was eliminated: the Mediterranean herbal register, rancio and lighter tannic grip are inconsistent with a Touriga-driven Douro. The warm sweet spice and bitter-chocolate finish, alongside the garrigue complexity, narrow the origin to Banyuls — Maury tends to show fresher primary fruit at a comparable stage.

**Wine 3** — Grenache/Shiraz blend, Barossa Valley, South Australia. Pale amber-tawny with slow viscous legs signals long oxidative ageing. Dried fruit, rancio, walnut, caramel and raisin, alongside very high spirit warmth (I estimate ~19–20%), confirm an old Australian tawny style. The rancio and butterscotch development is more pronounced than Wine 2, pointing to extended solera-style barrel ageing well beyond a 10-year Tawny in complexity.

## b) Method of production (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Grapes are harvested at full ripeness on the Douro's hot schist soils. Fermentation is halted early — when roughly half the natural sugar remains — by grape spirit addition to ~20% alcohol, preserving the dense black fruit and sweetness in the glass. Ageing in large seasoned oak vats for around four years before bottling explains the firm tannic grip and retained primary fruit, distinguishing this from the more oxidative Vintage Port style.

**Wine 2** — Grenache Noir is harvested at high ripeness in Roussillon's hot, wind-swept terroir. Fermentation is halted by mutage to ~16% alcohol, preserving generous sweetness. The subtle rancio and dried-fruit development suggest deliberate oxidative ageing in older demi-muids or foudres with oxygen exposure — though nothing approaching the extreme long-ageing of Wine 3 — yielding the characteristic bittersweet chocolate and garrigue complexity.

**Wine 3** — Harvested at maximum Barossa ripeness, fermentation is cut by spirit addition. Extreme rancio, caramel and walnut indicate long ageing in small seasoned barrels under a fractional blending system: progressive evaporation and oxidation over many years creates the intense concentration here. The very high alcohol warmth and extreme sweetness reflect the hot-climate source fruit and prolonged barrel maturation.

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, equivalent to a well-made LBV Port; retailing around £18–25. Best positioned in independent merchants and premium supermarkets across the UK and Scandinavia, where Port commands strong off-trade loyalty. A credible by-the-glass fortified for on-trade accounts seeking quality without the price of Vintage Port.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality, artisan Banyuls Vieilles Vignes level; retailing around €20–35 in specialist retailers. The appellation commands a devoted following in France and among specialist importers in the UK and US, but limited off-trade volume elsewhere. The rancio complexity justifies positioning against 20-year Tawny Port on a fine-wine list, though the appellation's relative obscurity limits broader commercial reach.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding quality, equivalent to a Show Reserve Australian tawny; retailing around AU$50–80. The rancio depth rivals VORS Amontillado in structural interest. Primary export markets are the UK and the US, where Australian fortifieds remain undervalued and represent a genuine commercial opportunity, though consumer unfamiliarity with the style outside Australia is the key barrier to volume growth.
