## Wine 1 — Identification (10 marks)

Pale lemon-green, high but refined acidity, low warmth (7–9%), lime and white peach over slate: Riesling. Gewürztraminer would give rose and lychee; Pinot Gris would be broader and lower in acid. Low alcohol with retained sugar and racy tartaric acid confirms Germany. The steely extract and intense citrus/stone-fruit weight favour the Rheingau over the Mosel, which at the same Prädikat would be lighter and more floral. Off-dry rather than lusciously sweet: **Rheingau Riesling Spätlese.**

## Wine 1 — Winemaking (8 marks)

Late but botrytis-free harvest of clean ripe fruit. Cool, slow stainless-steel fermentation to protect aromatics, arrested by chilling, sulphur and filtration once the sugar/alcohol balance was reached. No oak, no lees texture, no malolactic — the purity and absence of any dairy or savoury note confirm all three. Early bottling under screw cap or fine cork preserves freshness.

## Wine 1 — Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good; single-vineyard estate Spätlese level, £20–28. Off-dry, racy, versatile between aperitif and spiced or Asian food. Sells through UK independents and restaurant lists, where low-alcohol Riesling has a committed following; Germany itself, the US and Nordic markets are the key channels.

---

## Wine 2 — Identification (10 marks)

Burnished gold with amber hints, high viscosity, and marmalade, dried apricot, beeswax and saffron: botrytis. The waxy lanolin richness and full body indicate Sémillon-dominant rather than Sauvignon Blanc. Tokaji Aszú was weighed but the orange-peel spice and oxidative bite of Furmint is absent, and warmth suggests 13–14% rather than Tokaji's higher acid-driven leanness. Opulent, creamy, with concentration and length beyond Barsac's usual delicacy or Monbazillac's plainer fruit: **Sauternes, Premier Cru Classé level.**

## Wine 2 — Winemaking (8 marks)

Successive hand-picked tries through botrytised parcels; the concentration implies yields far below appellation maximum. Fermentation and ageing in new and one-year barriques give restrained vanilla and spice, and 18–24 months on lees explain the creamy texture. Malolactic suppressed to retain the acid that carries very high residual sugar.

## Wine 2 — Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding — the global benchmark for botrytis sweet wine, £60–100+ per half-bottle. Honeyed and concentrated but not cloying, with acidity promising 30 years' development; drinking now, it will gain marmalade and roasted-nut depth. Fine wine retail, starred restaurant lists and auction; US, Hong Kong, Singapore and the UK trade. Priced against Tokaji Aszú and German TBA.

---

## Wine 3 — Identification (10 marks)

Deep amber-gold, thick legs, moderate alcohol without spirit heat. Dried fig, roasted almond, candied orange peel, baked pear, dried herbs, and a faintly tannic, drying finish — dried-grape concentration, not botrytis (no saffron) or freeze concentration (no piercing acid). Among Italian whites, Trebbiano would be neutral and Malvasia grapier; the smoky hazelnut-almond signature with ripe, warm fruit depth indicates Fiano, and that ripeness places it in the south. **Campania, Fiano passito.**

## Wine 3 — Winemaking (8 marks)

Fully ripe fruit dried on racks for several weeks, concentrating sugar by evaporation; fermentation halted naturally as alcohol and osmotic pressure stalled the yeast, leaving high residual sugar. Toasted almond and light vanilla integration plus the amber tint and gentle oxidative edge suggest around twelve months in used oak — deliberately not new, which would bury Fiano's delicacy.

## Wine 3 — Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good, at Campania DOC/IGT passito level, £25–40 per 50cl. Richly sweet with a drying finish that prevents cloying. A specialist and on-trade by-the-glass dessert listing; domestic Italy first, then Scandinavia and the US Italian-wine trade. Awareness is the obstacle, differentiation from Vin Santo and Muscat the opening.

---

## Wine 4 — Identification (10 marks)

Almost water-white with green tints yet glacially viscous — extreme sugar at very low alcohol. Electric acidity, pure lime, lychee, concentrated peach, honeysuckle; no wax or saffron, so not Sauternes or German BA/TBA, and no dried-fruit oxidation, so not passito. Freeze concentration is the only mechanism that yields this purity with such sugar. Vidal would read more tropical and less mineral; this lime-and-slate line is Riesling. **Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Riesling Icewine.**

## Wine 4 — Winemaking (8 marks)

Naturally frozen grapes picked and pressed at –8°C or below, so only sugar-rich juice separates from the ice. Cold stainless-steel fermentation, no oak or lees influence, protects the frozen-fruit purity; osmotic stress stalls the yeast at low alcohol, leaving very high sugar. Screw cap holds the lime and floral aromatics.

## Wine 4 — Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding within its category, £40–70 per 200ml. Searingly acidic, intensely sweet, exceptionally pure. A luxury niche sold in small formats through specialists, duty-free and gifting; Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and the US. Tiny volumes and high price limit reach, but the Canadian category identity carries real prestige in Asian gift markets.

---

## Wine 5 — Identification (10 marks)

Gold, bright, medium-plus viscosity; candied citrus, apricot jam, dried peach, mango, honey and orange blossom. Fresh medium-plus acidity without Icewine's cut, no botrytis, no spirit heat, no oxidative dried-grape note, and warmth suggesting 10–11% — a vine-dried late harvest with fermentation stopped early. Chenin Blanc was weighed but its quince and beeswax are absent; the open, tropical aromatics read as Sauvignon Blanc grown warm. **Colchagua Valley, Chile, late-harvest Sauvignon Blanc.**

## Wine 5 — Winemaking (8 marks)

Extended hang time gave on-vine desiccation without noble rot — the fruit is clean, not funky. Cool stainless-steel fermentation, no oak, no malolactic, preserving primary fruit and bright acid; arrested by chilling, sulphur and sterile filtration near 11% with substantial sugar retained.

## Wine 5 — Style, Quality, Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good, Chilean Reserva late-harvest tier, £12–18 per 375ml. Forward, crowd-pleasing tropical sweetness with enough acid to stay fresh; drink within three years. Supermarket premium shelf and restaurant dessert-by-the-glass in the UK, US and Scandinavia. Its price and easy fruit recruit drinkers who find Sauternes costly, but it competes with many near-identical South American late harvests.

### a) Country and region (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 — France, Champagne; Côte des Blancs, Grand Cru village blend.** Fine, persistent bead and a nose of green apple, patisserie and hazelnut point to a long-aged traditional-method wine. Method aside, the origin argument is structural: very high, racy acidity against modest weight and a cool, lemon-oil fruit spectrum with no tropical ripeness, alcohol reading low-to-moderate (~12%). English sparkling was weighed — it can match that acid line — but it rarely carries this depth of chalky, saline extract or this quiet autolytic maturity; Crémant de Bourgogne was ruled out as the fruit here is too taut and the finish too mineral. The pure Chardonnay expression (no red-fruit breadth) narrows to Blanc de Blancs, and the crushed-rock, chalky signature points to the Côte des Blancs.

**Wine 2 — Italy, Veneto; Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore, Cartizze.** Soft, frothy mousse dissipating quickly, pear, lemon and lily florals, and a distinctly perceptible sweetness carried on medium(+) acidity at low alcohol (~11%). Asti was considered — comparable sugar and low alcohol — but the fruit is pear and grapefruit, not grapey Muscat terpene. Glera, therefore, and the honey/apricot depth plus a firmer acid spine than generic Prosecco DOC lift it to the hillside Superiore DOCG, at its most concentrated in the Cartizze cru.

**Wine 3 — Argentina, Mendoza.** A properly ruby sparkling red, dry, medium body, low soft tannin, medium acid, with juicy black fruit, violets and black pepper. Lambrusco was the first alternative but that would show higher acidity and a more savoury, sour-cherry frame; Australian sparkling Shiraz was rejected as those are sweetly dosed, densely oaked and far more concentrated. Violet-and-pepper black fruit with plush low-tannin softness reads as Malbec, and warm-climate ripeness held at medium acidity points to Mendoza.

### b) Method and style (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Traditional method: whole-bunch pressed base wine, full malolactic (buttered-toast roundness, no malic bite), second fermentation in bottle and around four years on lees. Style is vinous and gastronomic, low dosage — extra brut, ~5 g/L. *Under the skin:* the producer can go this dry only because extended autolysis and malolactic supply the mid-palate that sugar would otherwise fake — dosage is subtracted where texture has been earned.

**Wine 2.** Tank (Martinotti) method: a single short cool second ferment under pressure preserving primary florals, then sterile-filtered and bottled under counter-pressure, with fermentation arrested to leave ~20–25 g/L — the legal *Dry* tier, not Brut. Style is aromatic, frothy, immediate.

**Wine 3.** Tank method again, but reductively handled, no oak, no lees character, whole-berry or short-macerated for colour without tannin extraction. Style is unserious, chilled, fruit-forward.

### c) Quality and commercial (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding; grower Grand Cru Blanc de Blancs standard, £70–90, independent specialists and sommelier lists in London, New York, Tokyo. Drink now to 10 years.

**Wine 2.** Very good for DOCG Cartizze — the top of its appellation, €18–22, premium supermarkets and Italian on-trade; challenge is Prosecco's commodity image and a sweetness style out of fashion in the UK.

**Wine 3.** Good, no official tier; a $12–15 novelty for supermarkets and by-the-glass in Latin American and US markets. Drink within two years.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 (Sweet Wine Pair)

## a) Country, region, and grape variety (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Hungary, Tokaj; principally Furmint with Hárslevelű and probably Sárgamuskotály. Deep gold, viscous, with dried apricot, quince, marmalade, saffron and beeswax: clearly botrytised. Sauternes was the first candidate, but the searing acidity holding up the sugar, the saline mineral thread and bitter almond finish are Furmint, not Sémillon; smoky ginger notes point to Tokaj's volcanic tuff, and the oxidative nuttiness to Gönci cask ageing.

**Wine 2** — France, Alsace, grand cru granite; Riesling. Pale gold, viscous but markedly lower in perceived alcohol than Wine 1, so lighter on the palate. Lime zest, white peach, pineapple and petrol over honeyed botrytis rule out Sauternes and Vouvray, neither of which gives this citrus-petroleum register. Concentration far beyond Spätlese weight, with extreme sweetness at low warmth, places it at Sélection de Grains Nobles.

## b) Methods by which sweetness has been achieved (2 × 8 marks)

Both rely on noble rot, but the routes diverge.

**Wine 1:** botrytised berries picked individually over successive passes and worked into Aszú dough, then macerated 24–36 hours in base wine or must before pressing and fermentation. At 5 Puttonyos the finished wine carries roughly 120 g/L residual sugar; fermentation stops naturally as sugar suppresses the yeast.

**Wine 2:** botrytised fruit is also picked in tries, but whole clusters are direct-pressed — no maceration. At SGN level (minimum 256 g/L must sugar for Riesling) the sugar load itself arrests fermentation, leaving high sweetness at low alcohol.

The contrast that matters: Wine 1's maceration step lets the producer calibrate concentration by puttonyos, an assembled sweetness; Wine 2's sweetness is wholly given by the juice, preserving unmediated varietal purity.

## c) Style, quality, and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1:** outstanding Aszú 5 Puttonyos, around €60–90, oxidative and layered, with 20+ years ahead. Sold through independent specialists, auction and fine dining alongside Sauternes and German TBA; strong in Germany, the UK and the US. Its commercial problem is recognition — at this price it meets Sauternes Premier Cru Classé head-on.

**Wine 2:** exceptional SGN, roughly €100–150 per half-bottle. Style is crystalline and reductive where Wine 1 is oxidative, the acid giving extraordinary length. Aimed at collectors via specialist channels and auction, chiefly France, Germany, Switzerland, the UK and the US. Production is minute, so availability rather than price limits it.

Tank (Charmat) method: secondary fermentation in pressurised tank, cool fermentation to retain Glera's volatile terpenes, then isobaric filtration and bottling. Tank method, but — unlike Prosecco — from a single fermentation. ## a) Mechanism by which residual sugar has been achieved (5 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1 — Dried grape (passerillage/appassimento).** Concentrated stone-fruit and almond aromatics with viscous texture at moderate perceived alcohol point to post-harvest drying on mats or lofts. Water evaporates, concentrating sugars; fermentation is halted before all sugar is consumed, retaining sweetness without fortification.

**Wine 2 — Noble rot (botrytis cinerea).** Honey, saffron, apricot preserve, and ginger at very low perceived alcohol indicate selective harvesting of botrytis-affected berries. Fungal perforation of the skins concentrates sugars and acids while introducing glycerol, explaining the extraordinary weight and viscosity.

**Wine 3 — Cryoextraction (Icewine/Eiswein).** Piercing acidity cutting through extreme sweetness, pronounced tropical aromatics, and very low perceived alcohol indicate grapes harvested and pressed while naturally frozen. Ice crystals retain water, leaving hyper-concentrated juice that ferments only partially.

**Wine 4 — Arrested fermentation by fortification.** Spirit warmth clearly above table-wine strength combined with residual sweetness confirms that neutral grape spirit was added mid-fermentation, killing the yeast and locking in sugar before extended oxidative cask ageing.

**Wine 5 — Noble rot (botrytis cinerea).** As with Wine 2, botrytis has concentrated sugars and acids while generating honey, beeswax, and marmalade character. The mechanism operates in a warm climate, suggesting a narrower harvest window before rot turns grey.

---

## b) Region of origin and grape variety (5 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Recioto di Soave, Veneto, Italy; Garganega.** High viscosity at moderate perceived alcohol, citrus blossom, white peach, almond, and a saline mineral thread point to a non-fortified, non-botrytis dried-grape white from a cool volcanic terroir. Garganega's characteristic florality, stone-fruit generosity, and high acidity are all present. Muscat was considered but its overtly grapey profile is absent. The saline mineral thread and absence of oxidative development narrow origin to the Soave hills: Recioto di Soave.

**Wine 2 — Alsace Grand Cru, France; Riesling SGN.** Saffron, ginger, honeyed apricot, extreme sweetness, and very low perceived alcohol combined with electric acidity confirm top-level botrytis. The acidity is the diagnostic key: it has the tartaric, racy quality of Riesling rather than the broader glycolic acidity of Sémillon. Gewurztraminer was weighed against this, but its lychee and rose-petal profile is absent; a lime-pith tension and petrol-tinged mineral undercurrent confirm Riesling at Sélection de Grains Nobles level from a Grand Cru site.

**Wine 3 — Niagara Peninsula, Canada; Vidal.** Gold colour, extreme viscosity, tropical aromatics of pineapple and mango with orange peel, electric acidity, and very low perceived alcohol lock this into Icewine. Vidal — the hybrid dominating Canadian Icewine — shows exactly this tropical generosity and robust acidity. Riesling Eiswein was weighed against this but produces a lime-and-petrol character rather than mango-forward tropicality. The Niagara Peninsula's cold continental winters guarantee natural freezing at harvest.

**Wine 4 — Madeira, Portugal; Bual (Boal).** Elevated spirit warmth, rancio, caramelised fig, coffee, volatile acidity, and remarkable persistent acidity confirm a fortified wine from a volcanic Atlantic island. Medium-to-full sweetness eliminates the drier Sercial and Verdelho styles; sweetness falls short of Malmsey's luscious intensity. This is firmly Bual: the mid-sweet register retaining Madeira's signature tangy acidity with rich dried-fruit depth, and considerable complexity pointing to extended cask ageing.

**Wine 5 — Barossa Valley, Australia; Sémillon.** Honey, beeswax, and marmalade with moderate perceived alcohol and botrytis-derived glycerol weight point to a warm-climate botrytised wine. Sémillon is diagnostic: it produces a distinctive beeswax-and-lanolin texture that Chardonnay — the alternative candidate — lacks. The almost jammy marmalade note, without the cool-climate petrichor of a Hunter Valley expression, places this in the Barossa Valley, where botrytis infections occur under specific humid conditions in selected vintages.

---

## c) Style, quality, and commercial position (5 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** An elegant, medium-sweet DOCG white of very good quality, retailing around €30–45 in Italy's specialist market. The appassimento freshness — saline minerality, vibrant citrus, no oxidation — makes this refined rather than heavy. It appeals to Italian fine wine enthusiasts and specialist retailers in northern Europe and Japan, but Recioto di Soave's low consumer profile compared with Recioto della Valpolicella limits export volumes.

**Wine 2.** An outstanding Sélection de Grains Nobles retailing from €80 to over €150 for a half-bottle. With exceptional ageing potential, it belongs on fine dining lists and in collectors' cellars across France, Switzerland, Germany, the US, and Japan. Production is tiny and inconsistent, limiting commercial scale despite the prestige positioning.

**Wine 3.** A very good quality Niagara Peninsula Icewine retailing around CAD $50–80 for a 200ml bottle — typical of a category priced to reflect its tiny yields. The style is unambiguously sweet and gift-oriented, suited to premium retail and dessert pairings. South Korean and Chinese importers actively seek premium Canadian Icewine, though price resistance from consumers unfamiliar with the production cost remains the main commercial challenge.

**Wine 4.** A very good quality Bual Madeira — consistent with a 10-Year-Old house style — retailing around £25–35 in the UK specialist market. Its near-indestructibility once opened is a genuine competitive advantage for by-the-glass service in wine bars and fine dining. Growing consumer interest in oxidative and complex styles offers a real opportunity despite Madeira's persistently low category profile.

**Wine 5.** A good to very good botrytised Sémillon from the Barossa Valley, retailing around AUD $35–50 for a 375ml bottle. Rich and immediately approachable, it suits specialist off-trade and premium on-trade dessert lists in Australia, with export growth potential in the UK, Singapore, and the US. The principal challenge is competing for shelf space against Sauternes and German sweet wines at similar price points, where European origins currently hold stronger consumer recognition.

Barrel fermentation and roughly eighteen months in French oak, some new, gives the now-seamless vanilla and marzipan. Fermentation stopped by rising alcohol rather than sterile filtration, which preserves the energy; malolactic suppressed, keeping acidity tartaric and taut against the sugar.

**Wine 2** — Defined by time rather than fruit. Very ripe, shrivelled brown Muscat from old vines, fortified early to retain massive sugar. The decisive choice is decades of oxidative ageing in small old casks in hot sheds, concentrating the wine by evaporation and generating the coffee and rancio register. Fractional solera-style blending at the Rare tier draws on the oldest material, producing depth no single vintage could reach.

**Wine 3** — The opposite philosophy to Wine 1: no oak at all, so fruit and mineral stand naked. Berry-by-berry selection at Beerenauslese concentration is the labour decision that dictates the price. Gentle pressing, slow cool fermentation in stainless steel, arrested naturally by sugar at 7–8%, leaves profound sweetness held by acidity that was never softened by malolactic.

**Wine 4** — Fortification timing is everything: aguardente added mid-ferment, around half the sugar consumed, locking in sweetness and primary fruit. Rapid, warm, aggressive extraction — foot treading or pump-over — delivers the opaque colour and tannin in a very short maceration. Two years in large old wood adds no oak flavour, then bottling unfiltered, so all development is reductive in bottle.

**Wine 5** — A restrained, food-friendly sweet style. Hand-picked late-harvest fruit with only partial noble rot; barrel fermentation in second- and third-use oak with around ten months on lees gives creamy mid-palate weight without masking the varietal floral lift. Fermentation was allowed further than in Wine 1, leaving less sugar and higher alcohol.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding. Premier Cru Supérieur, the sole holder of that 1855 rank, at roughly £400–500 per half-bottle. Sold through fine wine merchants, auction and top restaurants in London, New York and Hong Kong to collectors and investors; its only quality peers are Germany's greatest TBAs. Sweet wine consumption is falling globally, but this wine trades as an asset, not a drink, which insulates it.

**Wine 2** — Outstanding, at the summit of the Rutherglen hierarchy above Classic and Grand, around A$120–150 per 375ml. Specialist merchants and premium off-trade in Australia, the UK, US and Japan; the buyer prizes concentration over freshness. The challenge is category confusion with Tawny or Sherry; the opportunity is by-the-glass sommelier listing, where its uniqueness and low relative price make it exceptional value.

**Wine 3** — Very high quality; Beerenauslese from a top Rheinhessen slate site, €80–120 per half-bottle. Specialist German importers in the UK, US and especially Japan, selling to committed Riesling drinkers. Younger consumers are retreating from sweetness, but at a fifth of Wine 1's price it is the strongest value argument in the flight, and tasting-menu listings are the growth channel.

**Wine 4** — Very high quality, consistent with a single-quinta Vintage rather than a declared shipper wine: £40–60 on release. Traditional Port markets — UK, US, Germany, Scandinavia — through specialist merchants and fine dining. Needs fifteen to twenty years; tannin and fruit are both ample, so it will improve, gaining fig, spice and sous-bois. The perception gap versus the great houses is exactly its commercial opening.

**Wine 5** — Good quality only: appealing citrus precision but lacking botrytis complexity and length, £15–20 per half-bottle. Premium supermarkets and independents in the UK, US and Scandinavia, plus casual-dining by-the-glass, aimed at drinkers who find Sauternes too rich. It competes against Bordeaux moelleux and Alsace vendange tardive, which carry stronger regional identity; Casablanca's rising cool-climate reputation is the credible counter-narrative.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Furmint, Tokaj, Hungary. Deep gold, viscous, with dried apricot, ginger, saffron and oxidative walnut. The discriminator is the electric tartaric acidity cutting the sweetness, far higher than a passerillage wine would give. Muscat is ruled out (rounder, lower acid); Chenin is closer but lacks the savoury saffron edge. The broad, oxidative, marmalade-edged sweetness rather than the tightly focused multi-puttonyos profile suggests Szamorodni Édes rather than Aszú.

**Wine 2** — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Samos, Greece. Orange blossom, apricot jam and lychee identify Muscat instantly; the spirit warmth at around 15% confirms fortification. Beaumes-de-Venise is the obvious alternative, but the pale gold and wholly primary fruit — no rancio, no colour development — rule out any aged VDN, including Rutherglen. A young, unaged Muscat VDN from Samos's schist-granite slopes is the most credible conclusion.

**Wine 3** — Cabernet Franc, Niagara Peninsula, Canada. Deep ruby-purple, hugely viscous, with blackcurrant, violet and red pepper. Alcohol is strikingly low and the body light despite the sugar: cryoextraction, not late harvest. Vidal Icewine would give tropical fruit and honey; Riesling Eiswein, lime and petrol. The pyrazine-edged red fruit with Icewine concentration points decisively to Niagara, the only significant commercial source of red-variety Icewine.

**Wine 4** — Malvasia with Grechetto and red grapes, Montepulciano, Tuscany, Italy. Very deep copper-amber, thick tears; raisin, chocolate, walnut husk, dried fig and orange peel indicate long oxidative maturation well beyond botrytis. Alcohol is high and warming but without spirit heat, which excludes a fortified wine. Oxidative concentration plus high natural alcohol equals Vin Santo; the copper hue signals Occhio di Pernice, made with red-skinned Malvasia Nera and Sangiovese. The depth suggests Montepulciano rather than Chianti Classico.

**Wine 5** — Malbec, Mendoza, Argentina. Deep purple, violet-scented, with dark plum, blackberry and mountain herb. Alcohol reads around 11%, far below a dry Malbec, indicating arrested fermentation. Late-harvest Syrah or Cabernet were weighed, but the blue-fruited violet signature with fine silky tannin is Malbec, and the herbal-mineral lift implies high altitude. Mendoza is the only major source of commercial late-harvest Malbec.

---

## b) Method of production — how sweetness has been achieved (5 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** *Botrytis cinerea* concentrates sugar, acid and glycerol in the vineyard. Crucially, botrytised and healthy bunches are harvested and pressed together — the defining difference from Aszú, where berries are individually sorted — which explains the broader, less surgical sweetness. Slow cool fermentation is arrested naturally by sugar and rising alcohol, leaving roughly 60–80 g/L. Oxidative maturation in partly filled Gönci casks, sometimes with a flor-like film, supplies the walnut character.

**Wine 2.** Grapes picked at full ripeness to protect terpene aromatics; fermentation begins in stainless steel and is arrested by *mutage*, the addition of neutral grape spirit at 95–96%, retaining roughly 120–160 g/L and lifting alcohol to about 15%. No oxidative ageing is applied, which is precisely why the fruit remains primary and grapey.

**Wine 3.** Grapes hang until temperatures fall to −8°C or below, then are pressed frozen so ice crystals retain water and only concentrated juice runs — must at 35–45 Brix. Fermentation is slow and stressed, halting naturally at around 8% alcohol with 200–250 g/L residual sugar. Unlike Wine 5, no intervention is needed to stop it.

**Wine 4.** *Appassimento*: grapes dried on *graticci* in ventilated lofts for three to six months, concentrating must to 40–50 Brix. Fermentation runs in small sealed *caratelli* seeded with *madre*, wild yeast lees from earlier vintages, and stalls from sugar and ethanol toxicity at roughly 120–180 g/L. Six or more years of oxidative ageing in partly filled barrels under the roof, with wide seasonal temperature swings, gives the colour and caramelisation. No fortification: the ~16% alcohol is entirely fermentative.

**Wine 5.** Harvested well after the dry programme, with partial on-vine dehydration in Mendoza's dry Andean air. Fermentation is cool and then arrested deliberately — by chilling, filtration and sulphur — at roughly 80–120 g/L, leaving about 11% alcohol. Brief barrel ageing adds spice without dominating. This is the only wine of the five where sweetness is achieved by cellar intervention rather than natural arrest.

---

## c) Style, quality, and commercial position (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Medium-rich oxidative sweet white, very good quality; approximately €25–40. Specialist retail and fine dining in Germany, Austria and the UK, where Tokaji retains a loyal following. Drinking now and will hold ten years, gaining waxy, nutty depth. Its commercial role is as the accessible entry to Tokaj beneath Aszú pricing.

**Wine 2.** Richly sweet, fresh, high-alcohol fortified Muscat, very good quality at Grand Cru level; around €15–25 per 500ml. Immediately accessible and ideal by the glass in Mediterranean restaurants and in specialist off-trade in France, Greece and the UK. Its competitive set is Beaumes-de-Venise, which it undercuts at comparable quality. Drink within five years — ageing would cost the primary fruit that defines it.

**Wine 3.** Outstanding within its category; roughly CAD $80–120 per 200ml. Using Cabernet Franc rather than Vidal is the point of difference, appealing to sommeliers and collectors seeking novelty inside an established prestige category. Key export markets are Japan, Hong Kong and the US. It will hold 15–20 years, drying into figgy, spiced complexity. The commercial obstacle is price per millilitre and the consumer education required to justify it.

**Wine 4.** Exceptional, outstanding quality; approximately €80–120 per 375ml for a mature vintage. Concentration, oxidative complexity and high natural alcohol place it among Italy's most serious sweet wines. Channels are fine wine merchants, top Italian lists and auction. Approachable now, it will develop 15–20 years further towards mahogany and rancio. The higher-order point is economic: six years in *caratelli* with heavy evaporative loss and tiny yields makes the price structurally unavoidable, yet the market still benchmarks Vin Santo against restaurant *cantuccini* wine — the category's core problem is that its cheapest expressions define its perception.

**Wine 5.** Good quality, approachable, fruit-forward; roughly USD $20–30. The opportunity lies in growing demand for sweet reds in China and the US, where Mendoza Malbec's brand recognition reassures new buyers. It suits off-trade retail alongside chocolate and blue cheese. The risk is that sweet red remains niche, so trial depends heavily on the strength of the producer's dry Malbec reputation.

---

### b) Method of production (9 marks)

Base wines fermented in stainless steel — no barrel character beneath the autolysis. Secondary fermentation in bottle confirmed by the fine persistent bead; brioche and toast development is consistent with at least four years on lees, well beyond the 15-month NV minimum. The creamy texture points to cool-cellar ageing at low pressure. Brut dosage leaves perceptible sweetness — around 8–10 g/L residual sugar — balanced by naturally high acidity.

No brioche, toast, or biscuit confirms Charmat (tank) method: secondary fermentation in sealed pressurised tanks, short lees contact to preserve primary aromatics. **a) Origin:** Germany, Mosel, Graach (Grosse Lage)

**b) Variety:** Riesling

**c) Sugar concentration method:** Pale gold, weightless in body, with laser acidity and very low perceived alcohol (7–8%) — no physical or fungal concentration of the must here, or the wine would carry far more weight and colour. This is late-harvest fruit at Auslese ripeness (roughly 83–110° Oechsle, selectively picked with some botrytised berries) whose must was rich enough that fermentation arrested before dryness, assisted by chilling and SO₂. Lime, green apple, peach and incipient petrol over slate minerality mark it as Mosel rather than Alsace or Austria.

**d) Residual sugar:** approximately 85–100 g/L

**e) Style and quality:** Crystalline and ethereal — the antithesis of the heavier styles in this flight — with extraordinary tension between acidity and peachy sweetness. Outstanding at Auslese Prädikat from a named Grosse Lage; drinking well now but will gain kerosene and honeyed depth over two to three decades. €30–50 per half-bottle.

**f) Commercial position:** Riesling specialists, fine wine on-trade and collectors in the UK, US and Scandinavia.

---

## Wine 5

**a) Origin:** Spain, Montilla-Moriles

**b) Variety:** Pedro Ximénez

**c) Sugar concentration method:** Near-opaque dark brown with slow mahogany tears, showing fig, date, molasses, coffee, rancio and old wood, with spirit warmth above 15%. The fortification and the depth of colour rule out every unfortified route in this flight. Grapes are sun-dried on esparto mats immediately after harvest (soleo), evaporation driving must sugars beyond 400 g/L; light fortification with grape spirit arrests fermentation, and prolonged oxidative ageing through a solera blends multiple vintages, darkening the wine and building the rancio and coffee notes.

**d) Residual sugar:** approximately 400–450 g/L

**e) Style and quality:** Among the most concentrated sweet wines made. The rancio from decades of oxidative solera ageing, and the seamless integration of spirit, give complexity beyond mere sweetness. Outstanding, of VORS-equivalent age and depth, at €25–40 per half-bottle — exceptional value against Wine 2.

**f) Commercial position:** Premium specialist off-trade and fine dining by-the-glass programmes in the UK, US and Benelux; increasingly used as a cocktail modifier.

## Wine 1

### a) Grape variety and origin (8 marks)

Intensely pure lime, green apple, and white peach with a pronounced slate-and-citrus mineral lift points directly to Riesling. Gewürztraminer and Pinot Gris were eliminated by the almost ethereally light body, absence of spice or phenolic grip, and perceived alcohol well below 9%. Within Riesling, slate-driven minerality, fierce acidity, and a nascent petrol note point firmly to the Mittelmosel. Alsace would show more body and higher alcohol; the Rhine appellations a rounder, fuller palate. The sweetness level — pronounced but perfectly counterbalanced — is consistent with Spätlese rather than Auslese.

**Conclusion:** Riesling, Spätlese, Mittelmosel, Germany.

### b) Residual sugar and winemaking decisions (9 marks)

Fermentation was arrested by chilling, centrifuging, and sulphur dioxide addition at the desired balance point. Slow cool fermentation allows progressive monitoring of the sugar-to-acid ratio. No oak character confirms neutral Fuder or stainless steel, preserving fruit purity. No malolactic fermentation was conducted; the searing acidity is fully intact.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Outstanding quality Mittelmosel Spätlese. The balance of approximately 75–85 g/L residual sugar against electric acidity is exemplary. Prädikat Spätlese tier with clear single-vineyard terroir expression.

### d) Commercial position (3 marks)

Specialist off-trade and premium restaurants in Germany, the UK, USA, and Japan. Retail approximately £30–50. Sweetness deters dry-wine drinkers, though versatility with Asian cuisine and charcuterie is an underexploited selling point.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Grape variety and origin (8 marks)

Botrytis-driven aromas of apricot jam, marmalade, saffron, and beeswax confirm botrytis-affected Sémillon. Muscat was eliminated by the absence of grapey floral character; botrytised Riesling would show a racier acid line with petrol development. Lanolin texture and marmalade character confirm Sémillon-dominant. Perceived alcohol around 13–14% and glycerol viscosity place this in Bordeaux rather than Monbazillac. A clean, uplifting acid line consistent with limestone soils points to Barsac rather than Sauternes proper, where richness tends to dominate.

**Conclusion:** Sémillon/Sauvignon Blanc, Barsac, Bordeaux, France.

### b) Residual sugar and winemaking decisions (9 marks)

Residual sugar was achieved through botrytis cinerea: multiple selective harvesting passes concentrate sugars by dehydrating berries on the vine. Fermentation proceeded slowly in French oak barriques — 30–50% new oak indicated by subtle toasty vanilla integration — terminating naturally at approximately 13–14% alcohol, leaving approximately 80–150 g/L residual sugar. Barrel ageing added oxidative complexity and textural integration.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Outstanding quality, equivalent to Deuxième Cru Classé level. Botrytis is fully expressed without heaviness; acidity lifts the sweetness cleanly. Long and complex finish.

### d) Commercial position (3 marks)

Specialist merchants and premium restaurant lists across France, the UK, USA, and Asia. Retail approximately £40–70 per 750ml; the 375ml half-bottle is the primary on-trade format. The category requires active sommelier advocacy to overcome declining consumption frequency.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Grape variety and origin (8 marks)

Deep amber with dates, dried figs, caramel, candied orange peel, hazelnuts, and a distinctive saline, volcanic minerality — a passito-style wine. Vin Santo from Tuscany was a strong alternative: both share the dried-grape mechanism, amber colour, and oxidative complexity. Vin Santo, however, shows more pronounced walnut and honey character without this maritime saltiness, and is built on Trebbiano and Malvasia rather than Assyrtiko. The saline edge and tangerine peel running through the finish resolve firmly in favour of Santorini Vinsanto, where Assyrtiko provides structure and acidity while Athiri or Aidani add floral complexity.

**Conclusion:** Assyrtiko-dominant blend (Vinsanto), Santorini, Greece.

### b) Residual sugar and winemaking decisions (9 marks)

Grapes are sundried on terraces for approximately 10–14 days; fermentation terminates naturally at around 11–12% alcohol, leaving approximately 250 g/L residual sugar. Dark amber colour and caramel-hazelnut complexity indicate extended barrel ageing — PDO minimum is two years, but the depth here suggests four or more — with partially filled barrels encouraging controlled oxidation. No MLF; underlying acidity remains structurally important.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Outstanding quality. The balance between extreme sugar concentration and Assyrtiko's acidity prevents heaviness and gives genuine freshness — Superiore level within the PDO.

### d) Commercial position (3 marks)

Specialist merchants and premium restaurants in Greece, Germany, the UK, and USA. Retail approximately €25–45 per 500ml. Even serious consumers rarely encounter Santorini Vinsanto, making by-the-glass service in specialist restaurants the primary route to discovery.

---

## Wine 4

### a) Grape variety and origin (8 marks)

Fresh peach, apricot, lychee, and wildflower honey — entirely primary and fruit-driven, with no botrytis funk or passito oxidation. Sugar concentration is enormous (estimated above 200 g/L) yet the fruit is pristine: the key diagnostic pointing to Icewine, where frozen grapes are pressed at sub-zero temperatures and ice is separated from concentrated juice. Riesling Eiswein would show petrol and lime; the tropical lychee and candied lemon profile points instead to Vidal Blanc, a French-American hybrid with thick skins that resist cold damage. Vidal is widely planted in Ontario precisely for Icewine, and the Niagara Peninsula is the world's leading producer: Great Lakes moderation ripens the fruit while January temperatures reliably reach the required −8°C.

**Conclusion:** Vidal Blanc, Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada.

### b) Residual sugar and winemaking decisions (9 marks)

Grapes are harvested at −10°C to −12°C and pressed immediately while frozen; ice remains in the press while concentrated juice flows through, yielding as little as 15% of normal volume. Fermentation proceeds slowly for weeks under osmotic stress, terminating naturally without any stopping agent. Pristine fruit confirms fermentation and ageing exclusively in stainless steel, with no malolactic fermentation and early bottling to preserve aromatic freshness.

### c) Style and quality (5 marks)

Very good to outstanding — a benchmark Vidal Icewine. Luscious sweetness is balanced by clean acidity with no cloying finish. Consistent with VQA Icewine designation.

### d) Commercial position (3 marks)

Canada's most internationally recognised style, sold through specialist off-trade and duty-free in 375ml or 200ml formats at approximately CAD $50–80, with key markets in the USA, China, Japan, and South Korea. The challenge is converting Icewine from a gift purchase into a serious dessert wine category alongside Sauternes and German TBA on specialist lists.

## a) Grape variety/varieties and region (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Chardonnay-dominant with Pinot Nero, Franciacorta, Lombardy. Fine persistent mousse and pale lemon-green colour indicate traditional method; white peach and melon over a satin, faintly buttery palate suggest Chardonnay dominance. Champagne was weighed but the fuller stone fruit and moderate-plus rather than racy acidity argue against the Marne; the absence of struck-match reduction and the softer acid line rule out England. The rounded, warm mid-palate fits a continental Italian climate, and 20–30 months' lees ageing shows in the biscuity texture.

**Wine 2** — Lambrusco di Sorbara, Emilia-Romagna. Vivid translucent ruby-pink with an ephemeral mousse. Fresh cherry, raspberry and violet with tangy cranberry acidity and light tannin grip mark a lightly sparkling red; the pale colour, aromatic lift and low perceived alcohol point to Sorbara rather than the deeper, fuller-bodied Grasparossa.

## b) Methods of production comparison (14 marks)

Both take a second fermentation, by opposite routes. Wine 1 is metodo classico: base wine fermented in stainless steel — the clean, untoasty fruit shows no oak — then tirage and bottle fermentation, with 20–30 months on lees before disgorgement and a low dosage giving a brut finish.

Wine 2 is tank-fermented in sealed autoclaves, which protects the primary cherry and violet aromatics that extended autolysis would erase. Fermentation is arrested to leave modest residual sugar and lower alcohol, balancing Sorbara's high malic acidity; the softer, quicker-dissipating mousse is the tank-method signature.

## c) Style and quality (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, elegant, very good quality; a non-vintage Franciacorta DOCG Brut at roughly €20–30. Lees texture and fruit concentration lift it above entry-level, but it lacks Riserva depth.

## d) Commercial position (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Aimed at export buyers of premium Italian traditional method, competing with entry-level Champagne and Cava Reserva at €25–30. Independent merchants and Italian-focused restaurant by-the-glass lists in Northern Europe, the US and Japan. Challenge: brand awareness against Champagne; opportunity: equivalent quality at lower cost.

**Wine 2** — On-trade and specialist retail, strongest in northern Italy and diaspora markets, plus the UK, Germany and the US where premium Lambrusco is shedding its cheap image. Low alcohol and food-friendliness suit aperitivo service; the category's residual reputation is the obstacle, the lighter-alcohol trend the tailwind at around €15.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, four wines / four countries

## a) Grape variety and origin (4 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Grenache-based Tawny, Barossa Valley, Australia.** Tawny-mahogany colour with a watery olive rim and high viscosity, plus obvious spirit warmth (high alcohol, ~19–20%) place this in the wood-aged fortified family before the nose is considered. Pronounced rancio — burnt orange, dates, salted caramel, varnish, black tea — with sweetness held by only medium(+) acid indicates very long oxidative cask ageing, almost certainly fractional-blending/solera. Douro Tawny was the leading alternative, but a Douro of this maturity shows a finer, drier walnut line and higher acid tension; this is broader, sweeter and more toffee-laden, pointing to a warm New World origin. Rutherglen Muscat was eliminated — no grapey, floral Muscat signature.

**Wine 2 — Ribolla Gialla, Goriška Brda, Slovenia.** Deep gold with a slight haze, plus real phenolic grip on a white wine, points to extended skin maceration rather than to colour from oak or age alone. Moderate alcohol and a saline, taut acid line rule out a warm-climate origin. Dried apricot, quince paste, beeswax, toasted almond and an oxidative walnut edge, with a whisper of brett, are the amber-wine signature of the Collio/Brda continuum. Friulano was considered but shows greener almond and less waxy weight; Georgian Rkatsiteli would carry more overt qvevri tannin and tea-leaf grip. The quince/beeswax weight over a firm acid frame favours Ribolla Gialla, and the Slovenian side of the border.

**Wine 3 — Gewurztraminer, Alsace (Sélection de Grains Nobles).** Deep gold, very high viscosity, and unmistakable rose petal, lychee and fresh ginger make the variety essentially unarguable; no other grape gives that aromatic. The critical structural read is the alcohol: distinctly low warmth, ~9–10%, against high sweetness, meaning fermentation stopped by yeast exhaustion at extreme must weight, not by fortification. That combination in Alsace is SGN rather than Vendanges Tardives. Emerging kerosene and lanolin indicate 15+ years of bottle age.

**Wine 4 — Tempranillo rosado, Ribera del Duero, Spain.** Cherry-red with a crimson rim — far deeper than Provençal pale-salmon convention — plus medium body and warmth at ~13.5–14%, yet high acidity. Provence Grenache/Cinsault was eliminated on colour depth and acid line; Tavel would be softer and more Grenache-herbal. The combination of ripe strawberry/pomegranate fruit with genuinely high acidity is the tell: this is not simply a hot site but a high-altitude continental one, where cold nights preserve acid at full phenolic ripeness — Duero valley, and the black-pepper/vanilla frame reads Tempranillo rather than Garnacha.

## b) Style and winemaking (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Grapes picked at high sugar, fermentation arrested early by neutral spirit to retain around 100 g/L sugar and 19.5% alcohol. The intensity of rancio and the drying, concentrating effect visible in the viscosity indicate decades in small, old oak in hot, un-temperature-controlled sheds, refreshed by fractional blending so the wine carries very old material within an NV blend.

**Wine 2** — Hands-off, low-intervention intent: whole-bunch or destemmed fruit fermented on skins for weeks, ambient yeasts, no SO₂ protection during ferment (hence the oxidative walnut and light brett), no fining or filtration (the haze). Ageing in large neutral wood — no oak flavour, only texture and gentle oxygen.

**Wine 3** — Multiple tries through the vineyard selecting shrivelled berries, part-passerillage with only partial noble rot. Slow, cool, spontaneous ferment over months, halted by alcohol intolerance; aged in old foudres, which leave no oak imprint — the purity of rose and lychee is protected rather than overlaid.

**Wine 4** — A serious rosé, not a by-product: short skin contact of a few hours to gain that cherry colour, cool-fermented, with a portion evidently fermented or aged in barrel and on lees to give the vanilla pod note and mid-palate breadth. No malolactic — the acid remains taut and citrus-edged.

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding for its category; the concentration and rancio complexity outstrip a 20-year Tawny and compete with 30–40 year age-statement wines. Sold in small formats through specialist independents and fine-wine lists at £70–100 per half; niche, ageless, a collector and sommelier wine rather than a volume line.

**Wine 2** — Very good quality within the amber category; the phenolic frame and length justify it, though the brett will divide opinion. Independent specialists, natural-wine bars and by-the-glass in progressive restaurants, £30–40; competes with Collio and Kakheti amber wines.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding, top of the Alsace legal ladder. The house has deliberately bottled below the sugar SGN permits, keeping the wine articulate rather than cloying — the second-order mark of a great address. £80–120 per half; fine-wine merchants, drink now to 2040.

**Wine 4** — Very good quality for rosé and unusually ageworthy, but commercially challenged: at £18–22 it sits far above Provence pricing in a category where consumers buy pale colour. Best placed on-trade, by-the-glass in Spain, and in export markets that already buy the estate's reds.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, five-country sweet/fortified flight

## a) Origin, production method and variety (5 x 10)

**Wine 1 — Austria, Burgenland, Seewinkel (Illmitz).** Deep gold and markedly viscous, with no spirit warmth whatsoever and a weightless, cool alcohol impression around 8–9%, this is an unfortified, naturally-stopped ferment rather than a fortified or muted style. The huge sweetness sits against fine rather than searing acidity, and the aromatics are stewed apricot, honey and pineapple — noble rot, not the pure frozen-fruit precision of Eiswein, which would show a shriller, more linear acid line. Riesling was considered and rejected: there is no lime or petrol, and the palate is broad and honeyed rather than incisive, pointing instead to a neutral-to-mildly-aromatic blend base such as Welschriesling with Chardonnay. The saline persistence on the finish is the origin marker — that brackish note belongs to the shallow lake-influenced botrytis vineyards east of the Neusiedlersee. Under the skin: at this sugar level with only ~8.5% alcohol the ferment stalled of its own accord at a must weight far beyond the legal minimum for its Prädikat, and the absence of overt oak means nothing masks it — a wine tasting a full tier above its label.

**Wine 2 — France, Roussillon (Banyuls, rimage style).** Garnet, high viscosity, and unmistakable spirit heat at ~16.5% with obvious residual sugar: this is a fortified red, made by mutage — grape spirit added mid-ferment to arrest fermentation and retain sugar. Port was weighed, but there is no firm tannic grip, no drying grip of long spirit-aged Tawny, and the fruit is red-toned cherry and raspberry with only hints of prune, so this is a young, reductively-handled vin doux naturel bottled early to preserve fruit rather than aged oxidatively. The savoury, faintly saline lift over Grenache Noir's raspberry signature points to the schist terraces of the Roussillon coast.

**Wine 3 — Italy, Emilia-Romagna (Romagna DOCG passito).** Deep gold, viscous, medium alcohol with no spirit heat, medium(+) acid and roughly 120 g/L of sugar. Candied orange peel, saffron and hay indicate botrytis working on grapes further concentrated by drying — a passito with noble rot, not a straight late harvest. Sauternes was considered and excluded: no beeswax-and-new-oak frame, and the acid is softer and the texture more enveloping than Bordeaux gives. The honeyed, hay-like neutrality with silky rather than nervy structure fits a native Italian white of moderate acidity — Albana — dried indoors and fermented to a natural stop.

**Wine 4 — USA, California (San Joaquin/Madera).** Gold, only medium viscosity, warm at ~15% with high sugar: a fortified Muscat where spirit was added early to leave a fresh, barely-fermented profile. The dried and fresh orange, mandarin and floral top note are varietally specific to Orange Muscat, and the slight spritz and short, medium(-) finish reveal an early-bottled, protectively-handled commercial style, not an oxidative one. Rutherglen was ruled out — that shows rancio, raisin and tawny colour from long wood ageing; this is pale, primary and simple.

**Wine 5 — New Zealand, Marlborough.** Gold, viscous, low alcohol ~9%, high acidity, sweet: again a naturally-arrested botrytis ferment. Lemon peel, lime, tangerine and white flowers over honey and a genuine textural grip identify Riesling; Chenin was considered but there is no quince-and-wax weight, and the acid is tartaric-bright rather than appley. The combination of high ripeness, retained aromatic lift and screaming acid indicates a cool, sunny, low-humidity site where rot was encouraged late rather than arriving early — Marlborough rather than the Mosel, which would show slatier restraint and less citrus-peel breadth.

## b) Quality and commercial position (5 x 8)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding, benchmark quality — the equivalent of a top Prädikat TBA or first-growth Sauternes. Independent specialists and fine-dining lists; around €40 per 375ml; strong in Germany, the US and Japan; competes with Sauternes Premier Cru and Tokaji 6 Puttonyos.

**Wine 2.** Very good quality within its category, appellation-level rimage rather than a long-aged rancio bottling. Around €25–30; French domestic on-trade, Benelux, specialist merchants; competes with Maury and young Vintage Port. The challenge is a structurally declining VDN category.

**Wine 3.** Very good, DOCG passito level, but its obscurity is commercial ballast. Around €30 per 500ml through Italian restaurant lists and specialist importers; a hand-sell against better-known Vin Santo and Recioto di Soave.

**Wine 4.** Good, sound commercial quality — no complexity, no ageing pretension. Around $18 per 375ml in US premium supermarkets and off-trade; an accessible entry point for consumers moving up from Moscato; competes with Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise on price.

**Wine 5.** Very good quality, comparable to a fine Auslese/BA; a small-volume flagship at around NZ$35 per 375ml through cellar door, independents and by-the-glass; competes with Alsace SGN. Volume is tiny and the sweet-wine market soft.

## c) Residual sugar and alcohol (5 x 7)

**Wine 1** ~150 g/L RS, 8.5% alcohol. **Wine 2** ~80 g/L RS, 16.5%. **Wine 3** ~120 g/L RS, 13%. **Wine 4** ~120 g/L RS, 15%. **Wine 5** ~150 g/L RS, 9%.

**Wine 3 — Touriga Franca-led Douro field blend, 10 Year Old Tawny.** Pale tawny-amber, olive rim, sweet, spirit ~20%. Walnut, dried fig, caramel and gentle rancio confirm long oxidative cask ageing. Not Australian tawny — no treacly muscat weight; not Amontillado — sweetness and a red-fruit remnant persist. Fruit still visible beneath the nuttiness indicates the ten-year tier, not twenty.

**Wine 4 — Gewürztraminer, Marlborough, New Zealand.** Medium gold, oily, off-dry (~8 g/L); lychee, rose petal, ginger, Turkish delight, with phenolic bitterness on the finish. Muscat ruled out — no grapey freshness. Alsace considered, but the moderate ~13% and retained acid line are too fresh; Alsace ripeness would give 14%+ and more unctuous weight.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 8)

**1.** Deliberately oxidative, textural, age-worthy. Wild-yeast ferment, full malolactic, extended ageing in large seasoned foudre. Critically, the honeyed patina carries no volatility or bruising — that indicates topped-up, protective handling over 18–24 months, an intentional style, not neglect. No new oak.

**2.** Very ripe, late-picked fruit; short warm skin ferment for colour and tannin, then fortification with neutral spirit at roughly half sugar to retain ~90 g/L, and a few years in large old wood — hence primary fruit and unresolved tannin.

**3.** A multi-vintage blend averaging ten years in seasoned pipes; controlled oxidation and evaporation deliver the tawny hue and rancio. Fortified early on skins, with polished tannin implying gentle extraction.

**4.** Reductive, protective handling: whole-bunch pressing with brief skin contact for aromatics, cool stainless ferment, no oak and no malolactic — the crisp line and absence of dairy notes — the ferment arrested to leave light sugar buffering the phenolics.

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 7)

**1.** Outstanding, far above its Côtes du Rhône tier — cru-level concentration and grip. Allocation-only through fine-wine merchants, £120+, competing with Château-Grillet and grand cru Alsace; drink now to fifteen years.

**2.** Very good within Australia's fortified category. AU$45, cellar door and specialist off-trade, modest UK/Nordic export; competes with LBV Port against a declining fortified market.

**3.** Very good, a genuine 10 Year Old age indication at £28–32. Premium supermarket and on-trade by-the-glass digestif or cheese listing.

**4.** Good quality estate-tier varietal, NZ$28. Independent specialists and premium supermarkets in NZ, UK and USA; competes with Alsace Pinot Gris, limited by Gewürztraminer's narrow following.

## a) Grape variety and region (5 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Petit Manseng, Jurançon, South-West France. Deep gold with thick, slow tears and a sweet, full palate: a concentrated sweet white. Very high acid plus tropical over-ripeness with no rot markers points to shrivelled Petit Manseng.

Youthful ruby, opaque and staining, sweet, with obvious spirit warmth well above 18% and medium(+) grippy tannin over blackberry, cassis, plum and dark chocolate. A fortified red. **Wine 3** — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Rutherglen, Victoria. Tawny-brown with an olive-green rim and viscous legs — extreme oxidative age. Old Tawny was considered but shows dried cherry and no grape musk; PX would be near-black and cloying with lower acidity.

**Wine 4** — Riesling, Mosel, Germany. Lemon-green, low alcohol around 8%, off-dry, with high, mouth-watering acidity, crushed stone, lemon rind, white peach and mineral drive. Austria and Alsace are ruled out by the alcohol alone; only Mosel Prädikat combines this fragility of alcohol with such acid tension. Spätlese level from a slate Einzellage.

**Wine 5** — Palomino Fino, Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Pale gold, watery-rimmed, bone dry, roughly 15%, with pronounced flor: sourdough, roasted almond, chamomile and marine salinity. Fino from Jerez city was considered, but the sea-spray delicacy and green-olive brine point to Sanlúcar. Manzanilla.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (5 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Sweetness achieved by passerillage, not noble rot: grapes left hanging into late autumn on Petit Manseng's thick skins, dehydrating to concentrate sugar and acid together. The absence of botrytis funk and the pure, lively fruit indicate healthy fruit picked in successive tries. Fermentation stopped by chilling and racking off yeast at around 50 g/l residual sugar, leaving moderate alcohol. Subtle spice rather than vanilla suggests a portion of old barrique with lees stirring; no overt new oak.

**Wine 2** — Sweetness from arrested fermentation: fortification with grape spirit at roughly 5–7% completed alcohol, killing the yeast and retaining around 100 g/l sugar, which explains the sweetness alongside the tannin. Robotic or foot-trodden rapid extraction gives colour and tannin in two to three days. Ageing in large old wood for three to four years — no bottle-age tertiary character — then blending across lots, fining and filtration for a stable, ready-to-drink Reserve.

**Wine 3** — A wholly different mechanism: grapes harvested raisined at very high must weight, briefly fermented then fortified early to retain massive sugar, followed by decades of oxidative maturation in old wood, warm and ullaged, then blended in a solera-style hierarchy of averaged ages. The rancio, burnt toffee and olive rim are all cask-derived; the seamless spirit reflects long marriage rather than recent fortification.

**Wine 4** — Sweetness natural and residual: high must weight from late picking on steep slate, whole-bunch pressed for purity, then a slow, cool, spontaneous fermentation halted early by chilling and sulphuring at around 45–55 g/l sugar. No malolactic — the acidity is razor-edged — and neutral vessels, most likely old Fuder, with no oak signature. Here the second-order point: a lesser grower would have chased sweetness for its own sake, but the low alcohol, mineral drive and light residual sugar show a deliberate choice to pick ripe fruit and stop early, using sugar only to counterweigh acid.

**Wine 5** — Base wine from free-run Palomino at low alcohol, fortified precisely to 15% to permit flor, then biological ageing in butts under a living veil in criaderas and solera. Bottled unclarified and unfiltered — the depth of texture and yeasty complexity confirm an *en rama* saca.

**Wine 1** — Very good quality for the appellation, top-tier Jurançon rather than a generic moelleux, at around €22 retail. Independent specialists and by-the-glass dessert lists; competes with Coteaux du Layon and Alsace Vendange Tardive. Challenge: the appellation's obscurity.

**Wine 2** — Good quality at Finest Reserve level — clearly above basic Ruby in depth, but without the concentration or fine tannin of a Vintage Port. Around £14 in premium supermarkets and multiples, sold on brand recognition in the UK and Northern Europe.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding within Rutherglen's Classic tier; the complexity approaches Grand, but the freshness and fruit definition keep it below that. Around AU$35 for 500 ml; specialist off-trade and cellar door, strong domestically, a sommelier's curiosity abroad.

**Wine 4** — Outstanding quality, Spätlese from a Grosse Lage-quality site, around €30. Independent specialists and Michelin lists in the USA, UK and Japan. Drink now to 2035 and beyond; the only commercial obstacle is consumer suspicion of sweetness.

**Wine 5** — Very good quality, a specialist *en rama* bottling rather than a standard Manzanilla, around €18 for 500 ml. Sherry bars, tapas on-trade and independents; delicate and short-lived once opened, which limits by-the-glass listings.

## b) Mechanism of sweetness and key winemaking decisions (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Passerillage — shrivelling on the vine through successive late tries, water evaporating through thick skins. Fermentation deliberately arrested before dryness. Integrated vanilla and spice confirm barrel fermentation and roughly 18 months in oak, with extract and sugar balancing the wood.

**Wine 2.** Selective harvesting of over-ripe and lightly botrytised fruit, fermentation halted at Auslese sugar levels by chilling and racking. The defining decision is preserving high tartaric acidity — sugar/acid tension is the style's signature. Absence of oak indicates stainless steel or large neutral casks, protecting terroir transparency.

**Wine 3.** The passito method: grapes dried on graticci for several months, then a years-long slow fermentation in small sealed caratelli under semi-oxidative conditions without topping up. Depth of colour and walnut-caramel complexity suggest five to six years' ageing; the clean finish confirms volatile acidity was held in check.

**Wine 4.** Cryoextraction: fruit left on the vine until roughly −8°C, freezing the water while concentrated sugar stays liquid, then pressed sub-zero. Slow stainless-steel fermentation is arrested at about 9% perceived alcohol; no oak or oxidative character. Harvest timing is the critical call — too early and concentration is insufficient, too late and the crop is lost.

**Wine 1 — Savagnin, Jura.** Deep gold, viscous, with walnut, curry, saffron, green olive and aged parmesan rind. Decisively, there is **no spirit warmth** — the palate reads warm and medium-plus, perhaps 14–14.5%, with a fine preserved-lemon acid line and no brandy edge — ruling out Amontillado and dry Sercial Madeira. That leaves unfortified *sous voile* ageing. The sotolon/beeswax with dried apricot points to Savagnin rather than oxidative Szamorodni (Furmint gives smoky stone fruit) or old oxidised Chenin (quince, but no sotolon).

**Wine 2 — Palomino, Jerez.** Amber, bone dry, high acid, and marked spirit heat near 18–19% confirms fortification. Roasted nuts, caramel and a persistent saline/iodine thread with a bready yeast note reads as flor-then-oxidative: Amontillado. Madeira is excluded by the absence of volatile lift and searing malic bite; straight Oloroso by the surviving flor markers.

## b) Method of production, with reference to oxidation management (2 x 9 marks)

Both are aged beneath a veil of yeast; the difference is that only one uses fortification as the lever.

**Wine 1:** fermented dry, then racked into old neutral 228-litre barrels deliberately left un-topped. That headspace allows a spontaneous *voile* to establish — only possible because natural alcohol sits below roughly 15%. Oxidation is managed *by the yeast*, which scavenges oxygen and generates acetaldehyde and sotolon, while ingress through wood is slow across six years or more. No new oak, minimal sulphur. The under-the-skin point: identical rancio complexity is reached with no fortification whatsoever.

**Wine 2:** Palomino fermented dry, then fortified to ~15% to keep flor alive for biological ageing. A second fortification above 17% kills the veil and switches the wine to fully oxidative ageing; fractional blending through criaderas and solera averages age and refreshes, while cask evaporation concentrates extract and lifts perceived acidity.

**Wine 1:** uncompromising, savoury, bone dry, built for cuisine and further decades. Outstanding quality at the summit of Arbois, comparable with Château-Chalon; around €70 in the 62cl clavelin. Very good quality; a premium bodega's aged Amontillado of perhaps 12 years average solera age, above entry level but short of VORS depth; around £22 for 75cl. # Mock answer — Paper 3, five sweet wines

## Wine 1

**a)** Gewurztraminer, Alsace, Vendanges Tardives level. Gold colour with slow, thick tears, and a pronounced nose of rose petal, lychee, Turkish delight and candied ginger — that trio of floral, lychee and sweet spice is varietally decisive and no other white gives it. Riesling was weighed and rejected: the emerging petrol note is there, but the low aromatic acidity, oily breadth and warm, generous ~12.5% weight are Gewurztraminer's, not Riesling's tartaric line. Germany was considered, but the cinnamon-clove spice and smoky, slightly phenolic edge point to the Vosges foothills rather than the Pfalz.

**b)** Passerillage on the vine — extended hang time concentrating sugars, with a minor botrytis contribution shown by the dried-apricot and honey layer. Not fortified (no spirit heat) and not frozen fruit (acidity is racy but not searing).

**c)** Off-dry to medium-sweet, richly textured, with sugar carried by acid rather than by alcohol. Winemaking is deliberately non-interventionist: no oak, no vanilla or toast, so old foudre or neutral tank; the clean, unbruised aromatics suggest a slow whole-bunch press and a long cool ferment arrested naturally as the yeast stalled, leaving perhaps 40–50 g/L. No malolactic — the acid is too pure and linear for that. Bottled young to preserve the floral top notes.

**d)** Outstanding quality, top-tier Alsace Grand Cru VT, retailing around €50–60. Independent specialists and gastronomy lists; strong in Japan, Scandinavia and the UK. Small-volume, sold to collectors of Alsace rather than to a generic sweet-wine buyer.

## Wine 2

**a)** A botrytis blend, Ruster Ausbruch, Burgenland, Austria. Gold, viscous, with marzipan, fresh fig and a distinctly bread-doughy botrytis lift. Sauternes was the obvious alternative but is ruled out by the absence of new-oak vanilla and the more red-fruited, fig-and-nut register; Tokaji Aszú was rejected because there is no orange-peel-and-saffron oxidative bite or Furmint's mouth-scouring acid spine. The moderate ~13% warmth with only medium(+) aromatic intensity fits Rust's neusiedl-lake botrytis over a mixed, non-aromatic planting.

**b)** Noble rot from lake-driven autumn humidity, hand-selected in successive tries; fermentation slows and stops of its own accord in the high-sugar must.

**c)** Sweet but restrained — juicy rather than unctuous, sugar around 100–120 g/L fully integrated. No dominant oak, so ferment and short ageing in large used casks; wild-yeast complexity is likely, given the bready nuance. Fermentation halted by alcohol and sulphur addition rather than by chilling alone.

**d)** Very good to outstanding, an official Prädikat-equivalent Ausbruch above Beerenauslese, around €40 per half bottle. On-trade by the glass in Austria and Germany, specialist retail elsewhere; the challenge is Austria's weak international recognition for sweet wine against Sauternes.

## Wine 3

**a)** Sauvignon Blanc with Sémillon, Central Valley, Chile — Colchagua. Gold and viscous, with candied citrus peel, peach conserve and mango over only light botrytis. The tropicality plus a modest, cool-feeling ~11% weight and refreshing but not racy acidity says warm New World, and the mango-pineapple thread is unlike Bordeaux's Sémillon lanolin. Australia was considered; the lack of oak and the pure, unsmoky citrus lift is more Chilean.

**b)** Late harvest — deliberate over-ripening with partial raisining, only marginal noble rot. Fermentation stopped early, most likely by chilling to near 0°C then sterile filtration and sulphuring, leaving low alcohol and high sugar.

**c)** Medium-sweet, clean, fruit-forward and unoaked: stainless steel, cool ferment with a selected aromatic yeast, no lees work, no malolactic — the acid is unbroadened. A commercial, technically precise style built for immediate charm; medium(+) finish, not built for cellar.

**d)** Good quality, a step below the flight's European examples, retailing around US$12–15 for a half bottle. Supermarket and mid-market off-trade in the US, UK and Brazil; excellent value entry point for consumers moving up from cheap Moscato.

## Wine 4

**a)** Riesling, South Island New Zealand — Waipara. Lemon-green, only medium viscosity, with lime zest, green apple, jasmine, wet slate and nascent petrol; the varietal call is secure. The candidate origin is Mosel Kabinett/Spätlese, and the low perceived alcohol — light-bodied, barely 8–9% — supports it. But the grapefruit-pith grip and riper white-peach flesh, with less of the filigree tartaric etch and slate-sourness of the Mosel, moves it to a cool maritime New World site.

**b)** Fermentation arrested with sugar still in the wine: chilled, sulphured, sterile-filtered, leaving roughly 45 g/L against very high acidity.

**c)** Medium-sweet but reading almost dry because of the acid; steely, reductive, unoaked, no lees influence, no malo — a purity-first style. Long finish. Youthful; will gain kerosene and honey over five to eight years and hold fifteen.

**d)** Very good quality, top-tier single-vineyard for its region, around NZ$35. Independent specialists and Asian on-trade, where its low alcohol and sweetness suit spice; the challenge is consumer resistance to sweet Riesling labelling.

Bone dry, high acid, and the warmth reads generous, around 14.5%, but never spirity — which rules out Amontillado or Palo Cortado, where fortification to 16–18% shows as heat across the finish. Oxidative white Rioja was weighed and rejected: Viura gives nuttiness but not this saline flor lift or curry depth. That combination points to Savagnin *sous voile*. Within Jura, the citrus-peel lift and surviving yellow plum indicate Arbois rather than the denser, more monolithic Château-Chalon. Under the skin: six-plus years under veil have not hollowed the mid-palate — fruit persists beneath the rancio — indicating a thick, healthy voile and limited evaporative loss.

Marlborough was eliminated: pyrazine is restrained, alcohol moderate, the finish chalky and saline rather than exuberantly tropical. The flight opposes deliberate oxidation against protective reduction.

Wine 2 is its mirror: gentle pressing, cool fermentation in stainless steel or large neutral vessels, malolactic blocked — the acid line stays taut with no lactic softness — a short lees period to build that muscular texture, then early bottling to preserve flint and fruit.

Crushed slate, Mirabelle, nectarine, jasmine and the first suggestion of petrol. Austria and Alsace excluded on alcohol and on the wet-stone signature. A single steep slate site; Prädikat Spätlese in weight.

**Wine 5 — Torrontés, Valle de Uco, Mendoza.** Gold, viscous, sweet, low alcohol ~11.5%, cut by medium(+) citrus acid: rose petal, orange blossom, lychee, dried apricot, candied peel, ginger. Muscat of Alexandria was the alternative; the ginger-and-orange-peel edge over pure grapey musk points instead to its Argentine offspring. High-altitude Uco.

## b) Style and defining winemaking decisions (5 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** A rich but dry-tasting-edged VT built on ripeness, not rot. Successive hand-picking tries produced must weight sufficient for both ~13% alcohol *and* substantial sugar — that dual outcome tells me fruit came in well above the legal VT minimum; the producer is buying concentration, not clearing a hurdle. Whole-bunch pressed slowly with no skin maceration (no bitterness on an already phenolic variety), fermented cool with ambient yeast in old, neutral wood, the ferment stalling naturally; malolactic avoided to keep what little acid there is, no new oak.

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Origin (10 marks)

Deep gold, high viscosity, dried apricot, marmalade, beeswax and almond paste indicate a sweet wine made by drying grapes rather than by botrytis alone. Riesling was excluded by the absence of lime, petrol and racy tartaric drive; Muscat by the near-total absence of primary floral lift. The hazelnut and gently oxidative nuttiness signal a passito with controlled oxidation during drying, and the saffron and chamomile markers point to Erbaluce di Caluso in Piedmont.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Rack-drying over several months is the defining decision, concentrating sugar and building the nutty complexity. Fermentation of such high-sugar must was slow and halted before dryness, leaving the sweetness that balances the intensity. The oxidative edge is stylistic, not faulty, and suggests maturation in older wood — measured oxygen without new-oak flavour — followed by extended ageing before release.

Very high quality, DOCG Erbaluce di Caluso Passito, £40–60 per half-bottle through specialist importers. Complexity and length sit at the top of a very small category. Riesling was the serious alternative — the acidity is high and taut — but there is no petrol or lime blossom, no linear citric austerity; instead the radish-herbal note and a slightly rounder, fuller body. Moderately elevated ripeness at Spätlese level with crystalline acidity favours the Kamptal's granite and loess over broader Niederösterreich, and over the warmer Kremstal, which would give less natural acid retention.

# Mock Answer — Sweet Wine Pair (Riesling Auslese / Recioto di Soave)

## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Riesling, Middle Mosel, Germany. Lime, wet slate and incipient petrol over piercing acidity. Chenin Blanc was weighed — it shares high acid and a botrytis-sweet tradition — but lacks this linear mineral tension and petrol lift. The near-weightless palate and very low perceived alcohol (~8%) rule out Alsace or Rheingau, both of which would carry more body and a broader acid line; the precise lime/apricot balance, rather than the Saar's steelier austerity, suggests a Middle Mosel premier site.

**Wine 2** — Garganega, Recioto di Soave, Veneto. Deep gold, viscous, with dried apricot, quince, roasted almond and beeswax. The warm, full palate (perceived ~13%) excludes Riesling- or Chenin-based passito. Vin Santo would show sharper nut-and-orange-peel oxidation; Sauternes would offer botrytis elegance without this raisined concentration and aromatic oak.

## b) How sweetness was achieved and key winemaking decisions (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Selective late picking of botrytis-affected berries at Auslese level; sugar concentration occurs in the vineyard through noble rot and shrivel, not in the cellar. Fermentation is arrested early — hence the low alcohol — leaving sugar suspended against very high natural acidity. Cool, slow ferment in inert vessels with reductive handling and no oak: the decisive choice is protection of fragile floral and citrus aromatics.

**Wine 2** — Appassimento: whole bunches dried on racks for some five months, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour. Honey, beeswax and saffron suggest botrytis intervened during drying. Fermentation is halted before dryness, retaining sugar at a higher alcohol than Wine 1. Roughly two years in French oak — integrated wood, toasted almond, balsamic — adds structure without masking the dried fruit. Where Wine 1 preserves, Wine 2 builds.

## c) Style, quality and commercial position (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding; upper-end Auslese approaching Beerenauslese intensity, €35–60. Fine-wine specialists and auction channels in Germany, the UK, US and Japan. Drinking now but will gain honeyed depth over 20–30 years — a collector's bottle as much as a table wine.

**Wine 2** — Very good, among the better Recioto di Soave DOCG, €25–40. A richer, Mediterranean alternative to Sauternes for drinkers who prefer dried-fruit concentration to botrytis lift. Independent specialists and premium Italian restaurant lists; reach is capped by the appellation's niche standing and depends on discovery selling.

## d) Level of residual sugar (2 × 2 marks)

**Wine 1** — Approximately 100–130 g/L.

**Wine 2** — Approximately 120–160 g/L.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Harvested at very high Brix for the preserves character; fermentation arrested by chilling or light fortification to retain sugar. Velvety texture with restrained vanilla indicates French oak, predominantly used cooperage rather than new. No reduction, so oxidatively handled with moderate SO₂ and a sugar-tolerant yeast.

**Wine 2** — The opposite philosophy: fortification early to leave high sugar, then prolonged oxidative ageing in old barrel with fractional blending of vintages, concentrating the wine through evaporation. **Wine 1** — Very good; premium single-vineyard tier, around $35–50. Its competitive set is PX Sherry and old Tawny, but the point of difference is that the base grape is aromatic, so Muscat's floral grapiness survives decades of oxidation — a niche no Port can copy, and one that sells on education rather than shelf presence.
