# Mock answer — Paper 3: three Muscats from three countries

## a) Region of origin and grape variety (3 × 8 marks)

Pronounced grapey musk, rose petal and orange blossom in all three glasses puts the Muscat family across the flight; the wines differ by mechanism and climate, not variety group.

**Wine 1 — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, southern Rhône.** Lemon-gold with no oxidative browning; sweet (~110 g/L) with discreet spirit warmth over a fresh mid-palate — perceived at roughly 15%, so mutage rather than natural sugar. Muscat de Rivesaltes was the real rival; this taut, faintly saline acid line and unbaked mandarin/lychee fruit point to cooler limestone slopes rather than Roussillon's flat schist heat. Setúbal is ruled out — no cask-derived oxidation.

**Wine 2 — Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge (Brown Muscat), Rutherglen, Victoria; Classic tier.** Mahogany with olive rim, staining tears, hugely sweet (200 g/L+), unmistakable spirit heat near 18%. Rancio, malt and cold tea sit over a vivid raisined-muscat lift, which eliminates Pedro Ximénez (fig, molasses, no floral musk) and aged Tawny (no grapiness).

**Wine 3 — Orange Muscat, California.** Pale lemon, almost no palate warmth — delicate, low alcohol around 4–5% — medium-sweet, high acid, explosive tangerine and orange blossom. Moscato d'Asti was the obvious alternative, but there is no persistent frizzante and the fruit is riper and more marmalade-inflected than Piedmont's; a warm New World site picked early to hold acidity.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — a reductive, aperitif-style Vin Doux Naturel. Fermentation arrested at 5–6% by adding neutral grape spirit; no skin contact, cool inert ferment, oxygen excluded and bottled young. The complete absence of nutty amber notes is itself the decision: oxidative ageing deliberately avoided to protect the floral primary fruit.

**Wine 2** — deliberately oxidative and concentrated. Very late-picked, part-shrivelled fruit fortified early, then long maturation in old small casks in hot above-ground stores. Crucially, the toffee/rancio layer sits *over* fresh raisin rather than replacing it: that betrays blending of a small proportion of much older reserve into young material — exactly the Classic (5–10 year average) intent, not Grand or Rare.

**Wine 3** — not fortified. Ferment stopped at ~4% by chilling and sterile filtration under pressure, leaving ~90 g/L. No oak, no malolactic, no lees; aromatic yeast, cool tank ferment, sterile bottling under screwcap for freshness.

## c) Quality and commercial position (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — very good quality, a benchmark for its cru VDN appellation: complex, long, sweetness beautifully cut by acid. Around €20/50cl, independent specialists and French on-trade; drink now to five years.

**Wine 2** — very good, top of the Classic tier but short of Grand's mid-palate depth. Around AU$30/375ml; specialist retail and sommelier lists in the UK and US. Distinctive but needs evangelising.

**Wine 3** — acceptable to good commercial quality; clean, one-dimensional, true to type. Around US$10 in supermarkets, aimed at new and sweeter-toothed drinkers, competing with Moscato d'Asti. Volume opportunity; price and low-alcohol perception cap trade-up.

Completed malolactic fermentation is evident in the rounded, creamy mid-palate. Whole-bunch pressing explains the clean colour and absence of bitterness.

### c) Quality (5 marks)

Very good, at the premium end of the Cava hierarchy. It competes credibly with entry-level Grande Marque Champagne NV at roughly £20–25, offering comparable autolytic complexity at a lower price point.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Targets the premium independent specialist and fine-dining channel. Export markets in the UK, Germany, and Scandinavia suit the Brut Nature style. The challenge is Cava's lingering reputation for cheap commercial production; the opportunity is clear value against Champagne.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Country and Region (7 marks)

More intense and better-integrated autolysis than Wine 2 — brioche, beeswax, and toasted bread fully absorbed into ripe pear and honeyed stone fruit — combined with a pillowy mousse and long mineral-edged finish points to **Champagne, France**. The fleshy Pinot Noir-derived red-fruit undertone alongside Chardonnay freshness, and precision exceeding any NV Grande Marque, indicate a **Brut Vintage Champagne** from a riper, warmer harvest year.

### b) Key Production Decisions (8 marks)

Traditional method with a minimum four years on lees, evidenced by the depth and full integration of autolytic character. A low but perceptible dosage integrates seamlessly, adding weight without apparent sweetness — a confident balancing decision reflecting the base wine's natural ripeness. The blend of black and white grapes is evident in the red-fruited undertone beneath the apple-citrus core. No oak influence is detectable; stainless steel fermentation preserves fruit precision and allows the vintage character to read clearly.

### c) Quality (5 marks)

Outstanding — at the apex of sparkling wine globally. The balance between generous fruit and lively acidity reflects deliberate assemblage of complementary parcels; the house philosophy is as legible as the vintage. Retails at £60–80+.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Premium on-trade and independent specialist, sustaining fine-dining lists and luxury hospitality. Key export markets: US, UK, Japan, Hong Kong, Australia. A vintage release creates a collectible dimension absent from NV wines, sustaining long-term brand equity. Price accessibility is the challenge; universal benchmark status is the opportunity.

---

## Wine 4

### a) Country and Region (7 marks)

Traditional-method autolysis — brioche, almond, baked apple — is layered with a pronounced saline, sea-spray mineral quality and warm stone-fruit generosity absent from Wine 3. California was considered but lacks this briny precision. Yarra Valley is a candidate, yet the sustained oyster-shell salinity and stone-fruit/sea-spray tension point more specifically to **Tasmania, Australia**, where maritime influence and cool diurnal variation produce exactly this fruit-mineral interplay.

### b) Key Production Decisions (8 marks)

Traditional method with several years on lees, confirmed by well-integrated brioche and almond autolytic character. The saline mineral quality is a terroir imprint from cool maritime viticulture, not a winemaking intervention. Harvesting at full phenolic ripeness — relying on Tasmania's cool climate to retain structural acidity — explains the stone-fruit generosity without heaviness. Malolactic fermentation appears complete, contributing to the creamy mousse; stainless steel base-wine fermentation preserves primary fruit and mineral clarity.

### c) Quality (5 marks)

Very good to outstanding — the apex of Australian traditional-method sparkling. It competes credibly with premium Champagne, demonstrating autolytic depth alongside cool-climate fruit precision. At approximately AUD 80–100 (£40–55), it offers strong value relative to Champagne.

### d) Commercial Position (5 marks)

Targets the premium on-trade and independent specialist in Australia, with growing export potential in the UK, US, and parts of Asia. It competes with premium Champagne on fine-dining lists and with English sparkling wine in the cool-climate traditional-method segment. Growing curiosity about non-Champagne prestige sparklers is the opportunity; limited brand recognition outside Australia is the challenge.

---

## a) Grape variety (2 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Sémillon-dominant, with a minority of Sauvignon Blanc. Deep gold, heavy slow tears, a warm medium-plus body and generous spirit-free warmth I read at around 14%, held by only medium-plus acidity. That structural combination rules out the two obvious alternatives: a botrytised Chenin from the Layon, or a German Riesling BA, would both show a far racier, more tartaric acid line and noticeably less alcoholic weight at this sugar level. The waxy honey, roasted apricot and mirabelle plum are squarely botrytised Sémillon; the preserved-lemon lift and slight herbal edge indicate a Sauvignon component.

**Wine 2** — a Chardonnay and Welschriesling cuvée. Low warmth, perhaps 9%, with the full, lush body carried almost entirely by sugar rather than alcohol. The aromatic core is neutral: no lime or petrol, which eliminates Riesling; no grapey musk, which eliminates Muscat; no smoky marmalade or oxidative rancio edge, which eliminates Furmint and a Tokaji origin. The broad, creamy mid-palate suggests Chardonnay, the tangy neutral apple-skin frame and saline close Welschriesling.

## b) Sweetness mechanism and key decisions (2 x 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — noble rot, picked in successive tries as botrytis advanced. Whole bunches, slowly pressed for the concentrated free-run juice. The vanilla and discreet sweet spice point to fermentation and maturation in barrique, perhaps half new, over 18 months. Critically, the ferment ended *naturally*, yeast exhausting itself near 14%, leaving perhaps 120–130 g/L — hence the alcoholic weight. Malolactic avoided to protect acidity; sulfured and sterile filtered before bottling.

**Wine 2** — also botrytis, from autumn mists off a shallow lake, but a wholly different intent. Very high must weights fermented cool in stainless steel and then deliberately *arrested* early by chilling, SO2 and sterile filtration at around 9%, retaining far more sugar than Wine 1. No oak and no malolactic: the purity of white peach and that saline persistence are the point. The sweetness sits well above the legal Beerenauslese minimum, and the salinity alongside such low alcohol argues lake-shore Seewinkel rather than a hillside site.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — outstanding, unmistakably 1er Cru Classé Sauternes/Barsac: length, elegance and structure beyond a generic bottling. Around £50 per 75cl, sold through Independent Specialists and fine-dining dessert lists, by the glass; UK, US and Japan. Competes with Tokaji Aszú 6 puttonyos.

**Wine 2** — benchmark quality at Beerenauslese level, top of Austria's sweet hierarchy. Around £30 per 375ml, via Monopolies in Scandinavia and sommelier-driven specialists. Competes with German BA and Sauternes half-bottles; the challenge is a shrinking sweet-wine category.

# Mock answer — Paper 3 Question 1 (sparkling flight)

## a) Production method (4 x 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Traditional method, with long lees ageing and a single superior vintage behind it. The mousse is fine and persistent rather than frothy, and the autolytic register is deep and *worked* — brioche, fresh butter, meringue, toasted almond — which tank fermentation cannot generate because the wine spends only weeks, not years, on gross lees. Transfer method was considered and rejected: the bead is too fine and the texture too creamy for a wine filtered under pressure. The chalky, saline grip through the finish points to a chalk-soil origin and to whole-bunch pressing of first-press juice, with no phenolic coarseness anywhere.

**Wine 2** — Traditional method also, but with a far shorter lees period. Bottle-fermented character is present in the fine, tight bead, yet the autolysis is barely sketched — green almond only, no bread. Charmat was the serious alternative; I rule it out because tank wines of this weight show pear-drop and softer, larger bubbles, whereas this is austere and dry-boned. The pale salmon tint with no red-fruit weight indicates a very brief press-cut of dark-skinned grapes rather than saignée or blending.

**Wine 3** — Traditional method, short-to-moderate lees, made deliberately to preserve varietal aromatics. The lees signature is a whisper of brioche behind green apple, lime and fresh ginger — the winemaker has stopped short of masking the grape. Reductive, cool handling in tank before tirage is evident in the unblemished white-blossom and wet-stone lift; malolactic has been blocked, since the acid line is malic-sharp and zesty rather than broad and lactic.

**Wine 4** — Traditional method with a moderate lees ageing of around eighteen months and full malolactic conversion. The cashew-and-cream texture with soft, buttery breadth over citrus fruit is the fingerprint of complete malo in a cool-grown base wine, used here to soften a naturally searing acidity. The mousse is fine and creamy but the autolysis is nutty rather than deeply toasty, consistent with a multi-vintage blend built on reserve wines.

## b) Style, quality, commercial position (4 x 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — A Blanc de Blancs of real seriousness: taut, chalk-driven, low in perceived alcohol warmth (light-medium body, ~12%) and built for the table rather than the aperitif. Outstanding quality, Grand Cru vintage Champagne level, retailing around £90–120. Here is the tension worth naming: the wine tastes drier than its dosage, because a decade of lees has provided the mid-palate flesh that sugar usually buys — a house working at this level can afford to dose low precisely because the base material carries itself. Independent specialists, fine-dining lists, collectors in the UK, US and Japan.

**Wine 2** — A lean, low-alcohol, gastronomic aperitif style with almost no sugar and no oak. Very good quality within its category, at the top of a regional Spanish traditional-method DO but short of Champagne depth — the medium-minus finish is the limit. Around €20–25. Sells to independents and natural-leaning wine bars in Barcelona, Scandinavia and the Netherlands; the challenge is that it lacks the fruit generosity supermarket shoppers expect.

**Wine 3** — Varietally-driven, dry, aromatic and site-marked; a modern alpine Sekt made to show the grape, not the method. Very good quality, comparable to a premium German Winzersekt, around €25–30. Domestic Italian restaurant sales and German-speaking export markets; hard to sell blind against Prosecco at half the price.

**Wine 4** — A rounded, fruit-forward, cool-climate house-style blend, creamy and commercially generous. Very good quality, premium New World traditional-method tier, roughly £22–28 — competing directly with Crémant and entry NV Champagne on UK and Australian retail shelves and by-the-glass lists.

## c) Dosage category (4 x 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Brut, at the low end (around 5 g/l). Tart apple and citron zest read bone-dry, but there is a fractional roundness that Extra Brut would not give.

**Wine 2** — Brut Nature, zero dosage. The finish is angular and short with no sugar-derived flesh at all.

**Wine 3** — Brut, around 8–10 g/l; the sugar is detectable only as a softening of the grapefruit-pith bite.

**Wine 4** — Brut, around 8–9 g/l, needed to balance the very high natural acidity of the base.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Country and Grape Variety (6 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Germany, Riesling. Pale lemon-green, with green citrus, white peach and orange blossom over piercing, crystalline acidity, a saline slate minerality and nascent petrol. Gewürztraminer was weighed and dismissed: no lychee or rose, and none of that variety's broad, low-acid frame. Low perceived warmth and a lean, linear palate place it in a cool northern German region; the iodine-tinged savoury edge alongside stony purity suggests the Nahe rather than the fruitier Mosel or broader Rheingau.

**Wine 2** — Germany, Riesling. Deep gold, high viscosity, with honey, dried apricot, marmalade, beeswax and saffron over steely acidity and very high residual sugar — the fingerprint of botrytised Riesling. TBA was considered but rejected: there is still citrus lift and freshness rather than the total desiccation and syrup-like weight of that tier, so Beerenauslese. The opulent, honeyed breadth rather than racy nervosity points to the Rheingau.

**Wine 3** — France, Chenin Blanc. Pale gold, honey, acacia, golden apricot and quince paste, with medium-plus acidity — firm but without Riesling's racy pierce — and a light botrytis inflection. Viognier was the alternative given the floral-apricot register, ruled out by the bracing mineral freshness and the absence of Viognier's oily, low-acid weight. Loire, in a lightly sweet Coteaux du Layon idiom.

**Wine 4** — France, Chenin Blanc. Same variety, greater concentration: gold, caramel, praline, toasted peach and white pepper over honeyed botrytis, fuller-bodied and deeper-coloured than Wine 3, with a long, fine finish and a stony mineral spine. Sauternes-style Sémillon was discounted — no oak vanilla, and the acidity is Chenin's high, mineral cut rather than Sémillon's rounder line. Loire, from an elite sweet appellation such as Quarts de Chaume.

**Wine 5** — Canada, Vidal. Gold, with lime, grapefruit, apricot, mango, raisin and honey over crisp citrus acidity and medium-plus finish. Riesling was the alternative and is excluded by the tropical generosity and rounder frame — none of the linear slate-and-petrol structure of Wines 1 and 2. Vidal, the French-American hybrid dominant in Ontario; the residual sugar level indicates late harvest, not freeze-concentration.

**Wine 6** — Canada, Vidal. Same variety in the concentrated register: peach, orange, mango, honey and lychee, creamy texture, luscious sweetness, low perceived warmth and lively citrus acidity, with a markedly longer finish than Wine 5. Riesling Eiswein was weighed but the lychee-pineapple register and broad texture rather than lime-and-slate linearity confirm Vidal, from the Niagara Peninsula.

---

## b) Method of Sweetness and Style (6 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Natural grape sugar retained by arresting fermentation before dryness, from physiologically ripe late-picked fruit; no concentration mechanism. Spätlese-level residual sugar. The razor acidity so completely counterbalances it that the wine reads almost dry on entry, sweetness surfacing only on the saline finish. Light-bodied, built on tension rather than richness.

**Wine 2** — Noble rot: *Botrytis cinerea* desiccating individual berries, concentrating sugar, acid and glycerol and contributing honey, beeswax and ginger. Fermentation arrests at very low alcohol, leaving exceptionally high sugar. Lusciously sweet yet never cloying, because the steely acidity remains intact — the structural difference from Wine 1 is not merely more sugar but sugar earned by concentration.

**Wine 3** — Selective picking of lightly botrytised Chenin, fermentation stopped at medium-sweet. Rich and honeyed but lighter-footed than Wine 4: sweetness plays a supporting role to mineral acidity. A moelleux style, drinkable young.

**Wine 4** — Botrytis again, but from successive *tries* through the vineyard selecting only the most rotted berries at much lower yield. Higher sugar, fuller body, deeper botrytis derivatives (caramel, praline). Liquoreux, with mineral tension lifting the concentration rather than leaving it heavy.

**Wine 5** — Extended hang time into autumn: dehydration on the vine concentrates sugar without freezing; the raisin note suggests some partial shrivel or incidental botrytis. Generous, fruit-forward, medium-plus sweet, kept fresh by citrus acidity — richer than an off-dry table wine, lighter than icewine.

**Wine 6** — Freeze-concentration: fruit left until −8°C or below, pressed frozen so that only the sugar-rich fraction runs, water remaining as ice. Very high residual sugar from tiny juice volumes, at low alcohol. Intensely sweet and viscous, yet the high citric acidity prevents heaviness. The style is a direct product of the process, not the variety.

---

## c) Higher Official Quality Designation (3 × 12 marks)

**Pair 1:** Wine 2. In the Prädikat hierarchy, Beerenauslese sits above Spätlese: Spätlese requires roughly 76–90° Oechsle depending on region and variety, Beerenauslese 110–128° from individually selected botrytised berries, achievable only in exceptional years. The glass agrees. Wine 1's lean, light-bodied linearity with sweetness as counterpoint is textbook Spätlese; Wine 2's deep gold viscosity, layers of saffron, truffle and candied citrus and luscious sugar over steely acid go well beyond Spätlese's primary-fruit clarity. Wine 1 is outstanding at its level — a top single-site estate Spätlese around £35–50; Wine 2 is exceptional, £80–150+ per half-bottle.

**Pair 2:** Wine 4. It shows the profile of Quarts de Chaume, one of only two Grand Crus in the Anjou sweet hierarchy, tiny in area, with a minimum natural alcohol requirement and sweetness built by successive selective passes. Wine 3 reads as a named Coteaux du Layon village — respected, but a clear tier below. The sensory case: Wine 4 is pronouncedly more concentrated, with deeper botrytis derivatives and a substantially longer finish, and its higher viscosity and fuller body reflect stricter yields, while the schist-derived mineral cut keeps that concentration buoyant. Wine 3's lighter honey-and-quince profile is very good at roughly £20–35; Wine 4 justifies £50–100+.

**Pair 3:** Wine 6. Under VQA rules Icewine outranks Select Late Harvest: it demands a minimum 35° Brix in naturally frozen fruit picked and pressed at −8°C or colder, with artificial freezing prohibited. Select Late Harvest sets a lower Brix minimum and relies on dehydration alone, so yields lower sugar and concentration. The glass confirms: Wine 6's tropical intensity, viscosity, very high sugar and low alcohol are unmistakably freeze-concentrated, while Wine 5's medium-plus body, moderate sweetness and shorter finish sit squarely at Select Late Harvest. Wine 5 is good quality at roughly CAD $30–50; Wine 6 outstanding at CAD $60–100 per 375ml.

---

## d) Commercial Position (3 × 6 marks)

**Pair 1:** Wine 1 sells through specialist independents to the Riesling-literate consumer at £35–50, with traction in the Nordic monopolies and the US East Coast; the hurdle is moving buyers beyond the Mosel name. Wine 2 is fine-wine territory — collectors, auction, Japan and the UK — where volumes are minuscule and demand rests on scores and cellaring reputation.

**Pair 2:** Wine 3 is the affordable moelleux alternative to Sauternes at £20–35, suited to French-focused restaurant lists and independent shelves. Wine 4 competes in the fine-wine specialist channel against Barsac and mature Vouvray moelleux. Both suffer the under-marketing of Loire sweet wine; both gain from a value-for-quality argument against Sauternes.

**Pair 3:** Wine 5 is the accessible entry point, at home in Ontario monopoly retail, domestic restaurants and gifting at CAD $30–50. Wine 6 is Canada's flagship export — travel retail, duty-free and premium merchants in Japan, China, the US and UK. The shared risk is vintage availability, acute for Icewine when winters fail to deliver reliable freeze conditions.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## Wine 1 — Mosel, Germany / Riesling Auslese

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Riesling, Mittelmosel, Germany, at Auslese level. Pale gold with green hues, piercing high acidity and very low perceived warmth — the palate is barely more than weightless. Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau were weighed and rejected: neither pairs lime-blossom aromatics with this near-malic acid attack. Rheingau or Nahe would carry more alcohol warmth and breadth; the steely, slate-inflected mid-palate and featherweight body argue for a steep slate site on the Mosel.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Sweetness is botrytis-influenced and over-ripeness-driven, from hand selection of shrivelled clusters over several passes. Fermentation was arrested very low in alcohol — the hostile high-sugar must plus cool cellar temperatures stalling the yeast — leaving substantial sugar carried by exceptional natural acidity. Complete absence of oak points to large neutral Fuder or stainless steel, and the reductive, primary character confirms a protective handling regime. No malolactic: the acid keeps its green edge, deliberately preserved.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, and consistent with Auslese Prädikat from a classified single site: roughly €50–100 through specialist fine wine merchants, with core demand in Germany, Japan and among US collectors. It will improve fifteen years or more, gaining petrol and toast while the citrus spine holds. Its commercial peculiarity is that virtually nothing competes at this intersection of sweetness, ageability and single-figure-to-low alcohol — which is also why it sells to enthusiasts rather than restaurants.

---

## Wine 2 — Sauternes, Bordeaux, France / Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Sémillon-dominant with Sauvignon Blanc and a trace of Muscadelle, from Sauternes. Deep gold, viscous, with dried apricot, saffron, spun sugar and acacia honey — noble rot on Sémillon, confirmed by the waxy lanolin texture. Full body and medium-plus warmth rule out German BA/TBA and Alsace SGN, which would show markedly higher acidity. Vouvray moelleux was considered for the honeyed weight but rejected: no quince, and the tartaric bite of Chenin is absent.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Botrytis alone, via repeated selective tris. Barrique fermentation with a high proportion of new oak is evident in integrated vanilla and spice, fermentation stopping naturally as sugar overwhelms the yeast. Lacquering texture indicates 18–24 months in barrel with gentle oxidative rounding and lees contact. The one structural tension: the finish lacks acid bite, suggesting a vintage of superb botrytis but modest acidity, so the balance tips toward texture rather than freshness — richness bought at the cost of drive.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very high quality, Premier Cru Classé level, on density, oak integration and length; around £180–250 retail, principal markets the UK, US, Hong Kong and France. The buyer is a cellaring collector, and the wine will reward twenty years. The commercial headwind is category-wide rather than specific to this bottle: Sauternes struggles for by-the-glass placement outside fine dining, so quality at this level does not convert into volume.

---

## Wine 3 — California, USA / Orange Muscat

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Orange Muscat, warm inland California. Orange blossom, apricot, mandarin and heady perfume identify the Muscat family; within it, the orange-blossom-and-dried-apricot signature separates Orange Muscat from the grapey rose-petal of Muscat Blanc and the broader, coarser Muscat of Alexandria. Alcohol warmth well above the Mosel or the Icewine, with generous warm-climate fruit and a thick texture, rules out European sweet Muscat and indicates partial fortification.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Fortification of partly fermented must arrests the yeast, retaining sugar and, critically, the volatile floral compounds — the Vins Doux Naturels mechanism in a Californian setting. Early spirit addition, before fermentation strips the terpenes, explains the aromatic purity. There is no botrytis: fruit is fresh and primary, not honeyed. No oak, so stainless steel or neutral vessel, with cold stabilisation and early bottling to protect the aromatics.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good within its category, achieving its stylistic aim with flair but no complexity. Around $20–30, sold through wine shops and restaurant dessert lists to casual drinkers wanting fragrance and sweetness; drink within three to five years. Export prospects are limited by its competitive set — Moscato d'Asti and Alsace Muscat both enjoy far greater name recognition.

---

## Wine 4 — Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada / Vidal

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Vidal Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario. Gold, highly viscous, with ripe peach, mango, candied citrus and honey. Riesling Eiswein was the alternative: rejected because the fruit is tropical and broad rather than citrus-driven, and the texture glycerol-heavy rather than racy. Vidal's thick skins survive the hard freeze that Riesling often does not. A faint metallic note and medium-minus length further separate it from the best Riesling Eiswein.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Cryoconcentration only: grapes left on the vine into winter, picked at −8°C or below and pressed frozen so water stays as ice and sugar-rich juice runs free. No botrytis, no fortification, hence high sugar with proportionally lower acid — the source of the syrupy rather than electric palate. Slow cold fermentation with sugar-tolerant yeast yields low alcohol; neutral steel and early inert bottling keep the fruit primary.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good to very good VQA Icewine; the short finish and metallic edge keep it below the top tier. Around CAD$60–80 per half-bottle through specialists, duty-free and the gift trade, with strong pull in China, Japan and South Korea where concentration and novelty sell. Drink within five to ten years.

---

## Wine 5 — Rust, Burgenland, Austria / Ruster Ausbruch

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Ruster Ausbruch from Rust, Burgenland — likely Welschriesling, Chardonnay or Furmint. Deep gold, musk and candied lemon lift, ripest apricot concentration. The acidity is the discriminator: broader than the Mosel yet far more present than the Sauternes, which fits the Neusiedlersee combination of morning fog and warm afternoons. Tokaji was weighed for equivalent botrytis intensity but rejected — no ginger or orange-peel Furmint signature.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Noble rot again, but Ausbruch occupies its own tier between Beerenauslese and TBA, demanding berry-by-berry selection consistent with this intensity. Unlike Sauternes, the musk-driven lift indicates neutral vessel or large old oak rather than new barrique, protecting botrytis aromatics rather than layering spice over them. Simultaneous high sugar and high acid held in tension points to early-arrested fermentation and no malolactic.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, above Beerenauslese and approaching TBA concentration; €80–150 per half-bottle, rarest parcels well beyond, through specialists in Austria, Germany, Switzerland and selected export markets. Twenty years or more of positive development, musk and candied lemon turning to dried fruit, honey and spice. The commercial problem is name recognition: the appellation is invisible beside Sauternes and Tokaji despite matching them in quality, so pricing is capped below its intrinsic worth.

---

## Wine 6 — Yarra Valley, Victoria, Australia / Viognier

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Late-harvest, partially botrytised Viognier, Yarra Valley, Victoria. Pale straw-gold — conspicuously lighter than the other botrytis wines here. White blossom, white nectarine, mandarin, crushed cashew and hazelnut read as Viognier. Riesling was considered on the bright acidity but rejected: no lime or petrol, and the stone-fruit richness plus toasty oak and almond praline are inconsistent with an unoaked Riesling.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Late harvest with selective, partial botrytis: enough concentration without the deep colour and marmalade of full transformation, so Viognier's floral identity survives — the deliberate opposite of the choices in Wines 2 and 5. French oak is the high-risk decision, since oak readily smothers botrytised wine; here it functions as texture rather than flavour. Fermentation was arrested at low alcohol by chilling and sulfur, not spirit; no malolactic, preserving acidity.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good, and a benchmark for a technically difficult style made as a statement rather than for margin. AUD$40–60 per half-bottle in specialist retail and premium restaurant lists, with modest UK and US fine wine export. Novelty is simultaneously its advantage and its obstacle: sweet-wine buyers default to Sauternes, Riesling or Icewine, so the education cost falls entirely on the seller. Drink within eight to twelve years, before tertiary development erases the varietal floral signature.

---

Wines 1-6 all have residual sugar. They are from six different countries.

a) For each wine, identify the country and region of origin as closely as possible, giving your reasons. (6 × 8 marks)

b) For each wine, describe the mechanism by which residual sugar has been achieved, with reference to the alcohol level and sweetness. (6 × 8 marks)

c) For each wine, comment on the style, quality, and commercial position within the context of its category. (6 × 9 marks)

wines.fullText: Château Suduiraut, 2015. Sauternes, France. (14%)
Donnhoff Kreuznacher Brückes Riesling Auslese, 2021. Nahe, Germany. (8%)
Vidal Estate Noble Riesling, 2022. Hawke's Bay, New Zealand. (10%)
Inniskillin Vidal Icewine, 2021. Niagara Peninsula, Canada. (9%)
Vietti Cascinetta Moscato d'Asti, 2023. Asti, Italy. (5.5%)
Bodegas Dios Baco Oloroso Dulce, NV. Jerez, Spain. (18%)

modelAnswer:
## a) Country and Region of Origin (6 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Deep gold, high viscosity, and a pronounced nose of dried apricot, quince and candied ginger point to botrytis. Warm, medium-plus perceived alcohol (~13–14%) with sustained acidity indicates France rather than Germany, where the equivalent style sits at markedly lower alcohol. The weight and marmalade concentration exceed Monbazillac or a lighter Barsac: classified Sauternes.

**Wine 2** — Very low perceived alcohol (~7–8%), crystalline acidity, lime, slate and nascent petrol confirm Riesling. Alsace was weighed and rejected: it would show broader body, higher alcohol and spice. The green-fruit purity and mineral tension fit Germany, and the combination of stony drive with fleshy peach points to the Nahe at Auslese ripeness.

**Wine 3** — Gold, viscous, with honeyed apricot, beeswax and lifted petrol: noble-rot Riesling. Medium-plus perceived alcohol (~10–11%) rules out German Auslese (lower) and Icewine (lower still, and purely frozen-fruit in profile, without botrytis funk). The tropical richness and fuller frame relative to a German counterpart suggest a warmer maritime New World zone with humid autumns — Hawke's Bay, New Zealand.

**Wine 4** — Pineapple, mango and orange peel with no botrytis character, very low perceived alcohol (~9%) and bracing acidity confirm cryoextraction rather than noble rot. The absence of petrol or lime steeliness suggests Vidal rather than Riesling. Canada dominates the category; Niagara Peninsula, with the Lake Ontario effect and reliable deep freeze, is the home region.

**Wine 5** — Lemon-gold, low viscosity, a fine spritz, and peach, rose petal and acacia at ~5–5.5% perceived alcohol: Moscato Bianco with fermentation arrested early. Moscato d'Asti DOCG, Piemonte. A Sicilian Zibibbo expression was considered but would show greater weight, higher alcohol and orange-blossom heaviness rather than this delicacy.

**Wine 6** — Old gold with copper rim, very high viscosity, roasted hazelnut, toffee and oxidised walnut with pronounced spirit warmth (~18%): oxidatively aged fortified wine. The sweetness makes this a Dulce rather than dry Oloroso; Tawny Port would show red-fruit and rancio, not this saline nuttiness. Jerez, Andalucía, Spain.

---

## b) Mechanism of Residual Sugar (6 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — *Botrytis cinerea* dehydrates Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc on the vine, concentrating sugar and acid. Fermentation runs further than in the German wines here — hence the medium-plus alcohol — before being arrested by the sugar concentration overwhelming the yeast, assisted by chilling, sulphuring and filtration. Pronounced residual sugar is balanced by retained acidity.

**Wine 2** — Selective harvest of late-ripened, partially botrytised bunches to Auslese must weight, then fermentation deliberately arrested early by chilling and sterile filtration. The very low alcohol shows how little of the sugar was converted; high Nahe acidity stops the sweetness reading as cloying.

**Wine 3** — Noble rot again, but arrest occurs at a higher conversion point than the German wine, giving 10–11%. Beeswax and botrytis spice confirm rot rather than simple late harvest or passerillage. Chilling and sterile filtration will have halted fermentation to preserve the sweet–acid balance.

**Wine 4** — Grapes picked at –8°C or below and pressed frozen; only concentrated juice runs, the water remaining as ice. No botrytis. The intensely sugary must ferments slowly and is stopped early, leaving ~9% alcohol with very high sugar and electric acidity.

**Wine 5** — Partially fermented Moscato must, arrested almost immediately by chilling and sterile filtration at ~5–5.5%. Fermented in sealed tank so that a fraction of the CO₂ is retained, giving the gentle mousse. No oak, no malolactic, no botrytis.

**Wine 6** — Distinct from all the above: the base Oloroso ferments to dryness, is fortified to ~18% and aged oxidatively. Sweetness is added post-maturation as concentrated Pedro Ximénez must or wine. The fortification level guarantees microbial stability, so no refermentation of the added sugar occurs.

---

## c) Style, Quality, and Commercial Position (6 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding, at a level consistent with Deuxième Cru Classé Sauternes, £60–100 per 75cl. Drinking well now at around ten years, it will hold and improve for a further decade or more, primary apricot giving way to dried fig, walnut and barley sugar. Sold through fine-dining lists and independent specialists in the UK, US and Japan. The perennial obstacle is consumer resistance to sweet wine at this price, which by-the-glass placement partly solves.

**Wine 2** — Very good; Auslese is a legal ripeness tier, not a quality guarantee, but this delivers. €25–40 per half-bottle. Youthful now, it will gain kerosene and honey over 15–20 years. Target consumer is the low-alcohol, food-pairing dessert-wine drinker; export markets the UK, Scandinavia and Japan. Nahe remains priced below Mosel equivalents — a genuine margin opportunity for independent buyers.

**Wine 3** — Very good, and richer and more approachable than the German wine above at comparable sweetness. NZ$35–50 per half-bottle, sold domestically through fine dining and specialists, with export appeal to Australia, the UK and the US. Best drunk within five to eight years, before the tropical fruit dulls. The commercial argument is botrytis complexity at a third of Sauternes money.

**Wine 4** — Excellent: purity, concentration and searing acidity, with none of the botrytis savouriness of Wines 1 and 3. CAD$60–80 per 200ml, justified by rarity and Canada's strong provenance story. Channels are Asian duty-free and the gift trade rather than the dinner table, which caps repeat purchase; volume growth depends on shifting it from souvenir to restaurant listing.

**Wine 5** — Very good and outstanding value at €10–15, the lightest and most immediate wine here. Aperitivo and fruit-dessert occasions; premium supermarkets, by-the-glass programmes and gifting in the US and UK. Low alcohol is an increasing asset. The risk is commoditisation at the mass end, countered by single-vineyard and vintage-dated positioning.

**Wine 6** — Very good and, at €20–30 per 75cl, the best value in the flight. The savoury-sweet tension differentiates it from the cloying sweetness of a straight PX, giving sommeliers a story to tell. It is stable in bottle and needs drinking within a year of opening rather than cellaring. The realistic route to market is on-trade by the glass at the meal's close, competing directly with 20-year Tawny, plus Sherry-specialist retail in the UK and US. Category obscurity, not quality, is the constraint.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Country and Region of Origin (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Spain, Jerez-Xérès-Sherry DO, Manzanilla. Bone-dry, saline, almond and bruised apple with a very pale straw colour and warmth around 15% place this in the biological ageing family. Oloroso was ruled out on dryness and colour; aged Tawny Port on the absence of red fruit and rancio. The marine lift and lighter frame indicate Sanlúcar de Barrameda rather than the rounder, weightier Fino of Jerez de la Frontera.

**Wine 2** — Portugal, Douro Valley, Late Bottled Vintage. Opaque ruby, staining legs, spirit warmth near 19–20% and sweetness braced by firm tannin place it in the Port family. Vintage Port was weighed and rejected: the extract falls short of a declaration and the peppery tannins are already resolved enough to drink. Rock rose, eucalyptus and black tea signal Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz.

**Wine 3** — Australia, Barossa Valley, fortified Muscat. Tawny-amber with an orange rim and very viscous legs — no tannic grip, no red-fruit freshness — separates it decisively from Wine 2. Raisin, Turkish delight, fig, toffee and rosewater confirm Muscat. Rutherglen was the alternative, but the vigour of the fruit and the freshness cutting the sweetness suggest a younger Barossa expression rather than a deeply aged Victorian blend.

## b) Method of Production (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Palomino Fino, gently pressed, free-run juice fermented dry in stainless steel to around 11.5%, then fortified only to 15% so flor survives. Ageing under a living veil in old botas within a solera consumes glycerol and generates the acetaldehyde-driven almond and bruised-apple notes; the flor also screens the wine from air, explaining the pale colour and light body. The solera guarantees consistency between releases.

**Wine 2** — Warm fermentation in lagares or autovinifiers extracts colour and structure from small, thick-skinned berries. Fortification with 77% grape spirit after two or three days arrests fermentation and retains substantial sugar. Four years in 550-litre pipes — larger than Wine 3's casks, so slower oxidation — softens tannin without the reductive concentration of a bottle-aged Vintage; unfiltered bottling leaves grip on the finish.

**Wine 3** — Late-harvested Muscat, raisined on the vine or on racks, gives extreme sugar concentration before fermentation even begins; fortification arrests it almost immediately at around 18%. Unlike Wine 1, oxidation here is deliberate: small old casks in warm Barossa conditions build toffee, orange peel and rancio. Solera-style blending with younger material preserves the lift that keeps the sweetness mobile.

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good; appellation-level Manzanilla at roughly £12–18. Precise and linear rather than profound, without the depth of En Rama or VORS. Best placed in on-trade tapas and Mediterranean restaurants in the UK, US and Benelux, and in wine bars trading on lower-alcohol aperitifs. Competes with Fino and dry vermouth; the constraints are cold-chain handling and rapid consumption after opening.

**Wine 2** — Very good; LBV tier at £18–25. It offers Douro concentration without the cellaring commitment or price of a declared Vintage, so it suits by-the-bottle service in steakhouses and fine dining, and premium supermarket and independent listings in the UK, US and Scandinavia. Its advantage is immediate drinkability; its obstacle is consumer confusion between LBV and generic Ruby.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding within its category, around AUD 45–65 — above entry-level fortified, below rare aged parcels. Its balance of lusciousness and freshness gives unusual versatility. Strongest in Australian premium off-trade and specialist retailers championing Australian fortified, with export potential in the US and in Japan and South Korea, where floral sweetness is prized. The category's small global footprint, and the assumption that Rutherglen owns this style, remain the barriers.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## Wine 1

### a) Region and Method (10 marks)

Champagne, France. The extremely fine, persistent bead and creamy mousse indicate traditional method, and the depth of autolysis — brioche, toast, beeswax — points to lees contact well beyond the eighteen-month minimum, consistent with a Grandes Marques NV. Three aromatic registers sit side by side: poached apple and quince (Chardonnay), red-fruited breadth (Pinot Noir), a honeyed softening mid-palate (Meunier). Cava and English sparkling were weighed and rejected: neither shows this mousse density combined with candied-lemon, cool-climate ripeness. Brut, roughly 8–10 g/L.

### b) Style and Quality (8 marks)

Benchmark NV quality, comparable to a leading house cuvée at £40–50. The style is generous rather than austere — quince, apricot jam and honeycomb sit alongside the autolytic frame rather than behind it, which distinguishes it from a leaner, more mineral house style. The dosage is fully integrated and supports the ripe Pinot Noir core. Outstanding balance; the fine mousse cushions high acidity.

### c) Commercial Position (7 marks)

Premium on-trade — fine dining, hotel bars, celebration occasions — plus specialist independents. Export is central: US, UK and East Asian luxury hospitality. Competes with the major houses' entry NV cuvées but positions above them on provenance narrative and mouthfeel. Challenge: high-quality English sparkling now undercuts this price band.

---

## Wine 2

### a) Region and Method (10 marks)

Penedès, Spain — Cava Gran Reserva. Traditional method (fine persistent mousse, clear autolysis), but several cues separate it from Champagne: broader texture, rounder white-peach and almond fruit, and a Mediterranean dried-herb edge inconsistent with northern France. Lower perceived alcohol and a linear mid-palate rule out California. Marzipan, walnut skin and dried apple indicate extended lees ageing consistent with the thirty-month Gran Reserva minimum; the nutty, faintly oxidative grip identifies a Xarel·lo-dominant blend. Brut Nature — bone dry, dosage effectively zero.

### b) Style and Quality (8 marks)

Very good; Gran Reserva tier, £25–35. Austere dryness with no dosage correction places this in the gastronomic, food-led niche rather than the celebration market. Considerable complexity — roasted almond, toasted bread, dried citrus peel — and the absence of sugar exposes firm acidity directly on the finish. Xarel·lo's waxy grip is the distinguishing quality marker here.

### c) Commercial Position (7 marks)

Independent specialist and premium on-trade, not supermarket. Spanish gastronomic restaurants matter domestically; Scandinavia and the UK specialist trade are growth export channels. Competes with premium Crémant and English sparkling at £25–35. Opportunity: the Gran Reserva tier gives consumers a navigable quality ladder as prestige Cava repositions upwards. Challenge: the denomination's residual commodity image undermines individual producer narratives.

---

## Wine 3

### a) Region and Method (10 marks)

West Sussex, England. Traditional method — fine persistent mousse, fresh-pastry autolysis — but acidity is more cutting and green-edged than Wine 1, with gooseberry, green apple and citrus rather than ripe pear. Very high acidity, medium-minus body and a lower ripeness register point to a cool maritime origin. Champagne was considered and ruled out: the fruit core is lighter, the mid-palate less enveloping, and the chalky austerity reads sea-climate rather than continental. Chardonnay-dominant with Pinot Noir and Meunier.

### b) Style and Quality (8 marks)

Very good; flagship NV from a mid-tier English house, £30–40. Precision and tension rather than richness. The brut dosage gives just enough cushion for the searing acidity without sweetening the impression. Autolytic development is genuine but lighter than Wine 1's extended profile — pastry and light cream rather than toast. Best as an aperitif or with delicate seafood.

### c) Commercial Position (7 marks)

Premium UK on-trade and specialist off-trade. Domestic prestige is strong; Japan, Scandinavia and the US are genuine export openings where provenance curiosity is high. Competes head-on with mid-range Champagne NV at £30–40, increasingly on equal stylistic terms. Opportunity: an English terroir and climate narrative no other region can borrow. Challenge: limited vineyard volume, and pricing above Champagne NV requires consumer education investment few producers can fund.

---

## Wine 4

### a) Region and Method (10 marks)

Valdobbiadene Superiore, Veneto, Italy — Prosecco DOCG. Tank method: the mousse is softer, larger-bubbled and less persistent than the traditional-method wines here, and the fruit is wholly primary — pear, white peach, acacia blossom — with no biscuit or toast. Lower perceived alcohol and delicate body fit cool-temperature tank fermentation of Glera. Aromatic definition and a mineral lift on the finish argue for Valdobbiadene rather than generic Prosecco DOC.

### b) Style and Quality (8 marks)

Good; Superiore DOCG, £15–20. Light, aromatic and fresh — the antithesis of Wines 1 and 2. Brut at roughly 10–12 g/L gives gentle fruit-forward sweetness balanced by medium-plus acidity. No pretension to complexity beyond primary fruit, but well-executed and varietally expressive within that idiom; the soft mousse is a positive in context.

### c) Commercial Position (7 marks)

On-trade by-the-glass and premium supermarket off-trade. Prosecco is the highest-volume sparkling category globally, and DOCG lets this producer trade upwards within it. Export is fundamental — UK, US, Germany by volume. Opportunity: the DOCG and Rive single-vineyard tiers offer a premiumisation ladder. Challenge: cheap Prosecco DOC constantly commoditises the category, making the DOCG distinction a permanent education cost.

---

## Wine 5

### a) Region and Method (10 marks)

Willamette Valley, Oregon, USA. Traditional method — persistent fine mousse, brioche, toasted hazelnut, lemon curd. The profile is warmer and more generous than Wine 3, with white peach and poached pear, yet the high acidity and restrained fruit rule out California or Washington, which would give softer acid and riper stone fruit. Medium body with high acidity suggests cool continental rather than maritime conditions. Extended tirage explains autolytic depth alongside intact primary fruit; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on volcanic Jory soils.

### b) Style and Quality (8 marks)

Very good; serious small-production American traditional method, $40–55. Extended tirage is the defining statement — toasted almond and hazelnut rival Wine 1's depth on a lighter frame, which is the more impressive achievement. Brut, fully integrated. The chalky mineral finish is the most distinctive feature and reads as genuine site expression rather than winemaking.

### c) Commercial Position (7 marks)

Premium US on-trade and specialist off-trade, with export interest in Japan, the UK and Scandinavia where Oregon carries prestige. Competes with high-end Anderson Valley and California sparkling at $40–60, differentiating on terroir narrative and the ageing commitment. Opportunity: American fine dining's appetite for premium domestic sparkling. Challenge: Oregon still means Pinot Noir to most consumers, so sparkling visibility is thin.

---

## Wine 6

### a) Region and Method (10 marks)

Tasmania, Australia. Traditional method — persistent if lighter mousse, brioche and fresh pastry. The fruit is cooler and more restrained than Wine 5: green apple, lemon curd, white blossom, with only a modest creamy mid-palate. Medium-minus body and medium-plus acidity indicate a cool maritime island. Within Australia, Adelaide Hills and Yarra Valley were considered but would show riper stone fruit and fuller body; Tasmania alone gives this Champagne-analogous restraint. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; the shallower autolysis suggests a shorter lees programme than Wines 1 or 5.

### b) Style and Quality (8 marks)

Good to very good; established Tasmanian house NV, AUD $35–50. The lightest of the traditional-method wines here — finer but less creamy mousse, subtler autolysis, less concentrated fruit core. This is stylistic positioning rather than weakness: the appeal is fresh, clean and floral. Brut dosage unobtrusive; chalky finish a positive regional marker.

### c) Commercial Position (7 marks)

Premium Australian on-trade and specialist off-trade, with export to the UK and Asia where Tasmanian provenance carries cachet. Competes domestically with mainland traditional-method producers but sustains a modest premium. Opportunity: Tasmania can make the same climatic claim as English sparkling to consumers already paying Champagne prices. Challenge: small vineyard area caps distribution scale and makes consistent year-on-year supply difficult for export partners.

# Mock Answer — 2025 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Identify the grape variety or varieties and country of origin (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, France.** Deep gold, viscous, pronouncedly sweet, with honey, apricot preserve, beeswax and orange marmalade: botrytis concentration on thin-skinned varieties. Full body with warmth suggesting around 14%, and the vibrant acidity holding that sweetness clear of cloying, is the Sémillon/Sauvignon Blanc signature of Bordeaux's sweet appellations. Moelleux Chenin was weighed — quince and high acid overlap — but the greater viscosity, deeper colour and lower perceived acidity at this sugar level rule it out; Tokaji Aszú lacks the orange-peel/ginger and oxidative lift. Sauternes-Barsac.

**Wine 2 — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Italy.** Lemon-gold, light-bodied, soft frothy mousse, minimal alcohol warmth (below 7%), with honeysuckle, fresh grape and peach blossom over a sweet, grapey palate: Muscat. The low pressure and ephemeral bead exclude traditional method and also Asti Spumante, which is fully sparkling and drier; this lighter spritz at lower alcohol is Moscato d'Asti. Piedmont.

**Wine 3 — Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and related Douro varieties, Portugal.** Opaque inky ruby-purple, viscous, with pronounced spirit warmth and very high dusty tannins over black fruit, mint, eucalyptus and liquorice: young fortified Douro red. Reserve Ruby was considered but the colour depth, slight haze from unfiltered bottling and the tannin concentration sit above that tier. Douro Valley.

**Wine 4 — Riesling, Australia.** Pale gold and viscous, with honeyed apricot, lime marmalade, ginger and emerging petrol, high acid at around 11% perceived alcohol. The pure lime thread beneath the honey, and acidity that is racy and linear rather than waxy, gives Riesling over Sémillon or Chenin. German BA/TBA was weighed but the alcohol is too generous and the lime-marmalade profile reads Clare or Eden Valley.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1.** Lush but structured. The absence of phenolic harshness at this sugar level implies whole-cluster pressing at low pressure; the concentration implies successive *tries*, selecting individual botrytised berries at heavy cost in yield. The vanilla-cream texture indicates barrel fermentation and maturation in French barriques, perhaps 30-50% new, for 18 months or more. Malolactic is unlikely — retained malic acid is what sharpens the finish.

**Wine 2.** Everything here protects primary fragrance. Arrested fermentation in sealed autoclave, stopped around 5-6% by chilling and filtration, leaving roughly 100-130 g/L sugar; the CO₂ is retained from that single fermentation rather than added by a second, hence the low pressure. No oak, no malolactic, minimal handling, bottled under crown cap or screwcap.

**Wine 3.** Built for the cellar, and the opposite of Wine 2 in every choice. A long maceration of 20-30 days extracts colour and phenolics from thick Douro skins; the fine-grained yet dense tannin is consistent with foot-treading in lagares. Fortification with neutral spirit mid-ferment at around 6-8 Baumé arrests fermentation and locks in sweetness. Around 18-24 months in large old oak, then bottled without fining or filtration — the haze confirms it.

**Wine 4.** Focused rather than opulent: sweetness disciplined by acidity, where Wine 1 achieves balance through richness. Selective picking of botrytised bunches at high sugar while diurnal range preserves malic acid; cool stainless-steel fermentation arrested before dryness. No vanilla or cream, so no oak, and the taut linearity suggests minimal lees work.

---

## c) Quality and commercial position (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1.** Outstanding — Premier Cru Classé Sauternes, at £80-120 per half-bottle. Fine wine specialists, independent merchants and starred on-trade lists; export to Japan, Hong Kong and the USA rather than domestic France. The category's problem is on-trade placement: dessert wine sells by the glass or not at all, so the opportunity is food pairing with blue cheese and foie gras. Will evolve 15-20 years into dried fruit, amber and honey.

**Wine 2.** Very good within its DOCG frame, at £10-14 through premium supermarket and online retail. Its real commercial asset is the low alcohol, which places it inside the moderation trend where no other sweet style can follow. Strong in the UK, USA and Germany. Perceived frivolity is the barrier; casual-dining by-the-glass and gifting are the answer. Drink now.

**Wine 3.** Very good to outstanding — single-quinta LBV pitched above commercial LBV and into Vintage territory, £25-40. Specialist merchants and serious on-trade. Quality-to-price is the argument: it competes with Vintage Ports at two to three times the money, for knowledgeable buyers wanting age-worthy Port outside declared years. UK and USA primary. Best from 10-15 years, holding 25 or more.

**Wine 4.** Very good — benchmark Clare botrytis Riesling, structurally near a good Auslese but with an Australian lime identity, AUD 40-60 (£20-30) per 375ml. Competitive set is Alsace Vendange Tardive and German Auslese, undercut on price. Australian fine wine specialists, and premium merchant export to the UK and USA. The challenge is that the category itself is barely recognised. Drink now to 10 years, gaining marmalade and toast.

## a) Region of origin and grape variety (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Jerez, Spain; Palomino Fino blended with Pedro Ximénez. Mahogany hue, viscosity and clear spirit warmth signal a fortified, oxidatively aged wine; dried fig, walnut and butterscotch over balsamic acidity point to Jerez. Dry Oloroso fits the nutty structure but not the generous residual sugar and raisined grapiness, which require a PX component — hence a Cream blend. Malmsey Madeira was rejected: no volatile lift, no curry-and-citrus acid signature.

**Wine 2** — Barsac, Bordeaux; Sémillon-dominant with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle. Deep gold and viscous but with no spirit heat, so concentration comes from noble rot: apricot jam, beeswax and malt candy confirm botrytis. The taut acid line and bitter-almond finish distinguish it from the broader, fuller texture of Sauternes proper; balance and length indicate Premier Cru Classé.

## b) Method of production and the role of oxidation (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Palomino fermented dry, then fortified to ~18%, killing flor and committing the wine to purely oxidative ageing in seasoned American oak butts under a solera. The absence of saline, aldehydic flor character confirms oxygen, not yeast, has been the agent. The PX component comes from sun-dried grapes, fermentation arrested by fortification at high sugar. Oxidation is transformative here: it destroys Palomino's neutral primary fruit and rebuilds the wine as tertiary complexity, with PX supplying sweetness and viscosity.

**Wine 2** — Oxidation is protective and subordinate. Botrytis itself drives enzymatic oxidation in the berry, giving the gold colour and malty register; harvest proceeds by successive tries. Barrel fermentation in French oak barriques with a new-oak proportion allows measured contact, but sulphur and careful élevage prevent development. The absence of rancio or aldehyde confirms a reductive-leaning approach after fermentation: oxygen builds texture and depth without competing with botrytis.

## c) Quality and commercial position (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding for the category, consistent with a very old solera blend, £40–60. Premium specialist tier: independent merchants, fine-dining lists, UK, northern Europe and Japan. Its commercial problem is category image — Cream is remembered as a supermarket commodity, so it must be sold as a dessert or contemplative wine, not on the Sherry name alone.

**Wine 2** — Very high quality, Premier Cru Classé Barsac at £80–120, competing directly with classed-growth Sauternes. Fine wine merchants, starred restaurants and auction, with US and Asian demand. Volume is small and sweet wine is out of fashion; the offset is decades of ageing potential and secondary-market strength in a fine vintage.

---

## b) Method of Production and Maturation (6 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Grapes are fermented fully to dryness before fortification raises alcohol above sixteen per cent. At this quality level, a multi-vintage Sercial is aged in cask in the warm upper floors of the lodge for a minimum of five years — the canteiro process. Sustained heat, oxidative ageing and the wine's naturally high acidity together produce the volatile lift, caramelized citrus and searingly fresh finish. The result is a dry fortified wine unlike any other style in the world.

**Wine 2** — Fermentation of red Douro varieties is arrested after roughly two to three days of skin maceration by addition of grape spirit, fixing colour and leaving forty to sixty grams per litre of residual sugar. The wine then ages in large old wooden vats for a minimum period. Minimal wood contact is precisely what preserves the fresh, juicy, primary-fruit appeal that distinguishes Ruby from the oxidative evolution of Tawny.

**Wine 3** — Palomino Fino is fermented to dryness and fortified lightly to around fifteen per cent, enabling flor to grow. The wine enters a dynamic Criadera and Solera system in American oak butts, where the living yeast veil excludes oxygen and generates the saline, almond-driven, high-acid style. For the En Rama bottling, minimal fining and no filtration preserve the slight haze and heightened aromatic intensity evident in the glass.

**Wine 4** — A Palo Cortado begins identically to a Fino — fermented dry, lightly fortified, entered under flor. When flor dies, naturally or by fortification above seventeen per cent, the wine transitions to full oxidative ageing. It inherits the fine, lifted aromatics of a Fino-type wine but develops the power and structure of an Oloroso over decades. VORS designation requires a minimum average age of thirty years, accounting for the extraordinary complexity of dried fruit, iron, beeswax and the smooth, unctuous texture.

**Wine 5** — Trebbiano and Malvasia grapes are dried on straw mats for several months, concentrating sugars and developing oxidative, nutty characters. Fermentation is slow in small sealed caratelli and ages for a minimum of three years, often considerably longer. Controlled oxidation and evaporative concentration produce the amber colour, caramel and almond complexity. Fermentation terminates naturally without fortification when alcohol and sugar reach equilibrium, explaining the absence of spirit heat at around fourteen per cent perceived alcohol.

**Wine 6** — Zibibbo grapes are sun-dried on Pantelleria for several weeks — appassimento — dramatically intensifying sugars and aromatics. Fermentation terminates naturally as sugar levels overwhelm yeast activity, producing around fourteen per cent perceived alcohol with substantial residual sugar. No fortification and no significant oxidative ageing explains why the wine retains its vivid orange blossom, dates and dried-fig character rather than developing the nutty, caramelized tones of Wine 5.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (6 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, equivalent to a five-year Finest Reserve tier. The balance of electric acidity against dried-citrus complexity is impressive for a blended wine. Strong commercial opportunities with specialist fine wine merchants and on-trade lists in the UK, USA and Nordic monopoly markets; Sercial is the most food-versatile Madeira style. Retail around £20–25. The core challenge is Madeira's image problem — consumers unfamiliar with dry styles price-compare unfavourably against Fino Sherry.

**Wine 2** — Good quality, entry-level Ruby tier, appealing but lacking the depth of a Reserve or LBV. Well-positioned for premium supermarkets, specialist merchants and brasserie by-the-glass lists in the UK, Netherlands and Belgium. Retail around £12–16. The Porto appellation retains strong consumer trust against New World competition, but persuading a younger generation to engage with fortified wine remains the broader challenge.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding quality among the finest expressions of Fino Sherry, equivalent to a single-pago selection. The En Rama premium over standard filtered Fino is justified and targets enthusiast consumers at ambitious restaurants and specialist merchants in Spain, the UK and Japan. Retail around £18–25. The constraint is short shelf life once bottled, requiring careful stock rotation and an educated retail partner.

**Wine 4** — Exceptional, genuinely world-class. Palo Cortado is already rare; a VORS from an accredited house competes against aged Vintage Port, old Tawny with age indication and fine Cognac at the premium end. The target is specialist fine wine merchants, top-end on-trade and high-net-worth collectors in the UK, USA and Japan. Retail around £80–120 for a half-bottle is realistic. The challenge remains that Palo Cortado is poorly understood by consumers relative to Fino or Oloroso.

**Wine 5** — Very good quality, Vin Santo del Chianti Classico DOC. The caratelli ageing and complexity indicate a serious, cellar-worthy sweet wine. Commercial appeal is strongest in Italian specialist restaurants and fine wine merchants, with export interest in the USA, Germany and Japan. Retail around £30–45 for a half-bottle. The obstacle is Vin Santo's perception as a restaurant digestivo rather than a collectible, competing against better-known French sweet wine styles.

**Wine 6** — Outstanding quality within the Passito di Pantelleria DOC. The aromatic intensity and balance of sweetness against freshness indicate a top-level producer. Declining island production and the difficulty of the terroir add genuine scarcity value. The target is specialist Italian merchants, premium on-trade lists and fine wine enthusiasts in the USA and Nordic markets. Retail around £35–55 for a half-bottle. The opportunity is the style's uniqueness — it has no real competitor; the challenge is communicating Pantelleria's identity to an unfamiliar audience.

---

# Mock Answer — Practice Paper 3: Nahe Riesling / Vouvray Moelleux

## a) Identify the origin and grape variety or varieties of each wine (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Riesling, Nahe, Germany. Pronounced citrus and stone fruit over sour apple and steely minerality, carried by searing acidity at very low perceived alcohol. Gewürztraminer is ruled out by the absence of rose and lychee and by acid too linear; Pinot Gris lacks this mineral tension. Within Germany, the mineral signature is lighter and more florally lifted than full-bore Mosel slate, and the stone-fruit richness exceeds a Mosel Spätlese's weight — Nahe.

**Wine 2** — Chenin Blanc, Vouvray Moelleux, Loire. Golden, honeyed quince and beeswax with nervous acidity; no spirit warmth, so not fortified. Sauternes was weighed for the shared botrytis-honey note but eliminated: the acidity is far more nervy and the texture lacks Sémillon's plushness. Residual sugar clearly beyond demi-sec level confirms moelleux.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Off-dry Spätlese with precision as the governing aesthetic. The light-to-medium weight despite substantial sweetness indicates fermentation deliberately arrested at low conversion, around 9% perceived alcohol, the sugar balanced against naturally high acidity. Primary fruit purity and no reduction point to cool stainless-steel fermentation; no oak, and malolactic clearly avoided, leaving the racy finish. Lees work is minimal — aromatic delicacy over structural complexity.

**Wine 2** — Richer and rounder by intent. Concentration suggests botrytised or heavily overripe fruit picked in successive tries. Unlike Wine 1's purely reductive steel, a faint creamy frame implies fermentation in older large oak. Fermentation stopped at a higher alcohol, so acidity does structural rather than aromatic work; malolactic again avoided, preserving the tartaric backbone that underwrites long ageing.

## c) Quality, commercial position, and value for money (2 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding, consistent with a single-vineyard Grosse Lage Spätlese rather than Gutswein: mineral complexity and length place it well above village level. Around £35–45, specialist independent and premium on-trade, competing with top Alsace Riesling. Scandinavia, UK, Japan and North America are the core export markets; the hurdle is consumer recognition of Nahe beyond Mosel.

**Wine 2** — Very good to outstanding, an established-domaine Vouvray Moelleux at roughly £25–35, sold to collectors, French fine dining and UK independents. It competes directly with Sauternes and Alsace VT/SGN at that price; its edge is acidity and food-friendliness for sommeliers.

**Value:** Wine 1. Few sweet wines at that price match its purity and ageing potential, and the Nahe's relative anonymity means the buyer pays for the glass, not the postcode. Wine 2 sits in a bracket where Sauternes owns the mindshare.

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — Jurançon, France (Petit Manseng, late harvest / passerillage)

**a) Mechanism (8 marks)**
Deep gold, viscous, with quince, orange marmalade and chestnut honey. Botrytis markers are absent — no saffron, no fungal lanolin — so noble rot is ruled out. Perceived alcohol is warm at around 14%, far too high for cryoconcentration, which arrests fermentation nearer 9–10%. The mechanism is therefore on-vine passerillage: Petit Manseng's thick skins allow the berries to shrivel and concentrate sugar without rot, and the combination of racy acidity with dried-tropical richness is that process's fingerprint.

**b) Quality (6 marks)**
Outstanding. Aromatic range from chestnut to pineapple, seamless integration of sugar and high acid, and a long layered finish put this well above entry Moelleux, at the ambition of a classed-growth Sauternes.

**c) Style (4 marks)**
Roughly 80–120 g/L residual sugar, yet balanced: Pyrenean acidity supplies the tension, so the palate is opulent without weight.

**d) Commercial position (7 marks)**
Premium specialist tier, around €40–70 per 50cl through independent fine wine merchants and gastronomic on-trade in France, the UK and Japan. It undercuts comparable Sauternes, which is both its selling point and its problem — recognition outside France is low, so it needs sommelier advocacy. Best export prospects: UK, Switzerland, Japan.

---

## Wine 2 — Wachau, Austria (Riesling Smaragd, arrested fermentation)

**a) Mechanism (8 marks)**
Sugar here is residual from a fermentation stopped just short of dryness. Botrytis is excluded (no amber hue, no honeyed funk), passerillage by the lack of dried-fruit concentration, and cryoconcentration by perceived alcohol around 13% with substantial body — far outside icewine parameters. Tartaric Riesling acidity and a flinty, saline finish show sugar as incidental cushion in a dry-leaning wine, not its purpose; that is what separates it from a Spätlese or Auslese.

**b) Quality (6 marks)**
Very good to outstanding, at Smaragd Erste Lage level. Precise gneiss-derived mineral identity and stony length lift it above generic Smaragd; ambition equivalent to a Burgundy Premier Cru.

**c) Style (4 marks)**
Only 8–15 g/L, perceptible against the body but reading almost dry — textural rather than sweet.

**d) Commercial position (7 marks)**
Collector's bottle at €45–80, via specialist importers in the UK, US, Germany and Scandinavia, and fine-dining lists with Austrian depth. The competitive set is grand cru Alsace Riesling and Mosel Spätlese at similar money; Austria's edge is site specificity and a modernist image, its constraint tiny volume.

---

## Wine 3 — Niagara Peninsula, Canada (Riesling Icewine)

**a) Mechanism (8 marks)**
Pale gold, extremely viscous, perceived alcohol only 9–10%, sweetness very high: cryoconcentration. Frozen berries are pressed at −8°C or below, water retained as ice, only concentrated juice extracted. Botrytis is excluded by the absence of saffron or spiced honey and by regulation; passerillage by the piercing lime-and-apricot freshness and low alcohol. Structurally this is the inverse of Wine 1 — concentration by freezing, not dehydration.

**b) Quality (6 marks)**
Outstanding, VQA Icewine. Extreme sugar matched by equally extreme acidity, with exceptional length; well above commodity icewine.

**c) Style (4 marks)**
Around 200–250 g/L, saved from cloy by acidity of equal magnitude — simultaneously sweet and bracing.

**d) Commercial position (7 marks)**
CAD $80–150 per 375ml. Domestic Canada plus the US, Japan, Hong Kong and mainland China, where icewine has entrenched luxury-gift positioning. The difficulty is justifying half-bottle value per ml; the opportunity is Asian gifting, still under-distributed relative to demand.

---

## Wine 4 — Montepulciano, Italy (Vin Santo Occhio di Pernice, appassimento)

**a) Mechanism (8 marks)**
Deep amber-gold, dark raisin, walnut and date, perceived alcohol around 16%: extended appassimento followed by oxidative barrel ageing. Grapes dry on mats for months, then a slow fermentation in sealed caratelli is halted by accumulating alcohol; ullaged cask ageing adds toffee and smoked hazelnut. The red-berry undercurrent and tannic extract identify Occhio di Pernice — Sangiovese, not Trebbiano — and set it apart from every other wine here. No other route yields concentration, oxidation and this density together.

**b) Quality (6 marks)**
Outstanding, at the top of Vin Santo di Montepulciano DOC; dried fruit, nut and oxidative notes fully integrated over very long ageing, comparable in ambition to vintage Madeira.

**c) Style (4 marks)**
Perhaps 120–180 g/L, but balance comes from tannin and extract rather than acid alone — serious rather than merely pleasurable.

**d) Commercial position (7 marks)**
€80–150+ per 375ml through specialist merchants and auction. Loyal but small followings in the US, UK and Japan. The real barrier is awareness: this is one of Italy's least-known great categories, dependent on sommelier advocacy; pairings with aged Pecorino and biscotti open doors but will not build volume.

---

## Wine 5 — Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia (Rare Muscat, fortification)

**a) Mechanism (8 marks)**
Tawny and viscous, Christmas pudding and burnt caramel, with obvious spirit warmth near 18%: sugar retained by mid-ferment fortification with neutral grape spirit, which kills the yeast. Spirit character alone excludes botrytis, freezing and passerillage. What then distinguishes this from other fortifieds is fractional blending in old casks, concentrating the wine by evaporation and generating the rancio depth present; that intensity places it in the Rare tier rather than Classic or Grand.

**b) Quality (6 marks)**
Outstanding, the summit of the Rutherglen classification — spirit, sugar and decades of oxidative development seamlessly knit, with an interminable finish and no true global analogue.

**c) Style (4 marks)**
Above 250–300 g/L, yet sweetness is checked by spirit, rancio bitterness and coffee grip; balance by concentration, not the acid equilibrium of Wines 3 and 6. A tiny measure suffices.

**d) Commercial position (7 marks)**
AUD $80–200+ per 375ml, mainly domestic with growing UK, US and Japanese interest. The best channel is premium by-the-glass dessert service, where one measure supports a high glass price and recruits new drinkers, plus luxury gifting. It competes with Tokaji Eszencia, aged PX and old Tawny, against which its handicap is recognition rather than quality.

---

## Wine 6 — Elgin, South Africa (Noble Late Harvest Riesling, botrytis)

**a) Mechanism (8 marks)**
Deep gold, viscous, dried apricot and frangipane, perceived alcohol around 10%: botrytis concentration. *Botrytis cinerea* degrades the skins, permitting dehydration and generating glycerol and apricot-floral notes. High fresh tartaric acidity rules out an oxidative passito treatment, and the fruit lacks the dried-tropical density of Wine 1's passerillage. Low alcohol confirms fermentation arrested with ample sugar remaining. Elgin's cool altitude gives the long, unhurried season that permits selective rather than destructive rot, and Noble Late Harvest is legally reserved for botrytised fruit.

**b) Quality (6 marks)**
Very good to outstanding. Sweetness, racy acid and aromatic intensity well managed, with a long clean finish; cool-climate specificity lifts it above generic Cape sweet wine, at German Auslese or Alsace SGN ambition.

**c) Style (4 marks)**
About 100–150 g/L, but freshness defines it — vivid rather than heavy, sitting between icewine purity and Sauternes richness, more tropical than a Mosel equivalent.

**d) Commercial position (7 marks)**
Roughly €22–35 per 375ml — exceptional value against German Auslese and Alsace Vendange Tardive at the same or higher prices, which is its strongest argument. Domestic South Africa plus the UK, Germany and the Netherlands, through specialist merchants and premium supermarkets; on-trade it gives lists a botrytis option without the Sauternes premium. Scandinavia and the US remain underexploited relative to quality.
