modelAnswer:
## a) Country and region of origin (2 × 8 marks)

Both wines show persistent fine mousse, pronounced autolytic character, high racy acidity and restrained alcohol: traditional method in a cool region. Chalk-driven tension and citrus precision narrow this to **Champagne, France**. English sparkling was weighed but ruled out — the depth of citrus complexity and structural weight exceed what it typically achieves. Cava was eliminated on finer mousse, higher acid tension and greater complexity.

**Wine 1** shows apple, white floral and caramelised citrus on a chalk-mineral finish, consistent with 100% Chardonnay from Grand Cru Côte des Blancs sites. The complete absence of red fruit or vinosity rules out any Pinot Noir component: a **prestige Blanc de Blancs**.

**Wine 2** is leaner and more austere: saline, green apple and gunflint, no creamy mid-palate. Dosage is evidently near-zero. The Chardonnay signature remains, but the suppression of sweetness points to a **Brut Nature Champagne** making a terroir-first statement.

## b) Method of production — compare and contrast (16 marks)

Both share the traditional method: bottle-fermented, extended lees ageing under crown cap, riddling, disgorgement, following the Champagne framework of pressing, assemblage and tirage.

The divergence is dosage and lees contact. Wine 1's brioche, caramel and toasted hazelnut alongside a creamy mid-palate suggest five or more years on lees, consistent with a prestige cuvée; the liqueur d'expédition is balanced, adding roundness without overt sweetness.

Wine 2 carries no such buffer: the stony finish and absent creaminess indicate 0–3 g/L, leaving acidity fully exposed and demanding impeccably ripe base wines. Suppressing the liqueur is a philosophical choice — terroir unmediated by sweetness — wholly distinct from Wine 1's voluptuous house style.

## c) Style, quality, and commercial position (2 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** is outstanding, retailing above £150, with seamlessly integrated citrus, floral and autolytic layers and a very long mineral finish. It sits among the great Blanc de Blancs prestige cuvées, targeting premium on-trade, specialist retailers and private clients, with export strength in the USA and East Asia. It will improve five to ten years as autolytic richness and citrus concentration integrate.

**Wine 2** occupies a distinct niche at £80–120, aimed at sommeliers and enthusiasts prioritising terroir over approachability. Quality is very high, equivalent to top vintage Champagne, but the austere finish limits appeal outside the specialist on-trade. Scandinavia and Japan, where zero-dosage resonates, are the strongest export opportunities. The commercial challenge is persuading non-specialists that stony austerity is a virtue rather than a deficit.

# Mock answer — Paper 3, Question 1 (rosé flight, six countries)

## Wine 1

**a)** Bandol, Provence, France; Mourvèdre-led with Grenache and Cinsault. Salmon-pink, medium viscosity, with wild strawberry and white peach lifted by unmistakable dried garrigue herbs. The killer evidence is structural rather than aromatic: a light but real phenolic grip on the mid-palate and a saline, stony, genuinely long finish, carried on a warm, medium-bodied frame reading around 13.5%. Provençal in idiom, but a generic Côtes de Provence would be shorter, softer and without that tannic edge; Tavel was weighed and rejected — it would show deeper colour and a broader, more alcoholic Grenache sweetness. The grip points to a late-ripening, thick-skinned Mourvèdre base, which narrows within Provence to Bandol.

**b)** Style is gastronomic, not aperitif. Whole-bunch pressing with only brief maceration explains a wine pale in colour yet phenolically present; cool stainless fermentation and a period on fine lees give the texture, and there is no oak signature at all. **Under the skin:** the tension between a pale, restrained colour and a firmly structured, saline palate tells you the fruit was picked at full phenolic ripeness and then pressed off fast — colour was sacrificed deliberately to keep the wine a table wine rather than a terrace wine, which is why the warmth reads as weight, not heat.

**c)** Outstanding for the category, at the very top of its appellation and comfortably the best wine in the flight; around €35–45 retail. Independent specialists and Michelin-listed restaurants in France, the US and Japan; competes with cru Provence and serious Tavel. Unusually for a rosé, it will improve two to three years and hold five.

## Wine 2

**a)** Brachetto d'Acqui, Piedmont, Italy. Method first: a light frizzante bead, low alcohol — perceptibly under 7%, almost no warmth — and clear residual sweetness places this as a partially fermented aromatic sparkling, made in tank with the ferment arrested under pressure. Ruby tending rosé, with pure crushed rose petal, strawberry and raspberry. Moscato Rosa and Lambrusco rosato were considered; Lambrusco is drier and firmer, Moscato Rosa less red-fruited. Rose petal plus red berry at this alcohol is Brachetto.

**b)** Grapes picked early to retain medium-plus acidity, crushed with very short skin contact for colour and perfume, then a cool tank ferment stopped by chilling and filtration at roughly 5–6% with around 80–100 g/L sugar retained. No lees work, no oak — everything is directed at preserving primary grape aroma.

**c)** Good quality within DOCG Brachetto d'Acqui, but a simple wine: medium-minus intensity, medium-minus finish. Retails around €12–15, off-trade and gift channels, strongest in Italy, Germany and the US. Sells to consumers wanting a low-alcohol sweet novelty; competes with Moscato d'Asti. Drink immediately; no upside from age.

## Wine 3

**a)** Rioja rosado, Spain; Garnacha-dominant with Tempranillo and a white component (Viura). Pale pink but far more substantial than the colour suggests: peach and stone fruit, white blossom, almond, and a strawberries-and-cream note over a silky, medium-bodied palate with pastry spice and a long finish, alcohol warm at around 13.5%. Provence was eliminated — no garrigue, and the texture is creamy rather than saline. Navarra rosado was the closer alternative, but the almond, pastry and barrel-derived breadth point to the traditionalist Riojan rosado idiom.

**b)** This has been treated like a white wine: a proportion barrel-fermented and aged in large oak on lees with bâtonnage, which explains the almond, spice and silkiness without any overt vanilla. Malolactic likely partial or blocked, as acidity remains fresh. Bleeding of red must plus co-fermented white grapes gives colour and aromatic lift.

**c)** Very good quality, well above generic rosado and equivalent to Crianza in ambition; around €15–20. Independent merchants and restaurant lists, exporting to the UK, US and Netherlands. Its competitive challenge is that consumers trained on pale Provence expect a lighter wine; its opportunity is textural rosé with two to three years of positive development ahead.

## Wine 4

**a)** Marlborough, New Zealand; Pinot Noir. Pale salmon, medium-minus viscosity, light-bodied with medium alcohol and mouthwatering medium-plus acidity. Fresh strawberry, raspberry, watermelon and citrus zest, floral on the finish, clean and short. Provence was ruled out — no herbal or saline dimension — and Chile ruled out for its riper, softer profile. The combination of very cool-climate red-berry purity, high natural acidity and zero phenolic grip is Marlborough Pinot Noir.

**b)** Machine-harvested at modest ripeness, direct-pressed or given a few hours' skin contact only, then cold-settled and fermented cool in stainless with aromatic yeast to accentuate the floral, watermelon character. No malolactic — the acid is sharp and malic. No lees texture, no oak; bottled early under screwcap.

**c)** Acceptable-to-good commercial quality, a branded varietal rosé at around NZ$20 / £11. Premium supermarket and by-the-glass volume listings in the UK, US and Australia. Target consumer is the Provence drinker trading sideways on price. Drink now, within twelve months.

## Wine 5

**a)** The curveball. Swartland, South Africa; Chenin Blanc-led with Viognier and Grenache Blanc. There is no pink here at all — the wine is gold — so the "rosé" designation must rest on a fleeting skin contact that has contributed texture but no colour. Nectarine, baked apple, honeysuckle, lemon rind and crushed stone over a creamy, medium-to-full palate with medium-plus finish and moderate warmth. Rhône white was the alternative; the granitic stony bite and apple-driven Chenin core point instead to old-vine Paardeberg fruit.

**b)** Old bush vines and low yields explain the concentration. Whole-bunch pressed with minimal settling, wild-fermented in older large-format oak and left on gross lees for texture — hence creaminess with no vanilla or toast. No new oak, minimal sulphur handling.

**c)** Very good quality for its tier, the second wine of a serious estate at around £14–16, independent specialists in the UK, US and Scandinavia. It will improve three to four years.

## Wine 6

**a)** Willamette Valley, Oregon; Pinot Noir. Salmon-pink, medium-minus body, high acidity, low tannin, dry, with cranberry, red cherry, nectarine, rose petal, spice and a slight struck-match reduction. Marlborough is already represented and this is riper and spicier; Sancerre rosé was considered but lacks this fruit concentration. Cool-climate Pinot with generous fruit weight fits Oregon.

**b)** Saignée or short cold maceration, then cool ferment in stainless and neutral barrel with lees contact and reductive handling — the sulphidic note indicates low-oxygen winemaking. Malolactic blocked to preserve acidity.

**c)** Good quality, estate-tier at US$25–28, sold cellar-door, DTC and on Pacific-Northwest restaurant lists. Drink now to two years.

# Mock Answer — Practice Paper 3: Four Fortified Wines

## a) Country and Region of Origin (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Madeira, Portugal; Sercial, 15-year-old or older. Pale tawny, with dried citrus peel, hazelnut and a salty, faintly curried lift. The discriminator against Sherry is the electric acidity slicing through residual sugar, giving a tension Jerez cannot produce. The lightness and freshness rule out Bual or Malmsey, which would be broader and lower in acid; the saline core and dried apricot fix Sercial.

**Wine 2** — Douro Valley, Portugal; Colheita Tawny. Brick-brown, viscous, with fig, prune, walnut, coffee and dark chocolate. The colour development alone eliminates Ruby and LBV. The nuanced, layered dried fruit rather than the flatter uniformity of a blended Tawny indicates a single vintage, aged in small cask for well beyond the seven-year minimum; the grape-spirit warmth and orange-peel edge confirm the Douro.

**Wine 3** — Jerez, Spain; Amontillado, VORS. Deep amber, high viscosity, pronounced hazelnut and savoury toast, bone dry. Oloroso was considered but lacks the fine, incisive structure left behind by an earlier period under flor; Palo Cortado would show more aromatic delicacy against that oxidative weight. The stratified complexity and extraordinary length argue for a minimum average age of 30 years.

**Wine 4** — Jerez, Spain; premium *en rama* Fino, single pago. Golden, medium viscosity, bready flor character, walnut, salinity. Perceived alcohol is clearly lower than Wines 1–3, consistent with the lighter fortification that permits flor. Unlike Wine 3, reductive lees character and fresh saline bite indicate recent flor activity rather than long oxidation. The fuller texture and cloudy, unfiltered presentation place it above standard commercial Fino.

---

## b) Quality Level Reflected in Method of Production and Maturation (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Quality here rests on *canteiro*: slow natural oxidation in small casks in heated lofts, not the three-month *estufagem* tank heating used for basic Madeira. Layered hazelnut, caramelised citrus and the taut sweetness–acid interplay cannot be manufactured by rapid heating. The age statement signals over a decade of cellar commitment, and the spirit is fully absorbed into the wine.

**Wine 2** — A Colheita requires a single vintage in small wood for at least seven years, and the seamless spirit integration plus the shift from dried fruit into walnut and chocolate suggests considerably longer. Where Wine 1 gains complexity from heat plus air, this gains it from cask surface area and evaporation alone. The precision of flavour is inconsistent with a generic Tawny blend, confirming vintage selection.

**Wine 3** — VORS is earned through biological then oxidative ageing in a solera whose average age exceeds thirty years, with rigorous selection at each *criadera*. A young Amontillado shows early oxidative character over a simple frame; here the flavour is stratified and the finish relentless. This is the reverse of Wine 4's philosophy — decades of controlled air rather than the protection of a living flor veil.

**Wine 4** — Standard Fino is fined and filtered for commercial stability and a lighter profile. *En rama* bottling straight from the butt preserves autolytic, flor-derived and reductive character, giving the yeasty depth, saline core and faint bitterness in the glass. The single-pago sourcing and fuller body indicate superior albariza base wine feeding the solera, and this shows in the length.

---

## c) Style and Commercial Position (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, high-acid, nutty: an intellectual style needing an engaged consumer. Independent specialists and fine-dining on-trade, at roughly £50–£80. Above generic Madeira blends, below single-vintage Frasqueira. The UK leads exports, with growth in Japan and among US sommeliers; low category awareness limits supermarket viability.

**Wine 2** — Sweet, rich, immediately rewarding — the most approachable wine of the four. Premium on-trade: by-the-glass dessert pours and after-dinner service. Around £40–£60 per 50cl, competing with 20-year-old Tawny but charging a premium for the stated vintage. France, the UK and Scandinavia are the receptive markets; the weakness is that Colheita is poorly explained on label and often mistaken for Ruby.

**Wine 3** — Bone dry and uncompromising, with a necessarily narrow audience. VORS is a trustworthy quality signal for specialist merchants, auction and top on-trade in Spain, the UK and the US, at £60–£100. Its competitive set is other VORS Sherries and old dry Madeira such as Wine 1. The commercial opportunity is food versatility, bridging umami savoury dishes and nut-based desserts across several service occasions.

**Wine 4** — Saline and yeasty, with more body than commercial Fino; sold on authenticity rather than polish. Independent specialists and premium by-the-glass lists, £30–£50 per 37.5cl, with the natural-wine audience in the UK, US and Japan the most receptive. The *en rama* premium is justified by complexity, but the wine must be chilled from arrival and drunk within months of release — a fragility requiring active retailer and consumer education.

---

# Mock Answer — Practice Paper 3: Sweet Wine Pair

## a) Country and Region of Origin (2 × 12 marks)

**Wine 1** — France, Sauternes, Bordeaux; Premier Cru Classé level.

Deep gold, viscous, very sweet, with dried apricot, saffron and acacia honey over integrated oak: noble rot on a Sémillon-led white blend. The lacquered texture and warmth (~14%) rule out German BA/TBA, where electric tartaric acid and far lower alcohol would dominate, and Tokaji, which would show orange peel and grip. Barsac was weighed, but the fuller body and deeper dried-fruit weight favour Sauternes. Seamless oak and length exceed generic AC level.

**Wine 2** — Austria, Rust, Burgenland; Ruster Ausbruch.

Similar gold and viscosity, but the sweetness is juicy rather than unctuous, with marzipan and fresh fig, a finer acid line and marginally lower perceived alcohol. Bread-like botrytis confirms noble rot; the absence of Furmint's orange peel and ginger rules out Tokaji, its closest structural rival. Concentration clearly exceeds Beerenauslese without reaching TBA density — the Ausbruch band.

## b) Mechanisms of Residual Sugar (18 marks)

Both derive sugar from botrytis cinerea, not enrichment or arrested must.

In Wine 1, mists off the Ciron and warm afternoons drive noble rot on Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc; successive *tries* select berries at optimum shrivel. Skin perforation evaporates water, concentrating sugar, acid and glycerol — the source of the unctuous weight. Barrel fermentation stalls around 13.5–14.5% through yeast fatigue and is arrested by SO₂ or chilling, leaving roughly 100–150 g/L.

Wine 2 uses the same biology under Pannonian lake mist, but a different legal threshold: Ausbruch demands higher must weight than BA, historically achieved by macerating shrivelled berries in fermenting must, now by whole-bunch selection. Fermentation ceases at lower alcohol, and Austria's tartaric-dominant acidity balances the sugar. Hence the key difference: sugar and acid are evenly matched here, vivid rather than lacquered, where Sauternes' glycerol and oak deliver richness.

## c) Style, Quality, Commercial Position (2 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding; £80–120 per bottle, classed-growth tier. Fine-wine off-trade, auction and Michelin lists in the UK, USA, Japan and Hong Kong. The category's problem is occasion, not quality: positioning with aged cheese and Asian cuisine widens the sale beyond dessert.

**Wine 2** — Very good to outstanding; £40–70 per 375ml. A vivid alternative to Sauternes at lower cost, sold through specialist independents in Austria, Germany, Switzerland and the UK. The constraint is awareness — Ausbruch needs education investment to hold premium pricing.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 2

## a) Country and Region of Origin (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Jerez, Spain. Pale gold with green rim, bone dry, ultra-light body, pronounced saline and bruised-apple acetaldehyde: biologically aged Sherry. Madeira is excluded by the absence of searing acidity and volatile lift; Vin Jaune by the lack of walnut and oxidative weight. Against Fino, the lighter frame and marine/chamomile lift point to Manzanilla, where Atlantic humidity sustains a thicker flor.

**Wine 2** — Banyuls, Roussillon, France. Deep garnet, viscous, warm spirit (~16%), with black cherry, fig, cocoa and candied orange over fine tannin — a vintage-style fortified, not an oxidative one, since rancio and tawny colour are absent. Vintage Port was the alternative, but the raspberry-and-garrigue Grenache Noir signature rather than Touriga/Tinta Roriz typicity moves this to the Mediterranean; Banyuls Rimage is the fresh, reductive expression of that style.

**Wine 3** — Barossa Valley, South Australia. Mahogany-amber, extremely viscous, very warm (~20%), with rancio, walnut, marmalade and Christmas cake. Aged Tawny is the reference point, but the concentration exceeds a 10-year bottling; Madeira is ruled out by the absence of volatility and firm acid. The generosity and sheer sweetness anchor it in the New World, in Australia's benchmark region for Rare Tawny (average age 20 years-plus).

---

## b) Style and Key Winemaking Decisions (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Neutral Palomino, fermented dry in stainless steel, then fortified only to 15–15.5%: a deliberately restrained addition, since higher alcohol kills flor. Ageing under a living flor veil in solera, with fractional blending refreshing nutrients and keeping oxygen away. The yeast consumes glycerol and produces acetaldehyde, which explains the thin, saline, apple-skin profile. Old neutral American oak botas contribute no oak flavour.

**Wine 2** — Grenache Noir picked at full phenolic ripeness, fermented on skins with pump-overs (fine tannin, good colour), then arrested by neutral spirit — *mutage sur grains* — retaining roughly 80–100 g/L sugar. The decisive choice is Rimage: early bottling in a reductive style, with only brief time in large neutral vessels, rather than the years in small oxidative barrels or outdoor bonbonnes that would create Banyuls Traditionnel's rancio. Hence the intact primary fruit.

**Wine 3** — Grenache and Muscat-family fruit picked at extreme sugars, fortified with high-strength grape spirit to leave massive residual sugar. Maturation in small seasoned hogsheads under Barossa heat, with fractional blending across decades: evaporation concentrates sugar and glycerol, warmth accelerates oxidation far beyond a Douro lodge, driving colour to mahogany and building rancio and marmalade intensity.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Outstanding for the category; an *en rama*/single-saca level bottling at roughly £12–18. The core channel is independent specialists and fine dining in Spain, the UK, Germany and the US, where Sherry's critical renaissance is strongest. The commercial obstacle is by-the-glass viability: refrigeration and rapid turnover are required. Tapas-led casual dining and the aperitif trend are the realistic growth route.

**Wine 2** — Very good to outstanding at Banyuls level, around €20–30 — pitched against entry-level Vintage Port. Approachable now and drinking well for 5–10 years from vintage; it will soften rather than gain complexity, as the reductive bottling caps development. Sold through independents in France, the UK and Northern Europe, with chocolate-pairing occasions its clearest hook. Weak category recognition against Port limits off-trade impulse purchase.

**Wine 3** — Exceptional, a benchmark aged Australian fortified, roughly AUD $80–120 (£45–65), competing with 20-year Tawny and Colheita. Fully mature and stable for years in bottle. Markets are domestic premium gifting, sommelier lists, and export to the UK and Asia. The unseen point: the Barossa's heat delivers a level of concentration that Portugal reaches only at far greater average age, so the category is systematically undervalued relative to Tawny — the sommelier's argument for listing it.

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (3 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Sweetness comes from the vine, not the still: grapes shrivel through autumn under dry Föhn winds, concentrating sugar so that fermentation stalls naturally, leaving substantial residual sugar at only moderate alcohol. A light toasty spice suggests older barrique; malolactic has been blocked, preserving the acidity that keeps the wine buoyant rather than cloying.

**Wine 2** — Fermentation arrested early by grape spirit, locking in primary grapey-floral character at very high residual sugar. Decades in small old casks under Rutherglen's extreme summer heat drive evaporative concentration and oxidative caramel-vanilla development; fractional blending of solera material explains the NV designation and the seamless spirit integration.

**Wine 3** — Fortification of fermenting red must retains sugar and anthocyanins; roughly ten years in small pipes then oxidises colour from ruby to amber and converts fresh fruit to nut and baking spice. The moderate viscosity, against Wine 2's syrup, marks a deliberately lighter sugar and extract level appropriate to the 10 Year tier.

## c) Commercial position (3 × 6 marks)

**Wine 1** — Around €25–40; independent merchants and specialists selling to consumers seeking a Sauternes alternative at half the price. Export to Belgium, Switzerland and the UK. The constraint is Jurançon's low name recognition.

**Wine 2** — Museum Reserve tier, roughly AUD $50–80 per half-bottle. Predominantly domestic, with selective premium on-trade export to the UK, USA and Japan; the collector and by-the-glass restaurant pour are the targets. Format resistance is the barrier.

**Wine 3** — £25–40 in the UK, strongest by-the-glass in restaurants and gastropubs as a dessert or aperitif pour. The 10 Year Old designation is a legible quality cue for trade buyers; key markets are the UK, France and Belgium. It competes against large-house Ports below it, but offers a better quality/price ratio than Vintage.

**Under the skin:** all three are sweet, yet each achieves it differently — by dehydration, by spirit into white must, by spirit into red must — and each is priced according to how much time, not how much sugar, it has absorbed.

modelAnswer:
## Wine 1 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Garganega, Soave Classico, Veneto, Italy. The aromas — white blossom, almond, chalky mineral, ripe pear — and the distinctive bitter-almond finish are the hallmarks of Garganega. The call was not immediate: moderate acidity and creamy mid-palate weight first suggested Pinot Blanc from Alsace or Alto Adige, but the absence of phenolic breadth rules that out. Verdicchio was also weighed, but the textural weight here is lower than a Marche interpretation typically shows. Warm medium body (~13.5%) combined with a volcanic mineral character and the bitter-almond close confirm Garganega. Concentration and richness beyond simple Soave DOC point to a single-vineyard Classico site on basalt soils.

## Wine 1 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Fermentation in large oak vessels with extended lees contact — a subtle toasty undertone beneath the fruit suggests both. Malolactic fermentation appears largely inhibited: the acidity stays bright rather than broad. Twelve or more months on lees accounts for the waxy, creamy mid-palate weight.

## Wine 1 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding quality, equivalent to a top single-vineyard Soave Classico. At €35–45 it competes with Village-to-lower-1er-Cru Burgundy while offering greater originality. Strong placement in Italian independents and fine restaurant lists across the UK, US, and Germany; the commercial challenge is limited consumer awareness of Soave as a serious category.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Gewurztraminer, Alsace, France. Deep gold, viscous, and intensely perfumed — rose petal, lychee, ginger, fresh mango — this is the most immediately identifiable wine in the flight. No other variety combines that lychee-and-rose aromatic profile with a broad, almost oily palate at ~14% perceived alcohol. Viognier was briefly considered but ruled out: the palate here is less defined by apricot stone-fruit, and phenolic grip is far lower than Condrieu shows. The slightly off-dry palate (~10–15 g/L RS), balanced against naturally low acidity, is consistent with a Réserve Personnelle or single-vineyard Alsace cuvée rather than a full Vendanges Tardives. Concentration and extract point to Grand Cru or leading domaine-level fruit.

## Wine 2 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Late harvesting maximises terpene expression. Clean, vibrant fruit with no reductive note points to whole-bunch pressing with minimal skin contact. No detectable oak — texture comes from natural glycerol and extract. Fermentation was likely arrested by chilling and SO₂ at ~10–15 g/L, preserving the perfume and providing structural contrast against the low acidity.

## Wine 2 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good to outstanding — above Réserve, approaching lieu-dit level. Retail €40–60. Strongest in the US, UK, Japan, and Germany among experienced consumers who appreciate richly perfumed whites; challenging by the glass but well-suited to premium restaurant lists alongside South-East Asian cuisine.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Sauvignon Blanc, Südsteiermark, Austria. White grapefruit, lime zest, cut grass, and a flinty mineral quality are confidently Sauvignon Blanc. Origin required closer analysis. Marlborough was the first alternative: eliminated because the acidity here is searing and tartaric rather than the broader malic acid line of New Zealand, and the body is leaner. Sancerre or Pouilly-Fumé was also considered, but this wine shows greater phenolic grip and density than the Loire typically produces, plus a herbal, white-pepper note consistent with Alpine influence. At ~13.5% with this taut acid structure, Südsteiermark GG is the compelling conclusion — limestone and slate soils, altitude, and a producer committed to demonstrating the variety's serious potential here.

## Wine 3 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Expressly mineral and reductive. Whole-bunch pressing with minimal skin contact preserves the pure citrus and herbal character. Fermentation and ageing in stainless steel or large neutral oak with no malolactic fermentation keeps the acidity cutting and clean. Extended lees contact adds a slight savoury, yeasty second dimension behind the primary fruit.

## Wine 3 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding — Austria GG equivalent, among the finest continental European Sauvignon Blancs. Retail €35–55. Commercial audience is specialist: top independent merchants in the UK, Germany, and Switzerland, and Michelin-starred restaurants where precision outweighs immediacy. Growing global interest in Austrian whites is the opportunity; low appellation awareness remains the obstacle.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Variety and Region (10 marks)

Riesling, Martinborough, New Zealand. Lime zest, green apple, bath talc, and nascent petrol (TDN) with very high racy acidity, lean body, and ~12% perceived alcohol point to Riesling. Alsace was ruled out — it would show greater phenolic texture and weight at comparable dryness. German GG (Rheingau, Pfalz) was considered but typically produces a richer, broader palate. Clare Valley was the closest call: both show a saline-mineral line and bone-dry electric style, but this wine has finer acid texture, a more delicate body, and less of the pure lime-oil character that defines Clare. The cooler maritime Martinborough climate — southerly latitude, Cook Strait winds — accounts for the elegant restraint and transparent acid structure.

## Wine 4 — b) Style and Winemaking (8 marks)

Stainless steel fermentation at cool temperatures preserves pristine citrus aromatics; no oak or lees complexity is detectable. No malolactic fermentation — the acidity retains its taut, high-tartaric cut. A slight residual spritz on the palate confirms early bottling for freshness. Modest RS (~4–6 g/L) frames the acidity without softening it.

## Wine 4 — c) Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good quality at GI single-vineyard level, retailing NZ$35–50 (£18–25 in the UK) — a style that over-delivers for its price. Consumer resistance to Riesling remains the central commercial challenge in most export markets. The opportunity lies with UK, German, and specialist US importers: the wine's austere, food-friendly character suits independent restaurants and educated consumers who have moved beyond Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc as a default.

## a) Identify the grape variety (10 marks)

Chardonnay. Both wines show pale lemon-gold with a fine, persistent bead. The aromatics — green apple, citrus zest, white flower, brioche — indicate traditional-method production with extended lees contact. Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier were considered but ruled out: both introduce red-fruit character, and Meunier adds a fleshier texture neither wine shows. The lean, citrus-driven precision points firmly to Chardonnay as the sole variety.

## b) Identify the region of origin (2 × 13 marks)

**Wine 1 — Côte des Blancs, Champagne.** Caramelised citrus, lime blossom, and deep brioche complexity indicate lees ageing well beyond the NV minimum. The palate shows searing linear acidity, considerable weight, and a long chalky finish — a vintage wine from a superior site. The tension between ripe grapefruit and chalky mineral precision is the signature of Chardonnay grown on the Côte des Blancs chalk. California was considered but lacks this austere minerality, tending toward riper stone fruit; English sparkling would show more pronounced green-apple crispness and less autolytic depth. Prestige cuvée level, around £150–200.

**Wine 2 — North Coast, California.** The structure is traditional-method but the feel is warmer: broader body, rounder acidity, and fruit tilting toward lemon curd and baked apple rather than steely lime. The mousse is creamy and generous. Champagne is ruled out by the lack of chalky austerity; English sparkling by the absence of green-apple sharpness. Good natural acidity and the absence of extreme ripeness point to a cooler North Coast sub-region rather than the Central Valley. Premium California sparkling, around $35–45.

## c) Compare and contrast style and method of production (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** is tightly structured, shaped by a long cool growing season. The absence of buttery texture indicates malolactic fermentation was blocked, preserving the racy acidity and mineral tension. Extended lees contact — likely five or more years — delivers pronounced brioche and pastry complexity. Richness is held in check by mineral precision; the wine is built for extended cellaring.

**Wine 2** is rounder and more immediately approachable. The creamier texture and broader palate suggest malolactic fermentation was partially or fully carried out, softening acidity and adding a weight absent in Wine 1. Lees contact appears meaningful but shorter, yielding biscuit notes without the deeper toasty layers of the first wine. The warmer growing season supplies naturally riper fruit, reducing the need for prolonged lees ageing to achieve balance. The wine is crafted for earlier enjoyment.

## a) Identify the grape variety (4 marks)

Riesling. Both wines share citrus, apple and a stony, slate-like mineral quality pointing toward a high-acid, low-phenolic white variety. The very high, racy acidity is the single most diagnostic structural marker — it eliminates Chardonnay, which rarely achieves this electric acid tension, and Sauvignon Blanc, whose pyrazine or tropical character is absent from both. Chenin Blanc was considered but its characteristic waxy, lanolin quality is absent, and neither wine shows phenolic grip. The two wines are stylistically divergent — one bone dry, the other carrying residual sugar at lower perceived alcohol — yet the varietal spine is consistent: high natural acidity, pure citrus-apple fruit, minimal oak, and slate minerality.

## b) Origin, style and winemaking (2 × 15 marks)

**Wine 1** — Clare Valley, Australia. Smoky citrus, sliced apple, incipient petrol and jasmine florals. The palate is bone dry and very crisp — medium-plus weight held in check by significant diurnal range, consistent with Clare Valley's elevated, continental conditions. Firm structure and dryness distinguish this from Wine 2: cool nights arrest ripening and preserve malic-dominant acidity, producing a lime-cordial grip rather than the lactic-rounded acidity of a German counterpart. Picked at close to full phenolic ripeness, gently pressed and cold-fermented in stainless steel to preserve primary aromatics. Residual sugar is perceptible but precisely balanced by high, steely acidity; very low perceived alcohol and light body confirm fermentation arrested early to retain RS. Hand-harvested from steep slate terraces — mineral intensity and fruit purity rule out mechanisation — then whole-bunch pressed and fermented in stainless steel or large traditional fuder, with no oak detectable.

## c) Quality, maturity and commercial position (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good quality, estate-level Clare Valley Riesling retailing around AUD $25–35. Primary aromatics indicate 1–2 years of age. Structural acid and concentration suggest improvement over 4–6 years, developing petrol and toast complexity, then holding for 3–4 more. **Wine 2** — Outstanding quality, retailing around €30–50. Primary white-fruit character suggests 3–4 years of age, barely approaching its drinking window. A specialist-merchant and fine-dining wine with a devoted following in the USA, UK and Japan.

modelAnswer:
## Section A · For the flight as a whole

### a) Grape variety and country of origin (6 marks)

The variety is Chardonnay; the country is France.

Evidence converges across all six wines: each is dry and still, with moderate-to-generous weight, moderate-to-high acidity, and no aromatic signature pointing toward an alternative. The absence of pyrazine-driven green-herb character rules out Sauvignon Blanc. The absence of petrol, racy lime, and acidity disconnected from body rules out Riesling. None shows the waxy lanolin, phenolic grip, or quince-skin of Chenin Blanc. The aromatic palette — white flowers, peach, citrus, green apple, nutty lees, integrated oak — is textbook cool-to-moderate-climate Chardonnay.

Pinot Gris briefly presents itself as an alternative: Wines 1, 4, and 5 carry stone-fruit richness consistent with Alsace Pinot Gris. But Pinot Gris at its most textured shows broad, almost flat acidity, and none of these six wines does so. Every wine here maintains a backbone of fresh, racy acid — malic-influenced in the cooler wines, tartaric in the richer — the structural hallmark of Chardonnay in a continental cool climate. The diversity of style, from the lean mineral Wine 3 to the concentrated toasty Wine 4, mirrors Chardonnay's adaptability across Burgundy's layered cru hierarchy.

---

## Section B · For each wine individually

### Wine 1

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Chablis, Premier Cru. The iodine and saline edge on the nose, combined with stone fruit and tangerine rather than pure chalk-and-citrus austerity, places this above entry-level Chablis. The rounder, more voluminous texture distinguishes it from a Grand Cru, which would show greater concentration and a more imposing mineral architecture.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Predominantly reductive winemaking in stainless steel or neutral vessels, preserving iodine and primary fruit. The fleshy texture and nutty note suggest limited lees contact — six to nine months on fine lees in tank or older oak. The absence of new-oak vanilla points to neutral maturation. Full or near-full malolactic fermentation contributes the round mouthfeel.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Very good quality, firmly Premier Cru — the length and volume exceed Village Chablis, but the wine lacks the structural density of a Grand Cru site. Retail around €30–45. The vibrant primary fruit suggests one to two years from vintage: ready to drink but with enough structure to improve for a further three to four years, developing honeyed citrus and a more pronounced mineral spine. Drink to approximately 2029.

---

### Wine 2

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Chassagne-Montrachet, Premier Cru. The citrus-mineral axis, slight bitterness on the finish, and focused power distinguish this from Chablis' saline iodine character, while the herbal aromatic nuance and tight structure are more consistent with Chassagne than the broader opulence of Puligny.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Fermentation and maturation in French barriques, likely 20–30% new oak for approximately twelve months. The silky texture and density indicate full malolactic fermentation in barrel and regular bâtonnage. Slight petrol-like reduction suggests reductive handling early, with careful sulphur management.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Outstanding quality at the top of Premier Cru level. The tight, coiled structure suggests this is currently slightly closed at two to three years old; a further two to three years of cellaring would be rewarding, peaking around 2027–2029 and holding to 2032. Retail around €70–100. The firm acidity reads as vintage character — precision rather than weight — consistent with a cool, structured year on the Côte de Beaune.

---

### Wine 3

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Bourgogne Blanc — the generic regional appellation. The lighter body, medium-minus finish, and broadly expressed nose of green apple, hay, and lemon meringue, without the concentration or site-specific mineral definition of Village level, points to a regional designation.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Almond-nougat character suggests some older barrel influence, but primary freshness remains dominant, indicating restrained oak. Likely a blend of tank and barrel lots, with partial or full malolactic fermentation. Light lees contact accounts for the subtle cashew note; reductive post-fermentation handling produces the faint smoke.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Good quality at its level — a Bourgogne Blanc that over-delivers for its appellation but cannot escape the structural limitations of regional fruit. Retail around €20–30. Bright primary aromas indicate one year from vintage. Ready to drink now; little to gain beyond two years. Drink through 2026–2027.

---

### Wine 4

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Corton-Charlemagne, Grand Cru. The pronounced aromatic intensity, toasted oak, chalk-and-flint minerality, saline finish, and — most tellingly — the concentration and creamy lees texture with underlying honeyed richness signal the top of Burgundy's white hierarchy. No Premier Cru delivers this combination of power, complexity, and length simultaneously. The anise nuance and honeysuckle are consistent with Corton-Charlemagne's calcareous, iron-rich soils.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Fermented and matured in French barriques with approximately 40–50% new oak for twelve to eighteen months. Full malolactic fermentation in barrel with sustained bâtonnage contributes the creamy lees texture. Careful oxidative handling during racking promotes hazelnut and honeyed complexity. The saline mineral finish is a structural correlate of the site's chalk substrates.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Exceptional — unambiguously Grand Cru, one of Burgundy's greatest white wine expressions. Retail around €150–250. The underlying honeyed richness signals a warm vintage, yet firm acidity holds the wine in tension — ripeness disciplined by the hillside's elevation and drainage. At approximately four years old, still relatively closed, with toast and oak currently dominating fruit. Will benefit substantially from five to seven further years of cellaring, peaking around 2032–2035 with complex hazelnut, white truffle, and candied citrus, holding at peak for a decade beyond that.

---

### Wine 5

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Santenay Blanc, Village level. The ripe peach-and-nectarine nose, light toasted hazelnut, and chalky mineral note are consistent with the southernmost Côte de Beaune commune producing white wine of genuine character. The medium-plus finish suggests Village quality: above Bourgogne Blanc, but without the precision or site-driven tension of a Premier Cru.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Ripe peach alongside light vanilla and brioche indicates barrel fermentation with perhaps 20–25% new French oak, followed by full malolactic fermentation. Approximately ten to twelve months maturation with moderate lees contact produces the almond note and accessible, fruit-forward style.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Very good quality at Village level — above the generic Bourgogne tier, comparable to a well-made Saint-Aubin Blanc. Retail around €25–40. Bright primary fruit suggests two years from vintage. Drinking well now; hold for a further two to three years at most. Drink through 2027.

---

### Wine 6

**b) Sub-region / appellation**
Mâconnais — a named-village Mâcon appellation. The ripe, slightly exotic character — yellow plum, mango, citrus blossom, melon — and the medium-minus finish point to the warmer, less structured wines of southern Burgundy. The absence of any serious mineral spine or oak complexity rules out Pouilly-Fuissé Premier Cru.

**c) Style and key winemaking**
Cool fermentation in stainless steel with no or minimal oak contact, producing the clean, neutral background and soft, juicy texture. The absence of buttery creaminess indicates either no or carefully managed partial malolactic fermentation. Light lees contact softens the mouthfeel. A deliberately accessible, early-drinking style.

**d) Quality and maturity**
Good quality for the appellation — a well-made Mâcon-Villages, retailing around €15–22, sitting at the entry tier of the Burgundian hierarchy. The vibrant ripe fruit indicates one year from vintage. No structural case for ageing: drink through 2026 before tropical fruit softens and freshness fades.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## Wine 1 — Mosel, Germany / Riesling Auslese

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Riesling, Mittelmosel, Germany, at Auslese level. Pale gold with green hues, piercing high acidity and very low perceived warmth — the palate is barely more than weightless. Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau were weighed and rejected: neither pairs lime-blossom aromatics with this near-malic acid attack. Rheingau or Nahe would carry more alcohol warmth and breadth; the steely, slate-inflected mid-palate and featherweight body argue for a steep slate site on the Mosel.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Sweetness is botrytis-influenced and over-ripeness-driven, from hand selection of shrivelled clusters over several passes. Fermentation was arrested very low in alcohol — the hostile high-sugar must plus cool cellar temperatures stalling the yeast — leaving substantial sugar carried by exceptional natural acidity. Complete absence of oak points to large neutral Fuder or stainless steel, and the reductive, primary character confirms a protective handling regime. No malolactic: the acid keeps its green edge, deliberately preserved.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, and consistent with Auslese Prädikat from a classified single site: roughly €50–100 through specialist fine wine merchants, with core demand in Germany, Japan and among US collectors. It will improve fifteen years or more, gaining petrol and toast while the citrus spine holds. Its commercial peculiarity is that virtually nothing competes at this intersection of sweetness, ageability and single-figure-to-low alcohol — which is also why it sells to enthusiasts rather than restaurants.

---

## Wine 2 — Sauternes, Bordeaux, France / Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Sémillon-dominant with Sauvignon Blanc and a trace of Muscadelle, from Sauternes. Deep gold, viscous, with dried apricot, saffron, spun sugar and acacia honey — noble rot on Sémillon, confirmed by the waxy lanolin texture. Full body and medium-plus warmth rule out German BA/TBA and Alsace SGN, which would show markedly higher acidity. Vouvray moelleux was considered for the honeyed weight but rejected: no quince, and the tartaric bite of Chenin is absent.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Botrytis alone, via repeated selective tris. Barrique fermentation with a high proportion of new oak is evident in integrated vanilla and spice, fermentation stopping naturally as sugar overwhelms the yeast. Lacquering texture indicates 18–24 months in barrel with gentle oxidative rounding and lees contact. The one structural tension: the finish lacks acid bite, suggesting a vintage of superb botrytis but modest acidity, so the balance tips toward texture rather than freshness — richness bought at the cost of drive.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very high quality, Premier Cru Classé level, on density, oak integration and length; around £180–250 retail, principal markets the UK, US, Hong Kong and France. The buyer is a cellaring collector, and the wine will reward twenty years. The commercial headwind is category-wide rather than specific to this bottle: Sauternes struggles for by-the-glass placement outside fine dining, so quality at this level does not convert into volume.

---

## Wine 3 — California, USA / Orange Muscat

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Orange Muscat, warm inland California. Orange blossom, apricot, mandarin and heady perfume identify the Muscat family; within it, the orange-blossom-and-dried-apricot signature separates Orange Muscat from the grapey rose-petal of Muscat Blanc and the broader, coarser Muscat of Alexandria. Alcohol warmth well above the Mosel or the Icewine, with generous warm-climate fruit and a thick texture, rules out European sweet Muscat and indicates partial fortification.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Fortification of partly fermented must arrests the yeast, retaining sugar and, critically, the volatile floral compounds — the Vins Doux Naturels mechanism in a Californian setting. Early spirit addition, before fermentation strips the terpenes, explains the aromatic purity. There is no botrytis: fruit is fresh and primary, not honeyed. No oak, so stainless steel or neutral vessel, with cold stabilisation and early bottling to protect the aromatics.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good within its category, achieving its stylistic aim with flair but no complexity. Around $20–30, sold through wine shops and restaurant dessert lists to casual drinkers wanting fragrance and sweetness; drink within three to five years. Export prospects are limited by its competitive set — Moscato d'Asti and Alsace Muscat both enjoy far greater name recognition.

---

## Wine 4 — Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada / Vidal

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Vidal Icewine, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario. Gold, highly viscous, with ripe peach, mango, candied citrus and honey. Riesling Eiswein was the alternative: rejected because the fruit is tropical and broad rather than citrus-driven, and the texture glycerol-heavy rather than racy. Vidal's thick skins survive the hard freeze that Riesling often does not. A faint metallic note and medium-minus length further separate it from the best Riesling Eiswein.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Cryoconcentration only: grapes left on the vine into winter, picked at −8°C or below and pressed frozen so water stays as ice and sugar-rich juice runs free. No botrytis, no fortification, hence high sugar with proportionally lower acid — the source of the syrupy rather than electric palate. Slow cold fermentation with sugar-tolerant yeast yields low alcohol; neutral steel and early inert bottling keep the fruit primary.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Good to very good VQA Icewine; the short finish and metallic edge keep it below the top tier. Around CAD$60–80 per half-bottle through specialists, duty-free and the gift trade, with strong pull in China, Japan and South Korea where concentration and novelty sell. Drink within five to ten years.

---

## Wine 5 — Rust, Burgenland, Austria / Ruster Ausbruch

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Ruster Ausbruch from Rust, Burgenland — likely Welschriesling, Chardonnay or Furmint. Deep gold, musk and candied lemon lift, ripest apricot concentration. The acidity is the discriminator: broader than the Mosel yet far more present than the Sauternes, which fits the Neusiedlersee combination of morning fog and warm afternoons. Tokaji was weighed for equivalent botrytis intensity but rejected — no ginger or orange-peel Furmint signature.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Noble rot again, but Ausbruch occupies its own tier between Beerenauslese and TBA, demanding berry-by-berry selection consistent with this intensity. Unlike Sauternes, the musk-driven lift indicates neutral vessel or large old oak rather than new barrique, protecting botrytis aromatics rather than layering spice over them. Simultaneous high sugar and high acid held in tension points to early-arrested fermentation and no malolactic.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Outstanding, above Beerenauslese and approaching TBA concentration; €80–150 per half-bottle, rarest parcels well beyond, through specialists in Austria, Germany, Switzerland and selected export markets. Twenty years or more of positive development, musk and candied lemon turning to dried fruit, honey and spice. The commercial problem is name recognition: the appellation is invisible beside Sauternes and Tokaji despite matching them in quality, so pricing is capped below its intrinsic worth.

---

## Wine 6 — Yarra Valley, Victoria, Australia / Viognier

### a) Region and variety (8 marks)

Late-harvest, partially botrytised Viognier, Yarra Valley, Victoria. Pale straw-gold — conspicuously lighter than the other botrytis wines here. White blossom, white nectarine, mandarin, crushed cashew and hazelnut read as Viognier. Riesling was considered on the bright acidity but rejected: no lime or petrol, and the stone-fruit richness plus toasty oak and almond praline are inconsistent with an unoaked Riesling.

### b) Mechanism and winemaking (10 marks)

Late harvest with selective, partial botrytis: enough concentration without the deep colour and marmalade of full transformation, so Viognier's floral identity survives — the deliberate opposite of the choices in Wines 2 and 5. French oak is the high-risk decision, since oak readily smothers botrytised wine; here it functions as texture rather than flavour. Fermentation was arrested at low alcohol by chilling and sulfur, not spirit; no malolactic, preserving acidity.

### c) Quality and commercial position (7 marks)

Very good, and a benchmark for a technically difficult style made as a statement rather than for margin. AUD$40–60 per half-bottle in specialist retail and premium restaurant lists, with modest UK and US fine wine export. Novelty is simultaneously its advantage and its obstacle: sweet-wine buyers default to Sauternes, Riesling or Icewine, so the education cost falls entirely on the seller. Drink within eight to twelve years, before tertiary development erases the varietal floral signature.

---

**Wine 1** — Saline iodine, bruised apple, bitter almond and dough signal biological ageing under flor: the Sherry triangle, Andalucía, Spain. #### Section B · For each wine individually

**Wine 1**

**a)** Riesling, Mosel, Germany. Very low perceived alcohol — the wine is almost weightless, below 9% in feel — combined with electric high-pitched acidity and restrained residual sweetness is the structural fingerprint of Mosel Kabinett. Gewürztraminer ruled out: no lychee or rose. Chenin Blanc considered and rejected — too delicate, and the acid too racy for the Loire. Crystalline slate on the finish over lime zest confirms a steep slate site rather than the broader Rheingau or Pfalz style.

**b)** Whole-bunch pressed, cool-fermented in large-format oak or stainless steel, preserving floral and citrus aromatics with no oak imprint. Fermentation arrested before dryness, leaving natural residual sugar. No malolactic conversion — the acidity is tartaric and unblunted.

## a) Country and Region of Origin (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Madeira, Portugal; Sercial, 15-year-old or older. Pale tawny, with dried citrus peel, hazelnut and a salty, faintly curried lift. The discriminator against Sherry is the electric acidity slicing through residual sugar, giving a tension Jerez cannot produce. The lightness and freshness rule out Bual or Malmsey, which would be broader and lower in acid; the saline core and dried apricot fix Sercial.

**Wine 2** — Douro Valley, Portugal; Colheita Tawny. Brick-brown, viscous, with fig, prune, walnut, coffee and dark chocolate. The colour development alone eliminates Ruby and LBV. The nuanced, layered dried fruit rather than the flatter uniformity of a blended Tawny indicates a single vintage, aged in small cask for well beyond the seven-year minimum; the grape-spirit warmth and orange-peel edge confirm the Douro.

**Wine 3** — Jerez, Spain; Amontillado, VORS. Deep amber, high viscosity, pronounced hazelnut and savoury toast, bone dry. Oloroso was considered but lacks the fine, incisive structure left behind by an earlier period under flor; Palo Cortado would show more aromatic delicacy against that oxidative weight. The stratified complexity and extraordinary length argue for a minimum average age of 30 years.

**Wine 4** — Jerez, Spain; premium *en rama* Fino, single pago. Golden, medium viscosity, bready flor character, walnut, salinity. Perceived alcohol is clearly lower than Wines 1–3, consistent with the lighter fortification that permits flor. Unlike Wine 3, reductive lees character and fresh saline bite indicate recent flor activity rather than long oxidation. The fuller texture and cloudy, unfiltered presentation place it above standard commercial Fino.

---

## b) Quality Level Reflected in Method of Production and Maturation (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1** — Quality here rests on *canteiro*: slow natural oxidation in small casks in heated lofts, not the three-month *estufagem* tank heating used for basic Madeira. Layered hazelnut, caramelised citrus and the taut sweetness–acid interplay cannot be manufactured by rapid heating. The age statement signals over a decade of cellar commitment, and the spirit is fully absorbed into the wine.

**Wine 2** — A Colheita requires a single vintage in small wood for at least seven years, and the seamless spirit integration plus the shift from dried fruit into walnut and chocolate suggests considerably longer. Where Wine 1 gains complexity from heat plus air, this gains it from cask surface area and evaporation alone. The precision of flavour is inconsistent with a generic Tawny blend, confirming vintage selection.

**Wine 3** — VORS is earned through biological then oxidative ageing in a solera whose average age exceeds thirty years, with rigorous selection at each *criadera*. A young Amontillado shows early oxidative character over a simple frame; here the flavour is stratified and the finish relentless. This is the reverse of Wine 4's philosophy — decades of controlled air rather than the protection of a living flor veil.

**Wine 4** — Standard Fino is fined and filtered for commercial stability and a lighter profile. *En rama* bottling straight from the butt preserves autolytic, flor-derived and reductive character, giving the yeasty depth, saline core and faint bitterness in the glass. The single-pago sourcing and fuller body indicate superior albariza base wine feeding the solera, and this shows in the length.

---

## c) Style and Commercial Position (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Dry, high-acid, nutty: an intellectual style needing an engaged consumer. Independent specialists and fine-dining on-trade, at roughly £50–£80. Above generic Madeira blends, below single-vintage Frasqueira. The UK leads exports, with growth in Japan and among US sommeliers; low category awareness limits supermarket viability.

**Wine 2** — Sweet, rich, immediately rewarding — the most approachable wine of the four. Premium on-trade: by-the-glass dessert pours and after-dinner service. Around £40–£60 per 50cl, competing with 20-year-old Tawny but charging a premium for the stated vintage. France, the UK and Scandinavia are the receptive markets; the weakness is that Colheita is poorly explained on label and often mistaken for Ruby.

**Wine 3** — Bone dry and uncompromising, with a necessarily narrow audience. VORS is a trustworthy quality signal for specialist merchants, auction and top on-trade in Spain, the UK and the US, at £60–£100. Its competitive set is other VORS Sherries and old dry Madeira such as Wine 1. The commercial opportunity is food versatility, bridging umami savoury dishes and nut-based desserts across several service occasions.

**Wine 4** — Saline and yeasty, with more body than commercial Fino; sold on authenticity rather than polish. Independent specialists and premium by-the-glass lists, £30–£50 per 37.5cl, with the natural-wine audience in the UK, US and Japan the most receptive. The *en rama* premium is justified by complexity, but the wine must be chilled from arrival and drunk within months of release — a fragility requiring active retailer and consumer education.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Country and Region of Origin (4 × 8 marks)

All four are fortified and sweet with pronounced oxidative or spirit character: **Portugal**.

**Wine 1** — Pale tawny-amber, medium weight, volatile lift with walnut and dried citrus. The electric, searing acidity cutting the sweetness is unlike any Port or mainland fortified style and points to **Madeira DOC**; medium-sweet rather than bone-dry (Sercial) or unctuous (Malmsey) suggests **Verdelho, 10-year**.

**Wine 2** — Deep opaque ruby, blackberry and chocolate, sweet palate, grippy but ripe tannin. Bright primary fruit and youth rule out tawny-style ageing; concentration falls short of a declared Vintage. **Ruby Reserve, Douro DOC**.

**Wine 3** — Tawny-amber, viscous, dried fig, orange peel, walnut, rancio; no fresh fruit remains. Long oxidative ageing in small wood. The focused vintage intensity, rather than the seamless homogeneity of a blended age statement, indicates a **Colheita, Douro DOC**, reading 12–14 years in cask.

**Wine 4** — Deep amber-gold, dried apricot, marmalade, roasted nut, and a persistent floral, grapey Muscat character absent from the others. Muscat typicity rules out Madeira's white varieties and the Douro's Touriga family. **Moscatel de Setúbal, Setúbal Peninsula**.

---

## b) Style and Method of Production (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 (Madeira)** — Fermented to partial dryness, then fortified with grape spirit to retain sugar. The defining feature is canteiro ageing: cask maturation under the warm lodge eaves for a decade, giving gentle oxidation at elevated temperature. This produces the volatile lift, caramelised toffee and rancio, while the island's naturally high acidity concentrates rather than fades — a wine simultaneously sweet, oxidative and searingly fresh.

**Wine 2 (Ruby Reserve)** — Rapid extraction in lagar or autovinifier, fermentation arrested with aguardente at around 77% abv after two to three days once target sugar is reached. Maturation is then in large wooden vats or tank for only 2–4 years, deliberately limiting oxygen exposure so the colour stays ruby and the fruit primary. Unlike Wine 3, no small-cask ageing has occurred at all.

**Wine 3 (Colheita Tawny)** — Fortified identically to Wine 2; the divergence is entirely in maturation. Ageing in 550-litre pipes gives high surface-to-volume oxidation over a single vintage, with slow evaporative concentration. Colour moves ruby to amber, tannin resolves, and rancio, nut and caramel build. The glycerol weight and integration exceed what a blended age-statement Tawny at similar price achieves.

**Wine 4 (Moscatel de Setúbal)** — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains fermented only briefly before fortification locks in high residual sugar and aromatics. Distinctively, additional Muscat skins are macerated in the young fortified wine for several weeks, extracting further terpenes — this explains why orange blossom survives alongside oxidative development. Subsequent cask ageing supplies the amber colour and roasted-nut layer without burying the varietal lift.

---

## c) Quality and Commercial Position (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 (Madeira)** — Very good; a 10-year varietal age statement, €30–45, clearly above a 5-year blend in acid-sweet tension and complexity. Independent specialists and premium on-trade in the UK, Germany, Japan and US, where the following is loyal but narrow. Consumer unfamiliarity is the barrier; the by-the-glass argument is its months-long stability once opened.

**Wine 2 (Ruby Reserve)** — Good to very good, €12–18. Clean spirit and sound fruit, but built for immediate drinking, not cellaring. Supermarket off-trade and on-trade by the glass in the UK, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, competing directly with branded Reserve peers under real commodity price pressure. Its role is recruitment: the entry point into the category for younger drinkers.

**Wine 3 (Colheita Tawny)** — Outstanding. Colheita outranks a blended 20-year in prestige among informed buyers; €40–65. Vintage specificity and rancio depth make this the flight's most complete wine. Independent specialists, fine dining and sommelier lists in the UK, US, Japan and Switzerland. The commercial obstacle is category literacy — buyers understand "20-year-old" instantly, but a bottling year on a Tawny still needs explaining at the point of sale.

**Wine 4 (Moscatel de Setúbal)** — Very good, Superior tier, €25–40. The genuine point of difference is that aromatic Muscat and long oxidative wood ageing coexist here; Beaumes-de-Venise offers the aromatics without the wood, Rutherglen the wood without the floral lift. Specialist off-trade and premium on-trade, best prospects in Northern Europe and Scandinavia. The DOC's near-invisibility in export markets, not the wine, limits it.

Under the skin, the flight is a study in how one variable — oxygen — divides Portuguese fortification. Wines 2 and 3 are the same must, fortified the same way, separated only by vessel size and time; Wines 1 and 4 show that oxidative handling preserves rather than destroys the raw materials' defining traits, acidity in one case and terpenes in the other.

# Mock Answer — 2024 Paper 3 Question 4

## Wine 1 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Sauternes, Bordeaux, France. Sémillon-dominant with Sauvignon Blanc. Deep gold, viscous legs, and a nose of marmalade, beeswax and dried apricot over a waxy lanolin note — the signature of Sémillon under noble rot. The acidity is moderate but structured rather than racy, and the palate is warm and broad at around 14%, which rules out a German Auslese or BA, where sweetness arrives at half that alcohol and far lower weight. Vouvray moelleux and Coteaux du Layon were weighed but lack the tropical botrytis signature and show quince instead. The layering of dried fruit over fresh citrus, closing on frangipane, argues Premier Cru Classé rather than generic AC.

## Wine 1 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Sweetness comes from botrytis cinerea, which dehydrates the berries to concentrate sugar while generating the beeswax, honey and saffron compounds on the nose. The evenness of that botrytis character and the total absence of green notes imply multiple selective passes (*tries successives*). Vanilla and toast sit beneath the fruit rather than on it, indicating barrique fermentation with perhaps 40–50% new oak, and the glossy, creamy mid-palate points to 18–24 months on lees. Freshness intact: careful SO₂ handling, no oxidative drift.

## Wine 1 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Outstanding. Premier Cru Classé Sauternes, £60–120 per half-bottle through specialist merchants and fine dining, with strong pull in the US, UK, Hong Kong and Japan. The commercial tension is structural: production costs per bottle are among the highest in France while sweet wine is losing younger drinkers, so the category survives on-trade, where cheese and foie gras pairings remain unrivalled.

---

## Wine 2 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Nahe, Germany. Riesling. Pale gold with a green tinge; slate, lime zest, white peach and a thread of petrol. The structure decides it: electric acidity slicing through the sugar, with a light body and only faint warmth suggesting roughly 8% — Auslese territory. Mosel was the serious alternative on the slate/lime axis, but the broader peach-apricot mid-palate and fuller extract fit Nahe's marly-clay sites, which sit between Mosel delicacy and Rhine breadth. Alsace Vendange Tardive is excluded by the low alcohol and lack of opulence.

## Wine 2 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Selective picking at Auslese ripeness, with fermentation arrested by chilling and sterile filtration, leaving perhaps 80–120 g/L. Whole-bunch pressing is implied by the clean fruit and absence of phenolic grip. No vanilla or toast whatsoever: stainless steel or old neutral casks. Acidity is linear and malic rather than lactic, so MLF was blocked — a reductive, aromatics-first approach, the opposite of Wine 1's oxidatively handled barrel regime.

## Wine 2 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Very good. Auslese, £25–40 per half-bottle, specialist merchants; UK, US and Scandinavia. Foil to blue cheese or stone-fruit desserts. Label complexity remains the barrier, but a sweet wine at 8% is precisely what the low-alcohol trend is asking for — the category's clearest premiumisation route.

---

## Wine 3 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

California, USA. Orange Muscat. Deep amber-gold and staining, with orange blossom, mandarin zest, apricot jam, dried rose and grapey exuberance — Muscat family beyond doubt. Perceived alcohol is full and warm, near 15%, with moderate acidity: a fortified style, not Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise's lighter frame or a German Muscat. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains was considered but does not deliver orange-peel marmalade at this intensity. Rutherglen would bring rancio, walnut and far deeper colour; this is brighter and more floral, and the jammy apricot ripeness reads Californian.

## Wine 3 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Fermentation arrested by grape spirit (*mutage*), preserving sugar and lifting alcohol to ~15%. The vivid primary grapiness indicates early fortification. No oak, and clarity suggests cold stabilisation. The decisive choice is varietal: Orange Muscat's linalool and orange terpenes do the stylistic work, so the winemaking is deliberately minimal — the inverse of Wine 1, where oak and lees build the wine.

## Wine 3 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good. Entry-to-mid fortified dessert wine, $20–30 per half-bottle: US premium supermarkets and large off-trade chains, by-the-glass in mid-market restaurants, plus travel retail. Competitive set is southern French VDN. Aromatics sell it instantly; the variety's name recognition is near zero, so it depends on shelf position rather than pull.

---

## Wine 4 — a) Region and Variety (10 marks)

Marlborough, New Zealand. Riesling. Bright gold; lime zest, lemon curd, peach compote, honeysuckle. High, bright acidity from Marlborough's diurnal swing lifts the sugar; light body and gentle warmth suggest around 9%, fermentation arrested early. Against Wine 2, the tell is what is absent — no crystalline mineral precision, no botrytis markers — so late-harvest concentration, not noble rot. Vouvray demi-sec was weighed on the honeyed stone fruit but the lime-dominant citrus and acid shape rule it out.

## Wine 4 — b) Mechanism and Winemaking (8 marks)

Late harvest with sugar accumulation by hang time, fermentation stopped by chilling and sterile filtration. No beeswax or saffron confirms passerillage rather than botrytis. Stainless steel throughout — the fruit is wholly primary. Gentle pressing and cool ferment preserve the lime and floral volatiles. Crucially the winemaker arrested early to hold acidity rather than chase maximum sugar, giving a commercial late-harvest rather than a BA equivalent.

## Wine 4 — c) Style, Quality and Commercial Position (7 marks)

Good. Late-harvest entry level, NZ$20–30 (£10–14), New Zealand supermarkets and off-trade chains, exported to the UK and Australia, with genuine by-the-glass dessert potential. Sitting in Sauvignon Blanc's shadow is the problem: the wine is well made and drinkable, but New Zealand Riesling has no premium equity, so price is capped by category rather than by quality.

# Mock Answer — 2026 Paper 3 Question 1

## a) Identify the region of origin and grape variety or varieties (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1 — Champagne (Côte des Blancs), France. Vintage Blanc de Blancs, 100% Chardonnay.** Citrus zest, white flower and pronounced chalk-flint minerality over toasted patisserie, mocha and hazelnut. The obvious alternative is English sparkling, which shares the acid tension and autolysis; the breadth, marshmallow texture and depth of pastry here exceed what Sussex delivers. No red-fruit note rules out Pinot Noir or Meunier.

**Wine 2 — Sussex, England. Blanc de Blancs, Chardonnay.** More restrained: tropical fruit and yuzu, light autolysis, medium-minus body, tight high acidity. Champagne is ruled out by the primary, unintegrated profile at this apparent quality; California by its riper stone fruit and softer acid. Cool-climate chalk fruit points to the South Downs.

## b) Winemaking decisions, with reference to ageing regime (2 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1:** Deep autolytic character implies five-plus years on lees. Broad texture indicates full malolactic; cocoa butter and toast suggest some base wine fermented in old oak, well integrated.

**Wine 2:** Lighter autolysis suggests 18–24 months on lees only. Clean primary fruit indicates reductive stainless-steel handling with no oak, and malolactic blocked or partial, preserving the acid backbone.

## c) Dosage (2 × 3 marks)

**Wine 1:** Round, softly textured despite firm acid — brut, around 6–8 g/L, enough to amplify the pastry richness without veiling the chalk.

**Wine 2:** Angular, with no perceptible sweetness — extra-brut or brut nature, letting the yuzu freshness read cleanly; more sugar would blunt the wine's defining precision.

## d) Quality and commercial position (2 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1:** Outstanding. Prestige-tier vintage Blanc de Blancs, above standard NV in complexity, length and integration; roughly £80–120. Sold through premium on-trade and specialist merchants in the UK, US and Japan, competing with grower Blanc de Blancs and other prestige cuvées. Drinking well now, with 10+ years ahead as citrus gives way to nut and truffle.

**Wine 2:** Very good. Upper-tier English estate Blanc de Blancs, around £35–45, sold via UK premium on-trade and independents; export to the US and Nordics is emerging but small. Its commercial problem is that Champagne sits at the same price with a century of brand equity — which is why provenance, sustainability and cool-climate typicity, not imitation of Champagne, are the levers. Drink over five years.

modelAnswer:
## a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin (4 × 10 marks)

**Wine 1** — Assyrtiko, Santorini, Greece. Lemon-gold with noticeable viscosity; ripe citrus, peach, and striking saline, chalky minerality that cannot be explained by oak or lees alone. Chardonnay was the first alternative — stone-fruit core and discreet vanilla are plausible — but the electric acid cut and absence of broad, buttery texture rule it out. Viognier was weighed for its floral lift, but is almost impossible at this acidity level. The combination of very high tartaric acidity, saline minerality, and warm-climate alcohol points firmly to Assyrtiko; Santorini's volcanic, basket-trained vineyards are the only origin that consistently produces this tension between extreme heat and extreme acid.

**Wine 2** — Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough, New Zealand. Pale lemon-green; lemon rind, green melon, orange blossom, and ripe stone fruit — thiols and pyrazines at the polished, riper end of the spectrum. Grüner Veltliner was briefly considered for the white pepper and citrus, but the structural weight and tropical tilt are inconsistent with that variety's lean frame. Sancerre was also in play, but the fruit generosity and juicy palate point to Marlborough rather than the Loire's more austere, flinty expression. Restrained tropical character rather than exuberant passionfruit suggests a cooler sub-region — Wairau Valley or Awatere.

**Wine 3** — Riesling, Rheinhessen (Westhofen), Germany. Crushed limestone, Amalfi lemon, lemon verbena, and flinty minerality; bone dry with no perceptible residual sugar rules out sweeter Prädikat styles. Power and concentration eliminate Mosel's lighter slate-driven profile and Alsace's broader, more phenolic expression. The chalky rather than slate minerality points to Rheinhessen's limestone-rich Westhofen plateau, making a Grosses Gewächs the logical tier.

**Wine 4** — Verdejo, Rueda, Spain. Lemon, green herbs, white pepper, pollen, and a slight smokiness, with a medium-minus bitter finish. Albariño was the obvious alternative but carries more saline extract and a rounder texture. Sauvignon Blanc was also considered, but the herbal register here is pithy and bitter rather than pyrazine-driven. The smoky finish and pollen-fennel character are typological for Verdejo; moderate weight and good ripeness are consistent with Rueda's high-altitude meseta vineyards.

---

## b) Style and key winemaking decisions (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1** — Rich, textured, dry white with marked freshness. Discreet vanilla and nuttiness suggest roughly 15–20% new French oak at fermentation, with the balance in stainless steel to preserve mineral purity. Extended sur-lie contact (6–9 months) and bâtonnage build mid-palate weight. MLF appears suppressed: acidity retains a sharp tartaric character rather than the softer lactic quality MLF would produce — a deliberate choice to preserve volcanic minerality.

**Wine 2** — Fresh, aromatic, and polished. Reductive handling throughout — cold settling, cool-temperature fermentation in stainless steel — protects the thiols. No new oak is detectable; palate richness comes from ripe fruit and brief lees contact (3–4 months). MLF is absent: acidity is fresh and persistent, and primary varietal character fully intact. A deliberately reductive style at the premium end of the Marlborough category.

**Wine 3** — Concentrated, dry, mineral. No oak influence detectable; fermentation in large neutral oval casks (Stückfass) is plausible given slight textural breadth without toast. Extended lees contact (10–12 months) explains the silky, savoury complexity. MLF avoided: acidity is high, racy, and unbroadened. The chalky grip and extractive detail are preserved through light fining and filtration.

**Wine 4** — Light-to-medium body, fresh, unoaked. Stainless steel fermentation at low temperature preserves delicate herbal aromatics. No oak, MLF, or significant lees contact is evident; early bottling keeps the palate clean and linear. The slight bitter finish is intrinsic to Verdejo, not a winemaking artefact.

---

## c) Quality, maturity, and commercial position (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1** — Very good to outstanding; single-vineyard Santorini PDO, approximately €35–45. Currently 2–3 years old and drinking well; sufficient structure to develop over 5–7 years, gaining nutty and honeyed complexity. Suits premium on-trade and specialist independents in the US, UK, and Scandinavia.

**Wine 2** — Good to very good; upper-mid-tier Marlborough, approximately £18–22 in the UK. At 2–4 years old it is at or near peak; primary aromatics will fade within 2–3 years. Targets premium supermarket and independent specialist channels in the UK, US, and Australia.

**Wine 3** — Outstanding; Grosses Gewächs tier, approximately €40–60. At roughly 4 years old it is in primary-to-secondary transition — excellent now but will reward patience. High acidity and genuine extract suggest continued improvement over 8–12 years, fruit shifting from citrus to honey and petrol, holding well for 15–20 years from vintage. Fine-wine specialist channel; export to the US, UK, Japan, and Scandinavia.

**Wine 4** — Good commercial quality; mid-tier Rueda DO, approximately €10–14. Clean and varietally accurate, but the medium-minus finish signals no classification-ladder ambition. Best consumed at 1–2 years old; will lose primary herbal freshness beyond 3 years. Sits in premium supermarket and entry on-trade in the UK, Germany, and the US, where Verdejo is gaining ground as a fresh alternative to Pinot Grigio at a comparable price.
